title: ‘A double entendre in every crevice’: what, beyond near-naked tennis, is Sydney Sweeney’s game? | Television | The Guardian
description: With her new, semi-nude advert for sports site Novig, the actor cements her reputation as the anti-woke poster girl. But is it real – or just provocation with a soft porn gaze?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: With her new, semi-nude advert for sports site Novig, the actor cements her reputation as the anti-woke poster girl. But is it real – or just provocation with a soft porn gaze?
Content: ‘A kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to sport’ … Sweeney in one of the images for the ad campaign.Photograph: NovigView image in fullscreen‘A kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to sport’ … Sweeney in one of the images for the ad campaign.Photograph: NovigAdvert reviewTelevisionReview‘A double entendre in every crevice’: what, beyond near-naked tennis, is Sydney Sweeney’s game?With her new, semi-nude advert for sports site Novig, the actor cements her reputation as the anti-woke poster girl. But is it real – or just provocation with a soft porn gaze?Zoe WilliamsMon 14 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBear with me here, but I’m beginning to suspectSydney Sweeneyis a very fine actor. It’s a skill she has been recognised for in the past, of course, winning nominations for Emmys for Euphoria and The White Lotus, but I mean it in a deeper sense, related to her work in advertising rather than drama – can she do more than play a role? Can she make you feel what she’s feeling?In her “controversial” new ad for the sports prediction site Novig (the scare quotes are because, when you’re begging for controversy this hard, you shouldn’t just be handed it on a plate), she adopts the garb of various sports. Her face, body, aspect, gait and mien are all carefully configured to amp up the erotic overtones to the maximum degree, and yet the feeling that beams out of each image is: “This is really going to piss people off, and I couldn’t be more delighted.” Her expression is so speechful that you cannot help but share in some of her hellion joy.‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes spark backlash against viral advertRead moreIn brief: the proposition of the betting site is that it’s only for betting on sports – no wars, no deaths, no politics, just sports. Even the captions, absent the Sweeney, are a red rag to a bull, since betting on wars and death is a disgusting and inhumane thing to do – the surge in people trying to spin cash out ofdeaths in Iran, in Ukraine, says something profound about where we’ve got to in late capitalism. Whatever that profound thing is, it’s definitely not funny.However, we are where we are, and that’s not Sweeney’s concern. She is there to wrinkle out the double entendre from every conceivable crevice. Do spherical things remind you of breasts? What if I get these two American footballs and put them in front of my actual breasts? Would it help if I was naked to the waist? Ah, better still if I were wearing no clothes at all and only the footballs stood between me and my modesty? The age-old tennis shot, immortalised by the80s Athena posterin which the viewer is invited to consider just how nearly they can see a player’s butt – well, that’s here, only this time minus the skirt.View image in fullscreenSweeney in another shot for the ad campaign.Photograph: NovigSweeney’s facial expressions are like a WikiHow gallery, “how to: soft-porn” – they often feel quite old-fashioned, pert or faux naive, more like 70s graphic novel erotica than modern, up-to-the-minute pornography. Yet, throughout, there is a layer of knowingness: “I know exactly how much I’m going to drive you mad, and why.”Truthfully, it’s hard (as a card-carrying member of the wokerati, just out here in the world, trying to keep up) to figure out what the fundamental provocation is. Sweeney famously last made headlines with the “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” ad for American Eagle Outfitters. It was taken by many to be a call back to Donald Trump’s “You have great genes, you know that?” speech, which itself was taken as a densely layered challenge to the world, that his supporters were better human specimens than everyone else. Was the speech white supremacist or simply Trumpian-supremacist? You couldn’t really stick anything on him because, as ever, it was only atmospherically decipherable. Sweeney, however – with her very blondness, her unarguable whiteness – people did stick a white-supremacist agenda on, one she soon decried, saying she was against “divisiveness”.11:05Sydney Sweeney naked sports ad controversy: what’s she playing at? - The LatestEver since, Sweeney has been taken as an anti-woke poster-girl, though since nobody can agree what “woke” means, still less what “anti-” it entails, this poster is more confusing than an avant garde typographer’s ball. She seems to want to kick that hornet’s nest with this Novig ad, but is it by inviting her own objectification? Or is there a complicated message in there about femaleness in elite sport, which has become such a lightning rod for anti-trans activism? Or are we supposed to disapprove of the pornification of the visual realm?None of the above! Ariarne Titmus, four-time Olympic gold medal-winning swimmer, explained on Instagram: it’s “a kick in the face to every woman who had dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity”. And now she says it, yes, that makes perfect sense. What Sydney Sweeney’s game is, beyond almost-naked tennis, is anyone’s guess.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionAdvert reviewSydney SweeneyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Richard Tice rallies to the defence of Reform’s crypto ‘patriots’  | John Crace | The Guardian
description: You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity though it could be argued that Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo just have
Author: John Crace
Headline: You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity though it could be argued that Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo just have
Content: Richard Tice’s main talent is the unfortunate ability to make Honest Bob Jenrick sound trustworthy.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenRichard Tice’s main talent is the unfortunate ability to make Honest Bob Jenrick sound trustworthy.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersThe politics sketchReform UKRichard Tice rallies to the defence of Reform’s crypto ‘patriots’John CraceYou can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity though it could be argued that Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo just haveMon 14 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareNever in the field of British politics has so much been given to so many by so few. You’d have thought Nigel Farage would have wanted to explain Reform’s sudden windfall fromChristopher Harborneand Ben Delo himself. To bask in the glory of the donations from two down-to-earth, anti-establishment crypto billionaires. Men who know what it’s like to graft, who know the meaning of an honest day’s work for an honest day’s pay.There again, Nige is keen not to appear as a one-man band these days and he could do with some downtime to enjoy his own £5m handout. And besides, he’s got a police investigation into Reform party funding to worry about. Even so, it wasn’t the best of looks to sendRichard Ticeout on to the morning media round. Dicky may have his talents, but he keeps them well concealed. His main talent is the unfortunate ability to make Honest Bob Jenrick sound trustworthy. But he does always leave you guessing. Is he being wilfully stupid or is he naturally that half witted?‘Party for sale’? Reform’s £72m donation causes backlash – podcastRead moreDicky began with a howl of protest. No rules had been broken. He made that sound as if it came as a surprise to him. I guess that’s an easy mistake for anyone to make. Everything was in the rules as they exist. Labour was mounting a coup against Reform for having passed legislation through the Commons that would prevent donors living overseas from giving more than £100,000 until they had lived in the UK for more than a calendar year, backdated to March 2026. You’d have thought Nige might have clocked this. But he probably hadn’t been in Westminster that day. And you can’t trust Dicky to be over the details.“Our money comes with no demands,” Dicky told Nick Robinson on the Today programme. Harborne and Delo were patriots. All they wanted was to save the country from being ruined by socialists and the rightwing Tories. Quite where he thought Reform fitted in on this particular continuum wasn’t clear. Presumably in the centre ground of British politics. Ordinary men and women who want to rescue their country from the do-goodery of the RNLI.“Patriots” was doing some heavy lifting here. Harborne had decamped to Thailand in the 90s, had become a Thai citizen in 2011 and had taken a Thai name. Now we learned that Dicky believed in dialectics. The more someone looked as if they were trying to put as much distance between themselves and the UK, the greater their commitment to the UK really was. Chris had just been playing very hard to get. The reality was he had been begging HMRC to ask him back so he could pay his fair share to the exchequer.Fine, said Robinson. When did he move back to the UK and does he now pay UK tax? Dicky was understandably clueless. He had no idea he was going to be asked whether Harborne complied with the law as it was going through parliament. I’m not his tax adviser, he protested, though if he was he would make sure he paid as little as possible. Dicky has always been upfront in his belief that only the little people pay tax. And as for Harborne’s whereabouts, he wasn’t his diary secretary. He just telepathically knew that Chris had complied with the law as it was and as it was proposed.It was the same with Delo. No man had ever loved his country more. From Hong Kong. Who wouldn’t want to receive money from a billionaire who had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with money-laundering laws and had been pardoned by Donald Trump? Dicky had no idea when Ben had come back to the country. That sort of level of detail was well above his pay grade. He was just here for the front-of-house stuff. The meet and greet. No one should expect any more from him than that.Then the killer line. “I hope you will trust the word of our compliance team,” said Dicky. They would assure listeners everything was above board. So touching. So sweet. Up till now, no one had any idea Reform even had a compliance team. They certainly hadn’t been much in evidence while James Orr and Dan Jukes had been negotiating a possible £500,000 gift from an overseas donor. And in the taped conversation, which Nige insisted he hadn’t been listening to, Farage had said, “it’s all above board”.So, if it’s all the same, we won’t be taking the word of an imaginary compliance team. Nick pressed on. What did Dicky think had attracted two crypto billionaires to a party that had promised to cut taxes on crypto, to limit regulation of the industry and had threatened to remove the governor of the Bank of England if he didn’t play ball?Dicky couldn’t quite put his finger on it. But he thought it was probably something to do with them really caring about a £500 tax break. And the pleasure of paying for Nige’s hideous suit. Champagne and oysters all round.There was just time for Robinson to point out that, far from getting nothing for their donations, the two men had already got everything they wanted and more. “Not at all,” Dicky insisted. Because Reform had promised to deregulate and cut tax before the two men had handed over the £72m. Where can you go with someone as dim as Dicky? A tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. You can’t buy Dicky’s level of stupidity. Though Harborne and Delo just have.It was left to Farage himself to clear up Tice’s mess later in the day in a BBC interview. Well, sort of. Yes, Delo and Harborne’s donations probably wouldn’t meet the necessary deadlines for the legislation going through parliament. But you couldn’t blame Reform for taking the cash. Rather it was the fault of the government for putting in place regulations that Reform might not now be able to get round. As so often with Nige, there was always someone else to blame.Not that Labour was immune from a little hypocrisy. It had been Burnham who had tried to bury the plan to limit donations to all parties. Something the unions had pushed back against. But the £72m has rather concentrated everyone’s minds. Once the current legislation was through parliament there would still be a good year to pass another law to impose a cap. Down in Brighton, Angela Rayner wanted the TUC to know she was on their side. There was no equivalence between Labour funding from the unions and money from two crypto billionaires. Politics could be bought. Just by the right sort of people.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchParty fundingRichard TiceNigel FarageChristopher HarbornecommentShareReuse this content

title: How did the Guardian cover Oasis at Knebworth 1996? Well … we didn’t | Oasis | The Guardian
description: Noel Gallagher told fans ‘this is history’ but the paper opted to review support act the Charlatans instead, as that band returned from tragedy
Author: Richard Nelsson
Headline: Noel Gallagher told fans ‘this is history’ but the paper opted to review support act the Charlatans instead, as that band returned from tragedy
Content: Liam Gallagher performing at Knebworth in 1996.Photograph: Roberta Parkin/RedfernsView image in fullscreenLiam Gallagher performing at Knebworth in 1996.Photograph: Roberta Parkin/RedfernsFrom the Guardian archiveOasisHow did the Guardian cover Oasis at Knebworth 1996? Well … we didn’tNoel Gallagher told fans ‘this is history’ but the paper opted to review support act the Charlatans instead, as that band returned from tragedyNews: Oasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concertsCompiled byRichard NelssonMon 14 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver two days in August 1996,Oasisplayed to 250,000 people at Knebworth House in Hertfordshire. Riding high on two bestselling albums, the concerts were seen as the crowning moment in their career.The Guardian covered the weekend but Caroline Sullivan’s review concentrated on the Charlatans, one of the support acts. There was a picture of the Knebworth crowds on page 7, but the main review that day was of folk-rock band Fairport Convention’sCropredyfestival. There was also a review of the“anti-Oasis”Divine Comedy.In fairness, the paper had recently carried a piece aboutOasis’s Loch Lomond gigs, and it continued to report all the latest news about the band including the constantfalling out/making upof the Gallagher brothers, and aSmurfs’ coverof Wonderwall. Read both pieces here:Blue tones: The Charlatans must have dreamt of upstaging Oasis. At Knebworth, they almost did. But it came at a horrible priceByCaroline Sullivan13 August 1996“This is history,” Noel Gallagher shouted on Sunday, all vestiges of Mancunian cool gone as he surveyed the 125,000 disciples jamming Knebworth’s green acres to the horizon. Despite his fondness for overstatement, he was right. Oasis’s weekend shows were the largest outdoor gigs ever staged in Britain by one band. And if that wasn’t enough, theMorning Glory albumwas last week certified 10 times platinum (3m copies under UK classification), making it the UK’s seventh-bestselling album ever.Today, as Noel and Our Kid ponder how to top it (Their own sitcom? A pub tour?), a handful of other bands will be nursing their own Knebworth memories. The Prodigy, Manic Street Preachers and Cast, though capable of headlining decent-sized venues themselves, became support acts for a day and were greeted with the mild enthusiasm reserved for introductory bands.Only one outfit distracted the crowd’s attention from its noodles and beer, but for all the wrong reasons. “This is going to be a fairly difficult gig,” said Radio 1’sJo Whiley, introducing the Charlatans. That they were playing at all, after the death of keyboardist Rob Collins in a car crash three weeks ago, elicited the biggest cheer of the day. Collins was responsible for the band’s trademark hypno-swirl sound, and his loss must put their future in doubt. However, they made a statement of sorts by honouring their Knebworth commitment, withPrimal Scream’s keyboardist, Martin Duffy, standing in.Aptly, it began to rain as they entered, a seagull soundtrack matching the mood. The drizzle stopped, but the sombreness remained, becoming a listlessness that dragged at the usually uplifting music (in which Collins’s Hammond flourishes were reproduced to the letter). Singer Tim Burgess, normally lost in a psychedelic trance, was blank-faced somewhere inside a hooded anorak. “New tune,” he murmured occasionally, as if feeling obliged to say something. After a while, they just seemed to stop. A sad, dispirited set, but one that deserves praise for having been done at all.View image in fullscreenThe Guardian 12 August 1996.Loch’n’roll: The setting, the passion, the chemical toilets … Oasis’s concert in Balloch was a classic of its kindBy Brian Logan5 August 1996Amble down Balloch’s main road any other day of the year and you’d be seduced – or bored – by its simplicity. You might stop at Corries tea shop for a cuppa and a scone; you might tinker with tartans in Loch Lomond Kilts. It’s a far cry from … well, from Manchester.When locals heard that Oasis were to visit loch’n’roll upon them, they kicked up something of a fuss. How could sleepy Balloch take the strain of these rock gods and 80,000 boisterous disciples? We have, they protested, only one public lavatory.Yet the horde that flocked to Loch Lomond this weekend was extended a warm(ish) reception. “West Dunbartonshire Council Welcomes You” read the signs; West Dunbartonshire residents, meanwhile, glared proprietorially from their windows.Their concern was misplaced. If the Gallagher brothers are sharing next week’s bill at Knebworth with the Chemical Brothers, this week they had chemical toilets for company. Hundreds, erected defiantly at the very entrance so passing Highlanders would see that the mighty Oasis could do without their measly lavatory, thank you very much.Rumour has it that forward-thinking revellers had come to Balloch Castle Country Park before the construction of the arena to bury their drugs beyond the investigation of the wiliest police officer. If there is an epidemic of blissed-out rabbits in the west of Scotland, we’ll know why.Continue readingView image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the 1996 Knebworth concerts.Photograph: Mick Hutson/RedfernsExplore more on these topicsOasisFrom the Guardian archiveCharlatansNoel GallagherLiam GallagherPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why has university become such a scam? | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Graduates are leaving with an average debt of £53,000 – while entry-level jobs plummet. It’s time for politicians to stop burying their heads in the sand, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Graduates are leaving with an average debt of £53,000 – while entry-level jobs plummet. It’s time for politicians to stop burying their heads in the sand, writes Zoe Williams
Content: Facing the future …  graduate vacancies were down 45% in August compared to the same month last year.Photograph: nirat/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFacing the future …  graduate vacancies were down 45% in August compared to the same month last year.Photograph: nirat/Getty ImagesOpinionStudent financeWhy has university become such a scam?Zoe WilliamsGraduates are leaving with an average debt of £53,000 – while entry-level jobs plummet. It’s time for politicians to stop burying their heads in the sandMon 14 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTShareIt wasn’t in relation to university that I first came across the organisation Rethink Repayment, which campaigns for a fairer settlement on student debt. I was looking into the astronomical numbers of young people who still live with their parents. It’s nowmore than a thirdof young men and more than a fifth of young women, statistics that get even crunchier when you realise that “young” describes anyone under 35.There were various reasons – some had gone home after a health crisis, some really liked their parents, some were battling unemployment, but the single unifying theme was student debt. Those on incomes too low to start repaying couldn’t make rent; those in the lower repayment bracket (an annual income of £25,000 or thereabouts, depending on your loan plan) still couldn’t make rent, because they were spending 9% of their income repaying. And those on more than £50,000 were keeping less than 50p in every pound they earn because of their marginal tax rate.It’s always been sold to students when they take on this debt that it won’t count against their mortgage raising capacity, which technically it won’t – but any affordability check by a mortgage company or letting agent will factor in the monthly repayments.It feels tactless to bring this up, just as a fresh wave of students heads off, with bigger, more exciting things on their minds than long-term debt. Yet it also feels remiss not to mention the fact that they’re being absolutely had. Florence, 29, who works as a solicitor in commercial litigation, is still living at home. She told me: “A lot of the time I’m reviewing contracts, and saying: ‘This is enforceable, sue them.’ The holes in what we were told are shocking. If student loans had come from an institutional lender, we would have a class action lawsuit.”Without lingering on the unedifying details, such as how we’re all feeling about Nick Clegg nowadays, a quick recap on what the debate around student fees looked like when they were first hiked to £9,000 in 2012. There was a lot of anxiety about whether the government would ever get its money back, or whether a huge amount of this debt would have to be written off – what we didn’t factor in back then was that, this being the government, they could make the rules. If they wanted the interest on student loans to be set at theRetail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation, plus up to 3%, they could simply snap their fingers and make it so. We talked a lot, too, about what those capped fees meant for universities – 10 years ago, £9,000 wasn’t enough for some courses but it was more than they needed for “classroom subjects” (a lot of humanities), which could then cross-subsidise. Now, with fees only increased to £9,790 in more than a decade, they often don’t even cover humanities courses – so worries about the sheer viability of what was previously one of the nation’s most successful sectors were well founded.‘I’m missing out’: the cash-strapped UK university students forced to live at homeRead moreThe students themselves were almost a side issue in this debate: the promise was that the debt would be more than offset by their increased earning capacity, once they had a degree, and, anyway, wouldn’t affect them until they could well afford it. This has turned out to be wildly untrue. Graduates are leaving with an average burden of £53,000, four or five times what it was in 2009, and the interest rates mean they can spend years repaying without making a dent in that amount. Graduate vacancies, meanwhile, were down 45% in August, compared with the same month last year, which is casually blamed on AI wiping out entry level jobs. Responsibility would be better situated with employers, who are choosing short-term cost-saving over their duty to their own companies, their society and the future.It’s one thing to deprioritise the younger generation, it’s another to straight up scam them. I don’t want to tell any political party its business, but the one that makes a better offer than “pretend the problem doesn’t exist” stands to make enormous headway, and not just with the under-35s.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: How Britain's kings and queens powered the slave trade – video | Slavery | The Guardian
description: From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade
Author: Nikhita Chulani
Headline: From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade
Content: How Britain's kings and queens powered the slave trade – videoEnslaving nationSlaveryHow Britain's kings and queens powered the slave trade – videoEnslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade.The kings and queens most heavily involved were those who ruled after the monarchy was restored in 1660. TheRegister of British Slave Tradersis the most comprehensive research project into the investors in the country's trafficking of enslaved African people. Its publication will further inform calls for the king to finally acknowledge the monarchy’s deep involvement in the trade.In response to the Guardian’s reporting of the new research relating to the monarchy, a spokesperson for King Charles said he was 'grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed'.The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave tradeMorgan Ofori,Stephanie Windeler,Albert Villa AlsinaandNikhita Chulani,Source: The GuardianMon 14 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsSlaveryEnslaving nationMonarchyColonialismAfricaKing Charles III

title: Ministers seek law change to make £72m donations to Reform illegal | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Plans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirements
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Plans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirements
Content: Nigel Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNigel Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianParty fundingMinisters seek law change to make £72m donations to Reform illegalPlans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirementsPippa Crerar,Jessica ElgotandKiran StaceyMon 14 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced.In a move that is likely to set off furious complaints from Nigel Farage’s party, the government will table amendments to legislation going through the House of Lords within weeks that puts the legality of Reform’s latest donations in doubt.Senior Labour and union figures had urged ministers to look again at party funding rules after Reform announced at the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who have both previously been based overseas, were each donating £36m to the party.Government sources, however, said the plans to strengthen the representation of the people bill had been under way for weeks, after MPs pushed for further action on domestic donations in the House of Commons.Under the proposals, which are expected to be tabled at the Lords committee stage of the legislation, individual donors will have to prove their ongoing physical presence in the UK, in line with the residence requirements applied to other areas of government policy, such as tax status.graphicThe extraordinary measure will be seen as a sign of the stakes attached to the donations, which would give Reform a vast advantage in organising supporters on the ground before the next election.However, Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors, although the party has said the £72m donations are in line with both current rules and those already voted on by MPs in the bill.The legislation currently restricts donations from expats to £100,000, which would also apply for the first 12 months after they return to the UK – backdated to 25 March this year.Ministers have already brought in a minimum residency requirement of the remainder of the calendar year in which they return, plus a further full year, meaning Reform may not be able to accept the £72m donations until January 2028.Delo has been based in Hong Kong but said in April he would return to the UK to avoid restrictions, while Harborne was based in Thailand but is believed to have registered to vote in Hampshire in June.“Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” Farage told the BBC. When asked if the two billionaires were UK residents as of 25 March, he replied: “All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.”View image in fullscreenLady Taylor told peers that the government was considering how it could strengthen the residency requirements of political donors.Photograph: HoLSharon Taylor, a Labour minister in the Lords, told peers that as well as donors having to demonstrate a “genuine and ongoing connection to the UK”, the government was also looking at further restrictions.“We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy,” Lady Taylor added.However, MPs and peers who have been pushing for a full domestic donations cap are unlikely to be satisfied by the new amendments. Government sources have said they do not want to delay the bill’s progress further by considering such a cap, but are open-minded on further legislation. MPs have voiced anger in internal WhatsApp groups that the chance has been missed to cap domestic donations in this bill while it was in the Commons.Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour.“How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” the communities secretary said.“It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.”Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations.The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed.Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations.Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”.However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day.In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.”The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality.Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps.“The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said.“But we have to ask the question, is this healthy for our democratic process to have more money coming from fewer people in bigger lumps?”MPs who have campaigned for a donations cap are working with peers on a number of amendments to the bill which would tighten it up without having to wait for another act of parliament.They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval.Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister in the Lords, said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling. “Even just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system,” she said.Reform denounced the government’s existing plans, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, describing them on X as “an unprecedented step from a leftwing government to plunge Britain into dictatorship and communism”.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Content: Shares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ developmentDonald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’Lauren AlmeidaMon 14 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 03.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for aslowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day.The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to“slow down”.However,Donald Trumpdismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”.In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!”The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”.OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fearsRead more“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote.Trump offered a similar assessment when he called Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, while the executive was on stage at an AI conference in California on Monday.“It’s a hoax,” Trumpsaid via speaker phoneto the audience. “The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That’s not going to happen.”The UN security council, meanwhile, is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week as international concern rises, Agence France-Pressereportedon Monday.Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer ofOpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chipmakers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.Shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%.In Europe, shares in the Dutch tech manufacturer ASML, Europe’s biggest company by value and an important supplier for the semiconductor industry, slumped by 6%.There was, however, a rally in shares that have been threatened by the rise of AI, including the advertising group WPP, which rose by 5% in London, and the analytics business Relx, which was also up 5%. The latter had suffered a sharp fall earlier this year after Anthropic launched a suite of new data and automation tools.Amodei has said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.His claims have beendisputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support forAmodei’s essayon slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder,toldthe BBC an AI “kill switch” that could be triggered by a third party may be necessary to prevent catastrophe.Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of UK MPs and peersidentified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them.Meanwhile, China’s top intelligence official warned that the use of AI by adversaries could pose a risk to the country’s political and social security.Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced US models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to Beijing’s critical information ​infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?Read moreDespite such concern about the risks around AI, Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares tolist on the US stock marketthis year.OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing tosafety concerns with the technology.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Stock marketsAsia PacificComputingTechnology sectorDatacentresDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Duke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UK | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Committee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residents
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Committee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residents
Content: Meghan’s risk assessment will be her first since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.Photograph: Kristina Bumphrey/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMeghan’s risk assessment will be her first since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.Photograph: Kristina Bumphrey/Variety/Getty ImagesPrince HarryDuke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UKCommittee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residentsPriya BharadiaMon 14 Sep 2026 18.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex will have a review of their publicly funded security following their return to the UK.The royal and VIP executive committee (Ravec), which oversees tax-funded security for royalty and public figures, is to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s level of police protection.The committee met last week to discuss the couple’s case, now they and their children are full-time residents in the UK and not just visitors.It will be the first risk assessment for Meghan since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.Harry was granted a review of his security in July but has yet to receive a decision.The Telegraph has reported that Ravec’s chair informed Harry last week the committee had commissioned a new risk assessment and a separate one for Meghan, in light of their return to the UK.The committee has reportedly asked the couple to provide their schedules and daily routine, including the school run, to inform their decision.Last year, Harry lost a legal challenge against the Home Office after the automatic tax-funded security for him and his family was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals.“The UK is my home,” said Harry in his witness statement. “The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil. I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.”The couple returned to the UK on 26 August. Soon after, a formal letter was issued on behalf of King Charles, reiterating their status as non-working royals.The letter stated the couple were “akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests” and “any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities”.The Sussexes also decided on Monday to switch their children to a new school just two days after they started, reportedly due to security concerns over the long journey and heavy traffic.“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a family spokesperson told Hello! magazine.“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.“This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham cancels engagements as his father’s death is announced | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: UK prime minister had been due to speak at the TUC conference in Brighton
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: UK prime minister had been due to speak at the TUC conference in Brighton
Content: Andy Burnham pictured with his parents, Eileen and Roy, in 2016.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham pictured with his parents, Eileen and Roy, in 2016.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAndy BurnhamAndy Burnham cancels engagements as his father’s death is announcedUK prime minister had been due to speak at the TUC conference in BrightonPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 08.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has cancelled his engagements for Monday and Tuesday after his father, Roy, died.Among other plans, the prime minister had been due to speak to the TUC conference in Brighton on Tuesday.Burnham’s father had Alzheimer’s and was in a care home. Inan interview Burnham gave in July, he said his father’s condition meant he was unaware that his son was about to become prime minister.“That’s a sadness because he would be [proud],” Burnham told the Times. “But the way I look at it, it’s his achievement as well. A whole family achievement, although he doesn’t know it.”Burnham has talked about wanting to improve social care, in part because of his experiences with his father.In one of his first speeches as prime minister, Burnham said it was humbling to see the “skill and the care and the professionalism” of care workers like those looking after his father, and that they should be paid more.Among those expressing their condolences was Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, who posted: “My thoughts are with Andy and his family at this terribly difficult and sad time.”In her own post on X, Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, offered her condolences to Burnham and his family, adding: “No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.“A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won’t ever be the same again.”At the start of the Commons session on Monday afternoon, Lindsay Hoyle, the speaker, said: “I am sure the whole house will want to send our best wishes to him and his family at this sad time.”In Head North, the 2024 book he co-wrote with Steve Rotheram, the Liverpool city region mayor, Burnham described what he said had been a happy upbringing with his father, his mother, Eileen, and his two brothers in Culcheth, near Warrington in Cheshire. Roy worked as a telephone engineer, while Eileen was a GP’s receptionist.“Neither my dad, Roy, nor my mum, Eileen, went to university. But both could have done if they had grown up in a different time and in a different place,” he wrote.“Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go. But that did not make them pushy parents in any way.“Their approach was one of quiet encouragement and confidence-building. Our family home in Culcheth was always full of music, life, laughter, love and support.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: British man accused of drugging and raping wife over two decades admits 60 offences | UK news | The Guardian
description: Man, who cannot be named to protect anonymity of his victim, admits scores of criminal offences
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Man, who cannot be named to protect anonymity of his victim, admits scores of criminal offences
Content: The man, appearing at Manchester Minshull Street crown court, admitted charges including sharing intimate images of his victim.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenThe man, appearing at Manchester Minshull Street crown court, admitted charges including sharing intimate images of his victim.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAUK newsBritish man accused of drugging and raping wife over two decades admits 60 offencesMan, who cannot be named to protect anonymity of his victim, admits scores of criminal offencesJosh HallidayandHannah Al-OthmanMon 14 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has pleaded guilty to drugging and sexually assaulting his wife over a period of 20 years as he admitted 60 criminal offences.The man, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim, is in his 60s and before his arrest lived in Stockport, Greater Manchester.He admitted 60 counts, which include 21 counts of rape and sharing intimate images of his victim.His estranged wife sat on the front row of the packed courtroom with other family members as he entered his pleas, occasionally sobbing as he did so.In June, the man pleaded guilty to 15 of the charges against him. On Monday he admitted the final 45 at Manchester’s Minshull Street crown court.The defendant also previously pleaded guilty to sharing intimate photographs or film of his wife, without her consent, for sexual gratification.Twelve co-defendants all deny various allegations involving the same woman.Rick Jackson, an assistant chief constable of Greater Manchester police, said: “Our focus remains on supporting the victim of this horrific campaign of abuse through what is a very complex investigation.“Specialist support continues to be provided to the victim at the centre of this case.“If you are concerned you, or someone you know, may be affected by drug-facilitated sexual abuse, please know that you do not need proof, certainty, or a clear memory to be taken seriously.“You are not expected to understand exactly what has happened or who was involved in order to be taken seriously. If you feel that something has happened, then please report it or ask for help.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: New special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of role  | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Alistair Burt speaks candidly about difficulties of tackling complex cases as families express concern over mandate
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Alistair Burt speaks candidly about difficulties of tackling complex cases as families express concern over mandate
Content: Alistair Burt is a former Middle East Minister.Photograph: James Drew Turner/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlistair Burt is a former Middle East Minister.Photograph: James Drew Turner/The GuardianForeign policyNew special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of roleAlistair Burt speaks candidly about difficulties of tackling complex cases as families express concern over mandateGeneva AbdulMon 14 Sep 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 17.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe special envoy for British citizens detained overseas has spoken about the difficulties he faces in his new role, as families express concern over the position’s mandate in complex consular cases.In his first public engagement,Alistair Burt, the former Conservative Middle East minister, spoke candidly about the difficulties and limitations of the new appointment, made following years of mounting criticism of how the Foreign Office handled the cases of British citizens detained overseas.“I don’t make policy. I’m not a minister. I don’t have that authority. It will ultimately be the foreign secretary and the prime minister who will need to make the changes in policy or changes in approach if required,” Burt told an audience in Westminster, following his appointment on Monday evening.“The best thing I can do is not disguise from you the difficulties of the role,” added the former minister.Foreign Office appoints first special envoy for Britons detained overseasRead moreBurt, who plans to meet the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, later this week, was tipped for the post more than a year ago. Burt was candid about the complexities of detention cases and of his role to “kick the tyres” of the policies involved.Burt, whose new role is appointed by the Foreign Office but not paid for by it, said he has already started to meet families of those with complex cases, and said there was “much to be gained” from stronger international condemnation.There is a strong view that the US special presidential envoy for hostages has secured more success and clout inside the diplomatic system, and used more innovative techniques to negotiate the release of Americans.Burt said he plans to meet his US and Canadian counterparts in the coming weeks, and is open to discussing broader cooperation with European leaders.The Foreign Office describes the purpose of the role as being to advance the government’s commitment to British nationals in the “most difficult and complex detention cases overseas” at the direction of the foreign secretary. The role is intended to advocate within and represent government, and engage with families.Speaking alongside Burt at Monday’s parliamentary event wasNazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, a dual national who was arbitrarily detained in Iran for six years before being released in 2022.View image in fullscreenNazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe expressed a fear of quiet diplomacy turning into an ‘excuse’ for government inaction.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesA documentary was played showing the ordeal her family went through to secure her release, as well as that of Anoosheh Ashoori, for whom a historic £400m debt was paid toIran.“I recognised the payment of the debt and I let my foreign secretary know repeatedly,” said Burt of Nazanin’s case, adding, “I got that one right.” That wasn’t the case, he admitted, forMatthew Hedges,a British academic sitting beside him, who was accused of spying for the UK government in the United Arab Emirates and was arrested and tortured.“Other cases I didn’t handle as well as I would have liked,” said Burt. “I’m very grateful that Matthew has seen me since to talk about his experiences.”While welcoming the appointment, Zaghari-Ratcliffe also expressed a fear of quiet diplomacy turning into an “excuse” for government inaction.Lawyers and campaigners at the event also expressed concerns over the limited mandate of the special envoy role, and called for the position to be independent of the Foreign Office and for the UK to be bolder in its diplomacy.In attendance was also Laila Soueif, who went on hunger strike in pursuit of freedom for her son, British-Egyptian activist Alaa Abd el-Fattah, who wasreleased from an Egyptian jail in 2025 after serving six years, as well as Naomi Connell, a friend ofLindsay Foreman and Craig Foreman, who has campaigned for the couple’s release from Iran’s Evin prison.Also present was Heather Cornelius, whose husband, Ryan, has been arbitrarily imprisoned in Dubai for more than 18 years. The family discussed their case with Burt when he was a minister in 2018, said Heather, expressing scepticism over whether the envoy role, which runs for 18 months, will do anything other than liaise with and reassure families.“He’s not going in there saying: ‘Yes, I know I can make a difference, I know I can help these people.’ He’s not saying that. He’s just saying: ‘Well, it’s very difficult,’” said Cornelius, who delivered a letter to Andy Burnham earlier on Monday, asking for the prime minister to help secure her husband’s release.“They’re relying on other countries being involved, and of course that’s good, but Britain can do something, and they can do more,” she added.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyNazanin Zaghari-RatcliffeIranMiddle East and north AfricaForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeHuman rightsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes lead backlash against viral advert | Sport | The Guardian
description: The actor is facing a backlash from Olympians and other athletes, who have accused her of demeaning and sexualising women’s sports by appearing in a controversial advert for a prediction company
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The actor is facing a backlash from Olympians and other athletes, who have accused her of demeaning and sexualising women’s sports by appearing in a controversial advert for a prediction company
Content: British sprinter Amy Hunt and Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus have called out Sydney Sweeney for her provocative advert.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskView image in fullscreenBritish sprinter Amy Hunt and Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus have called out Sydney Sweeney for her provocative advert.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskSport‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes lead backlash against viral advertAmerican actor accused of sexualising women’s sportsBritish sprinter Amy Hunt leads storm of protestSean IngleMon 14 Sep 2026 15.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US actor Sydney Sweeney is facing a backlash from female Olympians and other athletes, who haveaccused her of demeaning and sexualising women’s sportsby appearing in a controversial advert for a sports prediction company.In the viral commercial for Novig, which was viewed more than 22 million times in the first two days of its release, Sweeney’s nude body is covered by footballs, basketballs, and other sports equipment, as she tells users they can bet on “just sports”. After saying “sports” nine times, she appears topless on a pool table, before saying: “You can’t trade this, I just look good here.”Sydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sports | Jane McManusRead moreThe advert has led to a storm of protest led by the British sprinter Amy Hunt, who won four European Championship gold medals last month. After finishing fourth in the 200m at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship on Sunday evening, Hunt said: “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening.”That was a reference to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden’s winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth-fastest women’s 200m, and Hunt went on to reveal the painful realities she and other sports stars faced. “When you’re a woman in sport, it’s not pretty,” she said. “It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time, definitely.“There’s some low moments. Even turning up to this championship, my period started yesterday, so that’s not really ideal, and that’s not ever what you try to really plan for.”The British Olympic cycling gold medallist Sophie Capewell was also deeply critical of the advert. “Imagine a world where sexualised representation isn’t the most popular way of seeing women in sport,” Capewell said on social media.In Australia, there was also widespread fury with the four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus leading the charge. “I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” she wrote. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity.View image in fullscreenThe Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus said the ad campaign was ‘a kick in the face’.Photograph: François-Xavier Marit/AFP/Getty Images“How do we live in a world where monetising a woman’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?”Hundreds of athletes took inspiration from the American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted footage of her competing under the message “this is what a woman in sport looks like” onan Instagram postthat was liked more than a million times.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueSweeney appeared to respond to the criticism by posting a series of images of prominent female and male athletes posing naked for magazine shoots, including Serena Williams and the footballer Megan Rapinoe and the basketball player Sue Bird.The public relationship consultant Mark Borkowski, who has worked with everyone from Mikhail Gorbachev to Diego Maradona, said he felt the advert was “cynical soft porn”, but that the controversy would benefit Novig “given the number of eyeballs on it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBorkowski said: “Sex still sells. And the outrage, the culture war argument gets you one thing: enormous reach.”He also questioned whether Sweeney, who has starred in several successful TV series and films including Euphoria, The White Lotus and The Housemaid, may one day regret her decision.“Sweeney will make a lot of money over a short span of time,” Borkowski said. “But often it is about how your brand sustains over the years, not in the first flourish. And this sort of promotion can come back to haunt people.”The advert has been defended by Jacob Fortinsky, the founder and chief executive of Novig, which launched last month. “Sydney is great at captivating audiences and being the centre of attention,” he said. “In some sense, it forces us into the national discourse.”Fortinsky also pushed back against criticisms of the adult nature of the content, pointing out that Novig is restricted to users aged 21 and older. He added that Sweeney had approached the company about an equity partnership and helped to craft its message.This is not the first time an advert featuring Sweeney has attracted controversy. Last year American Eagle’s “Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans” campaignused a play on “jeans” and “genes”, including references to the blue-eyed actor’s inherited traits, sparked a culture war, with some saying it invoked eugenics.Several months after the controversy erupted, Sweeney said she had been unaware of it as she had been filming Euphoria. “Anyone who knows me knows that I’m always trying to bring people together,”she said. “I’m against hate and divisiveness.”Explore more on these topicsSportSydney SweeneyUS sportsAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade | Slavery | The Guardian
description: From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade
Author: David Conn
Headline: From Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave trade
Content: A close-up of a King Charles’s eyes beneath a jewelled crown, with silhouetted figures and ships collaged aboveComposite: Guardian/Diana EjaitaView image in fullscreenA close-up of a King Charles’s eyes beneath a jewelled crown, with silhouetted figures and ships collaged aboveComposite: Guardian/Diana EjaitaEnslaving nationSlaveryThe royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave tradeFrom Elizabeth I’s backing of early voyages to royal investment in trafficking companies, generations of monarchs were central to Britain’s slave tradeDavid ConnInvestigations correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.34 EDTShareEnslaved African people were seared with hot metal brands bearing the royal crown, according to research by historians who have documented the monarchy’s centuries-long involvement in Britain’s slave trade.TheRegister of British Slave Tradersidentifies thousands of people who invested in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans, including kings and queens.In response to the Guardian’s reporting of the new research relating to the monarchy, a spokesperson for King Charles said he was “grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed”.Dr Nicholas Radburn, a historian at Lancaster University, discovered evidence of the branding in the archives of the South Sea Company, a British crown-backed enterprise that trafficked thousands of enslaved African people to plantations in the 1700s.Radburn found a letter sent by the company’s board to its agents in Buenos Aires, instructing them to brand enslaved people with hot metal. The brand bore a crown, a symbol of the British monarchy’s role in the trade. A doctor had warned against the branding, but the board, whose members included figures from England’s establishment elite including MPs and Bank of England directors, instructed the agents to proceed.View image in fullscreenSouth Sea Company paperwork from 1714. This logo was used to brand enslaved people who were trafficked by the South Sea Company. The copy above it reads: ‘Mark for Negroes at Barbados’.Composite: South Sea Company“It now comes out, that you never mark the Negroes,” the letter said, “giving for reason that the French never did it, and that Dr Dover said your mark being so large, might endanger the Negroes.”Insisting the agents disregard the doctor’s advice, they wrote that it was “the most effectual … way to distinguish our Negroes from others”. The directors sent a crown brand with their letter and instructions for how to scar the enslaved African people with it.“Herewith you will receive a small silver mark,” they wrote. “As to the manner of using it, the method of our other factorys, is to mark the Negroes on the left shoulder heating the mark red hot.”The letter was signed: “Your affectionate friends, the court of directors.”Radburn said the letter illustrated how detailed the company’s dehumanising cruelty was – and its awareness of it.“These people were members of the London elite, in a boardroom, thinking in fine grain terms about the violence that needs to be done to enslaved people across the ocean,” he said. “And that will have happened as a result of that letter. People will have had their flesh seared with that brand.”The Register of British Slave Traders, thenew historical recordfor which Radburn was a lead investigator, documents how Britain’s enslaving and trafficking of more than 3 million African people for nearly 250 years was perpetrated as an official national enterprise, led by its monarchs.The publication of the register, themost comprehensive research projectinto the investors in Britain’s trafficking of enslaved African people, will further inform calls for King Charles to finally acknowledge the monarchy’s deep involvement in the trade.View image in fullscreenThe Register of British Slave Traders is expected to inform calls for Charles to acknowledge the monarchy’s deep involvement in the slave trade.Photograph: Arthur Edwards/ReutersThe kings and queens who powered the trafficking most ferociously were those after the monarchy was restored in 1660. James, Duke of York, who became King James II, was the governor and a substantial shareholder in the Royal African Company (RAC), founded in 1672, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.The RAC and its predecessor, the Company of Royal Adventurers, were established by James’s brother, King Charles II, and backed by royalist courtiers, politicians and financiers. These royal insiders, whose biographies are in the register, bore florid titles of the time: Edward Proger, “groom of the bedchamber”, the Earl of Falmouth, “groom of the stool”. The RAC meetings, where decisions about the trafficking of enslaved people were made, were held in James’s personal apartment in Whitehall Palace, the royal family’s London home before Buckingham Palace was built.Prof William Pettigrew, the register’s lead historian and investigator, said these royal enslaving companies were crucial to the kings of the Stuart dynasty striving to solidify the restored monarchy as an institution.View image in fullscreenThe Royal African Company’s coat of arms.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy“I view James II as the most important English slave trader of the 17th century,” Pettigrew said. “The African companies were central to the monarchy’s rehabilitation plan within the British constitution.”James ran the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people with his cousin, Prince Rupert of the Rhine, described in the register as “the visionary for England’s fully fledged, state-backed slave trade”. Other royals, including Charles II’s Portuguese wife, Queen Catherine of Braganza, were also investors in these companies.In her bookThe Crown’s Silence, Prof Brooke Newman haschronicled in detail the centuries-long involvementof the British monarchy in the enslavement of African people, from the first trafficking voyages backed by Queen Elizabeth I in the 1560s to King William IV, who relished drinking and debauchery on Caribbean plantations and opposed abolition for decades.Newman wrote that the RAC also branded the African people it enslaved at its coastal forts and factories, with DY for the Duke of York, and RACE for the Royal African Company of England. An agent in Sherbro, an island off Sierra Leone, was told by company directors: “You are to mark them … on the right breast RACE and the children of them at three years of age.”As part of a 1713 peace treaty, Queen Anne agreed with Spain’s King Philip V that Britain would be awarded theasiento– an agreement to deliver a stipulated 4,800 enslaved African men to Spain’s American colonies every year.View image in fullscreenThe RACE mark, for the Royal African Company of England, and the DY mark, for the Duke of York, used to brand enslaved African people.Anne announced it triumphantly in the House of Lords: “I have insisted and obtained, that theasientoor contract for furnishing the Spanish West Indies with Negroes, shall be made with us for the term of 30 years.”Queen Anne was a significant investor in the South Sea Company, which was established in 1711, and had rights to almost a quarter share of its overall profits. Anne gave theasientoto the SSC, which contracted the RAC to fulfil it.Anne’s successors, George I and George II, were also personal investors in and supporters of the SSC.According to theSlave Voyages database, the SSC trafficked 43,220 African captives fromwest Africa and Madagascarto the Caribbean and Spanish Americas between 1714 and 1740. From there, Radburn said, they were trafficked again, shipped and forced to march for hundreds of miles overland to the Pacific coast of South America. The company also moved more than 50,000 enslaved people within the Americas.The trafficking vessels, including ships named Crown, King William and William and Mary, all set off from London. Almost 7,000 people died in the ships’ notoriously appalling conditions.“It was a merciless, monarchy supported company,” Radburn said, “and the trafficking of enslaved people was the heart of it.”View image in fullscreenCharles has made several public expressions of regret about enslavement.Photograph: Anwar Hussein/AlamyPressure on Charles from African and Caribbean countries to acknowledge this history and go further than previous expressions of sorrow isexpected to buildbefore the nextCommonwealth heads of government meetingin Antigua and Barbuda in November.But successive governments have not formally apologised for Britain’s role in slavery and have rejected any discussion of reparations. Even if Charles wanted to, as king he is constitutionally bound by the government’s stated position.An official delegation from Jamaicadelivered a petition to Charleslast week, seeking a legal ruling from the privy council, the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories and some Commonwealth countries. It asks whether the forced transport of Africans to Jamaica was lawful, whether it constituted a crime against humanity, and whether Britain is obliged to provide restitution to Jamaica for slavery and its enduring consequences.Charles has publicly expressed sorrow over enslavement,describing it as an “appalling atrocity”and referring to “the most painful aspects of our past”, but has not formally acknowledgedand apologised forthe role of Britain or the monarchy in perpetrating it. In 2023 he signalled for the first time hissupport for researchinto the British monarchy’s historical links to transatlantic slavery.A spokesperson for the king said: “His majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today.“In that context, he is grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed.”David Comissiong, the Barbados ambassador to theCaribbeanCommunity, said he recognised that Charles’s constitutional role meant he must not contravene government policy.“But just as other British establishment families have acknowledged their involvement in the slavery enterprise and indicated a willingness to make reparation, anybody conscious of the British monarchy’s history would have to conclude that the British royal family should act similarly,” he added.

title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade | Slavery | The Guardian
description: St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans
Author: Morgan Ofori
Headline: St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans
Content: Animation: Alexander Purcell. Illustrations by Diana EjaitaEnslaving nationSlaveryThe London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave tradeSt Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved AfricansWritten byMorgan OforiandDavid Conn; Animation by Alexander Purcell; Photography by Wayne CrichlowMon 14 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.03 EDTShareInside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includesbiographical data on every known investorin Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.It reveals howwealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history.Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.View image in fullscreenThe grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOrnate boards adorn the walls of the Great Hall in St Barts, where governors recorded their philanthropic donations, many while investing in the companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe church of St Bartholomew the Less, in the grounds of St Barts hospital.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA portrait of King Henry VIII in the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, surrounded by the boards commemorating the hospital’s benefactors.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianPhillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.View image in fullscreenA diagram of a ship showing the cramped conditions in which enslaved Africans were trafficked.Composite: GuardianThe 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register.
