William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington,has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statueat the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nationRead moreThese connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.View image in fullscreenSeveral leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at St Barts.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAfter the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans formalised to become a lucrative source of funds for merchants.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Great Hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message. Its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – are tied to themes of healthcare.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored last year and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianThe private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688.Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

title: It’s a superfood but natto as we know it. Japan’s slimy fermented beans are coming your way | Japanese food and drink | The Guardian
description: Comprised of smelly soya beans held together by strands of mucus, the ancient dish is appearing in health food shops across the world
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Comprised of smelly soya beans held together by strands of mucus, the ancient dish is appearing in health food shops across the world
Content: There is evidence that regular consumption of the high-fibre, protein-packed food can boost the immune system, improve digestion and increase bone density.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThere is evidence that regular consumption of the high-fibre, protein-packed food can boost the immune system, improve digestion and increase bone density.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesJapanese food and drinkIt’s a superfood but natto as we know it. Japan’s slimy fermented beans are coming your wayComprised of smelly soya beans held together by strands of mucus, the ancient dish is appearing in health food shops across the worldJustin McCurryin TokyoMon 14 Sep 2026 19.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is smelly, slimy and contains bacteria – and a sizeable number of Japanese wouldn’t touch it with a pair of barge pole-length chopsticks. But after centuries as a breakfast food for Japanese diners with nerves of steel, natto is emerging as a global superfood to rivalkimchi, kombucha andkefir.Its exact origins are unknown. Some believe it was introduced toJapanfrom China by Buddhist monks during the Yayoi period (300BC-AD300), before becoming a staple among rural communities during the Edo period (1603-1868).A more prosaic explanation is that natto is the accidental byproduct of conflict, based on the legend of Minamoto no Yoshiie, a military commander during the Heian period (794-1185), whose troops discovered that simmered soya beans originally intended for their horses, but which had been left to fester in the heat for days after an enemy sighting, had taken on a viscous, pungent quality. Presumably famished by the demands of battle, they ate them anyway, and liked them enough to offer them to their master, who was similarly impressed.View image in fullscreenMinamoto no Yoshiie at the boundary to Nakoso, a painting by Suzuki Kiitsu, Japanese painter (1796-1858).Photograph: Culture Club/Bridgeman/Getty ImagesWhatever their origins, the beans – large, medium and small, or sometimes chopped,hikiwari-style – are finding their way into supermarkets around the world.Exports are packaged into Styrofoam trays of small paper cups and frozen, their nutritional value unaffected during transit, according to manufacturers.“We tend to try something new or unusual if we believe it will be good for our health, and that goes for people in the US, Australia and other countries,” said Hidefumi Ito, the president of Natto Kobo (Natto Workshop)Sendaiya, a chain of restaurants where diners can eat as many varieties as they like accompanied by rice, strips of simmered daikon radish and miso soup.View image in fullscreenA selection of natto on sale at Natto Bar Koganean, a specialist store in Tokyo.Photograph: Justin McCurry/The GuardianEaten as it is – or with topping ranging from mustard, shredded onion, wasabi and a splash ofdashi– natto’s appeal lies in its versatility. It works on toast or as a pizza topping, or mixed with pasta or avocado.But some Japanese are unconvinced. The dish is still more popular in the country’s eastern and northern regions, where it was used, often in soup, to see households through long, bitterly cold winters, while their counterparts in the west and south have traditionally been more sceptical.Consumers overseas, though, appear to have overcome any initial resistance to natto, whose smell has been compared to a particularly ripe stilton cheese, the beans connected by strands of mucus that diners can“whisk” into submissionwith repeated circular motions of their chopsticks.Ito suggested that natto novices add olive or chilli oil, or even use the beans as a topping for fish and chips, or mix them with ketchup. “Add some natto to something you would normally eat and push the envelope a little.”Natto exports tripled from 1,752 tonnes in 2017 to 5,248 tonnes in 2025, according to Japan’s finance ministry, with people in China the biggest consumers, followed by those in the US, Thailand and Hong Kong.View image in fullscreenExterior of Sendaiya, a natto restaurant in Tokyo.Photograph: Justin McCurry/The GuardianA member of staff atNatto Bar Koganean, a specialist store in Tokyo, said customers ranged from locals who eat the dish daily to foreign visitors who had tried it at home and wanted to eat the “real thing”.“Natto used to be something you’d put on rice, but now it’s becoming the centrepiece itself,” said the employee, whose store sells pots of additive-free natto with a choice of a dozen toppings, as well as versions encased in rice straw and bamboo.“We haven’t encountered a single person who was put off by its smell or consistency, and it’s really good for your health.”Those claims are supported by evidence that regular consumption of the high-fibre, protein-packed food can boost the immune system, improve digestion and increase bone density.In a 15-year study of 90,000 men and women between the ages of 45 and 74 that was published in 2020in the British Medical Journal, Japan’s National Cancer Centre said that eating fermented soy products, including natto, was associated with a lower risk of mortality. Packed with vitamin K2, the dish can suppress brain inflammation, while the bacteria that gives it its stickiness lowers blood sugar levels.View image in fullscreenNatto at Suehiro Japanese Restaurant in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Frederic J Brown/AFP/Getty ImagesSome of its popularity overseas has been driven by social media influencers who film themselves opening and eating natto. The American singer Lizzo, who has more than 26 million followers on TikTok, also fuelled interest in natto after she shared videos of hertucking into nattowithkarashimustard on rice.It is also challenging its “Marmite” status in Japan, where almost 19% of respondents to a 2023 survey by a natto industry group said they ate it daily – the highest proportion for a decade. Almost two-thirds ate it at least once a week.Wesley Smith, an American having lunch at Sendaiya in Tokyo, admitted he thought natto was “a little funky” when he tried it for the first time a few years ago. He added, though, that it had grown on him, “just like a strong cheese can”.Agence France-Presse contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsJapanese food and drinkVegetarian food and drinkJapanFoodAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to power | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing
Content: Presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APView image in fullscreenPresidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APBrazil‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to powerNeck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbingTom Phillipsin Juiz de ForaMon 14 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgiant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former presidentJair Bolsonarofluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.“Brazil is rudderless.Brazilhas no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.View image in fullscreenBolsonaro supporters float a giant balloon depicting the US president, Donald Trump, holding Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesBolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands ofa radical rightwing movementthat tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.Last September,Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentencefor spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.View image in fullscreenBrazil’s president Lula at a reelection campaign rally in Curitiba on Saturday.Photograph: Rodolfo Bührer/ReutersNearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused oftrying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favourthrough economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, thatJair Bolsonaro was stabbedin the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.View image in fullscreenDavi Frederico at the airport in Juiz de Fora.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianBolsonaro’sshock winushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part ofa plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.View image in fullscreenStreet hawkers at Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign event pay tribute to the US connection.Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’sattempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.View image in fullscreenSupporters gather to greet Flávio Bolsonaro at Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianMinas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, withone recent pollputting him ahead there.“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro addresses supporters at the spot where Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in Juiz de Fora during the 2018 presidential campaign.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty ImagesFor progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminalshis father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.View image in fullscreenLennon César: ‘Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.’Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianLennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’shostility to minorities.César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.View image in fullscreenGraffiti on Flávio Bolsonaro’s headquarters in the city of Juiz de Fora.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ancestors review – messy but moving ghostly drama about the Aids crisis | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Saipan standout Éanna Hardwicke is a soulful gay man looking for a missing friend in a striking yet muddled debut
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Saipan standout Éanna Hardwicke is a soulful gay man looking for a missing friend in a striking yet muddled debut
Content: Éanna Hardwicke in Ancestors.Photograph: Leanne SullivanView image in fullscreenÉanna Hardwicke in Ancestors.Photograph: Leanne SullivanFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewAncestors review – messy but moving ghostly drama about the Aids crisisToronto film festival:Saipan standout Éanna Hardwicke is a soulful gay man looking for a missing friend in a striking yet muddled debutBenjamin Leein TorontoMon 14 Sep 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not normal to regularly contemplate mortality in your twenties, to ask questions about where we might go after we die and whether any part of our legacy will even matter in the years following. But for gay men in the 1980s, death was everywhere.Prima Facie review – fiery one-woman play is flattened into a bland movieRead moreIn David Turpin’s intermittently impactful debut Ancestors, the director tries to make a connection with those men who lived through the very worst years of the Aids crisis. Turpin, born in 1982, might not have the first-hand experience but he bears the scars passed on from generation to generation and like many young gay men coming of age in the years after, likely experienced a watered down version of the shame and fear those before him once felt.His film is about how bridges are built between past and future, living and dead, old and young, and how those who have been pushed out of society work about trying to create and sustain their own. Set in a foggy, ghostly London in 1988, Turpin’s dreamy and mysterious film is trying to cast a spell (he hasreferredto it as a “séance” in interviews) and it’s one that works incredibly well at times and wears off far too easily at others. As with many a first movie, there’s a lot thrown at the wall here with scrappy ambition prioritised over laser focus and while that’s admirable, it can also be a little frustrating.What’s most consistent is a mesmerising performance from Éanna Hardwicke, the Irish actor who was also one of the best things about last year’s Toronto film festival, playing Roy Keane in underseen World Cup workplace dramaSaipan. Again he brings real, combustible angst to the role but here it’s of a far different kind, aimed at the rapidly disintegrating world around him and the one person he wants to save from disintegrating with it. He plays Beau, a gay man working in a caff owned by “Auntie” Maurice (Rupert Everett), an old queen who collects both framed pictures of the female actors he idolises as well as young strays. The latest of whom is Tiny (Jack Wolfe), a 20-year-old in need of work. When Beau later sees him cruising in the park and finds out he has nowhere to stay, he brings him back to stay in an apartment shared with his best friend, Shell (a luminous Jessica Reynolds).Refreshingly there’s no sexual tension between the pair (Beau says early on that Tiny isn’t his type) and instead they become friends, a far more compelling and under-explored gay male dynamic. Like Maurice did with him, Beau also feels a sense of responsibility for Tiny, an overwhelming weight at such a grim time and after Tiny reveals that he is positive, the objective changes from keeping him safe to keeping him alive. The film jumps back and forth in time, and to other places, as Tiny goes missing and Beau must try to find him. Early on Beau tries to get Tiny to read his collection of Jean Genet novels but he tells him that he isn’t interested in tales of detectives and instead prefers “love stories and ghost stories”. Turpin also has little interest in the fact-finding grind of actually tracking someone down and more about the love between the pair and the ghosts that surround them.From Chris Rock to Helen Mirren: 10 films to look out for at the Toronto film festival 2026Read moreFor a film that plays with reality, dreams, nightmares, the past, the future and the afterlife and slips between timelines and from colour to black and white, it often works best in its more grounded conversational scenes. His direction might get overly precious but Turpin’s dialogue is natural and direct and we never doubt Hardwicke’s authenticity. The film around him can meander a little, in its worst moments feeling like a short that’s been expanded beyond its means, and while some of the atmosphere is entirely enveloping, sometimes the visuals can be a little ropey. There are misfiring gambits like a transfixing but inconsequential Christina Hendricks as a golden age actor who comes to life and a few too many underwhelming musical interludes at a local gay bar (save for one wrenching cover of Tim Buckley’s Song to the Siren which is wisely played again at the end). I was moved by so much – a picture of Tiny added to an expanding wall filled with other gay men who got sick, Beau’s anxiousness over whether he might also have it and how intimate he should then be with Shell or Maurice, how Beau grapples with the idea of hopelessness without despair – but then alienated by so many others.The last act hinges on a more conventional reveal that feels a little at odds with the stranger, fuzzier movie that Turpin seems more focused on making. It doesn’t quite have the gut-punch impact it should, a more conceptually interesting idea than an emotionally effective one, but the very last scene does bring us back under that spell. In its swirl of emotions, ideas and styles, Ancestors can get a little lost in the mist but when, in its finest moments, it all clears, there’s something haunting in front of us.Ancestors is premiering at theToronto film festivaland is seeking distributionExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalFestivalsDrama filmsAids and HIVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Forever Home review – Graham Norton’s corpse-in the-basement thriller absolutely stinks  | Television | The Guardian
description: Norton’s best selling novel hits the small screen in a flurry of murder, bad gags and ex-soap stars in drab cardigans drinking fake coffees. What a total yawn
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Norton’s best selling novel hits the small screen in a flurry of murder, bad gags and ex-soap stars in drab cardigans drinking fake coffees. What a total yawn
Content: Half baked … the cast of Forever Home, from left: Moira (Denise Welch), Silent Dave (Kevin Whately), Sally (Jenny Walser), Carol (Amy Nuttall), Robert (Douglas Henshall), Kaden (Lewis Cope) and Dan (Shane Zaza).Photograph: Helen WilliamsView image in fullscreenHalf baked … the cast of Forever Home, from left: Moira (Denise Welch), Silent Dave (Kevin Whately), Sally (Jenny Walser), Carol (Amy Nuttall), Robert (Douglas Henshall), Kaden (Lewis Cope) and Dan (Shane Zaza).Photograph: Helen WilliamsTV reviewTelevisionReviewForever Home review – Graham Norton’s corpse-in the-basement thriller absolutely stinksNorton’s best selling novel hits the small screen in a flurry of murder, bad gags and ex-soap stars in drab cardigans drinking fake coffees. What a total yawnSarah DempsterMon 14 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘What in the name of the Virgin Mother is that terrible honk?” bellows Moira (Denise Welch) as she staggers disgustedly around her daughter Carol’s kitchen. “The smell!” she continues, cheeks ballooning in horror as Carol (Amy Nuttall) – who is, you suspect, familiar with such theatrics – busies herself with the teabags. “Carol?!The smell.”Moira – a vision of motherly forbearance in cerise elastane – is not the only one alarmed by the mysterious stench emanating from 7 Stable Row, the Edwardian domicile in which six-part thriller Forever Home does the bulk of its thrilling. Carol’s unblinking partner, Robert (Douglas Henshall, far better than he needs to be), wonders if the smell might be something to do with the drains. Robert’s son Kaden (Lewis Cope) suspects foxes. And Carol? Carol is as narked with the funk as the rest of them.That said, she thinks it’s probably best not to mention the fact that it’s all down to the corpse that’s currently defrosting in the faulty freezer she has just discovered in the cellar. Not just yet, anyway. Wouldn’t want to put anyone off their garibaldis. Particularly as said stiff appears to be Robert’s first wife, a “cow” who had, according to an increasingly shifty Robert, buggered off with his brother 20 years ago. Determined to prove to herself that Robert – who is in the early stages of dementia – is innocent, Carol soon finds herself in an investigational pea-souper, a tangled web of murder and blah in which long-buried secrets emerge from yawn and etcetera.All clear? Grand. And so, with nose pinched and buttocks clenched, we bash on.Based on the bestselling novel byGraham Norton, Forever Home is the latest emission from Channel 5’s Indistinguishable Domestic Thriller Processing Complex™, the shadowy facility responsible for such mechanically separated tubes of bunkum as Number One Fan, For Her Sins, The Fortune and no-me-neither classic of the genre, The Game.You know the deal: murder, betrayal, ex-soap actors in drab cardigans nursing visibly empty coffee mugs while standing alone in fitted kitchens from B&Q’s These Lies Are Tearing Your Marriage Apart Babes® range. Here, however, the custom blend of banality and absurdity is served with an unexpected accompaniment: humour. This is represented by lines such as “She doesn’t know her Van Goghs from her Van Dammes!” and a winking string motif that pops up whenever Forever Home wants us to know it’s safe to come out from behind the sofa.View image in fullscreenDark secrets? Carol Crottie (Amy Nuttall) finds herself in a tangled web.Photograph: Helen WilliamsSo here is Robert’s daughter Sally (Jenny Walser), a gullible leisure centre receptionist engaged in a saucy subplot with adulterous spanner Patrick (James Baxter). “We can get married in Las Vegas!” she swoons during one of their clandestine bums’n’tums workouts in the leisure centre’s store room. “Grumph,” replies Patrick, his faithless bum cheeks clacking like castanets.The soundtrack continues to tee-hee when an increasingly desperate Sally decides to befriend Patrick’s sweetly clueless wife, and refuses to let up even when, later, she starts secretly pawing through her underwear drawer.When Carol finally shares her cadaver-based discovery with Moira, it’s party time at the giggle factory. You can’t tell the police, shrieks Moira. There’ll be trophy hunters. “This place will become like a grisly house of horrors! Robert …AKAFred West!”Does this lighthearted approach to unhilarious subjects (eg dismemberment and stalking) work? It does not. Does it at least offer the odd moment of blackly comic respite from what would otherwise be an unremittingly bleak catalogue of domestic traumas? Again, no.Instead, we have a drama that crashes between tones and issues like a drunken soap, but without the earnestness or depth of characterisation that can make these things bearable. The only topic Forever Home considers a lol-free zone is Robert’s dementia. We know this because his scenes are accompanied by a sad piano rather than thigh-slapping and titters.Nobody turns up to a weeknight Channel 5 thriller expecting prestige subtlety or searing psychological insight. But is it too much to ask for a script that doesn’t honk like a defrosting corpse? Suffice to say: don’t go into the cellar.Forever Home is on Channel 5 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewGraham NortonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s about controlling your entire body’: how to start doing handstands | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Handstands display a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt – and they look cool. Experts share their advice for building up strength and practicing
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: Handstands display a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt – and they look cool. Experts share their advice for building up strength and practicing
Content: Although it looks like an upper-body exercise, the position requires nearly every part of the body to work together.Illustration: Carmen Casado/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlthough it looks like an upper-body exercise, the position requires nearly every part of the body to work together.Illustration: Carmen Casado/The GuardianHow to startWell actually‘It’s about controlling your entire body’: how to start doing handstandsHandstands display a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt – and they look cool. Experts share their advice for building up strength and practicingMadeleine AggelerMon 14 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy aspirations in life are modest: I want to write, spend time with my loved ones, and someday find a lipstick that flatters my skintone. But perhaps my greatest ambition is this: I want to be able to do a handstand.Why? It turns the world upside down. It seems fun. It displays a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt. And it looks cool! Maybe it has to do with that one time in third grade when all my friends could do a handstand and I couldn’t, but that’s for me and my therapist to sort out later.A handstand is an inversion, a type of position where one’s heart is above the head. Besides looking cool, there isa lot to gainfrom inversions. When the head is below the heart, oxygen-rich blood flow to the brain increases, according to theUC Irvine Integrative Health Institute. This helps “regulate neurotransmitters and nourish brain cells”. Other benefits include stress reduction and increased physical strength and mobility, says Antoinette Webb, a registered yoga teacher.Below, experts share advice onhow to startdoing handstands.A handstand is a full-body exercise“A handstand is a full-body inversion in which you support your weight through your hands while balancing upside down,” says Frank Medrano, a calisthenics athlete and coach.View image in fullscreenWhen the head is below the heart, oxygen-rich blood flow to the brain increases.Photograph: AleksandarNakic/Getty ImagesAlthough it looks like an upper-bodyexercise, the position requires nearly every part of the body to work together, he says. The hands and forearms helpmaintain balance; the shoulders, upper back, chest and triceps support and stabilize the body; and the core, glutes and legs create the tension necessary tokeep your body aligned.“A strong handstand is not simply about kicking your hands overhead,” Medrano says. “It is about controlling your entire body as one connected unit.”Because it is such an advanced exercise and it temporarily increasesblood pressurein the head and upper body, there are certain groups who should be cautious or avoid handstands and other inversions, says Webb. These include individuals with conditions including high blood pressure; osteoporosis; neck, shoulder or spine injuries; and heart and eye conditions.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Assess and build up your strengthFirst, you need to figure out howstrong your upper bodyis.“I would start with downward dog, and hold that position for about 90 seconds,” says Dianne Bondy, a certified yoga teacher and pilates instructor, referring to the popular yoga position in which the body forms an inverted V, with hips in the air and hands and feet on the ground.In order to prepare the rest of your body and help with mobility, Webb suggests working onyoga posesthat help strengthen the core and hips, such asplank,locust,boatandcobra.Use a wall for supportOnce yourupper body strengthis sufficient, Bondy suggests progressing to positions where your feet are against a wall. This helps familiarize you with “the feeling of going upside down and pressing weight into your hands”, she explains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVery difficult and extremely cool: how to start doing pull-upsRead moreWebb suggests building up comfort by learning to hold an L-shape against the wall, with your torso and legs at a right angle from each other, chest facing the wall. Your hands will be on the floor and your feet against the wall. How you get into this position is up to you – experiment safely to find your preferred method. This will help you learn how totap into your breathand alignment, and practice bracing your body while pushing the ground away with your hands, she says.As you progress, you can inch your feet gradually up the wall, says Medrano. The higher your feet go, the closer your hands, arms, torso and legs will move to the wall, until you are almost flush with it. Keep your body tight, and “only move as close as your strength and confidence allow”, he says. This process teaches body proper alignment without relying on the momentum of simply hoisting your legs into the air.Practice freestanding (briefly)When you can hold a controlled wall stand, Medrano says you can try removing one foot from the wall at a time. Eventually, this may progress to removing both feet from the wall. Keep these attempts short. “Quality is more important than duration,” Medrano says.Learn to fallWhen it comes to handstands, it’s not a matter of if you will fall, but when.“You are absolutely going to fall, so how you can do so safely is the question you have to answer,” says Webb.Medrano suggests “practicing stepping down deliberately”. One way to do this is learning how to turn out of the handstand, instead of falling over. This involves twisting from a handstand into acartwheel, so that your legs swing to the side and you land on your feet. Make sure you have adequate space. (If that is difficult to envision, an instructional video, likethis one, can help.)More from How to start:How to start meditatingHow to start weightliftingHow to start budgetingHow to start runningKeep practicing“When I learned to do a handstand for the first time, I wasin my 40s,” says Bondy. “I learned that it’snever too late. I still do them to this day.”Bondy says she also learned that handstands were a “use it or lose it” skill. If you want to be able to keep doing it, you have to keep practicing.View image in fullscreenAlthough it looks like an upper-body exercise, a handstand requires nearly every part of the body to work together.Photograph: fizkes/Getty ImagesEveryone’s progress will be different. If you’re miles away from doing a full handstand or wall stand, that’s fine.“Comparing your journey to someone else’s is going to keep you struggling to take the first step,” says Webb. “Your handstand or headstand on the wall, with blocks or supported by another person is just as valid as someone in the middle of the floor standing on one hand.”As with any physical goal, “give yourself grace and the space to see what you’re capable of,” says Webb.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyHow to startFitnessHealth & wellbeingYogafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Beck: Ride Lonesome review – stunning end to the heartache trilogy of Sea Change and Morning Phase | Beck | The Guardian
description: On his first album in seven years, Beck keeps the quality control extremely high as he surveys mid-50s malaise in the wake of divorce
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: On his first album in seven years, Beck keeps the quality control extremely high as he surveys mid-50s malaise in the wake of divorce
Content: Guess I’m doing fine … Beck.Photograph: Mikai KarlView image in fullscreenGuess I’m doing fine … Beck.Photograph: Mikai KarlBeckReviewBeck: Ride Lonesome review – stunning end to the heartache trilogy of Sea Change and Morning Phase(Iliad/Capitol)On his first album in seven years, Beck keeps the quality control extremely high as he surveys mid-50s malaise in the wake of divorceAlexis PetridisMon 14 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last timeBeckreleased an album it was 2019 and the singer-songwriter found himself in a strange and unenviable position. In some quarters, the arrival of Hyperspace was eagerly anticipated precisely because his personal life was in turmoil. Nine months before its release, his 15-year marriage to actor Marissa Ribisi had ended in divorce, an experience he understandably described as heartbreaking. Unfortunately for him, there exists a pervasive argument that Beck’s greatest work is born out of misery.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Ride Lonesome.Photograph: CapitolHis beloved 2002 album Sea Change featured a set of disconsolate acoustic songs written in the wake of a break-up with his long-term girlfriend Leigh Limon that Beck had initially thought were too personal for public consumption. They were certainly very different from the knowing, postmodern approach with which he’d made his name, but no matter: Sea Change went on to become a huge critical and commercial success. It wasn’t entirely clear what prompted the gloomy mood of 2014’s Morning Phase, but it very much seemed to be cut from similar musical and lyrical cloth. Some critics suggested it was the best album of his career; it subsequently won three Grammys, including album of the year. Given the circumstances, there was much pre-release speculation that Hyperspace would be a companion piece.Instead, Hyperspace was synth-heavy, produced by Pharrell Williams and clearly influenced by vaporwave: its tone was dreamily buoyant and noticeably light on wracked soul-bearing. After its release, Beck seemed to tacitly suggest to fans of Sea Change and Morning Phase that there wouldn’t be any more where they came from. “When I try to shoe-horn my life into a song,” he told the New Yorker, “it gets really ham-fisted.”Seven years on, he appears to have reconsidered. The first thing you hear on Ride Lonesome is a softly strummed acoustic guitar, echoey pedal steel and Beck’s voice. “Walk away, hang your head on the hollow moon,” he sings, as the album’s title track gets under way: should there be any lingering doubt about the mood it’s intent on evoking, it goes on to reference Julie London’s Cry Me a River and Johnny Thunders’ You Can’t Put Your Arms Around a Memory. “It feels like I’ve been here before,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him.He certainly has. There’s an intentionality about the way Ride Lonesome reconvenes the team responsible for Sea Change and Morning Phase – the former’s producer Nigel Godrich is once more behind the mixing desk, the backing musicians who appear on both albums are present and correct, the orchestrations are the work of Beck’s father David Campbell – and about the artists the music here evokes. As on Sea Change’s Round the Bend and Morning Phase’s Heart Is a Drum, the ghosts of Nick Drake and his string arranger Robert Kirby are very clearly summoned up, most noticeably on In the Night. On Run Away, we find Beck exactly where he was on Sea Change’s The Golden Age and Morning Phase’s Unforgiven: alone, behind the wheel of a car in the small hours, aimlessly driving around in an attempt to assuage his unhappiness.Beck’s greatest songs – ranked!Read moreSimilar sound, similar mood, similar lyrical themes: of course, the danger is of diminishing returns. But Ride Lonesome never feels like a pale imitation or a craven attempt to recapture past glories. That’s partly because of the standard of the songwriting. Beck has suggested that one reason the album took so long to make is because of stringent quality control: songs were recorded, then set aside for years, then reconsidered, a huge amount of material was discarded. You can tell: everything here, from the sparse country-rock of Slow Canyon to the lush, harmony-drenched Falling Through My Hands is melodically exquisite; every song has the requisite emotional impact.But it’s also because Ride Lonesome is clearly an album made by a noticeably older artist than either of its predecessors: its mood is marked not just by the collapse of a relationship, but a sense of time passing, of things – to borrow a phrase from Nick Drake – moving just a little too fast. “I don’t know where I’m going,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him, “but it feels like I’ve been here before”: a neat capturing of a very mid-50s kind of malaise. An affecting sense of weariness seeps into everything, even the ostensibly optimistic – and utterly lovely – closer Beyond the Light comes filled with evocations of lost “nameless days” and of “the dying of the light”.Unfortunately for Beck, Ride Lonesome does little to dispel the aforementioned theory about his best work being born out of unhappiness. There’ll be consolation in the fact it’s also that rarest of things: a sequel to a sequel that’s every bit as good as its predecessors.Ride Lonesome is released on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsBeckPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying’: how we made cave horror classic The Descent | Movies | The Guardian
description: ‘The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower’
Author: Alex Deller
Headline: ‘The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower’
Content: ‘I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked’ … Shauna Macdonald in the 2005 horror.Photograph: 1996-98 AccuSoft Inc., All rights reserved/PatheView image in fullscreen‘I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked’ … Shauna Macdonald in the 2005 horror.Photograph: 1996-98 AccuSoft Inc., All rights reserved/PatheHow we madeMovies‘The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying’: how we made cave horror classic The Descent‘The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower’Interviews byAlex DellerMon 14 Sep 2026 10.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeil Marshall, writer/directorI was introduced to Christian Colson at Celador Films off the back of [2002 horror film] Dog Soldiers, and I pitched them a project – actually a feature-length version of my student graduation film – about zombies on an oil rig. They liked it but said it was too expensive, so on the train back to Newcastle I was asking myself what would make a really scary horror film that could be contained and so made on a budget. I was thinking of things set in the dark and was like, well …caves. At the back of my mind was a school trip to a lead mine where the guide had said, “OK, everybody, turn your lights off” and, for the first time, I experienced a darkness that I just couldn’t fathom.We wanted the film to feel as realistic as possible: when you’re caving, the only lights you have are what you take with you. There are no beautiful shafts of light making everything look pretty. It meant having huge portions of the screen in total darkness, so only when a character turns around and shines a light you finally see what’s in the shadows.double quotation markAlex said her lines with an ice pick through her neck. Then I caved her head in with a stoneDarkness was definitely my friend, but it did mean a lot of planning because each character had to have something they could light the scene with, even if it was just a box of matches. Sam McCurdy, the director of photography, and I discussed lighting sources that we could potentially use, and I structured the film around who had which light at which time. This gave us a lighting scheme: if you’re with the fire, it’s Sarah. If it’s a torch, it’s Juno.There isn’t a single real cave in the whole film. It was a mixture of amazing sets by Simon Bowles, a couple of matte paintings and a miniature set built by Leigh Took – the water pouring down the waterfall wasn’t water, it’s salt.For the crawlers, I wanted something very basic-looking, not too many lines or details. The challenge was how to make them scary but keep them human, because the notion is that these are the cavemen who stayed in the cave rather than those who left the dark and started building cabins in the open. Visually they were a hybrid of Nosferatu and Iggy Pop, but movement-wise I thought we should make them like spiders – the way they’ll stop and be perfectly still before suddenly going off at 100 miles an hour and then stopping again.I conceptualised the film as Sarah’s descent into being this primal savage: her undergoing a rebirth in order to survive, even though you’re not sure she’s going to be able to go back to society afterwards.View image in fullscreen‘I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked’ … a crawler in The Descent.Photograph: PatheShauna Macdonald, played SarahThis was the era of FHM, Loaded and all those lads’ mags, so I initially thought it was going to be girls looking sexy in tight spaces covered in blood and gunge. I wasn’t interested in that. When I read the script, though, it was excellent. It was about a grieving mother and I also needed to be physically strong and brave. I thought, “I have to do this part because I don’t know if I’ll be able to pull it off.”We weren’t allowed to see the crawlers or even any pictures of them. I was the first to see one because we were shooting chronologically once we got into the caves. The others were all asking “what does it look like?!” but I didn’treallyknow because it was quite far away. I just knew it was grey or white and slimy, and it looked a bit like Gollum.I think Neil was right to keep us apart, because when we were faced with them, I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked, who’d been training for months and months – that really focuses the mind. When we came to fight them, they were so animalistic it was really unnerving. The actors had figured out how the crawlers’ system worked and their different characteristics. You felt like you were fighting a pack with all its dynamics, and that was pretty intimidating.That whole sequence where Sarah goes into survival mode was great. First I had the dying scene with Alex Reid, who played Beth, just making it look really easy. It was like, “OK, Alex, you’ve had an ice pick through your neck, but it’s really important that you tell these plot points …” And she was, “Yeah, cool, no problem.” And then, of course, I cave her head in with a stone. Then I get leapt on by a child crawler. He was only like 11, bless him, and I crushed his head with my boot, which was actually me stamping on a cauliflower. Then the mother finds out, and we have this fight sequence where one mother has to kill another to survive. The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying. Then another crawler comes along and I bash his head in too. Afterwards I’m submerged in this pool of blood, which was a Jacuzzi that they’d overflowed. This amazing stunt girl had to do the run and jump, because the pool was so shallow they couldn’t insure an actor to do it. All I had to do was emerge and take the glory.In the press, it was all about “girl power”. But we were like: “Have you seen what we do to each other?!” Whatwasvery girl power was how fiercely we actors supported each other and we continue to do that. The only way you can really show love is by turning up for your friends, and the six of us have done that repeatedly for the last 21 years or so. We’ve got a WhatsApp group and still meet regularly. I do wonder, if we’d met on a different project, would the same thing happen? Or was it the film? If you throw a group of people in a cave, maybe you all come out bonded for life.The Descent is available on 4K UHDExplore more on these topicsFilmHow we madeHorror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Phones are the new cigarettes: why restaurants are discouraging and even banning them | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: Would you hand in your phone at the door in exchange for a free bottle of wine? One restaurateur has tried that – and there are now many other gambits that are encouraging us to connect
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: Would you hand in your phone at the door in exchange for a free bottle of wine? One restaurateur has tried that – and there are now many other gambits that are encouraging us to connect
Content: A sign discouraging mobile phone use in the White Horse pub, Soho, London.Photograph: Tony Smith/AlamyView image in fullscreenA sign discouraging mobile phone use in the White Horse pub, Soho, London.Photograph: Tony Smith/AlamyPass notesRestaurantsPhones are the new cigarettes: why restaurants are discouraging and even banning themWould you hand in your phone at the door in exchange for a free bottle of wine? One restaurateur has tried that – and there are now many other gambits that are encouraging us to connectTim DowlingMon 14 Sep 2026 11.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Phone bans.Age:Their provenance is considerable; their time is now.Appearance:Groups of people eating together, talking together and laughing together, while also twitching slightly from withdrawal.So this is specifically to do with banning phones in restaurants?Restaurants and bars, yes.Hardly a new thing, is it?No. Ironically, a decade ago many fine dining establishmentswereunbanningmobiles, surrendering to the idea that people couldn’t be stopped from posting photographs of their food.I suppose it was considered good for business.Not any more – at the Spy Bar in London, they put a sticker over your phone’s camera lens at the door.What’s the point? People can just peel the sticker off.It’s supposed to work on a psychological level – to preserve privacy and allow people to enjoy themselves without distraction.Shouldn’t a ban be more, erm, enforceable?They certainly can be. At Antagonist, a bar in Charlotte, North Carolina, customers are required to put their phones in a locked pouch of the type used to enforce phone bans in schools. At the Trophy Room in Phoenix, Arizona, guests’ phones are stored in a vintage filing cabinet during their visit.Sounds like prison.At the Clink restaurant in London they lock all phones in an outside cabin, but that’s because the restaurant is actually inside HMP Brixton, where possession of a mobile phone is prohibited.OK, maybe a phone ban should be less enforceable than that.Some places use a carrot instead of a stick. At Al Condominio in Verona, Italy, customers are offereda free bottle of wineif they surrender their phones before the meal.Does that work?Apparently 90% of customers accept the challenge.As would Ifor free wine.Other restaurants simply have a no phones policy, in a bid to encourage conversation and to re-establish focus on the food and the experience.And the clientele are in favour?For the most part. “I strongly encourage people to give it a chance, and sometimes they don’t and they go somewhere else,” Antagonist’s general managertold the Wall Street Journal.Still, it sounds as if it’s becoming more widespread.Big chains are now beginning to crack down. Pizza Express initiatedphone-free afternoonslast summer, and evenWetherspoons has drawn a line.There’s no way I would go into a Wetherspoons without my phone.No worries – they just want you to keep it on silent.Do say:“Take my phone, please. Anything that encourages human connection is worth sacrificing a few hours of doomscrolling for.”Don’t say:“I can still do my podcast from here though, right?”Explore more on these topicsRestaurantsPass notesMobile phonesPubsFoodSocial etiquettefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: As Reform celebrates £72m in donations, tell me this: are you ready to see two rich men buy our democracy? | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: It’s not just that Nigel Farage claimed his movement abhorred the super-rich. It’s also the obscenity of individuals seeking so much sway over who runs the country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: It’s not just that Nigel Farage claimed his movement abhorred the super-rich. It’s also the obscenity of individuals seeking so much sway over who runs the country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Nigel Farage after his closing speech at Reform UK’s annual conference in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage after his closing speech at Reform UK’s annual conference in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionReform UKAs Reform celebrates £72m in donations, tell me this: are you ready to see two rich men buy our democracy?Owen JonesIt’s not just that Nigel Farage claimed his movement abhorred the super-rich. It’s also the obscenity of individuals seeking so much sway over who runs the countryMon 14 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTShareAs£72m in donationsmakes its way to Reform UK’s bank accounts, consider what Nigel Faragesaidon the eve of Britain’s vote to leave the European Union a decade ago. “This referendum is the people versus the establishment,” he declared. “It is the vested interest, it’s the rich, it’s the big business.”Just two years ago,Farage assailed“an unholy alliance of big business, big banks and big government”. He is also the same man who, when he debated with the then Liberal Democrat leader, Nick Clegg, in 2014,claimed to“represent the mercantile, trading, entrepreneurial end of society”, while his opponent “represents big banks, big government and big business”.To be clear, Farage’s political outfit isbeing bankrolledby two cryptobillionaires. One of them is Ben Delo, who once developed high-frequency trading systems for JP Morgan.That investment bank was a particular bete noire of Farage: when it backed the Remain campaign,he savaged“the unholy alliance of big banks and big politics”. The other is the Thailand-based cryptobillionaire Christopher Harborne, who gave Farage hispre-election £5m giftand provided two-thirds of Reform’s funding – until now, that is.Neither of them is the plucky small merchant evoked by Farage’s rhetoric. The man who denounced banks buying political influence is now dependent on two wealthy figures from the world of finance. Predictably, Reform says its benefactors want “nothing” in return for their colossal donations. Yet the two businessmen who have just coughed up the biggest donations in British political history will surely be delighted with Reform’s plans to slash taxes on crypto assets and set up a “bitcoin reserve”.The political fraud that is rightwing “populism” is quite something to behold. These movements claim to champion the little guy against the elites. Whether embodied by wealthy tycoon Donald Trump, whose relatives and friends are making a killing from his administration, or the privately educated millionaire ex-City broker Farage, the formula is straightforward. Dupe struggling people into believing their problems are caused by migrants, refugees and minorities – while championing the interests of the mega-rich who actually hold the power.Sure, British democracy has always come with heavy caveats. Political parties and politicians have always received hefty donations from an economic elite that, to be clear, does not give money away without expecting a return. They can also rely on powerful lobbyists to advance their interests. Then there’s the “revolving door” through which politicians and civil servants leave public office for lucrative jobs with companies in the very industries they were previously responsible for overseeing and regulating. And there’s a British newspaper industry mostly owned by rich moguls with a vested interest in defending a status quo they profit from.View image in fullscreenA protest placard near the Houses of Parliament in London on 9 September.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersBut these latest donations take the corruption of our democracy to a whole new level. That two donations to Reform in a single weekend now eclipse the total amount spent by all political parties at the last general election tells its own story. Indeed, these donations amount to about14 timesthe total spent by Farage’s party at the last election – when, it should be noted, it won more than 4m votes, or one in seven votes cast.The party can now pay for hundreds of full-time staff, build local political hubs and massively expand its polling and research infrastructure. Crucially, it can throw vast sums at digital advertising, which can be uniquely tailored to the interests and concerns of individual voters. We know fromresearch in the USthat digital ads can shift voting intention. The more money a political party has, the more it can afford to experiment until it finds the ads that work.Indeed, all the evidence suggests that money wins votes. A recentpeer-reviewed studyexamined every British general election between 1857 and 2017, and found a strong relationship between relative campaign spending and votes. Rich donors really do shower political parties with money for a reason. Reform’s mega-donations underline that democracy is for sale.But could this spectacularly backfire? Reform is, after all, already embroiled in multiple controversies over gifts and donations from wealthy donors, andits ratingshave taken a bad beating.Polling earlier this yearfound that 83% of Brits believe that “wealthy individuals use political donations to influence the government to further their own personal interests”. That figure was only four points lower among Reform voters, who were also nearly 10 times as likely to say they would view a party more favourably if it promised to cap donations as to view it less favourably.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFarage hints that Reform’s £72m donations may not be legal under new elections bill - UK politics liveRead moreIt would be naive, alas, to believe that this will finally burst the gilded Reform bubble. What it does do depends on what the national political conversation is about. Labour has had long enough in government to change the law to block such donations, and tragicallyAndy Burnham has retreatedfrom his stated desire to cap them at £500,000.But that would mean a Labour party that was determined to confront wealthy vested interests. Because Starmerism had no desire to replace an economic order rigged in favour of elites, it was unable to redirect anger away from the scapegoating of migrants. Instead, it simply replicated Farage’s xenophobia, which only ever legitimises the arguments of the anti-migrant right.A different approach, based on redistributing wealth and power, would force a different conversation. So far, thanks to pressure from Zack Polanski’s Green party, Burnham has shifted some of the rhetoric. But if Labour were to, say, hike taxes on wealth in order to invest in crumbling services, it could pair that with a sustained attack on Farage as the plaything of wealthy vested interests.Otherwise, the outrage over these donations will fade. The old poison will remain – and this time it comes with £72m behind it.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is released in October.
