title: Canada should become an EU state in all but name. Here’s how to make that a reality | Fabian Zuleeg | The Guardian
description: From the UK to Japan, so many countries need to quickly be brought inside the European tent without the rigours of full membership, says economist Fabian Zuleeg
Author: Fabian Zuleeg
Headline: From the UK to Japan, so many countries need to quickly be brought inside the European tent without the rigours of full membership, says economist Fabian Zuleeg
Content: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and European Council president Antonio Costa in Brussels in June 2025.Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPAView image in fullscreenEuropean Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and European Council president Antonio Costa in Brussels in June 2025.Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPAOpinionEuropean UnionCanada should become an EU state in all but name. Here’s how to make that a realityFabian ZuleegFrom the UK to Japan, so many countries need to quickly be brought inside the European tent without the rigours of full membershipMon 14 Sep 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTShareThe worst conclusion to draw from Iceland’sEU referendum resultlast month would be that the country, apparently nowon Donald Trump’s imperial mapalong with Canada and Greenland, wanted to distance itself from Europe. Rather, the decision to refuse the reopening of EU accession talks shows that asking voters to choose between membership of the 27-nation bloc and staying outside the club is too binary. Some countries want to be inside the European tent without necessarily becoming members. The EU needs a new status for them.There are existing models of close cooperation. Iceland and Norway, for example, participate in much of the single market through theEuropean Economic Area (EEA). A range of other partial, gradual or associated membership options for candidate countries is being debated.What I am proposing is different from any of them. It is not about setting up a stepping stone to accession, nor is it primarily about access to the single market. Instead, it is about letting like-minded countries combine with the EU when geopolitical and geo-economic necessities demand it, without them having to sign up to a predetermined constitutional outcome.The main criterion for the novel status I call “integrated partnership” would be geopolitical rather than geographical. A country would not have to aspire to EU membership to qualify. It would not even have to be situated in Europe.Iceland, the UK and Norway are obvious potential candidates, but so are Canada, Japan and South Korea.These countries would be inside the tent wherever legally and politically possible, pooling sovereignty across specific policy areas. This relationship could ultimately amount to quasi-membership, with corresponding rights and obligations. Unlike membership of the EEA, however, it would extend beyond the economy. Defence, security, economic security and foreign policy would be as fundamental to the relationship as trade and the single market.Countries already seeking full EU membership, of which there are nine at the moment, will continue to prioritise that end goal. But the EU will struggle to deliver on its promises to all of those in the queue within a reasonable timeframe. Political resistance to the union’s expansion beyond the 27 existing members could intensify ifkey national elections next yearcreate a shift in the EU’s majority political outlook. Already, internal reforms, budgetary concerns and the complexities of accession could leave some countries waiting for years.All sides would benefit from giving these queueing nations another option. Ukraine or the western Balkan countries should not remain stranded in a geopolitical waiting room simply because the EU lacks the political will or administrative bandwidth to admit them. Of course, safeguards are essential: this kind of advanced partnership must be a bridge to membership for those seeking it, not a car park that allows governments of existing EU nations to renege on promises if they become electorally unpopular.The defining test for partners must be genuine like-mindedness around democratic values: a sustained commitment to liberal democracy, the rule of law, political sovereignty and an international order based on rules.Canada should be among the first candidates. TheEU-Canada summit in Octobershould go beyond another list of worthy deliverables and start the process of establishing a special status so deep that the country could eventually become the equivalent of an EU member state in all but name. Ursula von der Leyen should announce as much in her annual state of the union address this week. With Canada’s relationship with the USon the ropes, Brussels has an eager partner in Mark Carney, who said on Sunday that he wants a “unique alliance” with the EU.But that would require clear commitments from Ottawa as well as Brussels. Integrated partners should not get a free ticket to the benefits of EU policies without corresponding obligations and costs.The case for this is becoming easier to make. Democracies face increasingly aggressive behaviour from authoritarian powers. Middle powers risk being isolated, divided and picked off individually.As Carneyhas argued, they must act together in response to the rupture of the old international order. Integrated partnership could help operationalise Carney’s argument.There is also a more uncomfortable reason for new geopolitical architecture. It cannot be assumed that countries, even those supposedly joined at the hip through the EU, will always continue on a like-minded path. France or Germany could in the future be governed by illiberal anti-European forces unwilling to defend the principles on which European integration rests.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA network encompassing democratic EU members and their close partners could then become a political counterweight, helping to preserve collective action when consensus inside the EU becomes impossible. This should not become an alternative EU. But Europe cannot base its geopolitical strategy on the assumption that every one of its governments will remain committed to European integration or even liberal democracy.The European project emerged from the ruins of the second world war. Now, in a very different geopolitical context, we need ambitious mechanisms for bringing like-minded democracies together. But full EU membership cannot be the only route to deep integration. Maximum integration without a predetermined end point should now become the objective.Iceland’s vote, driven by concerns over fisheries and other totemic national issues, shows why new thinking and geopolitical ambition are needed. Geography should no more determine who can be inside Europe’s tent than the time it takes to conduct painstaking enlargement negotiations. Increasingly, the decisive question is whether Europe can club together with all countries that are prepared to defend democratic principles together.Fabian Zuleeg is chief executive and chief economist at the European Policy CentreExplore more on these topicsEuropean UnionOpinionCanadaMark CarneyIcelandInternational tradeGlobal economyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Sydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sports | Sport | The Guardian
description: The actor’s latest promotion has stirred outrage but will no doubt be good for the prediction markets hoping to lure in young men
Author: Jane McManus
Headline: The actor’s latest promotion has stirred outrage but will no doubt be good for the prediction markets hoping to lure in young men
Content: Sydney Sweeney has promoted a series of brands since her ascent to fame.Photograph: NovigView image in fullscreenSydney Sweeney has promoted a series of brands since her ascent to fame.Photograph: NovigSportSydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sportsJane McManusThe actor’s latest promotion has stirred outrage but will no doubt be good for the prediction markets hoping to lure in young menMon 14 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrediction markets are a cynical business.Many customers will lose money, and the real product may just be the delightful dopamine hit that comes in that brief window between placing a bet and its outcome – which is statistically more likely to be a disappointment than a victory. So the bettor has to think they are buying more than their own fleecing.Enter Sydney Sweeney, the icily beautiful actor who stars in a sports prediction market company’s ad campaignwearing little more than a bat and balls. She’s not a professional athlete, but she functions to remind us that plenty of people want us to believe the best woman in sports is the one who appeals to men.Sydney Sweeney under fire for ‘sexualising women’s sport’ in sports prediction adRead moreIt’s the same ethos that puts capturing the male gaze on a list of hiring criteria for TV sideline reporters, and made Olivia Dunne therichest athlete in college sports. But of course Dunne put in years of training as an elite gymnast, and didn’t serve to make a mockery of women’s sports.Does Sweeney? After her American Eagle campaignwas criticizedas eugenics-adjacent, she eventually issued vague comments about how, yawn,surprised she was at the outcry. If she were actually bothered, she might check the optics of campaigns like the one causing so much outcry at the moment. Certainly once she saw how her blond, blue-eyed image was being utilized and perceived, she would be more discerning when sifting through the endorsement opportunities that came her way.Her lack of apparent concern must be as well-compensated as her one-note acting. The prediction company she is promoting in this campaign lists her asa strategic partner and equity holderand, if the company can negotiate shifting legal terrain, that could make Sweeney orders of magnitude richer for absorbing the critique.Olympic swimmer and four-time gold medalist Ariarne Titmus is one of many professional athleteswho have expressed disappointmentand anger with the provocatively regressive campaign.“How do we live in a world where monetising a women’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?” shewrote on Instagram.Women’s sports are being professionalized at a pace eclipsing anything we’ve previously seen. Leagues are expanding,ratings and attendance are up, and some teams have been valued atmore than $500m. Female athletes have real power – financially and with their social media platforms. Any company looking to get into the space has a pick of champions who would communicate the company’s message.But for all that progress, there are executives and fans who would prefer that sports looked how they did back when they were kids. Many of them are gatekeepers in traditional media, and many outlets still treat women’s sports less seriously than men’s. Purdue academic Cheryl Cooky’snew researchdetails the trend in all its glory.In an era in which stoking outrage can win elections andmake you a wealthy sports bloviator, there are fewer actual consequences to stop a company from trying to offend potential consumers.Of course, it is still possible to create a marketing campaign so disastrous it can severely damage a company.Look no furtherthan the golf content specialist Good Good, which recently ran and then retracted a commercial which appeared to make light of violence against women.Good Good’s front office has been shaken up. But the company lost a partnership with industry stalwart Callaway Golf, a reality show it launched was cancelled, stores pulled merchandise off the shelves, and its name was pulled off a PGA Tour tournament. Co-founder Garrett Clark eventually posted an eight-minute apology video, but whenever you have to announce that you don’t condone domestic violence, you’ve lost control of the narrative. Maybe golf isn’t the best place to go for edgy.Prediction markets, however, are in a particularly calculating line of business. As was the case with cigarette companies before them, few people believe the product is actually good for anyone.There are allegationsthat people with inside information on war and troop movements are placing bets in the liminal space between planning and action.So what is there for a prediction market to lose by stoking outrage with a proven outrage-stoker like Sweeney? Unlike with Good Good, there is no established brand partner to disappoint. The sports prediction consumers that the maker of the Sweeney ad is likely courting are the same young men who will be titillated by the actor and delighted by the subversive naughtiness of all the froth.The message cynically fits the audience.Even though prediction markets aren’t the same as traditional sportsbooks, they are in the same general family. Sports consumers can’t escape the ads, the conversations, the sponsorships when watching a game. It seems everyone wants a piece of the action.What those behind the Sweeney ad are actually predicting is a column like this, and the outrage of athletes who are trying to push back the regressive tide. I’d wager they hope to use it to attract more young men to open accounts. After all, poison in the discourse is good for business.Explore more on these topicsSportUS sportsSydney SweeneyPrediction marketsGamblingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Islamophobia is rising – and Britain’s politicians have been dangerously complacent in tackling it | Arun Kundnani | The Guardian
description: Mainstream figures have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties, says Arun Kundnani, editorial director of Monthly Review Press
Author: Arun Kundnani
Headline: Mainstream figures have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties, says Arun Kundnani, editorial director of Monthly Review Press
Content: Anti-Islamophobia protest outside Conservative party headquarters in London, 29 February 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenAnti-Islamophobia protest outside Conservative party headquarters in London, 29 February 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAOpinionIslamophobiaIslamophobia is rising – and Britain’s politicians have been dangerously complacent in tackling itArun KundnaniMainstream figures have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political partiesMon 14 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.10 EDTShareFive years ago, many Muslims wondered if the prejudices they faced were set to fade away. The “war on terror” was dwindling in prominence, and new enemies such as Russia seemed to be displacing fears of Islamic terrorism. Yet Britain’s Islamophobia has only intensified since then. A poll published in July found thattwo out of five Britons believe Muslims cannot integrateinto British society. Earlier in the summer, it was reported thatmore than half of Muslims in Britain had personally experienced anti-Islam prejudicein the last year, and a quarter in a public place.The evidence of a worsening climatefor Muslims has been mounting since two summers ago, when racist riots erupted across the UK, targeting mosques and asylum hostels. Watchingvideos of those events,I was disturbed by the parents who brought their young children to watch while mobs attempted, with apparently murderous intent, to break into the buildings.It was not only hardened far-right activists but a much broader cross-section of British societythat was willing to participate in racist violence directed at Muslims or asylum seekers assumed to be Muslim.But it is the widespread indifference to anti-Muslim racist violence that is most distressing. Last October,a white man raped a Sikh womanin her Walsall home while shouting Islamophobic abuse, believing her to be Muslim, and telling her he was a “British master”. The case attracted little public comment, despite seeming to be part of apattern of racist sexual crimesin the region. Likewise, there was only modest coverage of therampaging knife attackthat began at an Edinburgh mosque in June that left a number of men injured.To understand why Islamophobia is so pervasive, we need to grasp the deeper forces that enable it. The first is a bedrock of anti-Islam attitudes set during the 1990s when, with the cold war over, neoconservative intellectuals began to see in Islam a new enemy to replace communism. After Muslim protests against Salman Rushdie’s The Satanic Verses, some liberal commentators also began to declare that Islam was incompatible with western values. That all might have remained a problem of cultural adaptation to be solved through community-building, but during the “war on terror”, anti-Muslim racism was institutionalised in the daily functioning of the British state by the Labour government. Ministers made regular speeches singling out Muslim communities as threats, while under the Prevent policy, thousands of public sector workers were trained to regard ordinary Muslim political and religious behaviours asindicators of extremism.The second has to do with Palestine. The groundswell of opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza has been profoundly disconcerting to Britain’s foreign policy establishment. In turn, the hundreds of thousands of people who marched on demonstrations have been depicted as supporters of, or aligned with, Islamic extremism. That has restored a virulent atmosphere of animosity towards Muslims, who are again seen as dangerous and disloyal.We might think, for example, of Keir Starmer’s description ofplannedprotests on 7 October 2025 as“un-British”, his suggestion that further protests could be banned and hiscall for prosecutionagainst demonstrators using contested phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – despiterepeated explanationsthatsuch slogansarenot calls for violence. His comments reflect a widespread belief that ordinary protest – against a genocide! – is actually something else: the importing by Muslims and their allies of dangerous foreign ideologies. But to say that is to demonise the bond of allegiance between Muslims in the west and Muslims in other parts of the world fighting colonial occupations. That community-based international solidarity, of the kind that Britain used to hold up as evidence of its tolerance, should only be welcomed.Third, there are the barriers that make it hard to even raise the issue of anti-Muslim racism in a fruitful way. Talk about Islamophobia in the mainstream of British public life and you will face the ritual demand that you also condemn Islamic extremism and acknowledge antisemitism among Muslims. Of course, an attack on a synagogue is to be condemned as forcefully as an attack on a mosque. But the harder political question is how to create the conditions in which neither one of those attacks is made likely. In this, Jewish communities have the resolute support of the British government. Muslims do not. For decades, they have been on the receiving end of official disdain, and when they attempt to assert a modicum of political representation they areaccused of “family voting”.This matters because racism is about power. Its function is to divide society so that certain groups can be subjected to exceptional forms of exploitation or elimination. It is typically experienced as routine and structured powerlessness: the daily struggle to eke out a living in the face of discriminatory employers, public services riddled with suspicion, oppressive policing, immigration enforcement. Twenty-five years ago, policymakers at least paid lip service to racism as “institutional”, which helped to make visible some of its structural features. But that is no longer true. Racism is nowadays framed mainly as a problem of extremist individuals radicalised by hateful and polarising ideologies.Tackling racism means overcoming that lack of power. But the opposite is happening as governing elites continuously reinforce racist attitudes. A decision, for instance, to allow Ukrainians fleeing warpreferential entry to the UKwhile many Afghans fleeing war have to risk their lives in dangerous sea crossings – a policy of racial segregation that is as absolute and violent as those of the Jim Crow south of the US – is also a form of public messaging. Policymakers can hardly be surprised when ordinary people take their cue from such policies and decide that non-white immigrants must indeed be a threat to national identity. Racism applied at the border inevitably seeps into other areas of public life.Then there is the other response to talking about Islamophobia: to switch the conversation to a victimhood competition, the never-ending game of fighting over whose oppression is greater, as if there were some way to rank Black people, Jews and Muslims by the scale of horrors they have experienced. What this misses is that the fate of Muslims is inseparable from the fate of all people of colour in the UK. What Britain does to Muslims today it is likely to do to Black people tomorrow, and vice versa. And if a future government of Britain decided to carry out the mass deportation of Muslims from the country, I have no doubt it would decide soon afterwards to do the same to Jews. When supporters of Israel promoteIslamophobia, they are playing with fascist fires that will end up engulfing us all.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor decades, Britain’s mainstream political leaders have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties. They continue to do so, sleepwalking to social disaster with an unconscionable recklessness and complacency. It is high time they woke up.Arun Kundnani is editorial director of Monthly Review PressDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: There’s a surprisingly simple reason for England’s high antidepressant use: lots of people need them | Dean Burnett | The Guardian
description: The idea that GPs are ignoring guidelines and ‘overprescribing’ doesn’t hold water. Instead, look to our social and economic crises, says doctor of neuroscience Dean Burnett
Author: Dean Burnett
Headline: The idea that GPs are ignoring guidelines and ‘overprescribing’ doesn’t hold water. Instead, look to our social and economic crises, says doctor of neuroscience Dean Burnett
Content: Illustration: Nash Weerasekera/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nash Weerasekera/The GuardianOpinionMental healthThere’s a surprisingly simple reason for England’s high antidepressant use: lots of people need themDean BurnettThe idea that GPs are ignoring guidelines and ‘overprescribing’ doesn’t hold water. Instead, look to our social and economic crisesDean Burnett is a doctor of neuroscienceMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTShareAnew NHSreporthas revealed the highest ever levels of antidepressant use recorded in England, with roughly one in seven people prescribed an antidepressant item in 2025-26. This has resulted in a swathe of media coverage expressing alarm over the increase, with questions about what could, or should, be done to reverse the trend.Such a high level of antidepressant use should, of course, prompt concern and reflection. But the popular claim that has taken hold is that antidepressant use is too high because of “overprescribing”, as Dr John Read, a professor of clinical psychology, says in the Daily Mail. This is the idea that patients are being prescribed antidepressants when they shouldn’t be, or when better, safer alternatives are available.This idea is worth challenging – but first it’s important to consider how we got here. The increase in antidepressant use is strongly correlated with a rise in diagnoses in common disorders including depression and anxiety. Much of this is the afterlife of the Covid-19 pandemic and its associated lockdowns: according to ONS data, across Britain, the rate of depressive symptoms in adultsdoubledduring the crisis to almost one in five. As of April 2025, the figuresremain almost as high. This surge has particularly affectedyoung people in England, with one in four having a mental health condition, according to NHS data.So with this rise, an increase in antidepressant use is predictable. Lockdown, however necessary for public health, has had lasting implications for the country’s wellbeing.But it’s not only the consequences of the pandemic. What this data also indicates is that persistent regional inequalities have a worsening effect on mental health outcomes, and therefore antidepressant use. The most dramatic increases in antidepressant use are found in themost impoverishedregions of England, while more affluent regions report modest levels of antidepressant use.The highest rate of antidepressant use was seen in patients treated under the North East and North Cumbria integrated care board, with 200 in every 1,000 people prescribed antidepressant medication. Consider that this ICB contains some of the country’smost deprived areas, which have “faced longstanding inequalities and poor health for decades”, and you have further proof of something that has long been clear: poverty isinextricably linkedto poorer mental health outcomes. One key element that underpins many cases of depression, anxiety and related disorders ischronic stress. It’sour brain’s achilles heel. And a guaranteed source of chronic stress is a life of constant poverty.The argument presented against wide antidepressant prescription, as laid out in the Daily Mail, is that “doctors [are] increasingly being expected to treat wider social and life problems with medication”. Such a position assumes that a neat division can be drawn between these social problems and the mental health conditions they produce.These socioeconomic factors also explain why antidepressants are used more and more as a first-line treatment. It’s all well and good to argue that less severe cases of depression should be treated with talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, but these involve regular one-one-one sessions with trained counsellors, andthe wait for such interventionson the NHS regularly lasts months, if not years.In the most deprived areas,access to such servicesis even more difficult, whereas for the most part, antidepressants are accessible straight away. It should also be said that GPs followstrict clinical guidelinesfor prescribing antidepressants, as set out by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. These state that practitioners should “not routinely offer antidepressant medication as first-line treatment for less severe depression unless that is the person’s preference”. So it is clear that GPs are not simply handing out pills, but rather responding to legitimate patient demand.Of course, antidepressants can’t be a magic bullet – mental health services are evidently in need of deep reform and increased funding. We have already heard pledges to improve services, including with the government’s announcement in May this year of anew mental health strategyin England to drive a shift from crisis intervention to preventive care. And there are already technological interventions being recommended, includingdigital therapiesfor depression and anxiety that “could free up thousands of NHS therapist hours”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government’s callout for frontline workers, clinicians and mental health experts to share views on transforming mental health care shows that there are likely several creative solutions to tackle this crisis, without the need for medication. Still, there should be no doubt about the simple reality: more people than ever are taking antidepressants because they genuinely need them.So the point here is not that the record rates of antidepressant use in England isn’t a problem. It undoubtedly is. But to determine that this is due to “overprescription” is to mistake a symptom for a much deeper social and economic crisis as its cause.Dean Burnett is a doctor of neuroscience and the author of The Idiot Brain and Emotional IgnoranceExplore more on these topicsMental healthOpinionDepressionPovertyHealth policyNHSAnxietyHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Touring can take musicians to isolating, anxious extremes. Access to therapy on the road is a vital support | Music | The Guardian
description: I know from our early days how high-pressure road life can be. While big tours often hire therapists, grassroots acts can’t afford it. I’m pleased to back a new scheme that aims to change that
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I know from our early days how high-pressure road life can be. While big tours often hire therapists, grassroots acts can’t afford it. I’m pleased to back a new scheme that aims to change that
Content: Thom Yorke and Philip Selway of Radiohead performing in 2006.Photograph: Jo Hale/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThom Yorke and Philip Selway of Radiohead performing in 2006.Photograph: Jo Hale/Getty ImagesMusicTouring can take musicians to isolating, anxious extremes. Access to therapy on the road is a vital supportPhilip Selway, RadioheadI know from our early days how high-pressure road life can be. While big tours often hire therapists, grassroots acts can’t afford it. I’m pleased to back a new scheme that aims to change thatMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTShareWhenRadioheadstarted touring, it was hugely exciting, but we got signed when we had been going for five or six years and had only really played in Oxford. Suddenly you’re entering a new world: the first flush of fame, being compared to everyone else, the furnace-like experience when a band takes off and a whole new routine of late nights, bad food and everything else that goes on around live music. Everything is heightened and it can be very isolating.In 1992 we were playing small venues in a van and then suddenly in 1993 we were spending the second half of the year in the US. On our second long tour that year, everything caught up with me. I kind of withdrew into myself. Something about being in the US made me feel “impostor syndrome”. I really did feel a very long way from home. All that anxiety has to come out somewhere – for some it’s drink and drugs – but for me it came out in my playing. There was one particular show where we were opening for Tears for Fears and another band who had [Blondie’s] Clem Burke on drums. Clem was my absolute drummer hero but I just hit peak overwhelm, and my drumming went off a cliff. Every limb seemed to be going at its own speed. The kick drum became like trying to open a heavy door.By the end of the tour it was very noticeable. I was lucky in that I could speak to my wife – this was pre-Zoom or FaceTime, so meant very expensive phone calls! – but after that tour one of our managers asked me to go and have a chat and broached it with me very nicely. Having that space to begin talking about it was absolutely invaluable. Similarly, when we opened for James and then REM, they became kind of mentors: seeing how other people navigate it all was fascinating.On Radiohead’s tour last autumn, with the help of the Music Industry Therapist Collective, we were able to put an initiative in place to support the health and well-being of all tour personnel. The MITC provided introductory sessions during rehearsals and production build, and confidential drop-in therapy sessions were available to anyone in the touring party during the tour if they wanted them. But until now there’s been nothing like that available for bands playing venues like the ones we did when we started.At that level, your margins are nonexistent, your workload is much greater – loading the gear and so on – and you’re driving yourself between shows. You’re expected to get your head down and get on with it, but it can mean times when you’re not necessarily looking after yourself physically and you can feel very isolated. There’s an emotional and geographical displacement in moving from place to place and living on top of each other. There’s the sound check, the gig, meeting people afterwards, anxiety that some people guiding you may not have your best interests at heart. You can feel really vulnerable, and there’s no way of getting off that roundabout until you get home. It’s difficult to talk about because nobody wants to rock the boat, and other people might be going through the same thing, so you don’t want to burden them.‘The working class can’t afford it’: the shocking truth about the money bands make on tourRead moreThat’s why I’m supporting a new project called the Pay It Forward Fund, which has been set up by Tamsin Embleton and the Music Industry Therapist Collective to provide much-needed mental health support for musicians and crews on smaller tours, having grown out of the kind of help MITC already provides to larger tours. If someone is looking to reach out to a therapist, it can be really good to talk to someone who has lived experience in the music industry, so this project will mean people have someone to talk to who understands what they’re going through. I’ve volunteered for the Samaritans since I was a student and know how important it is to talk.I’d have really appreciated something like the Pay It Forward Fund back in Radiohead’s early days, so that’s the kind of space I hope it can provide. Initially £272,000 is being provided to finance 150 tour teams of practitioners over a three-year period, an occupational health, mental health education and pastoral care programme for crews and artists on smaller tours. Hopefully after that it will become an everyday part of touring and make the sort of difference it would have done for me. You might be on the other side of the world, but you can reach out and talk to somebody face to face.Applications for the Pay It Forward Fund are now open. MITC’s bookTouring and Mental Health: the Music Industry Manual, edited by Tamsin Embleton, is published by OmnibusAs told to Dave SimpsonExplore more on these topicsMusicMental healthRadioheadHealthCounselling and therapyIndieMusic industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Reform UK: crypto billionaires must be stopped from undermining democracy | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The vast sums given to Nigel Farage’s party in recent days must lead to action on political funding
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The vast sums given to Nigel Farage’s party in recent days must lead to action on political funding
Content: Nigel Farage speaking at the Bitcoin Conference in Las Vegas in 2025.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenNigel Farage speaking at the Bitcoin Conference in Las Vegas in 2025.Photograph: GettyOpinionReform UKThe Guardian view on Reform UK: crypto billionaires must be stopped from undermining democracyEditorialThe vast sums given to Nigel Farage’s party in recent days must lead to action on political fundingMon 14 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.36 EDTShareThestaggering sumsgifted to Reform UK over the weekend have transformed the context for the representation of the people bill making its way through parliament. The announcement of two £36m donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, both crypto billionaires who have lived abroad, makes Andy Burnham’s decision not to impose a limit onpolitical donations– a move he supported before becoming prime minister – look even more misguided. Fortunately the House of Lords still has the chance to amend the bill. It should take it by imposing meaningful limits on both political donations and party spending.It is unclear whether either man meets the criteria set out in the Rycroft review into foreign influence in politics. It set a maximum of £100,000 per annum for people who have not been in the UK for at least a year. Mr Delo previously lived in Hong Kong while Mr Harborne is based partly in Thailand;Nigel Faragesaid on Monday that he does not know the details of their movements. While ministers will view the prospect of a legal fight over eligibility with trepidation, they must do what it takes to ensure rules are met.View image in fullscreenBen Delo.Photograph: The Ben Delo FoundationReform UK’s support has fallen since a year ago, when polls showed it ahead of Labour, and again since May when it won more than 1,400 seats inlocal elections. After a summer dominated by investigations of its finances, and with thepolice widening their inquiriesto include footage, aired on Channel 4, of officials apparently discussing ways to get around electoral law,Nigel Farage’s unfavourability ratinghas hit a 10-year high. But while this reversal of fortune has brought relief to opponents, there is no room for complacency. In 2024,34% of votessecured a huge majority for Labour. The danger of a Farage premiership and all that it could mean for UK politics and civil society remains real.Mr Farage no longer advertises hiscloseness to Donald Trumpin the way he once did. But he shares the US president’s enthusiasm for crypto currencies, which is part of a wider agenda of aggressive financial deregulation. Last year he told a conference that he wants to turn the UK into“the world’s premier hub for cryptocurrency”. No wonder that Mr Harborne appears to be competing to be the party’s top supporter with Mr Delo – who was pardoned by Mr Trump following a 2022 conviction for failing to implement adequate anti‑money laundering controls.The Rycroft review focused on foreign influence for good reason; it is for UK voters to choose their government. But ministers must look beyond the narrow question of outside interference. As well as donation and campaign spending caps, they should regulate party expenditure across the electoral cycle. Otherwise mega-rich donors can pay for years of polling, advertising, data and staff, before election-period limits apply.A statement fromunionsis expected to signal a change of heart and support for a cap on donations. Ministers will need to find a carve-out protecting contributions from their members. A mechanism to prevent charities becoming a back door for rich individuals to fund parties is also needed. Democracy is undermined when the vastly wealthy make politics look like an auction, upending norms built up over decades. It is entirely wrong that two wealthy individuals should be able to spend their way to such an influential role in Britain’s political life.Explore more on these topicsReform UKOpinionNigel FarageCryptocurrenciesChristopher HarborneLabourDonald TrumpUS politicseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the united Ireland debate: shifting dynamics need to be treated with caution | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Donald Trump’s blithe comments at the weekend were characteristically unhelpful. A careful and considered discussion on the subject has yet to begin
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Donald Trump’s blithe comments at the weekend were characteristically unhelpful. A careful and considered discussion on the subject has yet to begin
Content: Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, and Donald Trump at the trophy presentation of the Irish Open in Doonbeg on Sunday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenIreland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, and Donald Trump at the trophy presentation of the Irish Open in Doonbeg on Sunday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAOpinionIrelandThe Guardian view on the united Ireland debate: shifting dynamics need to be treated with cautionEditorialDonald Trump’s blithe comments at the weekend were characteristically unhelpful. A careful and considered discussion on the subject  has yet to beginMon 14 Sep 2026 14.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTShareAdecade ago, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) viewed Brexit as a potential gamechanger in the struggle to resist future pressure for a united Ireland. As the author and journalist Fintan O’Toole wrote in an essaypublishedlast year, the DUP hoped that the 2016 referendum would deliver “a double exit. Brexit would not simply mean the UK’s departure from the EU. It would also be an act of separation from the Republic. It would reverse the slow drift towards integration.” That proved to be, to put it mildly, a deeply flawed judgment.The direction of travel since 2016 has instead been the opposite. Rather than leading to a hard border between Northern Ireland and Ireland, which would have disastrouslyunderminedthe Good Friday agreement, the UK’s divorce agreement from Brussels eventuallyplacedone in the Irish Sea. The logic of further economic integration between north and south within the EU’s single market was reinforced.At the same time, demographic change has meant that people with a Catholic background now outnumber those with a Protestant one in Northern Ireland, changing the political calculus. In 2022, Sinn Féinwona historic victory in Stormont elections, leading to Michelle O’Neill’s appointment as the first nationalist first minister. On Monday, during a meeting with the heads of the UK’s other devolved nations, Ms O’Neill welcomed off-the-cuff remarks by Donald Trump during an unofficial visit to Ireland, in which he said he would “love” to see unification. The US president’s comments, she claimed,reflectedthe fact “that there is a growing conversation around constitutional change”.That is undoubtedly the case. But it is a debate that has barely begun, and one which needs to be conducted with care and caution. The 1998Good Friday agreementwas intentionally vague about the criteria for holding a border poll. Successive governments in London and Dublin have since preferred to concentrate on promoting and developing cross-border co-operation.Given the history, and the level of political risk involved, that was a sensible strategy. But the dynamics of the debate have shifted. Mr Trump’s blithe remarks followed hard on the heels of an early spat between Ms O’Neill and Andy Burnham,afterthe prime minister said during a visit to Belfast that a poll on a united Ireland was “off the table”.In the short and medium term, Mr Burnham’s position makes sense. Sinn Féin’s commitment to a referendum on Irish unity by 2030 is wildly unrealistic. But for all sides, sleepwalking into a vote without adequate preparation is equally unpalatable. In the absence of a proper debate, commitment to unity in the Irish republic is broadbased but shallow. In Northern Ireland a disturbing revival oftensionsover Orange Order marches in Catholic areas suggests deepening polarisation, fuelled by ongoing political dysfunction at Stormont.A sober, lengthy and detailed public conversation is required over what form unification might take, and the possible trade-offs involved. In an interview with the Guardian last month, the former prime minister Gordon Brownsuggestedthat “of course, in the long term, Ireland will be united”. Unlike Mr Trump, though, he added a significant rider. Reaching that outcome would be “a long process where people have got to come together and find a way of agreeing. Basically, that is the issue: whether people can actually agree.” Leaders on all sides of the debate should heed that caveat.Explore more on these topicsIrelandOpinionNorthern IrelandSinn FéinMichelle O'NeillDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamGood Friday agreementeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Keeping women out of prison must be the focus | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on overcrowded jails and plans to convert parts of the women’s prison estate for use by men
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial on overcrowded jails and plans to convert parts of the women’s prison estate for use by men
Content: ‘If the government is serious about a reduction in the number of women in prison, it should ensure that women leaving prison are supported.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If the government is serious about a reduction in the number of women in prison, it should ensure that women leaving prison are supported.’Photograph: Mark Harvey/AlamyPrisons and probationLettersKeeping women out of prison must be the focusReaders respond to an editorial on overcrowded jails and plans to convert parts of the women’s prison estate for use by menMon 14 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTShareYour editorial (The Guardian view on the prisons crisis: moving men into women’s jails is not the answer, 10 September) is right to argue that the prison capacity crisis cannot be solved through a series of short-term fixes. Victims need confidence that the government has a credible long-term strategy for the criminal justice system, not another piecemeal intervention designed to buy time.I share your concern about the pressures facing probation services. There are also legitimate questions about the impact on policing, but we cannot discuss the prisons crisis without confronting the crisis in our courts.About one in five prisoners are now awaiting trial, often because cases are taking so long to be heard. Some defendants spend so long on remand that by the time they are sentenced, they are released from court, having effectively already served their sentence. Victims will rightly ask whether that is justice, and the public will rightly ask what it means for public safety.The government points to the removal of foreign offenders as part of the solution to prison overcrowding. Yet a third are held on remand awaiting their day in court due to a court system in crisis.Prisons, courts, probation and policing are interconnected. The government cannot hope to resolve the prisons crisis if it does not also resolve the crisis in our courts. Delays leave victims waiting years for justice, drive up the remand population and place further pressure on an overcrowded prison estate. As victims’ commissioner, I need assurances that the prime minister is focused on pursuing a strategy for the whole justice system, not simply responding to the latest emergency.Claire WaxmanVictims’ commissioner forEngland and WalesWe are a collective of women’s charities, frontline services and women with lived experience of prison. We saw first-hand the devastating impact that Holloway prison’s closure had 10 years ago. For 170 years, it wasa paradoxical space– a place of trauma, but also a crucible of feminist resistance and home to dozens of frontline services. From thesuffragettesto the activistChris Tchaikovsky,women’s history unfolded there. Now it has been razed.This invites the question: what could we build instead? Your editorial offers some answers when it referencesthe Corston review. However, one crucial element is missing: women’s centres. These are spaces where women’s services are brought together under one roof, offering support with housing, domestic abuse, employment, childcare, therapy and more. They help women holistically, rather than simply fixing one area of their lives. Women in Prison reports that forevery £1 invested in a women’s centre, £2.75 is saved.Women’s centres stop women entering the criminal justice system, keep children out of care and relieve pressure on emergency services. We’ve spent a decade campaigning for one on the Holloway prison site. The public are supportive and building work is under way, but funding is still not secured.If Andy Burnham wanted to pursue a visionary policy, he could champion a women’s centre programme across the UK, starting with the Holloway Women’s Building.Polly CreedHolloway Women’s Building Collective, LondonMeasures to reduce the number of women behind bars are long overdue, but it must be more than a short-term fix to try to free up capacity (Ministers propose converting female prison estate into cells for men, 7 September).Women in, and leaving, prison face particular challenges. Many have also been victims of crime or have children they hope to be reunited with. Rates of homelessness are higher among women than men when they leave prison.These challenges also lead to higher numbers of women being recalled to prison.Our analysisfound that there was one recall for every four women under post-release supervision in the community in the first three months of this year, compared with one recall for every five men.In some cases, recall will have been needed to protect the public. But in others, better community support could and should be put in place.If the government is serious about a long-term reduction in the number of women in prison, it should start by ensuring that women leaving prison are supported to stay out.Enver SolomonChief executive, NacroThe reported proposal to convert parts of the women’s prison estate to accommodate male prisoners may initially sound controversial, but the more important question is why so many women need to be imprisoned in the first place.A pilot women’s court inBristoloffers a potentially much more constructive answer. By taking a trauma-informed, problem-solving approach, the court seeks to address the circumstances underlying offending – including domestic abuse, addiction, mental ill health and homelessness – while still holding women accountable for their crimes.This seems preferable to the familiar cycle of short prison sentences, release and reoffending. It also recognises something often overlooked in the debate: imprisoning women can have consequences far beyond the offender herself. Many are mothers and primary carers, so custody can profoundly disrupt children’s lives and family relationships.If the Bristol experiment demonstrates that intensive community supervision and properly funded support can reduce reoffending while keeping women safely out of prison, it deserves to be expanded.The real test of a successful prison policy should not be whether we can find more cells, but whether we can reduce the need for them.Stuart HarringtonBurnham-on-Sea, SomersetHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Middle-class parenting neglects life skills that are essential for students | Parents and parenting | The Guardian
description: Letters: We owe it to our young people to teach them how to do laundry and prepare food, writes Melissa Scallan, while Pippa Keech recalls her son’s university halls baptism of fire
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: We owe it to our young people to teach them how to do laundry and prepare food, writes Melissa Scallan, while Pippa Keech recalls her son’s university halls baptism of fire
Content: Student living. ‘Conjuring up a decent chilli, cleaning a loo properly and washing a sheet are lifelong useful skills.’Photograph: Janine Wiedel Photolibrary/AlamyView image in fullscreenStudent living. ‘Conjuring up a decent chilli, cleaning a loo properly and washing a sheet are lifelong useful skills.’Photograph: Janine Wiedel Photolibrary/AlamyParents and parentingLettersMiddle-class parenting neglects life skills that are essential for studentsWe owe it to our young people to teach them how to do laundry and prepare food, writesMelissa Scallan, whilePippa Keechrecalls her son’s university halls baptism of fireMon 14 Sep 2026 12.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTShareZoe Williams’ university-bound son won’t be the only one among his peers not to know how, or indeed why, bed sheets are laundered (I went to Ikea with my son – and was confronted with my parenting failures, 8 September).Modern day, middle-class parenting tends to direct kids away from domestic pursuits, focusing instead on academic achievements and sporting prowess or music grades, scouting activities and Duke of Edinburgh awards. With their waking hours consumed by so many outside interests, there’s little time for learning life skills such as cooking, cleaning and laundering.I visit schools giving talks to sixth-form students about preparing for university. In advance, I invite the students to share any questions or concerns they may have. Alongside issues such as finding their future friends and whether they’ll cope academically, they often question how they’ll live independently. Many of them have never had to do a full supermarket shop, prepare a meal from scratch, wash a kitchen floor or iron a shirt.They anticipate focusing on their studies and socialising with their flatmates, coursemates and people they meet through clubs and societies. They do worry about how they’ll also take care of themselves and how they’ll juggle everything.We owe it to our young people to teach them essential life skills along the way – not just in the week before they head off to university – so they have one less thing to worry about. After all, conjuring up a decent chilli, cleaning a loo properly and washing a sheet without it shrinking, fading or changing shape, are lifelong useful skills.Melissa ScallanAuthor, Starting UniversityFive minutes after dropping my son off at his Birmingham halls of residence, we received a WhatsApp message: “I cut my hand on a knife when I opened the packaging. There’s quite a lot of blood. Any advice?” As we turned the car round, while rummaging for plasters in the glove box, we got another message. “It’s OK, my new flatmates have bandaged me up.” All six are still close mates, 10 years later.Pippa KeechLyndhurst, HampshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Severe mental illness and the risk of violence | Psychiatry | The Guardian
description: Letters: A new willingness to acknowledge the risk that some people with severe mental illnesses may become violent is welcomed by Prof John F Morgan
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: A new willingness to acknowledge the risk that some people with severe mental illnesses may become violent is welcomed by Prof John F Morgan
Content: Flowers laid in Nottingham city centre after the stabbing of three people by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFlowers laid in Nottingham city centre after the stabbing of three people by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianPsychiatryLettersSevere mental illness and the risk of violenceA new willingness to acknowledge the risk that some people with severe mental  illnesses may become violent is welcomed byProf John F MorganMon 14 Sep 2026 12.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.12 EDTShareYour report of Sarah Hughes’s acknowledgment that mental health organisations have sometimes “softened the truth” about the relationship between serious mental illness and violence marks an important change in the public debate (Mental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chief, 5 September).There is some historical irony here. Mind grew from the National Association for Mental Health, an organisation in which psychiatrists and other mental health professionals played an important part. From the 1970s onwards, Mind increasingly defined itself as an independent campaigning organisation and, at times, a vigorous critic of psychiatric practice and authority.As a psychiatrist who previously chaired the Royal College of Psychiatrists group concerned with risk, and who gave evidence to theNottinghaminquiry, I have seen the consequences of our difficulty in discussing this subject plainly.Psychiatrists have long had to hold two propositions together. The overwhelming majority of people with mental illness are not violent and should not be stigmatised as such. But some severe mental disorders, particularly when accompanied by factors such as substance misuse, disengagement from treatment or a previous history of violence, can materially increase risk. Acknowledging the second proposition does not contradict the first.Indeed, avoiding discussion of risk for fear of stigma can itself have consequences for patients, families and the wider public. Properly resourced services, continuity of care, assertive follow-up and thoughtful risk assessment protect patients as well as others.It is therefore significant that Mind is now prepared to say publicly that the mental health charity sector has sometimes been too reluctant to acknowledge an uncomfortable reality. This should not become an argument between psychiatry and its critics. It is an opportunity for clinicians, patients and campaigning organisations to recover a more mature position: opposing stigma while being equally willing to speak honestly about risk.ProfJohn F MorganConsultant psychiatrist, Harrogate, North YorkshireExplore more on these topicsPsychiatryMental healthSchizophreniaCrimeNottinghamlettersShareReuse this content

Author: Guardian staff reporter

Content: One reader insists that their expression is a result of thinking, not judging.Photograph: Kryssia Campos/GettyView image in fullscreenOne reader insists that their expression is a result of thinking, not judging.Photograph: Kryssia Campos/GettyBrief lettersSocial etiquetteLettersIf looks could kill, I’d be in real troubleDefault facial expressions | Coffee thermometer | Quitting Britain | Nominative determinism delightsMon 14 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTShareAdrian Chiles is lucky that his face is merely “miserable” (I’ve spent my whole life looking miserable. It’s time for a change, 9 September). On the advice of my estimable wife, when I introduce myself to new colleagues I alert them to the fact that if I look as though I want to kill them, it’s my default expression and I am merely thinking, not judging.Trevor LawsonHaddenham, BuckinghamshireSince Oxford University, no less, tells us that it is now vital to know the temperature of hot drinks (Drinking very hot drinks could triple risk of oesophageal cancer, study finds, 9 September), I look forward to the delivery of my NHS coffee thermometer – and the award of next year’s Ig Nobel prizes.Anne ArcherOban, Argyll and ButeIt’s striking that billionaires departing the UK merit a headline (Billionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UK, 8 September), but the carers and their families, as well as couples who don’t meet the ever stricter financial rules for immigrants, do not.Claire PillarGaitsgill, CumbriaOn the nominative determinism debate (Letters, 13 September), I think we should now tie this correspondence up and put it back in its box.Christopher PackerLondonMy wife and I find we are generally far ahead in any nominative determinism game.David and Gisele JonesGlasgowI am finding these letters very informative.Gill LearnerReading, BerkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: From influencers to brutal finishes, US Open 2026 was worst grand slam in recent memory | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Despite the drama on the court, the poor condition of Arthur Ashe Stadium was just one problem among many
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Despite the drama on the court, the poor condition of Arthur Ashe Stadium was just one problem among many
Content: Ben Shelton sprawled out on the court during his men’s singles final defeat against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreenBen Shelton sprawled out on the court during his men’s singles final defeat against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026AnalysisFrom influencers to brutal finishes, US Open 2026 was worst grand slam in recent memoryTumaini CarayolDespite the drama on the court, the poor condition of Arthur Ashe Stadium was just one problem among manyMon 14 Sep 2026 15.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareAt the end of another comically late night and early morning in Flushing Meadows, when the remaining spectators were departing, a familiar scene was unfolding on the US Open tournament grounds. A handful of workers had congregated directly beneath a hole in the ceiling inside one of the tournament shops as they tried to stop water from flowing out of a broken pipe and ruining thousands of pounds worth of merchandise below.This was not a surprising sight. Upon entering Arthur Ashe Stadium this year, fans were greeted by some ominous signs: “Pardon our appearance while we write the next chapter of Arthur Ashe Stadium.” The tournament’s appearance, it must be said, was hideous. Inside the corridors and rooms at one of the biggest sporting events in the world, it felt like its main building was falling apart.Dogs, bands and pre-match outfits: best images from the US Open tennis 2026Read moreSeemingly every other day a new leak revealed itself in the media centre, with long plastic sheets attached from the ceiling to buckets on the floor containing the splashing in various parts of the room. In the nearby workers’ restaurant, a dramatic burst of water from the ceiling caused its closure for one day. Throughout the tournament, a colleague joked that most sane human beings would not return every day to work underneath a ceiling that seemed ready to collapse at any time. Elsewhere, numerous photographers reported feeling sick after inhaling fetid fumes from the drains in the photo pit.This was the worst grand slam tournament in recent memory for various reasons. When people look back, 2026 will be remembered as the US Open’s year of the influencers, a group united by their talent for making everything about them. It takes a special level of foolishness to bring ring lights to a tennis match, loudly film TikTok videos in the middle of games and repeatedly stand up to take selfies during points. There is a widespread belief that everyone involved in the sport should help to “grow the game” at all costs. Sometimes, though, gatekeeping is great. Meanwhile, the general conversation on Ashe was so loud at times that even Aryna Sabalenka’s screams were drowned out.Although the 16 hours of tennis between 11.30am on Tuesday and 3.33am on Wednesday provided one of the most spectacular quarter-final days in recent history, with four dramatic final sets in four matches, it is an obvious sign of dysfunction in this sport that tournament organisers still have not prioritised finding a real solution to these early morning finishes.In the heat of battle, though, there was still so much to enjoy. Women’s tennis stole the show again as the entire top six reached the quarter-finals and, for the first time in 51 years, the top four shut out the rest of the tour in the semi-finals.Sabalenka’s comeback victory against Linda Noskova, the 21-year-old Wimbledon champion, was one of the best matches of the year and she will eventually reflect on how well she recovered just to reach the final after such a nightmare summer.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina’s excellence was a reflection of the high standard of women’s tennis at the tournament, one positive amid the negatives.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/Imagn Images/ReutersElena Rybakina dealt spectacularly with so many obstacles: the No 1 ranking, an achilles injury and one of the toughest possible drawsto win the title. Her level on hard courts over the past year has been incredible and her quiet, reserved nature is the perfect foil to the intense extroversion of Sabalenka.Meanwhile, Zheng Qinwen’s back-to-back comebacks from 0-5 to 7-5 in the third set of her third-round match against Madison Keys, and then in the first set ofher fourth-round match against Iga Swiatek, were astonishing and she greatly deserved her dramatic return to the big stage. Iva Jovic and Alexandra Eala showed relentless competitiveness can sit comfortably with strong friendship as they battled into the night. A year after the pitiful state of her serve reduced her to tears on the court, Coco Gauff’s semi-final run was a reflection of her great progress.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionConversely, 2026 has been a miserable year for men’s tennis, primarily due to the shocking amount of injuries sustained by younger players. The difficulties ofCarlos Alcarazand Jannik Sinner are only the tip of the iceberg: Jack Draper, Holger Rune, Lorenzo Musetti, Arthur Fils and João Fonseca have all missed a significant amount of the past year. Even those who competed in New York are still working through the consequences of missing so much action.The men’s draw still produced one of the memorable sporting moments of the year courtesy of a special champion. At 3.40am on Wednesday, after Ben Shelton’s monumental victory against Alcaraz, the Spaniard finally made his exit from Ashe. He had pushed himself to the limit for 4hr 28min, vomiting repeatedly, only to lose by narrow margins in a fifth set tie-break. However, after being away for four and a half months because of a wrist injury and unsure about how his body would react upon his return, he was finally able to again participate in the sport he loves and he left the court feeling like himself. As Alcaraz walked through the tunnel leading to the locker room, a place that had seen so many tears, his face broke out into a wide, joyful smile.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna SabalenkaCarlos AlcarazUS Open tennisTennisanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Calvert-Lewin shows the way as Leeds thrash limp Newcastle and rise to third | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Leeds romped to 4-1 victory over Newcastle, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin leading the way as Daniel Farke’s side stayed unbeaten
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Leeds romped to 4-1 victory over Newcastle, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin leading the way as Daniel Farke’s side stayed unbeaten
Content: Dominic Calvert-Lewin takes the acclaim from the Leeds supporters after putting Leeds ahead 3-0.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersView image in fullscreenDominic Calvert-Lewin takes the acclaim from the Leeds supporters after putting Leeds ahead 3-0.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersPremier LeagueCalvert-Lewin shows the way as Leeds thrash limp Newcastle and rise to thirdAaron Bowerat Elland RoadMon 14 Sep 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt what stage does a good start become something more significant? Perhaps we are not quite there yet; maybe we are. But as the goals flew in on a chaotic night at Elland Road, it was difficult not to think the boundaries of expectation for Leeds were potentially being redrawn.Ask those close to the action over the summer at Leeds and the feeling was that there was a possibility of something special materialising this season. Having found their feet in thePremier Leaguein the last campaign, the platform had been set and a very good summer transfer window seemed like the catalyst for even brighter days to return to West Yorkshire.VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood downRead moreBut even with that optimism in mind, this night felt significant. Leeds did not just beat a Newcastle side who themselves have started brightly under Matthias Jaissle, they dismantled them. And with the manner of this victory, Daniel Farke’s side sit third in the table.Perhaps, in this world of demanding success overnight, there is a lesson here in patience for both clubs too. As Elland Road’s patrons likely pinched themselves when the outstanding Dominic Calvert-Lewin made it 3-0 before half-time it was easy to forget that, under a year ago, large swathes of supporter were suggesting time was up for Farke.His decision to change to a back three against Manchester City last November saved his job and sparked an upturn in form that saw Leeds secure safety beforestarting this campaign in magnificent fashion. If this start continues with another win over Crystal Palace on Sunday, perhaps this side can do greater things than many first thought.As for Jaissle, this was his first large bump in the road as Newcastle manager and there will possibly be more over the coming months as he imprints his vision on this team. But the decision-making of the Leeds side who vanquished them is evidence enough that patience can often pay off and Jaissle and his team could have no complaints about the scoreline.Leeds were magnificent from start to finish. The opening goal was perhaps a touch fortuitous as Ao Tanaka’s shot bounced off the substitute Sean Steur and Lewis Miley to wrongfoot Lukas Hornicek, but it was the least Leeds deserved. Two minutes later, the lead was doubled when Jayden Bogle headed home a James Justin cross.View image in fullscreenDominic Calvert-Lewin’s header for Leeds’ second was deflected in off Jayden Bogle.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesBogle has quietly been one of Leeds’ standout performers for some time and he is one of a few Leeds players who Thomas Tuchel may find difficult to ignore before naming his latest England squad later this week. The man who slotted home Leeds’ third in first-half stoppage time has perhaps even greater a claim for a call-up.Calvert-Lewin’s latest goal was brilliantly taken; a measured finish that made it 3-0 at half-time.With James Trafford between the sticks, Leeds have a clutch of players who may be fancy their chances of international recognition if they keep this up; a surefire sign of a club trending upwards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey may have a manager in that bracket as well. “There’s never a perfect performance in football but that was top class for more or less the whole game,” Farke said. “We know we have to stay humble; we might not have the best individual quality but we can be an outstanding team.”The prospect of a grand Newcastle comeback appeared unlikely from the moment Sven Botman carelessly gave away possession to Anton Stach shortly after half-time and Stach spurned a glorious chance to make it 4-0. But Leeds did not have to wait long for their fourth goal, as Noah Okafor struck through a crowded penalty box to put the result beyond doubt.Jaissle’s demeanour became more and more exasperated as the evening wore on and unsurprisingly he cut a frustrated figure afterwards. “We couldn’t match the intensity of Leeds and you see how difficult it can be to win a game in the Premier League,” he said. “We’ll have some ups and downs and this was a big down. A tough night.”There was at least a consolation in the final moments as Bazoumana Touré, a bright spark after coming on, capitalised on a rare Leeds error to make it 4-1.But the damage had long since been done – and the party among the home support by this time was already well under way.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueLeeds UnitedNewcastle Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood down | Video assistant referees (VARs) | The Guardian
description: The VAR officials who failed to disallow Erling Haaland’s winning goal in the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down this weekend
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: The VAR officials who failed to disallow Erling Haaland’s winning goal in the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down this weekend
Content: Erling Haaland’s goal was given even though Enzo Fernández (right) was in an offside position and regarded as likely to have affected the passage of play.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenErling Haaland’s goal was given even though Enzo Fernández (right) was in an offside position and regarded as likely to have affected the passage of play.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesVideo assistant referees (VARs)VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood downMatt Donohue and his assistant not used this weekendPro Ref said allowing winner was ‘error of judgment’Paul MacInnesMon 14 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe video assistant referee officials whoallowed Erling Haaland’s winning goalin the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down. Matt Donohue and his assistant, Blake Antrobus, have been told by Pro Ref they have not received appointments for this weekend’s round of Premier League fixtures.Howard Webb, the chief ­refereeing officer, took the decision with his management team after a review of the weekend’s action. Their availa­bility will be reconsidered after the international break.VAR controversy decides Manchester derby as City keep pace with Arsenal: Football Weekly – podcastRead moreDonohue was called on to check Michael Oliver’s decision to ­disallow Haaland’s 60th-minute goal for offside. Using semi-automated ­offside technology, Donohue was able to establish that theManchester Citystriker was onside and he overturned ­Oliver’s call. But he failed to spot Enzo Fernández had ­influenced play from an offside position, an ­infringement which Pro Ref said should have led him to recommend an on-field review.This is the first time officials have been made to stand down this season owing to an error. Donohue, an EFL referee since 2018, has taken charge of three Championship matches this season as well as his VAR work. His EFL profile says he has completed Pro Ref’s “Enhanced VAR ­Training Programme”. ­Antrobus is also an assistant referee in the ­Premier League and ran the line in the first three matchdays.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Pro Ref acknowledged an “error of ­judgment” in the Haaland incident in a statement on Sunday night and is understood to have contacted ­Manchester United to explain the mistake.Explore more on these topicsVideo assistant referees (VARs)RefereesPremier LeagueManchester CityLaws of footballManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Pollock denies signing Northampton deal and is ‘open to every opportunity’ | Northampton | The Guardian
description: Northampton remain confident Henry Pollock will stay at the club, but he has insisted he is prepared to be ‘selfish’ when maximising his earning potential
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Northampton remain confident Henry Pollock will stay at the club, but he has insisted he is prepared to be ‘selfish’ when maximising his earning potential
Content: Henry Pollock has insisted he is ‘open to new opportunities’ as Saints seek his signature on a new contract.Photograph: Nations Championship/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHenry Pollock has insisted he is ‘open to new opportunities’ as Saints seek his signature on a new contract.Photograph: Nations Championship/Getty ImagesNorthamptonPollock denies signing Northampton deal and is ‘open to every opportunity’Flanker says: ‘You almost have to be quite selfish’Northampton still confident 21-year-old will stayRobert KitsonMon 14 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHenry Pollock insists he has not yet re‑signed forNorthamptonand is “open to every opportunity” including playing abroad and trying out other sports. The England back‑row is still widely expected to agree a deal to remain at Franklin’s Gardens but, for now, is refusing to publicly confirm his intentions beyond the end of the season.While the 21-year-old flanker, who toured with the British & Irish Lions last year,has been offered a significant pay rise to more than £400,000 a yearto stay with the English champions until 2029, his new promoter Eddie Hearnhas been touting Pollock as “a seven-figure player”in terms of what he brings on the field and commercially. Prem salary cap regulations, however, mean that few, if any, other English clubs are in a position to afford him at that level.Greatest Rivalry swagger showed South Africa will take some beating at World CupRead morePollock has made clear that he is prepared to be “selfish” when it comes to maximising his earning potential in company with Hearn’s Matchroom agency. “I’m very much working through different scenarios and avenues I can take,” he said. “I’m very open to new opportunities and exploring that. I’m so young so I think it’s only right I assess those options and find the best decision for myself.“I’m not going to say no to any opportunity. I’m in contract until the end of the year for Northampton and then after that I guess we’ll see what happens. You almost have to be quite selfish and think what’s right for you. If that is staying here, that’s great. I’ll be here for however long. If it’s not, then I’ll be open to new opportunities.”Well-placed sources at Northampton remain confident Pollock will opt to stay put but any future suitors will also be encouraged by the player’s clear desire to venture beyond the East Midlands at some point in his career. “I definitely want to go and live in different countries and explore new sports and new avenues. At the minute rugby is my main priority but you never know what’s happening around the corner.”Saints’ director of rugby, Phil Dowson, who has seen several high-profile England players depart Northampton in recent years for more lucrative pastures, acknowledged a new deal for Pollock had not been fully nailed down but said an agreement was “getting closer” with the new season kicking off next week. “As you can imagine it’s complex,” said Dowson, whose side will commencethe defence of their titleagainst Newcastle on Friday 25 September. “There’s a few moving parts that we need to put together. But I’m hopeful. As I’ve said before, he wants to stay and we want to keep him. Obviously there’s some negotiation between that but those two things are very positive.“It would have been good to have it sorted three weeks ago but that’s the case across the board. There’s lots of guys out of contract … the best way of getting paid is to play well so that’s what we expect the lads to do.”Dowson also believes Pollock’s fast-growing public profile will not necessarily affect his personality or have an impact on his playing performances. “He has always been honest and energetic. Sometimes that gets misconstrued. I don’t think he’s arrogant, I think he’s bloody talented.
