If I was that talented I would be pretty confident, too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But no, I don’t think he’s changed. The boys still take the piss out of him. He goes on private jets to boxing matches and as long as that’s not impacting how he plays the game, which it hasn’t done yet, I have got no problem. I did ask him if we could borrow the private jet to get to Sri Lanka on tour, but he said he was using it!”Explore more on these topicsNorthamptonRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pietersen has England players ‘buzzing’ but McCullum delivers Carse warning | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Brendon McCullum, the England white-ball head coach, has said he was the driving force behind the recruitment of Kevin Pietersen as a specialist mentor
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Brendon McCullum, the England white-ball head coach, has said he was the driving force behind the recruitment of Kevin Pietersen as a specialist mentor
Content: Kevin Pietersen (left), England’s specialist mentor, with the white-ball head coach, Brendon McCullum, during training in Southampton.Photograph: Steve Bardens/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Pietersen (left), England’s specialist mentor, with the white-ball head coach, Brendon McCullum, during training in Southampton.Photograph: Steve Bardens/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamPietersen has England players ‘buzzing’ but McCullum delivers Carse warningFormer England batter starts role with white-ball teamsFleming also ‘right person’ to take Test team forwardSimon BurntonMon 14 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrendon McCullum has revealed that he was the driving force behind the recruitment of Kevin Pietersen as a specialist mentor to England’s white-ball teams and said the new arrival had specific orders to “look across the environment and challenge me”.Pietersen spent his first day in the role monitoring training at the Utilita Bowl after delivering an address that had the players “buzzing”, according to McCullum, England’s white-ball coach.One constant menace and post-Bazball malaise: England’s winners and losers | Simon BurntonRead moreMcCullum revealed that Pietersen had “thought I was joking” when he made the initial approach to the 46-year-old. “Then he mentioned: ‘I’ve been quite critical of you guys in the past’,” McCullum said. “And I said: ‘I have no problem with that, mate’.”“That’s the beauty of Kev coming in. He’s obviously got an incredible pedigree as a player and a lot of the guys grew up idolising Kev when he was in his pomp. He’s brought a ton of energy to the setup within the last 24 hours.”With Marcus Trescothick returning to duty as assistant coach with a focus on batting, 48 hours after the conclusion of his time as interim coach of the Test team, Pietersen has been told not to focus on any single discipline. “I’ve mentioned to him that I don’t want him to be buried in one specific skill set,” McCullum said. “I want him to look across the environment and challenge me privately around ways we can improve things or can do differently.“The way he looks at the game is quite different to a lot of people. Having someone that has a different take on things is no bad thing. You don’t know what you don’t know, but if someone can see something slightly different and point out something that can make you a better side, or a better coaching structure, I see that as no bad thing. Kev will do that and I’ve encouraged him to do that. From my point of view I see only up side.”View image in fullscreenStephen Fleming was appointed in July as England’s new Test head coach.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesMcCullum’slong-term replacement as red-ball head coach, Stephen Fleming, arrived on Monday in the country for a hectic and brief reintroduction to the domestic game, to include visits to several counties and to the national cricket performance centre at Loughborough, and meetings with the Test captain, Joe Root, as well as with the white-ball squad at their third T20 against Sri Lanka in Manchester – the final game of a series that starts on Tuesday in Southampton – before he returns to New Zealand next week.“I think the team will really respond to his style and his approach,” McCullum said. “He’s a brilliant man, a brilliant tactician and a brilliant coach. I think he’s going to do a great job with that side.”The two coaches are close friends, and inevitably discussed the offer before Fleming accepted his new job. “He said: ‘What do you think?’ I said: ‘I think you’d be brilliant. It’d be a great opportunity for you.’ I absolutely loved the job. They were the things I passed on to Flem. And I also thought for the group, for English cricket, he would be absolutely the right person to take this team forward.”England will start the series against Sri Lanka without Phil Salt, Jacob Bethell and Sam Curran for fitness reasons, with Jofra Archer rested after his recent exertions with the Test side and with Brydon Carse absent for disciplinary reasons. In their absence Aneurin Donald, the Derbyshire batter who scored 31 off eight balls for the Lions against Sri Lanka last week, will make his debut as opener. “He’s a cricketer who has been on our radar for a long time,” McCullum said. “He’s got a game where he can go from ball one. He’s got raw power. Incredible amount of talent.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarse’s absence stems from a late-night fracasat a Derby bar last month, with McCullum saying this was an opportunity for the 31-year-old “to get his house in order”. In a change to the approach that has marked much of his time as England coach, the New Zealander said he was now unwilling to select players who cannot guarantee full commitment to a professional culture.View image in fullscreenDerbyshire’s Aneurin Donald is poised to open for England in their T20 series against Sri Lanka.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty Images“I want us to be the fittest, strongest, most robust, dynamic one-day and T20 side in the world,” McCullum said. “That comes with hard work, commitment to training, but also the high octane style we want to play comes with responsibilities off the field to look after yourself. I know in the Test setup this has been talked about, and that’s completely consistent with what we expect from our players. If we want to play this style of cricket then we need to be living it daily, not just with our skills but our decisions off the field too.“It’s the same message, not just to the guys within the squad at the moment but also to those who have got aspirations of representing England in white-ball cricket over the next 12 to 18 months. You need to make good decisions off the field that allow you to be the best version of yourself. I hope it’s crystal clear what is expected.“There is a lot of talent around. If you’re not prepared to do that, there are other guys who will be given those opportunities.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamKevin PietersenBrendon McCullumCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hunt and Kerr have lit up summer, but will star athletes make Spoty shortlist? | Athletics | The Guardian
description: While there is caution over the BBC’s informal policy of not picking two athletes from the same sport in its six-person shortlist, Josh Kerr and Amy Hunt are still hopeful of getting well-deserved recognition
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: While there is caution over the BBC’s informal policy of not picking two athletes from the same sport in its six-person shortlist, Josh Kerr and Amy Hunt are still hopeful of getting well-deserved recognition
Content: Amy Hunt (left) has said it would be ‘incredibly special’ if she and Josh Kerr (right) both made the Spoty shortlist.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via PA/Shutterstock)View image in fullscreenAmy Hunt (left) has said it would be ‘incredibly special’ if she and Josh Kerr (right) both made the Spoty shortlist.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via PA/Shutterstock)AthleticsHunt and Kerr have lit up summer, but will star athletes make Spoty shortlist?‘It’s not a given, that’s the reality,’ Kerr says in BudapestAthletes cautious over BBC’s informal shortlist policySean IngleMon 14 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt should be the biggest no-brainer of the sporting year. After a summer where athletics has captured hearts and headlines, and made so many fans fall back in love with it again, either Amy Hunt or Josh Kerr should win the award for BBC Sports Personality of the Year.The bookies’ odds suggest many others think the same way: Hunt is the even-money favourite, Kerr is second, with Harry Kane a stride or two back in third. Yet Kerr knows he cannot take anything for granted.‘Just making a joke’: Usain Bolt retracts claim stairs got him out of breathRead moreIn 2023 the 28-year-old Scotwon the world 1500m titlein a clash for the ages against Jakob Ingebrigtsen. But then he fell foul of the BBC’s curious reluctance to pick two athletes from the same sport in its six-person shortlist. Instead the wheelchair tennis player Alfie Hewett, and Rory McIlroy, who won four of his five Ryder Cup matches that year, got the nod ahead of him.“Spoty is massively important,” Kerr saidafter winning the Ultimate Championship in Budapest. “Everyone grew up watching it. It’s a massive award, and I would be truly honoured to be on that shortlist up against some of the best athletes of all time this year. I would love to go, but it’s not a given, that’s the reality.”Kerr is right to be cautious given that only twice since 2017 has the BBC veered off its informal policy. The first came in 2019 when the athletes Dina Asher-Smith and Katarina Johnson-Thompson were selected. Then it happened again when the footballers Hannah Hampton and Chloe Kelly got the nod.However, on both occasions, those selections helped to balance the male-female split. But in a year where Kane could win the Ballon D’Or, Matt Weston has won two Winter Olympic medals, Luke Littler has dominated darts, and McIlroywon the Masters again, it is not a given the BBC will necessarily go for both track and field stars.Kerr’s claims are surely stronger than anyone givenhe obliterated a world mile record that had stood for 27 years, and backed it up by winning the world indoor, Commonwealth Games and Ultimate Championship.Late on Sunday night he accepted that amounted to pretty much the perfect season. “Outside of an Olympic year, I can’t give any more than that,” he said. “I’m a clean athlete doing it the right way, trying to show the way that I’m doing it. And you know, that’s all I can give. This, genuinely, has been the best year of my career.”Next year he wants to go for the world 1500m record, but he stressed it would not be easy. “People don’t know what that toll is on your body,” he said. “It feels like getting hit by a bus the next day.” Kerr also wants Hunt on the shortlist. “She’s had a fantastic season,” he said. “She deserves to be there.”Last month Hunt became the first person in the 96-year history of the European Athletics Championships to win four gold medals. Few athletes have a bigger personality as she showed again at the weekendby speaking out against Sydney Sweeney sexualising sport, and about the difficulties of performing when on her period.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This year has been all about finding how to paint a beautiful picture out of all the chaos,” Hunt said. “If I had a camera crew with me at all times, it would have been like a horror film.“I’ve done 40-plus races, 60 flights. There’s not going to be a single year that will be harder. It’s not pretty. It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time. It’s rare you turn up on the start line, fully fit without anything going on.”Yet she kept powering through. Now Hunt, like Kerr, is hoping the BBC does the right thing by selecting both of them for the Spoty awards night as a reward for the impact they have had.“I think it would be incredibly special if we could get two track and field athletes on the Spoty shortlist,” she said. “I get messages every day from people saying I fell out of athletics, I stopped watching it, I stopped doing it. But watching Europeans has really made me kind of fall back in love with it, and I’m training again, or I’ve done my first parkrun, and that’s really incredibly special.”Explore more on these topicsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: USA’s Solheim Cup inquest begins amid early celebrations and stats complaints | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: Angela Stanford, the USA captain, was frustrated by the lack of in-play statistics and has offered a warning to her Ryder Cup counterpart Jim Furyk
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Angela Stanford, the USA captain, was frustrated by the lack of in-play statistics and has offered a warning to her Ryder Cup counterpart Jim Furyk
Content: Angela Stanford, the USA captain, looks on during the 15-13 Solheim Cup defeat against Europe.Photograph: Naomi Baker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAngela Stanford, the USA captain, looks on during the 15-13 Solheim Cup defeat against Europe.Photograph: Naomi Baker/Getty ImagesSolheim CupUSA’s Solheim Cup inquest begins amid early celebrations and stats complaintsLosing captain frustrated by lack of in-play statisticsStanford offers warning to Ryder Cup leader Jim FurykEwan MurrayMon 14 Sep 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe latest inquest into failure by an American team on European soil involves slow greens, the perception of a premature celebration and a curious absence of statistical backup. Angela Stanford, whoseSolheim Cupteam were defeated by Europe in the Netherlands on Sunday, warned Jim Furyk’s Ryder Cup contingent to take note.Stanford used the numbers-based evidence of Justin Ray to assist with decision-making and Furyk will do likewise at Adare Manor next year. In the aftermath of the 15-13 defeat and assessing Ray’s input, Stanford clearly had an underlying gripe. “I’m wondering how honest to be,” she said.Europe win Solheim Cup against USA to give captain Anna Nordqvist last laughRead more“Justin Ray is extremely helpful. We were missing some pieces this week. Like, in Spain [in 2023] we had people giving us strokes gained in each match, even in practice. And we didn’t have that this year.“Because I know he’s working with Jim in the Ryder Cup, just now in the locker room, I told him exactly what he needed to do for Jim. Those things do matter and Justin was a huge help. He got us to this point.“It’s easy to get blown out over here. So I think we had the right formula and he helped us make that formula, so Justin Ray is awesome.”Pressed on why there was not the adequate backup resource she had referenced, Stanford said: “We just didn’t. See, that’s why I couldn’t be so honest with you.”It should be remembered that the teams were level, at 8-8, before a Sunday singles session where the USA team stood as the favourites. Following Stanford’s logic, she appears to be implying her team were denied the opportunity to take a lead into day three.Saturday’s conclusion had felt significant. Extraordinary pieces of play by Jennifer Kupcho on the last two holes meant she and Lindy Duncan claimed an unlikely point against Carlota Ciganda and Céline Boutier. Social media lit up with video of the USA team celebrating with beers on the bus back to their hotel. “They drink on Saturday, we drink on Sunday,” Europe’s team chanted when they made the same journey a day later.Stanford disputed any sense of untimely euphoria. She had been unwilling to ask the American players to tone down their joy. “That’s kind of tricky because you don’t ever want to take away from that moment,” she said. “The worst thing I could have done is go in there and be like: ‘OK, y’all. Come off this high.’ You don’t want to take away from those moments. We’re never going to see anything like that again.“I think they handled it very well. We’ve never seen that so we don’t really know how to react. I talked to Kupcho and everybody and they’re like, ‘Yeah, we got good rest, but it did take a minute to come off because it was a pretty high, high.’”Another element was the putting surfaces. Anna Nordqvist, Europe’s captain, shrugged off any notion of gamesmanship by pointing out “we are in Europe in September”, but the pace of the greens had caught out the USA team.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Apparently I didn’t get to know the [greens] superintendent as well as I should have,” Stanford said only half in jest. “Even when we showed up in July here, they were faster. And I don’t think it had anything to do with the rain either.View image in fullscreenAnna Nordqvist, the Europe captain, lifts the Solheim Cup.Photograph: Naomi Baker/Getty Images“Now, saying that, it’s my responsibility to get the team ready. This is the one thing I am kicking myself [about], is that I just didn’t keep pushing, ‘We [have] got to figure out how to hit our putts a little bit harder.’ Which is really difficult, to change the way you putt.“I’m a little frustrated with myself. Nobody complained about it at all. It’s me saying this right now that I wish I would have maybe hammered it home more; they’re going to be slow, they’re going to be slow, they’re going to be slow. We don’t play on greens this slow usually.”There is more than enough blame to go around, it seems.Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spanish GP plans to change Madring after fierce criticism from F1 drivers | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Discussions are already under way to change the layout of Formula One’s newest circuit after driver condemnation of the Madring during its inaugural Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Discussions are already under way to change the layout of Formula One’s newest circuit after driver condemnation of the Madring during its inaugural Grand Prix
Content: The Spanish Grand Prix race was far from thrilling with drivers largely circulating behind one another.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Spanish Grand Prix race was far from thrilling with drivers largely circulating behind one another.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Spanish GP plans to change Madring after fierce criticism from F1 driversNew track for Spanish GP frustrated drivers and fansMcLaren’s Stella: ‘It’s impossible to attempt overtaking’Giles Richardsin MadridMon 14 Sep 2026 06.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiscussions are already under way to change the layout of Formula One’s newest circuit after driver condemnation of the Madring during its inaugural grand prix. The race in Madridwas won by Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, but it was notable for being a procession with overtakes failing to reach double digits over 57 laps. Drivers were left frustrated and disappointed at an opportunity that had been lost, resulting in a chorus of criticism.“I don’t know how someone looks at this design and goes ‘mint’,” said the defending world champion,Lando Norris, who finished third. “There’s a lot of opportunity. They can make it into a track that’s good for racing and I’m excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes.‘No stopping him’: Hamilton admits defeat as Antonelli charges towards F1 world titleRead more“The fact you have to turn and brake basically defeats the whole object of racing. They can do some simple changes. I hope they do it because then it should be more exciting for everyone.”The race was far from thrilling with drivers largely circulating behind one another, albeit at high speed, but unable to find any opportunity to make a move. Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto dismissively categorised it as uninvigorating to drive in as it had been to watch. “I almost fell asleep as well,” he said.The Madring, a hybrid circuit of part public roads and part purpose-built track, has been constructed in north-east Madrid around a conference centre on the way to the airport. Logistically, it has been a success, with transport to and from the track managed well, despite the huge numbers of fans, which F1 puts at 352,000 for the weekend.The teams enjoyed the facilities and space and it presented a high-speed and spectacular challenge on a narrow, technical circuit many drivers enjoyed over a single lap in qualifying. However, in racing terms, the track, built at a reported cost of approximately £71m, was frustrating.It was designed by the Italian Jarno Zaffelli who said he hoped “people walk away recognising it’s possible to build a street circuit that is not boring”. That was a goal left sorely wanting after the race, with people walking away looking bored.“There are some corners that need to be changed to create more overtaking opportunities because it’s nice over one lap, but in the race you’re just stuck behind,” said Antonelli.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli’s victory gave him a lead of 81 points over his teammate, George Russell.Photograph: David Davies/PAHis feelings were echoed by Max Verstappen who finished second. “If you just drive a little bit in the middle, then you can’t pass,” he said. Verstappen had warned of the poor design from the moment he had first driven the track in a simulator.The Mercedes team principal,Toto Wolff, acknowledged there were discussions about changes taking place even before the race. “The tricky bit [is] doing a track that is spectacular for the drivers and then building it in a way that there is lots of overtaking,” he said. “I had a discussion [on Saturday] with the CEO of the circuit and they are totally open-minded about next year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’ve had the discussions with the FIA. What is it we should do? How is it that we should lay the track out when it comes to overtaking? There is a constant discussion and they are on it and understand we can tweak it a little bit.”The Madring has a 10-year contract to host the Spanish Grand Prix and theMcLarenteam principal, Andrea Stella, was clear he expected there to be considerations of layout changes. “It’s a shame it’s so difficult. It just requires a large, large lap-time difference to be able to overtake,” he said. “What F1, we’d like to review, is there’s some modifications required in order to introduce an overtaking possibility.“At the moment the straight may be long enough, but there’s absolutely no way the two cars can enter the corner together. It’s basically impossible to attempt overtaking.”Antonelli has a lead of 81 points in the world championship over his teammate George Russell, with nine meetings remaining and the next round at Baku in two weeks.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportLando NorrisKimi AntonelliToto WolffMercedes GPnewsShareReuse this content

title: WSL talking points: Olid must weather United storm, Arsenal wasteful again | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Manchester United need to regroup after a heavy home loss to Chelsea while Crystal Palace frustrated the Gunners
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Manchester United need to regroup after a heavy home loss to Chelsea while Crystal Palace frustrated the Gunners
Content: Crystal Palace’s goalkeeper Pauline Peyraud-Magnin, West Ham's Riko Ueki and Kelly Gago, the Manchester United head coach, Eva Olid.Composite: Getty; ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCrystal Palace’s goalkeeper Pauline Peyraud-Magnin, West Ham's Riko Ueki and Kelly Gago, the Manchester United head coach, Eva Olid.Composite: Getty; ShutterstockWomen's Super LeagueWSL talking points: Olid must weather United storm, Arsenal wasteful againManchester United need to regroup after a heavy home loss to Chelsea while Crystal Palace frustrated the GunnersSuzanne Wrack,Sophie DowneyandEmillia HawkinsMon 14 Sep 2026 07.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs Olid under pressure?The frustration among Manchester United fans at full-time was evident at Leigh Sports Village after they had watched their team being thrashed 5-0 by a rampant Chelsea. There are certainly things to be worried about, but perhaps judging United’s new manager, Eva Olid, on the basis of how they performed against Sonia Bompastor’s established side is a little premature. The likelihood of United taking three points was always slim, despite the false hope afterChelsea’s 1-1 draw with Aston Villalast weekend. Chelsea have not been an easy opponent for the Red Devils, who have lost three WSL games by more than three goals, all against Chelsea. Having had three weeks with her side, Olid had a harsh WSL baptism with losses to London City Lionesses and Chelsea. United face Arsenal next. “These are difficult games to build the confidence in attack, but I’m here to build an identity and I have to be faithful to that,” said the Spaniard.Suzanne WrackMatch report: Manchester United 0-5 ChelseaArsenal lack finishing touch againThere was a strong sense of deja vu at the Emirates Stadium as Arsenal’s annual early season woes continued with goalless draw at home to Crystal Palace. For much of the game, it felt like they were re-winding the tape from seasons gone by, frustrated by resolute defensive visitors and their own lack of clinical finishing. Arsenal dominated every attacking metric – they had 79% possession, created 30 shots (nine on target) and recorded 70 touches in the Eagles’ area. The Gunners hit the woodwork twice, wasted golden opportunities and were denied by a standout performance from Pauline Peyraud-Magnin, who made eight saves. “Yes, there were good things, but it’s about scoring,” the head coach, Renée Slegers, said. Arsenal’s title tilt last season was ended by six draws and they will have to improve on that if they are to challenge this season.Sophie DowneyWSL roundup: Arsenal rue misses in Palace drawView image in fullscreenChloe Kelly and Leah Williamson were part of a dominant, but goalless, Arsenal display against Crystal Palace.Photograph: Eddie Keogh/WSL/Getty ImagesWest Ham expose London CityAfterbeating Manchester Unitedlast time out, London City Lionesses were brought back down to earth by an inspired West Ham to suffer their first defeat of the campaign. West Ham put in a performance that caught the eye for their own qualities as well as highlighting the early frailties of Eder Maestre’s team. If you were to just glance at the stats, you would think the visitors dominated, but it felt anything like that at Dagenham: Rita Guarino, the Hammers manager, set up her team perfectly. The burgeoning midfield relationship between Katie Zelem and Saki Kumagai nullified the threat of Alexia Putellas and Rosa Kafaji, Riko Ueki swept everything up in front of them, while the combined transitional threat of Viviane Asseyi and Kelly Gago had London City’s right side teetering. West Ham’s French duo found their touch in front of goal after precise counterattacking moves to secure a first win of the new season.SDMatch report: West Ham 2-1 London City LionessesFlexibility helps Liverpool close the gapTwo games, four points and frustration that it is not all six: Liverpool have come a long way in a year. Last season, it took them until 25 January to earn a win and that win came against their opponents on Sunday, Tottenham, a similarly resurgent side who are possibly a few steps further ahead in their project. It was tactical flexibility that helped Gareth Taylor’s side earn a draw, with Liverpool responding well after Signe Gaupset’s effort took a heavy deflection off Sam Kerr to give Spurs a lead, somewhat against the run of play. The half-time introduction of Aurélie Csillag, who joined in January and grabbed the goal that gave them a point, was key. “They’re not going to give up the spaces easily,” said Taylor. “At times the spaces changed. Aurélie coming on to the pitch is a different type of proposition for back-fours as she’s physically very good.”SWChampions flex their muscleThe only team with a perfect record after two games, Manchester City, the reigning WSL champions, showed they can be ruthless, with a comprehensive 4-1 defeat of Aston Villa. Yes, City have played a promoted side, Birmingham, and an unconvincing Aston Villa. Yes, we are yet to see how City fare when they add Champions League football into the mix, but the firepower at Andrée Jeglertz’s disposal is enviable. Khadija Shaw has three goals from two games and City had 55 touches in the opposition area to Villa’s 15 and 23 shots to Villa’s five. Chelsea’s profligacy cost them last weekend and Arsenal’s cost them this weekend, but City are scoring for fun.SWskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenManchester City’s Khadija Shaw scored her third goal of the season at Aston Villa.Photograph: Andrew Couldridge/Action Images/ReutersHills’ regret after red cardThe Charlton manager, Karen Hills, said she was disappointed after the second-half red card for Ashleigh Neville against Everton led to a 1-0 defeat. Neville was sent off in the 58th minute for a high boot on Ruby Mace. While Hills suggested there was more hip-to-hip contact than anything else, she did not outright criticise the officials. “I don’t think the referee made the decision, it’s the fourth [official] and I guess they have to work together. Yes, her foot is a little bit high, but disappointed because that changes the game.” Charlton went down to nine players after Hawa Cissoko received two yellow cards in quick succession.Emillia HawkinsView image in fullscreenAshleigh Neville was sent off in the 58th minute for a high challenge.Photograph: Molly Darlington/WSL/Getty ImagesBirmingham’s lack of WSL experience showsOn paper, Birmingham’s 2-2 draw against Brighton is an impressive feat for a promoted side, but the head coach, Amy Merricks, did not look too happy at the final whistle. Her team led the match by two goals with 15 minutes left to play, but Olivia Garcia got one back for Brighton in the 77th minute before Kiko Seike snatched a point with a last-gasp equaliser. The difference in experience between the two sides probably played a part in the later stages, with Birmingham in the WSL for the first time since 2022. “We’ll take a massive lesson today from those dying moments and how we see that out a bit better,” said Merricks. “What we can’t question is this group’s application and intent. They were on the front foot, they were tenacious. We look improved from last week, which, for me, is brilliant. We’re going to go up a notch because I know this team, they won’t settle, they’re very hungry.”EHPosTeamPGDPts1Man City Women2562Chelsea Women2543Liverpool FC Women2444Tottenham Hotspur Women2245Arsenal Women2146Crystal Palace Women2147London City Lionesses2038Everton Women2039West Ham Women2-1310Brighton & Hove Albion Women2-1111Birmingham City Women2-2112Aston Villa Women2-3113Charlton Women2-5014Man Utd Women2-60Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballManchester United WomenChelsea WomenArsenal WomenCrystal Palace WomenWest Ham United WomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Democracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data shows | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Trump administration undermining rule of law at home and worldwide, according to intergovernmental report
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Trump administration undermining rule of law at home and worldwide, according to intergovernmental report
Content: Police officers arrest a protester during a ‘No Kings’ protest against Donald Trump’s perceived authoritarianism in Los Angeles in March.Photograph: Étienne Laurent/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice officers arrest a protester during a ‘No Kings’ protest against Donald Trump’s perceived authoritarianism in Los Angeles in March.Photograph: Étienne Laurent/AFP/Getty ImagesTrump administrationDemocracy indicators in US at lowest levels for 50 years, data showsTrump administration undermining rule of law at home and worldwide, according to intergovernmental reportJason BurkeInternational security correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKey indicators of democracy in the US have fallen to their lowest levels in 50 years, with the global rule of law significantly undermined by the Trump administration’s “threats and actions”, data from a leading thinktank shows.Around the world, judicial independence, credible elections and freedom of expression, press freedom and access to justice are all at their lowest levels for at least 30 years, according to the Stockholm-basedInternational Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International Idea).The intergovernmental organisation’s annual Global State of Democracy report is considered the most comprehensive of its kind, covering 174 countries and measuring democratic performance since 1975.International Idea said the decline in the US was particularly marked, but part of a global trend, with 2025 the 11th consecutive year in which more countries declined than improved democratically – the longest continuous downturn since the thinktank’s records began.“In 2025, the global challenges to democracy and the difficulty in stemming its erosion were both exemplified and compounded by political developments in the United States,” the report’s authors said.“President Donald Trump quickly amassed power in the executive branch and wielded it to further a narrow set of personal goals and pursue retaliation against perceived enemies … The results have been far-reaching, undermining the rule of law domestically and internationally and testing longstanding alliances and multilateral cooperation.”View image in fullscreenDonald Trump has made repeated false claims about the integrity of US elections.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesKevin Casas-Zamora, International Idea’s secretary general, warned that the risk of conflict rose as democracies deteriorated.“The key message from our research is that investing in democracy should be at the heart of any country’s security strategy,” he said. “The connection between the erosion of the quality of democracy and increasing conflict is not being made either in policymaking or in the public debate.”The separateUppsala Conflict Data Program, based at Uppsala University in Sweden, shows that 2025 had the most violent conflicts – including the most interstate conflicts – of any year in its dataset, which goes back to 1946.The International Idea report did highlight some positive developments, including in Australia – wherecivil society groups were consulted on an anti-racism strategyand children’s online privacy among other issues – and in Syria, where the repressive dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad was overthrown.In Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka,youth-led popular protests unseated long-serving leaders, but, the report noted, “it has proven difficult to create far-reaching, meaningful reform in a short period of time”.Casas-Zamora said it was clear that events in the US influenced other countries.International Idea added the US to its list of “backsliding” democraciesfor the first time in 2021, pointing to a “visible deterioration” it said began in 2019.View image in fullscreenYoung voters celebrate in Nepal after the election of a new government in March.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersThe thinktank bases its assessments on 50 years of democratic indicators, assigning countries to one of three categories: democracies, “hybrid” governments and authoritarian regimes.Globally, it found rule of law was the weakest area of democracy in 2025, with 71 countries – 41% of those assessed – ranked as low-performing. It was also found to be deteriorating quickly, with 29 countries registering downturns.“Whatever happens in the US goes global. There is now an epidemic of election denialism, of which the patient zero is the current occupant of the White House,” Casas-Zamor said.“I am not willing to say the deterioration of the quality of democracy is inevitable or permanent. It can be reversed,” he added. “We live in a volatile world and that means things can happen which create very positive political openings.”Yet, despite the positive signs in Nepal, Bangladesh and elsewhere, the report paints a bleak picture overall.“While people continue to push back against democratic deterioration, civic space is narrowing,” its authors wrote. “Civil society and civic engagement have suffered, due in part to the widespread use ofstrategic lawsuits against public participation, foreign agent laws, and the criminalisation of peaceful protests.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationInternational lawGovernanceCivil liberties - internationalUS politicsThinktanksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Member of British armed forces killed in Ukraine crash, says MoD | Military | The Guardian
description: Ministry of Defence says person, who has yet to be identified, died in road traffic incident not believed to be result of hostile action
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Ministry of Defence says person, who has yet to be identified, died in road traffic incident not believed to be result of hostile action
Content: A small number of British military personnel in Ukraine provide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PAView image in fullscreenA small number of British military personnel in Ukraine provide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PAMilitaryMember of British armed forces killed in Ukraine crash, says MoDMinistry of Defence says person, who has yet to be identified, died in road traffic incident not believed to be result of hostile actionPriya Bharadiaand agencyMon 14 Sep 2026 15.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA member of the UK armed forces has been killed in a crash in Ukraine, theMinistry of Defencesaid.The person, who has not yet been named, died in a road traffic incident on Saturday. It is understood the incident was not a result of hostile action.The person’s family has been informed and has asked for some time before more details are made public.“Our thoughts and our sympathies are with the individual’s loved ones at this difficult time,” an MoD spokesperson said.The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on X: “This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our Armed Forces.“My deepest condolences go to them all.”The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, said on X he was “saddened to hear this news” and offered his condolences to the person’s family and friends.A small number of British personnel inUkraineprovide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces.British paratrooper George Hooley, 28, was killed in Ukraine in December while watching Ukrainian forces testing defensive capability.‘He served with honour’: Starmer pays tribute to British soldier killed in UkraineRead moreThe MoD described his death as a “tragic accident” that occurred “away from the frontlines”.Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine is in its fifth year and the conflict continues with fresh strikes on Ukraine, including an attack on a gasworks and a drone attack on a train station on Sunday.The attack hit a train at Yahodyn station, on the Polish border, shortly after a train carrying Boris Johnson had left ahead of schedule.Ukraine’s railway operator said the attack may have been aimed at the train carrying the former prime minister, among other dignitaries.Johnson had been returning from a major conference in Kyiv along with former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt and a number of European security advisers.According to a translation from Ukrainian, rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in a post on Telegram it was “quite possible” the drone had been aimed at Johnson’s train.Explore more on these topicsMilitaryMinistry of DefenceUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Experts quit Lucy Letby’s defence team over ‘scientific credibility’ concerns | Lucy Letby | The Guardian
description: Some of the arguments inconsistent with ‘available evidence, science and established physiology’, say pair
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Some of the arguments inconsistent with ‘available evidence, science and established physiology’, say pair
Content: Lucy Letby is serving 15 whole-life orders after she was convicted across two trials.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenLucy Letby is serving 15 whole-life orders after she was convicted across two trials.Photograph: Publicity imageLucy LetbyExperts quit Lucy Letby’s defence team over ‘scientific credibility’ concernsSome of the arguments inconsistent with ‘available evidence, science and established physiology’, say pairJosh HallidayNorth of England editorMon 14 Sep 2026 10.47 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo leading experts have withdrawn from Lucy Letby’s defence team over concerns about the “scientific credibility” of some of its evidence.The former neonatal nurse is challenging her convictions for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at the Countess of Chester hospital in north-west England.The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the UK’s miscarriage of justice watchdog, is considering a dossier of evidence submitted last year by experts on her behalf.Two experts withdrew from Letby’s defence team on Monday. They said that although they stood by their assessment that it was “very unlikely” two of the babies were poisoned, some of the arguments being put forward on her behalf were “inconsistent with the available evidence, science and established physiology”.Helen Shannon, a British chemical engineering expert, and Geoff Chase, a professor of bioengineering based in New Zealand, produced a 100-page report last year casting doubt on her convictions for poisoning two babies with insulin.Theytold the Guardianlast year there was a “very strong level of reasonable doubt” about those two convictions, which formed a central part of the prosecution case against Letby. The 36-year-old nurse was convicted in 2023 of trying to murder two newborn boys, known as Baby 6 and Baby 12, by spiking their feeding bags with insulin.Letby is serving 15 whole-life orders after she wasconvicted across two trials at Manchester crown courtof murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, with two attempts on one of her victims, between June 2015 and June 2016.Shannon and Chase said on Monday they stood by their assessment, but could not support other evidence used by Letby’s defence team relating to the insulin cases.In a letter to the CCRC, the experts said: “Whilst it is entirely legitimate for the defence to advance multiple arguments, some of the other arguments now being put forward we cannot support as scientifically credible and which have, in our view, fundamental unresolvable problems.”They said the strategy of Letby’s defence team, led by her barrister Mark McDonald, was “placing the long-term interests of Ms Letby at serious, unnecessary and unacceptable risk” and that those “consequences also extend to the families” of the babies who died and were injured.View image in fullscreenThe barrister Mark McDonald began representing Letby in August 2024.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesThey added: “We cannot, with integrity, support arguments which are inconsistent with the available evidence, science and established physiology … After disclosing these concerns, continued association with arguments we believe are demonstrably inaccurate creates a serious ethical issue under the professional engineering codes governing us in New Zealand and the UK, and exposes us to professional sanction.”McDonald, Letby’s barrister, said: “We now have evidence from a number of leading international experts in insulin, endocrinology and laboratory medicine which fundamentally undermines the scientific evidence relied upon at trial. Importantly, the case does not stand or fall on any one expert.Cheshire constabulary rejects criticism by David Davis over Letby investigationRead more“The strength of the new evidence lies in its breadth and convergence, with independent experts from different disciplines and jurisdictions identifying fundamental problems with the scientific basis upon which the jury were invited to conclude that babies [6] and [12] had been deliberately poisoned.”The CCRC, which has been reviewing the convictions for 18 months, declined to comment.A public inquiry into the murders will publish its findings on Tuesday. Thereview, led by Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall, is expected to highlight a number of missed opportunities for bosses to intervene after doctors raised the alarm about a spate of unexplained deaths on the neonatal unit in 2015 and 2016.A criminal investigation is ongoing into potential corporate manslaughter and gross negligence manslaughter at the Countess of Chester hospital.Explore more on these topicsLucy LetbynewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding  | Donald Trump Jr | The Guardian
description: US president’s eldest child married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: US president’s eldest child married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands
Content: Umar Kremlev, a Putin ally, reportedly paid a significant amount of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding.Composite: Getty Images, SOPA Images/LightRocketView image in fullscreenUmar Kremlev, a Putin ally, reportedly paid a significant amount of Donald Trump Jr’s wedding.Composite: Getty Images, SOPA Images/LightRocketDonald Trump JrRussian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish weddingUS president’s eldest child married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in three-day celebration across two exclusive private islandsUS politics live – latest updatesLucy CampbellMon 14 Sep 2026 18.28 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 14.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed on Mondaythat a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following aProPublicareport revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events.Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest child, married the Palm Beach socialite in a lavish three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands in May.Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show.In astatement signed by the coupleand shared on Bettina Trump’s Instagram after ProPublica’s report was published, they confirmed Kremlev’s contributions to the celebrations and characterized them as “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful”.Democrats to investigate ‘miraculous’ rise of Trump Jr’s investment firmRead moreA top Democrat demanded answers on the Trumps’ ties to Kremlev.“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” posted Robert Garcia, the ranking member and lead Democrat on the House oversight committee, on social media. “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”Kremlev has a longstanding relationship with Putin. He is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), a sporting body that has beenbackedby the state-owned Russian energy company Gazprom. According to ProPublica, the wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions.In the days before the wedding party, he reportedly went to China as part of a delegation accompanying Putin, and the month prior the Russian president hadbestowed him with a state honor, the Order of Friendship. The Ukrainian government has imposed sanctions on Kremlev, citing his closeness to Putin and Russian security services.Alexander Lagutin, a businessperson who has held senior roles at a Russian defense contractor and a state-backed energy company, had been with Kremlev on the China trip. Kremlev’s right hand at the IBA, Elena Sobol, attended the wedding, too.While the event was extravagant, the guest list was intimate, with only about 50 people attending, most of whom were immediate family, close friends and business partners of the couple. Then there was Kremlev, who reportedly didn’t attend the ceremony itself, which was limited to just 18 guests, but was present with a large contingent of Russians at the party, much to the confusion of the other guests. The group reportedly sometimes stood off by themselves speaking Russian, according to ProPublica.The affair has raised questions about the implications of a member of Putin’s circle financially supporting and gaining such intimate access to the US president’s family. In recent years Trump Jr has emerged as a leading campaign surrogate for Trump and has even been touted as a potential political heir.Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew), said it is in the public interest for Congress to strongly consider requiring financial disclosure statements of a president’s adult children, in addition to the president themselves.The crux of the issue is the nature of the friendship, and whether the giving of gifts is genuine or designed to influence, Sherman said. “We know that private companies and foreign governments have been seeking to gain Don Jr’s favor in order toservetheirownfinancialinterests. And so, it’s important that there is a measure of transparency when folks tied to the Russian government are lavishing the president’s rich adult son with expensive gifts.”He added: “Most of us learn as children that ‘there’s no such thing as a free lunch’. It’s one thing if, in the nature of this friendship, there’s a mutual exchange of lavish gifts. It’s another if someone’s daddy becomes president and then all of a sudden this new friend starts giving gifts – that context very much matters.”In similar vein, retired FBI official Frank Montoya Jr told ProPublica: “If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something. This should be unthinkable for the son of the president.”It remains unclear why Kremlev helped pay for the wedding and why he was there, when he appears to have only met Trump Jr – the executive vice-president of the Trump Organization, who has a personal net worthsomewhere in the ballpark of $300m– quite recently.Donald Trump famouslydidn’t attend the wedding. “He’d like me to go, but it’s going to be just a small, little private affair,” the US president told reporters a few days before the nuptials. “I said, you know, this is not good timing for me. I have a thing called Iran and other things.”In response to detailed questions from ProPublica, a spokesperson for Trump Jr did not deny that Kremlev had helped fund the wedding. “Umar is a personal friend of Don,” the spokesperson said, adding Kremlev is “not someone he has a business relationship with” and that the men met through a mutual friend in the hunting world.In their joint Instagram statement, Trump Jr and Bettina Trumpthanked“our dear friend Umar” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding”.They said they “got married privately” on 22 May “surrounded ONLY by our family”, and said the Russian businessman had simply given them a gift.“Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” they said.Explore more on these topicsDonald Trump JrDemocratsDonald TrumpRussiaVladimir PutinnewsShareReuse this content

title: US ‘super-emitters’ of planet heating methane identified by satellite analysis | Gas | The Guardian
description: Energy Transfer, whose CEO is a major Trump donor, named as biggest single methane producer in new rankings
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Energy Transfer, whose CEO is a major Trump donor, named as biggest single methane producer in new rankings
Content: A flare burns natural gas at an oil well in August 2021, in North Dakota.Photograph: Matthew Brown/APView image in fullscreenA flare burns natural gas at an oil well in August 2021, in North Dakota.Photograph: Matthew Brown/APGasUS ‘super-emitters’ of planet heating methane identified by satellite analysisEnergy Transfer, whose CEO is a major Trump donor, named as biggest single methane producer in new rankingsOliver MilmanMon 14 Sep 2026 16.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 20.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDown a short gravel track in a largely nondescript corner of Louisiana sits a gas processing facility, operated by a company whose chief executive is a major donor to Donald Trump. It may be the largest emitter of methane in the US.TheEnergyTransfer site, located near the city of Shreveport,is named as the biggest single “super emitter” in new rankings of US oil and gas operations for the largest releases of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas that is rapidly overheating our planet, according to a new UCLA study, which is based on satellite data.From January 2025 to June this year, the Shreveport facilityspewed out methaneat an average emission rate of 1.56 tonnes an hour, which is 15 times larger than the thresholddefinedin a Biden era program by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) as a super emitter event,according to the study. The Trump administration has put implementation of that program on hold but climate experts and advocates say reducing methane emissions is vital to limit the climate crisis.The new rankings combine satellite data and public records to indicate a “potentially responsible operator” for each of the largest methane plumes, researchers at UCLA’s Emmett Institute say. Such a task can be complicated by a lack of official records naming sites with large methane emissions as well as ascertaining ownership of pollution coming from tight clusters of differing oil and gas leases.Dallas-based Energy Transfer oversees a huge network of pipelines and processing properties in the US and is linked to four of the 15 sites highlighted in the new rankings, with the company responsible for 75 methane plumes in total over the study period – three times as much as the next operator. Other major corporate methane producers include Enterprise Products, Targa Resources and Enlink.Kelcy Warren, Energy Transfer’s billionaire chief executive,donated millions of dollarsto Trump’s last election campaign and has previouslydescribed as an “insanity”when asked what he thought about a newspaper editorial that said net-zero carbon emissions policies would ultimately mean oil was no longer needed.A map showing the plume from Energy Transfer facility on 24 February 2026Energy Transfer did not respond to questions on what it is doing to stem methane from its facilities or whether the Shreveport site has been intentionally venting the gas or has experienced some sort of leak. The company has previously described efforts it was taking to reduce methane emissions in company reports includingoptical gas imaging inspections across hundreds of its facilites.“Many of these sites are repeat offenders linked to not one but multiple mega plumes,” said Cara Horowitz, executive director of the UCLA Emmett Institute and author of the new report. “As America’s oil and gas industry ramps up production, it can no longer ignore what can only be described as super-sized pollution events seen from space.”Horowitz said that the satellite record is “spotty but important”, as it shows emissions “that used to be frankly invisible and historically undercounted. Now they are plainly visible, they deserve public and regulatory attention. These numbers are unacceptably large, these emissions seem very wasteful and very inefficient.”A chart showing top ‘super emitters’ of methane in US’s three biggest oil and gas basins, according to analysisThe new report draws upon data from the Tanager-1 satellite, compiled by the non-profitCarbon Mapper, of spotted plumes in the Permian, Appalachian and Haynesville-Bossier basins, resource-rich hotspots which span several states and account for about two-thirds of US gas production.A total of 1,097 methane plumes were detected from oil and gas sources in these regions between January 2025 and June this year. The UCLA team was able to assign an operator responsible for a plume in around a third of these cases, using publicly available data. Horowitz said, though, it is “a real cause for concern when it comes to transparency” that so few operators can be identified as responsible for this pollution.While satellites have helped reveal previously unknown methane emissions, such pollution is still vastly underreported,with researchers recently estimatingactual US oil and gas methane emissions are around 64% higher than official EPA figures.Activists have long argued that drilling sites and pipelines often experience regular,sometimes dangerous, leaks or purposely vent methane into the air, to release the pressure of gas build-up in equipment, with little reporting or oversight. Even satellites are unable to capture thefull extent of these emissionswhen they are obscured on cloudy days. It is not illegal to release methane in these ways and operators face no penalizing regulations for doing so.“I’ve been in the Permian basin and seen methane blowdowns happening everywhere for days but nothing got picked up on the satellites because it was overcast,” said Sharon Wilson, director ofOilfield Witness, an advocacy and monitoring group.Wilson, a former fossil fuel industry worker, has spent the last 14 years acting as a “methane hunter” by filming oil and gas sites with a special camera that makes methane emissions visible. In 2024 she documented a Energy Transfer facility in Pecos county, Texas, that is fifth on UCLA’s top 10 producers list. The video from her visit shows gusts of methane, resembling smoke, spiraling from the site.“Just a fraction of what is happening is being reported,” Wilson said. “I don’t see any improvement from the industry, what I see is just continued expansion. I have been to a lot of Energy Transfer sites and they are by far, in my opinion, the worst midstream operator I’ve seen. They always have massive methane plumes.”The UCLA researchers chose to focus on the three large oil and gas basins, rather than every single emitter in the US, as they are the fulcrum of a booming liquified natural gas (or LNG) export industry. The US hasleapfroggedother countries in recent years to become the world’s leading exporter of LNG,constructing a slew of vast terminalswhere gas is chilled and then shipped overseas. Trump hassoughtto fast-track the growth of this industry.Proponents of LNG exports contend burning gas is cleaner than coal, although the repeated expulsion of methane during the export process can in fact make it even worse than coal for the climate, research has found.“While US industry players often talk about reductions in methane intensity, this analysis reveals a concerning number of super-emitter events from the regions that ship LNG overseas,” said Mary Nichols, former chair of the California air resources board and now distinguished counsel for the UCLA Emmett Institute.Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, trapping around 80 times more heat than carbon dioxideover a 20-year period, and is responsible fornearly a thirdof the global heating that has occurred since the industrial revolution. It is released via oil and gas drilling and transportation, as well as from landfills and agriculture.There has been a “scary” surge in global methane emissions since 2007, according to scientists, although the gas doesn’t linger in the atmosphere as long as CO2. This means that reducing methane emissions from leaky pipes, venting and burning gas as a fuel can act as a rapid “emergency brake” amid a climate crisis that is dangerously barreling past safe limits.Some progress can be achieved by identifying unseen methane leaks and fixing them, ashas occurred recently in Turkmenistan. The country was previously releasing more methane than the entire emissions of the UK, a situation described as “mind-boggling” and “infuriating”, but has since started to plug some of the leaks emanating from its aging oil and gas infrastructure.Such remedial work has been happening in some instances in the US, too, with the industryclaiminga recent “profound shift” in pinpointing and dealing with leaks. In the UCLA study, three of the top 10 methane producers, including the first and second placed sites, had no methane plumes detected in their most recent satellite observations, suggesting some improvements may have taken place.“The goal of shining a light on these emissions is to prompt action, which may already be under way at a few of these sites,” said Horowitz.But critics argue that leaks of methane will continue for as long as the oil and gas industry faces little financial or regulatory pressure to change its ways, or until it is eclipsed entirely by clean energy.Trump has set about eliminating enforcement, reporting requirements andfeesaimed at driving down US methane emissions, with his EPA pushing ahead with therollbackof Joe Biden-era rules aimed at slashing this pollution. Lee Zeldin, the EPA administrator, has previously said these requirements “weaponized environmental regulations to regulate the oil and gas industry out of existence”.Wilson said the only way to force down methane emissions is to stop issuing new permits to the fossil fuel industry. “We have all these emissions blasting into the air and no one even knows about it,” she said.“We’ve gone so far past trying to rein in the industry. We don’t need oil and gas to energize our world anymore, it’s silly. Ironically Donald Trump has helped everyone realize the need to move on from oil and gas because of this (Iran) war.Gasisn’t energy security, it’s a vulnerability.”All of the companies named in UCLA’s top 10 sites and among those responsible for the largest number of plumes were contacted for comment. None of them provided a response for the story apart from Boardwalk Pipeline Partners, which said it has reduced emissions in recent years from the 10th placed site, a gas storage facility which is also near Shreveport, Louisiana.“Natural gas storage facilities require periodic inspections, testing, and maintenance activities to help ensure safe and reliable operations,” said a company spokeswoman.“During some of these activities, natural gas may be released to safely reduce pressure before work can be performed. This is part of the safe operation and maintenance of the facility and is not necessarily indicative of equipment leaks.“The Bistineau Storage Station operates in full compliance with all state and federal regulations. While there is more work to do, our emission reduction journey reflects Boardwalk’s ongoing commitment to responsible operations and continuous improvement.”Explore more on these topicsGasEnergyFossil fuelsClimate crisisOil and gas companiesGreenhouse gas emissionsEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Tidal wave’ of Pfas being launched to satisfy AI industry, campaigners warn | Pfas | The Guardian
description: Big manufacturers planning to produce more of the forever chemicals to meet demand from datacentres
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Big manufacturers planning to produce more of the forever chemicals to meet demand from datacentres
Content: Increased production risks undermining moves to restrict Pfas in Europe, the UK and US, said ChemSec.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenIncreased production risks undermining moves to restrict Pfas in Europe, the UK and US, said ChemSec.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersPfas‘Tidal wave’ of Pfas being launched to satisfy AI industry, campaigners warnBig manufacturers planning to produce more of the forever chemicals to meet demand from datacentresDamien GayleEnvironment correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePfas companies are launching a “tidal wave” of forever chemicals production to meet demand from the AI industry, a campaign organisation has warned.Despite alarm over the chemicals, which have been linked to cancer, a survey of the 10 biggest manufacturers found most had plans to increase production.Many frame their investments around the “AI revolution”, because of the role Pfas play in semiconductor production and next-generation datacentre cooling systems.But opponents warn that the chemicals, which never degrade in nature, are a ticking timebomb for human and planetary health. They say increased production risks undermining nascent moves to restrict Pfasin Europe,the UKandparts of the US.“These companies’ expansion plans show that unless governments and regulators insist on a rapid phaseout, we will face a new tidal wave of forever chemicals,” said Anne-Sofie Bäckar, the executive director of ChemSec, the Swedish chemicals watchdog that carried out the research.ChemSec’s survey found nearly all of the10 biggest manufacturers of Pfashad plans to increase production, at sites in Europe, Asia and North America.The boom in AI tech was leading demand, with Pfas used for “eco-friendly” datacentre cooling and in various stages of semiconductor manufacturing.Japan-headquarted Daikinsaidit was launching a “datacentre hub” to meet demand, and promised to “maintain and expand our top share in the industry by expanding sales of existing fluorine products and introducing new products”.The French multinational Arkema was expanding its refrigerant offering, with a new $60m (£44m) production unit in Kentucky thatit said“will enable us to follow the rapid expansion of datacenters’ cooling needs”.And the US Pfas producer Chemours was expanding to meet demand from “advanced datacenters and AI hardware”. Itsaidits “innovative liquid cooling solutions” lower the energy, water, space, maintenance and investment costs of datacentres.Critics have said Chemours – recentlyordered to pay $450mto settle a lawsuit over Pfas discharges –downplays the chemicals’ toxicityand climate impact.Other companies increasing production were Japanese multinational AGC, Chinese conglomerate Dongyue, India-based chemicals giant Gujarat Fluorochemicals, secretive Russian Pfas producer HaloPolymer, Mexico’s Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials, US-based fluorinated gases producer Solstice and Belgian multinational Syensqo.Producers also cited Pfas coatings and binders for lithium-ion batteries, used in EVs, laptops and phones, as a parallel growth area. Gujarat Fluorochemicals’ chief executive, Bir Kapoor,recently identified batteries as one of several “sunrise sectors”, alongside datacentres, semiconductors and green hydrogen. “There is a tremendous growth opportunity there,” he said.The only clear exceptions were the Swiss company Archroma, which was switching to marketing Pfas-free alternatives, and the German giant BASF, which has said it will exit Pfas production by 2028.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAdvocates raise alarm over Pfas pollution from datacenters amid AI boomRead morePfas are used for a new form of datacentre cooling touted as more water- and energy-efficient. In “two-phase immersion cooling” systems, servers are immersed in a pool of Pfas with a low boiling point. As the hardware gets hot, the fluid boils, drawing heat away as vapour. That rises to a water-cooled condensing coil at the top of the tank, cools back to a liquid state and re-enters the cycle.Pfas also play a crucial role in the fabrication process for semiconductors, another sector booming to meet demand from the AI industry.According to a recent investor note from Danske Bank: “In the world of microchips, these ‘forever chemicals’ are not merely peripheral additives; they are essential ingredients integrated into as many as 1,000 distinct steps at the nanometric level.”But analysts also warned Pfas were “the hidden risk of the AI boom” with “escalating potential for multibillion-euro remediation and litigation liabilities”.The carbon-fluorine bonds in Pfas, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are among the strongest in organic chemistry, rendering them incredibly resistant to heat, water and corrosion.That makes them useful for a range of industrial processes and consumer products. But it also makes them virtually indestructible in the natural environment. As a result, they continue to be recycled through planetary systems, leading to their accumulation in air, water and soil, and up the food chain.Although Pfas have existed for less than a century, scientists have warned that their accumulation in the environment has alreadybreached a planetary boundary.Already the chemicals are thought to contaminate the blood of nearly every living person.Research links themto cancer, liver disease, kidney issues, high cholesterol and birth defects.ChemSec sent finger-prick blood tests to the chief executives of all the European companies in its top 10, encouraging them to test Pfas levels in their own blood and share the results publicly.“The people who lead them must understand that they too are affected by the toxins they produce, which have been detected in the blood of more than 99% of people worldwide,” said Bäckar.Explore more on these topicsPfasDatacentresAI (artificial intelligence)Chemical industryPollutionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Scientists find nine new sponge species in glimpse of Alaska’s deep-sea diversity | Alaska | The Guardian
description: But their habitat is threatened by bottom trawling in the region and Trump’s plan to expand seafloor mining
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: But their habitat is threatened by bottom trawling in the region and Trump’s plan to expand seafloor mining
Content: Deep-sea sponges and other invertebrates collected during a bottom-trawl survey.Photograph: Noaa FisheriesView image in fullscreenDeep-sea sponges and other invertebrates collected during a bottom-trawl survey.Photograph: Noaa FisheriesAlaskaScientists find nine new sponge species in glimpse of Alaska’s deep-sea diversityBut their habitat is threatened by bottom trawling in the region and Trump’s plan to expand seafloor miningMaya YangMon 14 Sep 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScientists have discovered nine new deep-sea sponge species offAlaska, offering new insights into the region’s largely unexplored marine biodiversity.The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa)announcedthe discovery on Thursday, saying the species were found in the Gulf of Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. The findings bring the total number of known sponge species in Alaska to 232.Could this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports?Read moreThe specimens were collected during Noaa Fisheries’ annual bottom-trawl surveys, which monitor groundfish and shellfish stocks. Researchers analyzed samples collected as far back as 2012, describing the new species intwo recentscientific papers.Often described as living water pumps, sponges are among Earth’s earliest multicellular animals, dating back more than 600m years. They filter seawater and help create habitats on the seafloor, despite having no brain or complex organs.“Sponges are ecologically important,” said Sean Rooney, a Noaa fisheries biologist and co-author of the studies at the agency’s Alaska Fisheries Science Center. “They aren’t plants, but like trees in a forest, they provide complex structure along the seafloor that creates habitat and refuge for commercially important fish and crabs,” he added.“Each time we find a new species, it opens up new doors … Deep water is hard to access, especially rocky places we can’t reach with bottom-trawl surveys. There are now more than 232 identified species of sponges in Alaska, and probably hundreds more that we don’t know about yet. The future in this field is exciting,” he continued.View image in fullscreenBiologists use guides to try to identify species of sponge and fish collected during a bottom-trawl survey.Photograph: Noaa FisheriesUnlike most marine animals, which can be identified by visible traits such as fins and body shapes, sponges can be much harder to distinguish. Because they lack complex organs and other distinctive external features, scientists often rely on their microscopic skeletons and genetic material to identify them.“DNA barcodes provide a quick genetic reference,” said Meredith Everett, a biologist at Noaa’s Northwest Fisheries Science Center. “Sponge DNA can be tricky because they filter-feed, and within their tissues we may find foreign DNA and biochemicals that inhibit testing. But despite the challenges, we successfully developed several new barcodes for Alaskan species,” she added.Dense sponge communities are consideredessential fish habitatby Noaa because they provide shelter that supports fish survival, growth and population recovery.Sponges also produce chemicals to defend themselves against predators and competing organisms. Some of these compounds have shown promise for potential use incancer treatments.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYet despite their ecological importance, Alaska’s deep-sea sponge communities face growing threats from Donald Trump’s proposals toexpand deep-sea miningfor critical minerals such as nickel and copper – used in military and technological applications – as well asbottom trawlingin the region.Environmental groupshave opposed the proposals,warningthat the activities could damage fragile seafloor ecosystems as theclimate crisisintensifies.Cooper Freeman, Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, said: “Alaska’s sponge gardens do so much for a healthy ocean, including providing shelter and serving as vitally important nurseries for all kinds of fish and crabs. Bottom trawl fishing is so damaging and unsustainable because it indiscriminately destroys the habitats that support future generations. Adding seafloor mining to the picture adds insult to injury, scraping up and devastating life on the bottom of the ocean.“Instead of stewarding Alaska’s precious sponge gardens so they can support Alaskan coastal communities and wildlife, theTrump administrationis pushing extractive marine activities on these irreplaceable seascapes for nothing but short-term profit,” Freeman added.In addition to Alaska, the Trump administration has proposed exploring deep-sea mining across millions of hectares of fragile Pacific ecosystems, including areas around the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam – a plan that has drawnbacklashfrom the US territories.Explore more on these topicsAlaskaMarine lifeMiningFishingDonald TrumpTrump administrationFishing industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: US ends limits on coal and gas plant emissions, removing key tool to battle climate crisis | US Environmental Protection Agency | The Guardian
description: Trump’s EPA strips itself of regulation ability, gutting Clean Air Act in what experts say is a gift to planet polluters
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Trump’s EPA strips itself of regulation ability, gutting Clean Air Act in what experts say is a gift to planet polluters
Content: A flue-gas stack blows exhaust at a coal-fired power plant in Ghent, Kentucky, on 14 February 2026.Photograph: Jon Cherry/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA flue-gas stack blows exhaust at a coal-fired power plant in Ghent, Kentucky, on 14 February 2026.Photograph: Jon Cherry/Getty ImagesUS Environmental Protection AgencyUS ends limits on coal and gas plant emissions, removing key tool to battle climate crisisTrump’s EPA strips itself of regulation ability, gutting Clean Air Act in what experts say is a gift to planet pollutersOliver MilmanMon 14 Sep 2026 17.17 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the heels of the hottest summer everrecordedin the US, the Trump administration has said it will erase any limits on emissions from coal and gas plants that are dangerously heating up our planet.TheUS Environmental Protection Agencysaid it will strip itself of its ability to regulate greenhouse gas emissions coming from power plants under the Clean Air Act, removing a key tool to address the climate crisis.By erasing any limits on such emissions from coal and gas plants, theTrump administrationhas severely limited any future administration’s ability to curb this pollution.The EPAcalculatedthe move will result in 123m metric tons of additional carbon emissions in the next decade, and save power plant operators $370m in direct compliance costs. Lee Zeldin, the agency administrator said the Trump administration is protecting American energy from a “war on coal”.US ‘super-emitters’ of planet heating methane identified by satellite analysisRead more“Americans will see a decrease in electricity prices, but this is just the beginning,” said Zeldin, who unveiled the reversal of the 2024 carbon pollution standards at a G20 meeting in Houston on Monday.“We are working to go even further so that American energy can be fully unleashed. Realizing the full potential of American energy means more jobs, lower prices and a more prosperous America.”The EPA said that greenhouse gas emissions from power plants have “no material impact on global climate change”.
