This is despite the fact that US electricity generation is responsible for aquarterof the country’s greenhouse gas emissions. If the sector were itself a country,it would bethe fifth largest carbon polluter in the world, after China, the US, India and Russia.Trump, who has called the climate crisis “bullshit” and “a hoax”, earlier this yearoverturnedthe foundational 2009 EPA endangerment finding – spurred by a supreme court ruling – that greenhouse gases pose a significant threat to public health and the environment.This has opened the way for the administration to scrub out any limits on the planet-heating gases that are causing our world to rapidly overheat and worsen deadly heatwaves, drought, wildfires and floods. In February, the EPA eliminated pollution standards for cars and trucks as part of a series of actions Zeldin described as “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the climate change religion”.Environmental groups immediately vowed to challenge the latest rollback in court. “This is full-throated climate denial while the climate crisis happens in real time and a shocking betrayal of the American public,” said Holly Bender, chief program officer at the Sierra Club.“The Sierra Club will fight back against this reckless and dangerous proposal with everything we have in the courts, in Congress, and in communities across the country.”When it issued the latest carbon pollution standards for power plants under Joe Biden’s administration in 2024, the EPA found the rules would slash 1bn tonnes of greenhouse gases by 2047 and deliver $370bn in net benefits.The rules also would have prevented 1,200 premature deaths and 360,000 asthma attacks in 2035 alone, due to air quality improvements. Under Trump, however, the EPA has eliminated the dollar benefit of saving lives through reduced air pollution in its calculations.“Every American deserves to breathe clean air, but time and again this administration gives a green light to more pollution at the expense of our health,” said Gina McCarthy, who was administrator of the EPA under Barack Obama.“Everyone will be affected by their actions, but the most vulnerable among us, our kids and grandkids, will suffer the most. Today’s decision lets the nation’s biggest industrial polluters off the hook by reversing findings the agency itself established.”Trump has long championed the use of fossil fuels, such as coal and gas, pushing a “drill, baby drill” approach that has opened up more land for extraction while demolishing clean air and water regulations the industry said it found too onerous.As well as handing out hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer funds to prop up coal plants, which have struggled economically in recent years, the Trump administration has sought to directly strangle clean energy projects such as solar and offshore wind.The latest EPA intervention will probably be significant, if it survives legal challenge, as it will stymie any future attempt to restrict carbon pollution from power plants. It is the latest episode in a decade-long saga over how, or if, the US tames its power emissions.In 2016 the supreme court knocked down Obama’s clean power plan. A more narrow version, with the parameters set again by the court, was then enacted under Biden.Explore more on these topicsUS Environmental Protection AgencyTrump administrationDonald TrumpGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisPollutionFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sunday in the Park With George musical cancelled, after Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey both drop out | Musicals | The Guardian
description: The star-studded Sondheim musical has hit the buffers after a second star, Jonathan Bailey, joined his Wicked colleague Ariana Grande and left the production
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: The star-studded Sondheim musical has hit the buffers after a second star, Jonathan Bailey, joined his Wicked colleague Ariana Grande and left the production
Content: Never on a Sunday … Ariana Grande, left, and Jonathan Bailey have both now left the production of Sunday in the Park With George.Composite: Shuttershock, GettyView image in fullscreenNever on a Sunday … Ariana Grande, left, and Jonathan Bailey have both now left the production of Sunday in the Park With George.Composite: Shuttershock, GettyMusicalsSunday in the Park With George musical cancelled, after Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey both drop outThe star-studded Sondheim musical has hit the buffers after a second star, Jonathan Bailey, joined his Wicked colleague Ariana Grande and left the productionTim JonzeMon 14 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst, it wasAriana Grande who dropped out. Then her co-starJonathan Baileyfollowed her out the door. Now, the London revival of Sunday in the Park With Georgehas been cancelled altogether, with organisers perhaps anticipating that it would be hard to sell tickets for a star-studded musical without the stars.Grande and Bailey, who appeared together as Glinda and Fiyero in Wicked andWicked: For Good, had originally been cast as Dot and George in Stephen Sondheim’s hit musical. It was set to debut at the Barbican in the summer of 2027.But in August, Grande pulled out, citing the need to take a break from “endless public scrutiny”. The pop star, who was coming to the end of her Eternal Sunshine tour, had been the subject of press speculation surrounding her weight loss and general health, which intensified after the release of the music video for her song Petal.The production vowed to soldier on, with new casting promised, but was then hit with the news earlier this month that Bailey had also had second thoughts. In a statement, the Bridgerton star announced his departure, saying: “Ari is one of my dearest friends. After much consideration, I have decided to also step back from Sunday in the Park With George. This brilliant, introspective musical has been a real passion project for me, and I feel incredibly lucky to have shared in its journey with this team. I look forward to seeing what the team, and the two actors who will now take on these roles, will create with it.”Sadly, it seems that what production company Empire Street Productions have decided to do with it is cancel it, at least in the short term. A statement from the company said: “The planned 2027 production of Sunday in the Park With George at the Barbican will no longer proceed as scheduled. Empire Street Productions will retain the rights with a view to presenting the production in 2028. Further details will be announced in due course.”The musical, created by Sondheim and James Lapine, made its Broadway debut in 1984, starring Mandy Patinkin and Bernadette Peters as George and Dot. A year later it won the Pulitzer prize for drama. The musical’s story is inspired by the Georges Seurat painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, and follows the artist as he attempts to finish the pointillist masterpiece, while exploring his relationship with Dot, his lover and muse.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsStephen SondheimAriana GrandeWickedWicked: For GoodJonathan BaileynewsShareReuse this content

title: Oasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concerts | Oasis | The Guardian
description: After 2025’s wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, and revisit the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumph
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: After 2025’s wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, and revisit the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumph
Content: Liam Gallagher (left) and Noel Gallagher of Oasis, who are to return to Knebworth in 2027.Photograph: Joshua Halling/Oasis/PAView image in fullscreenLiam Gallagher (left) and Noel Gallagher of Oasis, who are to return to Knebworth in 2027.Photograph: Joshua Halling/Oasis/PAOasisOasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concertsAfter 2025’s wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, and revisit the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumphFrom the archive: How did the Guardian cover Oasis at Knebworth 1996? Well … we didn’tLaura SnapesMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOasis have finally confirmed new tour dates for 2027, including their long-rumoured return to Knebworth for a run of shows 30 years after they played a historic two nights at the Hertfordshire venue in 1996.“Start the celebrations!”, the band said in a statement. “After a period of reflection, The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force in Recent British History” – a quote froma Guardian opinion pieceabout the band – “has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people. Come witness the fitness. It shall be a sight to behold.”Titled Oasis Live 27, the dates encompass the UK, Ireland, mainland Europe and the US, beginning in Glasgow on 21 May, and touring through Manchester, Munich, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome, Boston, Las Vegas and Slane Castle (north of Dublin), ending with four nights at Knebworth in September.The band had teased the news in a massive drone display above Manchester’s Etihad stadium last week, after hinting at the dates on Instagram.The tour follows Oasis’s acclaimed 2025 reunion, which saw them play 41 dates spanning the UK, Europe, North and South America, east Asia and Australia, 16 years after they split in 2009. “You struggle to think of another artist that’s received such a vociferous reception,” wrote Guardian critic Alexis Petridis ina five-star reviewof the first night of the tour in Cardiff.The 2027 tour will be Oasis’s first visit to mainland Europe since their reunion and adds US cities they didn’t visit during that run. Their return to Paris will be particularly poignant, given it was shortly before a 2009 set at the city’s Rock en Seine festival that the band first split up.In the UK, tickets will cost between £71.50 and £266.60. Those hoping to buy them will have a happier experience than those in the same position last year: all pricing information for Oasis Live 27 has been shared in advance after action by the competition watchdog forced Ticketmasterto change how it advertises tickets, including ending “misleading” information about seats, after fan backlash over its handling of the 2025 tour.Last year, the use of “tiered” pricing meant that some fans, expecting to pay £148.50 per ticket, found themselves faced with costs of £350 at the checkout – and only a matter of minutes in which to decide whether to go ahead with their purchases. Now, Ticketmaster must tell fans 24 hours in advance if tiered pricing will be used, which tickets it covers and how the system works. When the sale is live, the price range must be shared and updated as tickets sell out.Anyone wanting a ticket for 2027’s tour mustregisterbetween now and 4pm BST on 17 September. The registration has been introduced “to reduce queuing times and organised ticket touting in order to give genuine fans the best possible chance to buy tickets,” according to organisers.View image in fullscreenOasis pictured at Knebworth in 1996.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyFans had a chance to revisit the 2025 tour – or catch up on what they missed – as a documentary about the reunion,Don’t Look Back in Anger, hit cinemas last week after premiering at the Venice film festival. It earned glowing reviews for its emotional portrait of the band’s fans.The documentary didn’t touch on the furore around ticket prices, other than one onstage comment from Liam Gallagher: after referring to the people in the cheap seats, he added: “Actually there are no cheap seats, sorry about that.”The news that Oasis would return toKnebworth was first teased by an unlikely suspect, the British peer Baroness Taylor of Stevenage. In October 2025, she suggested in the House of Lords that Oasis would be playing five shows “in the fantastic venue of Knebworth House”, just a mile away from her own residence.Don’t Look Back in Anger trailer – videoShe quickly retracted her comments in the chamber,clarifying to the Guardianthat she was “speaking hypothetically following speculation that they would play Knebworth again as they did in August 1996”.In August, it was reported that SJM Concerts managing director Simon Moran had secured an events licence for Knebworth, prompting further speculation about an Oasis appearance. The licence would cover audiences of 125,000 people.At the original 1996 dates, the band played to 250,000 fans – just one tenth of the number who applied for tickets, estimated at the time to be more than 4% of the entire British population. “This is history,” Noel Gallagher told the Knebworth crowd on the second night. The bandrecently started selling replicasof Noel and Liam’s respective outfits on the night.A 2021 documentary, the prosaically titled Oasis Knebworth 1996, positioned the concerts as “the peak of British culture” wrote Guardian music editor Ben Beaumont-Thomas ina four-star review. The film’s voiceovers, he continued, implied that “all live music went downhill afterwards. It’s a lie every generation tells itself.” Liam subsequently headlined the park in June 2022.UK Music estimated that the band’s five nights at Manchester’s Heaton Park last year led to music tourist spending in the north-westrising 16% year on year to £1.4bn. Momentum behind the tour was alsocredited with boostingthe UK’s ongoing vinyl revival.Do you remember the first time? Why Britpop nostalgia just won’t go awayRead moreOasis are also rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027, the festival’s return after a fallow year in 2026.Their reunion poured more fuel on the fire of enduring Britpop nostalgia, sparking acritically panned playdocumenting the rivalry between Oasis and Blur, an album called Britpop by Robbie Williams and evenan embrace of Oasis in the US, a country that had been historically immune to their charms.Oasis Live 27 tour dates in fullCeltic Park, Glasgow: 21, 23, 25, 28, 29 MayEtihad Stadium, Manchester: 4, 6, 8, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19, 22, 25, 26 JuneAllianz Arena, Munich: 2, 3 JulyEstadi Olímpic Lluís Companys, Barcelona: 10, 11 JulyJohan Cruijff Arena, Amsterdam: 16, 17 JulyStade de France, Paris: 23, 24 JulyStadio Olimpico, Rome: 29, 30 JulyGillette Stadium, Boston: 10, 13, 14 AugustAllegiant Stadium, Las Vegas: 20, 21, 24 AugustSlane Castle, Ireland: 4, 5 SeptemberKnebworth, Hertfordshire: 11, 12, 18, 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsOasisNoel GallagherLiam GallagherPop and rockBritpopnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Signs of violence’: asylum seekers arriving in France injured after being deported from UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: French health service documents injuries including fractures and bruising after detention and return under ‘one in one out’ scheme
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: French health service documents injuries including fractures and bruising after detention and return under ‘one in one out’ scheme
Content: Samusocial de Paris’s report includes a case of one person who arrived in France in such a bad state he was sent to A&E.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenSamusocial de Paris’s report includes a case of one person who arrived in France in such a bad state he was sent to A&E.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAImmigration and asylum‘Signs of violence’: asylum seekers arriving in France injured after being deported from UKFrench health service documents injuries including fractures and bruising after detention and return under ‘one in one out’ schemeDiane TaylorMon 14 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMultiple injuries including bruising and fractures have been documented by a health service supporting people returned toFranceunder the controversial “one in, one out” scheme.The pilot scheme involves one asylum seeker who crosses the Channel in a small boat being returned to France in return for another in northern France being legally brought to the UK to claim asylum. The scheme isdue to end on 1 October.Samusocial de Paris (SSP) has been commissioned by Île-de-France’s regional health agency to provide healthcare for asylum seekers returned to France in the first eight days after their deportation from the UK, when they are accommodated in a shelter in Paris.They have documented the cases of 90 returnees between 22 January and 7 June 2026. All are young men, mostly in their 20s and early-30s, who sought sanctuary in the UK after fleeing a variety of conflict zones including Eritrea, Sudan and Afghanistan.About 1,400 people have been forcibly removed to France by the Home Office since the scheme began in August 2025, althoughsome have subsequently returnedto the UK in lorries or small boats.The evidence compiled by SSP has been submitted to the French Assembly’s cross-party inquiry into the impact of the Anglo-French border deals known as Le Touquet agreements. This evidence comes from their own clinical consultations with returnees and some hospital reports from those sent to A&E.Many of those detained in the UK for “one in one out” have fled torture and other forms of persecution in their home countries, and have been subjected to modern slavery on their journeys in countries such as Libya. However, the focus of the report is on what happened to people while they were detained in the UK as part of the scheme and during their removal to France.View image in fullscreenPeople wade into the water at Gravelines, France, hoping to board a small boat to the UK.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesAccording to the report: “Consultations are revealing signs consistent with recent physical and psychological violence as well as the consequences of prolonged detention in conditions described as particularly degrading.” It states that the physical and psychological conditions documented are “explicitly linked to the implementation of the France-British agreement”.The report adds: “The frequency and recurrence of the incidents reported by people transferred under the Franco-British agreement appear particularly worrying.”One A&E medical report from a returnee who arrived in France in such a bad state that he was sent to hospital reads: “The patient’s general condition was marked by significant suffering and shock upon arrival necessitating referral to the hospital emergency department. The medical certificate mentions reports of physical violence in England, including diffuse bruising, injuries consistent with restraint (lacerations with handcuffs) and abdominal pain resulting from repeated blows.”The report includes 13 case studies documenting a range of injuries, including problems that worsened due to a lack of medical treatment, while people were in detention in the UK. Concerns were also raised about mental health conditions such as PTSD.In one case, a man was referred for emergency psychiatric treatment because he was too disoriented to find his way back to the dormitory while in the shelter, suffered from body tics and incoherent speech and was deemed to be at risk of suicide. The report highlights limited options for ongoing psychiatric treatment for this group.SSP recommends that a mechanism should be established to collect information on allegations of mistreatment by the British authorities that can be sent to the UK. It also suggests reporting this issue to the French prosecutor under article 40 of the French code of criminal procedure.Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, which also provides health support for this group of returnees, said: “This one in one out agreement is a machine for psychological destruction.“The deeply concerning physical injuries sustained whilst in detention in the United Kingdom, which we have documented among those deported, must be viewed in the light of a serious psychological deterioration.”Mitie, a contractor providing the guards for the asylum seekers, has been approached for comment.AHome Officespokesperson said: “We take the welfare of those returned to France incredibly seriously. Migrants have regular access to healthcare while in detention and anyone unfit to travel will not be returned.“Contractors must adhere to strict standards of dignity and respect throughout the removal process.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumFranceRefugeesEuropeHome OfficenewsShareReuse this content

title: Top civil servant sacked by Starmer received record £860,000 payout | Civil service | The Guardian
description: Special approval needed for amount that surpassed what Chris Wormald was ‘contractually entitled to’
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Special approval needed for amount that surpassed what Chris Wormald was ‘contractually entitled to’
Content: Chris Wormald, pictured here in 2020, now sits in the House of Lords.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenChris Wormald, pictured here in 2020, now sits in the House of Lords.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyCivil serviceTop civil servant sacked by Starmer received record £860,000 payoutSpecial approval needed for amount that surpassed what Chris Wormald was ‘contractually entitled to’Jessica ElgotDeputy political editorMon 14 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 19.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former head of the civil service Chris Wormald received a record payout of almost £860,000 when he was forced out of the top job in Whitehall byKeir Starmer.Cabinet Office accounts have revealed that the former cabinet secretary, who wassacked earlier this year, was paid £859,496 upon departure. The figure is an unprecedented amount, which required civil servants to seek a special direction from ministers to approve it because it was “greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to”.Wormald has since been made a member of theHouse of Lords, after serving as cabinet secretary for just 14 months. He was replaced by Antonia Romeo earlier this year.It was revealed earlier this summer that the size of the payout to Wormald was so vast that Cat Little, the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office, had to request a ministerial direction from Starmer in February to override value-for-money concerns before she could approve it.In her letter to the prime minister at the time, Little wrote that she needed special permission to grant such a high award, saying “in respect of value for money, I have consulted civil service HR and legal advisers and have had due regard to managing public money and the consideration of Sir Chris Wormald’s employment rights in the circumstances. The proposed award is greater than what Sir Chris Wormald would be contractually entitled to.”Little said she had been informed a settlement of that level was “necessary given that this is a departure from a high-profile, unique role that has been agreed at very short notice”.She said the prime minister could take into account “the public interest in bringing this matter to a conclusion and the prevention of distraction from the effective operation of government”.Civil service chief got record £500,000 payout after Starmer dismissalRead moreTheConservativessaid the payout was an “appalling waste”. The shadow Cabinet Office minister Alex Burghart said: “Chris Wormald was just one of many civil servants and advisers fired by Keir Starmer as he tried to save his own skin.“This payout is another appalling waste of taxpayers’ money byLabour. Whether it’s big payouts for fall guys, or gimmicky giveaways, this government is always happy to spend our money if it thinks it will benefit the Labour party.”The settlement with Wormald dwarfs the previous record amount given to the former Treasury permanent secretary Tom Scholar, who was forced out by Liz Truss in one of her first acts as prime minister. He was given £457,000, including severance pay and compensation in lieu of notice and leave.Wormald became a crossbench peer after he was nominated by Starmer as the former prime minister left office.At the time, No 10 had been criticised over its handling of Wormald’s departure, with his allies saying he had been badly treated and learned of his fate through the media.Dave Penman, the general secretary of the senior civil servants’ union the FDA, said the briefing against Wormald had been extraordinary and that it was “no way to run a country”.Explore more on these topicsCivil serviceKeir StarmerLabourConservativesHouse of LordsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sweden’s political parties launch coalition talks as both blocs try to secure power | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Centre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battle
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Centre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battle
Content: The Social Democrats’ party leader, Magdalena Andersson, has started a long and difficult process of trying to form a new government.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Social Democrats’ party leader, Magdalena Andersson, has started a long and difficult process of trying to form a new government.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPASwedenSweden’s political parties launch coalition talks as both blocs try to secure powerCentre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battleMiranda BryantNordic correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSweden’s political parties have launched coalition negotiations as the Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, started the long and difficult process of trying to form a new government.Full results from Sunday’s election are not expected until after overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, but with 95% of the votes counted, the Social Democrats and the centre-left bloc had a narrow but growing lead of 176 seats to the right-leaning parties’ 173.The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remainsRead moreAfter losing support for the first time since they were founded, the far-right Sweden Democrats, who were hoping to enter government for the first time, appear to be out of the picture. But many of its policy ideas – on immigration laws, integration and crime – have become mainstream, including in the centre-left.Both Andersson and the outgoing centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, of the Moderates have each said they want to explore possible coalition options to secure power.View image in fullscreenSweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, leader of the conservative Moderates, has said he wants to explore possible coalitions to secure power for another term.Photograph: Christine Olsson/TT/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesAfter a long election night during which there was just one seat between the two blocs, Social Democrat leaders met Andersson on Monday morning at the party’s Stockholm headquarters.Questions remain as to whether the bloc is willing to work with the Left party (Vänsterpartiet), which the Centre party has previously ruled out.The Social Democrats press secretary, Tobias Baudin, said he had been in contact with colleagues from opposition parties and called for the resignation of Kristersson, who led the rightwing Tidö coalition government with the support of the Sweden Democrats.“Now the voters have had their say and they have given him a failing grade for himself and his government,” Baudin told the Swedish broadcaster SVT, adding: “He should resign himself. In fact it doesn’t matter, if he doesn’t resign he will be removed. How he does it is up to him.The Centre party said that in talks with the Social Democrats it would be seeking a government with a “desire for political stability” and a “clear centre-right character” with no “fringe politics”.The Social Democrat Morgan Johansson, who under the last Social Democrat-led government was deputy prime minister, said the Centre party’s announcement was a positive development and that overall there were “good prospects”.All of the left-leaning parties want a change of government, he said. “That is the starting point. I don’t think anyone wants us to end up in a situation where blockages lead to a new election.”Meanwhile, Kristersson appears to be keeping his options open.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Sunday night he said the result could lead to a “complicated government formation, where it ends remains to be seen”. On Monday, before a meeting with his fellow Tidö coalition leaders, he declined to elaborate, saying he would wait for a full result before having conversations. “If all the red lines remain then Sweden won’t have a government at all,” he added. “I plan to pursue a number of possibilities that may exist.”The Liberals and Christian Democrats have both said they will not work with the Social Democrats.After the overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, the final election results are not expected until the weekend.The new parliament will meet for the first time on 28 September and the earliest date that the speaker can suggest a prime minister is 29 September, but talks could take considerably longer. If, when parliament votes for a prime minister candidate, more than half say no, then the speaker must find a new candidate. If there are four failed votes there will automatically be a new election.After the 2022 election, it took 37 days to form a government; in 2018 it took 134 days to form a new coalition.Fredrik Furtenbach, the senior political correspondent at Sveriges Radio (Radio Sweden), said: “I think it will end with either the Left or Centre party having to give way. It might take several failed prime minister votes first.” But he does not believe the Social Democrats and Moderates, who he describes as “traditional archenemies”, will end up working together. “You cannot share the position of prime minister.”Explore more on these topicsSwedenEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gulf states postpone strait of Hormuz talks with Iran as Yemen conflict intensifies | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Impasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipeline
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Impasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipeline
Content: Houthi armed forces patrol Sana’a over the weekend  as the rebel group swept down the west coast of Yemen and seized the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHouthi armed forces patrol Sana’a over the weekend  as the rebel group swept down the west coast of Yemen and seized the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesStrait of HormuzGulf states postpone strait of Hormuz talks with Iran as Yemen conflict intensifiesImpasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipelineOil prices rise after drone attacks shut down Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipelinePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 14 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGulf states have postponed a critical meeting with Iran on the future of the strait of Hormuz owing to a lack of Arab consensus and growing Saudi Arabian anger with Tehran for helping the Houthis loosen Riyadh’s grip in Yemen.The stalemate over the vital waterway came as Houthi rebels launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A Houthi military spokesperson claimed its forces had attacked the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, hitting fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways and landing strips, ammunition depots and additional targets.Last week, Tehran-backed militias in Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close a critical east-west pipeline that had been acting as a means for Riyadh to export oil afterIraneffectively closed the strait of Hormuz.The closure of the pipeline, the postponement of the Hormuz meeting, and the Houthis’ seizure last week of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – which gave the group control over another vital waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait – combined todrive up oil pricesabove $108 a barrel on Monday.Later in the day, Houthi officials said they had seized the strategic islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish in the southern Red Sea just inside the mouth of the strait, according to the AP.View image in fullscreenA screengrab of video released by the Houthi authorities shows fighters during an offensive in the port city of Mocha, Yemen.Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPAAlso on Monday, the Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, held urgent discussions with the US ⁠Central Command chief ⁠Adm ​Brad Cooper in Jeddah to discuss “the latest developments in the region”, according to Saudi media. Sources told US media last week that the Saudi de facto ruler had sought military assistance ‌from Donald Trump to help fight theHouthis. So far the US has provided only logistical and intelligence backing,Middle East map 14 SeptemberThe Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting was postponed at the last minute, deferring a proposed agreement on a new temporary route for commercial shipping when the strait of Hormuz is reopened.In a statement, Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, said the meeting had been delayed in the interests of consensus. “We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting co-operation in our region,” he wrote on X. He gave no further details.The meeting would not have led to the immediate opening of the strait, since Tehran has set a series of other preconditions: including requiring the US to lift a blockade of Iran’s oil ports, the handing over of many frozen Iranian assets and a ceasefire in Lebanon.But it would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member countries for two years. The planned agreement on a temporary route for ships to use would have formalised Iran’s control of the strait, since the entry route would have been entirely in Iranian waters.Washington has not expressed publicly an opinion over the proposed deal, and some of Trump’s recent social media posts – claiming full US control of the strait – seemed to bear little relationship with what shipping companies have been reporting.The atmosphere surrounding the meeting, in preparation for weeks, had been rapidly souring because of the advance by the Houthis inYemenand the drone attack on the Saudi pipeline by an Iran-backed Shia militia in Iraq.Vantor Technologies released high-resolution satellite images showing the damage to the east-west pipeline pumping station near Al Mesba’ah, Saudi Arabia. The station appears to be almost completely destroyed.View image in fullscreenA satellite shows damage to a pumping station along the east-west pipeline near Al Mesaba’ah, Saudi Arabia.Photograph: Satellite image ©2026 Vantor/AFP/Getty ImagesIran’s foreign ministry spokesperson denied any Iranian involvement in the pipeline attack, or on events in Yemen.US military bases throughout the Gulf have been attacked by Iran in response to the Iran war.Saudi Arabia, which backs the UN-recognised Yemeni government based in Aden, is trying to regain the initiative after Houthi forces swept down the west coast of Yemen from the port of Hodeidah last week and seized the Bab al-Mandab strait, a narrow waterway that links the Red Sea with Asia and is viewed as second in strategic importance to the strait of Hormuz.It was claimed that a Saudi air bombardment was making it difficult for the Houthis to gain full control of the Yemen waterway or the strategic islands in the Red Sea.View image in fullscreenA commercial vessel anchored off Yemen’s coast at Bab al-Mandab. The Houthis leadership says it is seeking to block only Saudi-linked ships.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe Houthi leadership says is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea but only Saudi-linked ships. It is also offering cut-price fees in the ports it controls on the west coast of Yemen in an effort to lure traffic away from the ports controlled by the Aden-based government in the south.It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, but the group also operates independently of Tehran. The rebels ultimate aim is to oust Saudi Arabia from the country, and take full control of the territory.Saudi Arabia has tried different tactics in handling the Houthis during the decade-long civil war in Yemen, including making concessions in the hope the highly ideological group would reach a power-sharing deal.The Yemen government said preliminary tolls indicated that 150 civilians had been killed and 200 others injured in the course of the recent Houthi advance. About 85,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzYemenSaudi ArabiaHouthisIranSaudi Arabia drone attacksUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Alligator Alcatraz held detainees in cages the size of phone booths, DHS watchdog says | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Office of inspector general’s report says practice at Florida immigration jail is not aligned with ‘humane treatment’
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Office of inspector general’s report says practice at Florida immigration jail is not aligned with ‘humane treatment’
Content: Small cages that were used in the ICE detention facility in Ochopee, Florida.Photograph: OIG/DHSView image in fullscreenSmall cages that were used in the ICE detention facility in Ochopee, Florida.Photograph: OIG/DHSUS immigrationAlligator Alcatraz held detainees in cages the size of phone booths, DHS watchdog saysOffice of inspector general’s report says practice at Florida immigration jail is not aligned with ‘humane treatment’Richard Luscombein MiamiMon 14 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore the facility wasshuttered, detainees atFlorida’s “Alligator Alcatraz” federal immigration jail were frequently locked in outside metal cages no bigger than a phone booth, according to a damning government watchdog report that said the practice “does not align with standards for humane treatment”.The findings from the office of the inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) werepublishedon its website – and offer rare criticism of the Trump administration by one of its own agencies.The report also provides the first official confirmation that guards repeatedly used the highly restrictive cages on detainees in direct contravention of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rules.In December, the Guardian was the firstto reportan Amnesty International dossier detailing multiple alleged human rights abuses at the controversial camp in the remote Florida Everglades, including how people were regularly shackled outside in metal cages for hours as well as exposed to brutal heat, sunshine and swarms of mosquitoes.At the time, a spokesperson forRon DeSantis, the Republican Florida governor whose administration ran Alligator Alcatraz on behalf of the federal government, dismissed the claims now confirmed by the DHS report as “fabrications” – and the Amnesty report as “a politically motivated attack”.Call for inquiry into Alligator Alcatraz’s ‘abuse of Everglades’ despite closureRead moreOn Monday, his office declined to answer why it falsely denied using the cages and instead attempted to portray the detainees – with no evidence – as “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful while awaiting deportation”.In a statement, Alex Lanfranconi, DeSantis’s communications manager, contended that “the leftwing media wants to focus on a confinement area” which “adheres to all federal standards for criminal confinement”.His statement added: “We’d make it even smaller if we could.”Amy Fischer, Amnesty International USA’s director for refugee and migrant rights, said in a statement: “The findings confirm what we documented months ago: the horrific treatment of people detained at Alligator Alcatraz was real, not a hoax, as Trump administration officials wereon the recordsaying.“This report should serve as a reminder that the public must never simply take the government’s word when officials deny that human rights violations are occurring.”Thenotoriousimmigration jailclosedin June after a year of operation during which DeSantisboastedof detaining and deporting more than 21,000 immigrants. Officials cited the risk of holding detainees in tents during hurricane season for the closure.Critics, however, said the$1.2mof taxpayers’ money that DeSantis was spending on the camp daily was fast becoming a political millstone – while separate lawsuits swirled over the jail’s impact on the environmentally fragile Florida wetlands, and the harsh mental and physical treatment of detainees that several Democratic lawmakers decried as akin to “torture”.The inspector general’s office report exposed numerous failings found during an unannounced January 2026 visit by DHS inspectors to Alligator Alcatraz, which theyreferto as the Florida Soft-Sided Facility (FSSF). Many of the shortcomings, they said, posed “significant risks to detainee health and safety”.“FSSF did not provide detainees with sufficient living space, creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units, which may harm detainees’ physical and mental health,” the report said.Additionally, it studied records that revealed 79 instances between July 2025 and January 2026 in which guards placed detainees in the metal cages for up to two hours at a time.Each cage, the report noted, offered only about 18 sq ft of floor space, less than half the minimum 37 sq ft required for single-person spaces by ICE’s own publishednational detention standards. The inspector general’s discovery of cases in January means detainees were still being confined in the cramped cages more than a month after Amnesty International exposed the practice and DeSantis’s office denied it was taking place.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe report acknowledged concerns raised by the Democratic US senators Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Dick Durbin of Illinois in March over the use of the cages known to detainees as “The Box”. But the report said facility staff insisted they were used as “calming areas” for detainees “to deescalate and have time alone”.“Staff further maintained that detainees asked to spend time” in them, the report said.However, inspectors found at least one time in which a cage was documented to have been used as a disciplinary tool: for a detainee who “failed to comply with a lawful command”. Inspectors noted that there were locking mechanisms on the cages.“Use of these small metal enclosures for any reason is unprecedented among ICE facilities inspected by OIG,” the report said. “Confining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and wellbeing.”Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and chief executive of the immigration advocacy group Global Refuge, said in a statement: “There is no euphemism that can sanitize caging human beings. Calling a metal box a ‘calming area’ is an affront to the English language and to human dignity alike.“The stark reality is that human beings, many of whom came to this country seeking protection, were crammed into spaces unfit to accommodate them, denied adequate medical care, food and basic hygiene. That is not immigration enforcement. It is cruelty.”Human cages and overflowing toilets at $1m a day: the brutal legacy of Ron DeSantis’s ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ jailRead moreOther failures noted by the DHS inspectors during their tour of detention spaces, and kitchen and bathroom areas, included overcrowding, a lack of sufficient recreation time for detainees, and inoperable telephones preventing detainees from contacting their attorneys or families, and poor food hygiene standards leading to the risk of contamination and illness.Multiple detainees told the inspectors in January they had limited or no access to clean drinking water. The Guardianreported in Junethat the practice appeared to be continuing, with detainees complaining that guards were withholding clean water and food as punishment – or until they signed documents in English that they did not understand.TheFloridadepartment of emergency management, which oversaw the operation of the facility using private guards, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationFloridaTrump administrationICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Ron DeSantisUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bob Mackie, costume designer to stars daring to be noticed, dies aged 87 | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Famous for his flamboyant outfits, he helped celebrities including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John cause a stir
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Famous for his flamboyant outfits, he helped celebrities including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John cause a stir
Content: Cher, left, and designer Bob Mackie arrive at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Gala on 25 September 2021, in Los Angeles.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APView image in fullscreenCher, left, and designer Bob Mackie arrive at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures Gala on 25 September 2021, in Los Angeles.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APCostume & cultureFashionBob Mackie, costume designer to stars daring to be noticed, dies aged 87Famous for his flamboyant outfits, he helped celebrities including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John cause a stirLauren CochraneMon 14 Sep 2026 14.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBob Mackie, the costume designer behind some of the most sexy and glamorous outfits worn by celebrities in the past 50 years, has died at the age of 87.“He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a fashion and costume designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” read a statement posted on his Instagram account. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”View image in fullscreenCher wears a creation by Bob Mackie as she poses with actor Don Ameche after presenting him with the Oscar for best supporting actor at the Academy awards in Los Angeles, 24 March 1986.Photograph: Lennox McLendon/APMackie’s work can be seen in the wardrobes of stars ranging from Marilyn Monroe to Carol Burnett, Liza Minnelli, Elton John, Dolly Parton, Tina Turner and – perhaps most memorably – Cher. He designed the ‘naked’ dress the singer wore to attend the Met Gala in 1975, the midriff-baring outfit with an oversized Mohawk headdress she wore to the Oscars in 1986 and the transparent body stocking she wore for theIf I Could Turn Back Timevideo in 1989.The Met Gala outfit has since become a reference for a younger generation. Kim Kardashian wore a dress modelled on it for the same event in 2015.More recently, Taylor Swift wore one of Mackie’s original Jubilee! cabaret costumeson the cover of her 12th studio album, The Life of a Showgirl, while Sabrina Carpenter and Zendaya have also worn archival looks by the designer. In 2024, the singer Miley Cyrus paid an undisclosed sum to buy the Mackietasseled mini dressshe had worn to perform at the Grammys.Last year at an auction, Cher’s “naked” bodysuit fetched $57,600 (£42,600),seven times its estimated price, while a silver and gold fringed bodysuit with lamé wings that Mackie designed for Tina Turner for a 1977 performance sold for $19,200 (£14,200).The designer first began working withCherfor The Sonny and Cher show in the 1960s and remained a collaborator for decades. Cher has paid tribute to his contribution to her career, saying that without Mackie “I would have been a peacock without feathers”.Mackie’s first notable design has another connection to Kardashian – as assistant to designer Jean Louis, he sketched the dress Marilyn Monroe wore to sing Happy Birthday to president John F Kennedy in 1962. Kardashianwore the original dress to the Met Gala in 2022– to the disapproval of much of the fashion world, who thought it should be preserved. Mackie was one of the people who spoke out. “I thought it was a big mistake,” he said toEntertainment Weekly. “It was designed for [Monroe]. Nobody else should be seen in that dress.”In 1963, he began to work on The Judy Garland Show, and met his collaborator and partner Ray Aghayan. Work for the Supremes, and then Diana Ross, followed. The duo were nominated for an Oscar for the costumes Ross wore in the 1973 Billie Holliday biopic Lady Sings the Blues.Mackie’s motto was “dare to be noticed” and his costumes certainly gained attention for the people wearing them. Elton John’s duck costume, worn in 1980, has become notorious. But the designs also sometimes made points. Cher’s outfit for the Oscars in 1986 was so flamboyant because the star felt she was snubbed for her performance in Mask and wanted to take revenge when she was presenting an award.Speaking to the New York Times a year latershe said: “OK, you can go in a simple black dress and be just like everyone else. But then I decided, I’m going to remind them of what they don’t like about me.” Mackie obliged with his creation.Turner’s “flame” dress, worn in 1977 after her split from her abusive partner and musical collaborator, Ike, turned the star into a gloriously unsubtle phoenix rising from the ashes.The designer hasn’t always been harmonious with his clients. His work with Cher had tensions. In 2018,talking to the Guardianabout the raunchy Turn Back Time outfit, he said he thought it was “vulgar and horrid”. “I told her: please, I don’t want any credit for this,” he said. In2019, he described Garlandas “a big handful” and said he refused to design costumes for a recent Cher tour. “I’m in touch with clients only when they need clothes,” he said. “I never want to be their best friend.”Mackie diversified beyond costume design. He launched a clothing line in 1982 and made Bob Mackie collectible Barbies. Working with QVC from 1999, Mackie’s aesthetic has been utilised on everything from fragrance to luggage to high-end jewellery – and in 2009 he appeared as a guest judge on RuPaul’s Drag Race.Mackie gained plaudits for his unique take on glamour in recent years. The Fashion Institute of Technology staged the Unmistakably Bob exhibition in 1999, and he received the prestigious Geoffrey Beene CFDA Lifetime Achievement award in 2019. He wasfront and centreof the Diva exhibition at London’s V&A in 2023, with Turner’s flame dress a highlight. The exhibition showed how Mackie’s design accentuated Turner’s showmanship and made her performance even more memorable. This was, ultimately, Mackie’s talent. “I’m very serious about this,” he said in 2018. “It’s not just flamboyant, crazy stuff. It’s all very worked out.”Several celebrities paid tribute to the designer on social media.Carpenter wrote on Instagram that she felt “so lucky to have met Bob.“His one of a kind creations have inspired and brought so much happiness and confidence to my world and they will continue to always x Mackie girl forever.”Kathy Lennon, a member of the vocal group The Lennon Sisters, described Mackie as “always so welcoming and complimentary when we went to his amazing costume showroom.”“In a sea of ego, he seemed to have none,” Elton John wrote on Instagram. “One of the most courteous, incredible people I ever had the pleasure of working with.”The Canadian model Coco Rocha said it was an“enormous privilege”to work with Mackie and wear his designs.“There are designers whose work defines a moment, and then there are those rare few whose imagination teaches fashion something for generations,” Rocha said on Instagram. “Bob was one of them. His clothes had wit, drama, fantasy and joy.”Explore more on these topicsFashionCostume & cultureCherTina TurnernewsShareReuse this content

title: Government moves to nationalise Speciality Steel UK to protect 1,300 jobs | Steel industry | The Guardian
description: Firm, once part of Sanjeev Gupta’s empire, fell into administration last year but has failed to find buyer
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Firm, once part of Sanjeev Gupta’s empire, fell into administration last year but has failed to find buyer
Content: An electric arc furnace at Speciality Steel UK’s plant in Rotherham. The steelmaker also has sites in Stocksbridge, Brinsworth and Wednesbury.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn electric arc furnace at Speciality Steel UK’s plant in Rotherham. The steelmaker also has sites in Stocksbridge, Brinsworth and Wednesbury.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesSteel industryGovernment moves to nationalise Speciality Steel UK to protect 1,300 jobsFirm, once part of Sanjeev Gupta’s empire, fell into administration last year but has failed to find buyerBusiness news – live updatesAlex DanielMon 14 Sep 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Britain’s steelworks is to come into public ownership after the government said it would take over Yorkshire-based Speciality Steel UK (SSUK).Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said officials would “work towards” acquiring the company to protect the jobs of its 1,300 workers in Rotherham, Stocksbridge and Brinsworth in South Yorkshire and Wednesbury in theWest Midlands.The insolvent steelmaker,formerly part of the tycoon Sanjeev Gupta’s industrial empire, fell into administration last year and its day-to-day operations have since been run by the government’s official receiver.The Norwegian steel startup Blastr Green Steel had been in talks to buy SSUK, but hopes had faded over the summer for a private sector takeover after a deadline to finalise a deal passed in June.The steelworks and its staff have been described by Reynolds as important strategic assets for the UK. SSUK is the largest producer of “green steel”, made using less-polluting electric arc furnaces.Reynolds said: “We do not intervene in private companies lightly. But nor can we simply stand aside and allow the future of this company and over 1,300 jobs to be decided by default.“Working towards public acquisition will keep options open while we work with local leaders, workers, industry and investors to determine the best long-term future for these sites, which could play a vital role in the future of the growth-driving sectors in our industrial strategy, including defence and advanced manufacturing.SSUK went bust last year after longstanding financial issues under previous ownership, particularly after the collapse of its primary lender Greensill Capital in 2021. A high court judge at the time found the company was “hopelessly insolvent”, with only £650,000 in the bank after running down its reserves.Since then, the government has been funding the wages of its workers, costing £3.5m a month. The plantshave not been producing steelfor the last year, though some staff remain on its sites to maintain equipment.Ministers’ preference was for a private sector buyer, but after what were described as “extensive discussions” with Blastr, officials decided the company’s offer could not provide the desired long-term stability for SSUK.A Blastr spokesperson said: “We are disappointed by the government’s decision today concerning Speciality Steel UK, and we were not informed in advance. Over the course of several months, we have advanced our plans for a private sector solution to acquire SSUK – and were today on site in South Yorkshire with investors and strategic partners. We have a fully-funded proposal – at no cost to the British taxpayer – that is ready to complete within 12 weeks.”Mark Bula, the Blastr chief executive, quit the company unexpectedly at the end of last month, with its finance boss, David Morant, taking his place.The shadow business minister Bradley Thomas said it was “surprising” that the government had moved away from a private sector buyer after picking a preferred bidder. Speaking in parliament, he asked Reynolds: “Other than a new prime minister who’s committed ideologically to nationalisation, what has changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReynolds added there was “nothing ideological” about the move and that he would “not go into the detail” about why Blastr’s bid fell through. He accused the Conservatives of a “legacy of neglect” during their 14 years in government.The government has committed to spending up to £2.5bn on the steel industry through thenational wealth fund. About £500m of that was put towards converting Tata Steel’s blast furnaces into electric arc furnaces.The South Yorkshire mayor, Oliver Coppard, said he was pleased the government had taken action, adding: “It’s the next important step forward, giving us more time to find the best possible outcome for our steelmaking communities – places where people have faced economic challenges and real barriers to opportunity for far too long.”Roy Rickhuss, the general secretary of the Community union, welcomed the intervention but said the lack of a credible buyer was “a disappointing outcome”.He added: “SSUK is a unique and integral component of the UK’s steelmaking capabilities, without which we would be entirely reliant on foreign suppliers for high-value speciality inputs to our critical energy infrastructure and our advanced manufacturing base, including the defence industries. We cannot allow British industrial sovereignty in these areas to be lost.”Explore more on these topicsSteel industryManufacturing sectorNationalisationIndustrial policyRotherhamYorkshireWest MidlandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Crispin Odey loses appeal against lifetime ban from UK financial services industry | Financial sector | The Guardian
description: Judges uphold ruling that financier tried to ‘frustrate’ investigations into harassment claims against him
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Judges uphold ruling that financier tried to ‘frustrate’ investigations into harassment claims against him
Content: Crispin Odey during his appeal hearing in March, where judges say he ‘expressed no contrition’.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCrispin Odey during his appeal hearing in March, where judges say he ‘expressed no contrition’.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFinancial sectorCrispin Odey loses appeal against lifetime ban from UK financial services industryJudges uphold ruling that financier tried to ‘frustrate’ investigations into harassment claims against himKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 11.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former hedge fund boss Crispin Odey has lost a legal challenge to overturn his lifetime ban from the City for trying to “frustrate” investigations into sexual harassment allegations against him.A ruling by judges at the upper tribunal upheldthe ban imposed by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in March last year, while reducing a proposed fine of £1.83m to £1.53m.“We have found that Mr Odey lacked integrity,” the tribunal ruling said, referring to the Conservative party donor’s behaviour at Odey Asset Management (OAM) between December 2021 and November 2022.“Mr Odey is not a fit and proper person and it is reasonable for the authority to have concluded that a prohibition order is appropriate.”Numerous allegations against Odey by female members of staff came to light after OAM launched an internal investigation into sexual harassment at the business in September 2020.Odey, who resigned in 2023 after the allegations were reported in the media, tried to block executives of his hedge fund from taking any action, including by twice firing its entire executive committee (ExCo).“He misused his power as controller to remove the ExCos as a means to protect his own interests and attempt to achieve his objectives,” the tribunal ruling said.The judges also saidthe Brexit-backing hedge fund chieffailed to acknowledge any potential harm during a three-week appeal hearing in March. “He has expressed no contrition,” they added. “He sees nothing wrong with his approach, and indeed he wrongly sees himself as the victim.”The hearing involved a series of controversial admissions, including Odey blamingan incident in 2005 when he was alleged to have groped a colleague’s breastson the effect of sedatives he had taken after root canal treatment. He said the woman had accepted his apology and continued to work for the company for another eight years.He also told the appeal judges he did not remember cornering a female employee after a boozy lunch and saying to her“I could attack you now”.The allegations against Odey werefirst reported by the Financial Timesin summer 2023. OAM ceased trading months later.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCommenting on the ruling, the FCA’s executive director for enforcement and market oversight, Therese Chambers, said: “Mr Odey clearly thought he could act with impunity. He twice sacked those tasked with protecting female employees from his inappropriate behaviour when they tried to hold him to account. He felt the rules shouldn’t apply to him and acted to save his own skin.“During the hearing he reinvented history, painted himself as a victim and displayed no contrition. That arrogant entitlement and the resulting complete disregard for proper governance means Mr Odey is unfit to work in financial services.”Odey’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsFinancial sectorSexual harassmentFinancial Conduct AuthorityHedge fundsBankingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nine EU countries further delay EES border checks | European Union | The Guardian
description: Holiday hotspots including France and Greece plead for more time to implement changes in busy airports
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Holiday hotspots including France and Greece plead for more time to implement changes in busy airports
Content: The EU border entry-exit system was supposed to come into full force across the bloc on 6 September.Photograph: Jc Milhet/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe EU border entry-exit system was supposed to come into full force across the bloc on 6 September.Photograph: Jc Milhet/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesEuropean UnionNine EU countries further delay EES border checksHoliday hotspots including France and Greece plead for more time to implement changes in busy airportsWhat are the new EU border checks and how will they affect your holiday?Lisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNine EU countries, includingFrance, are delaying the introduction of fingerprinting for non-EU citizens as they plead for more time to introduce the new border controls at busy airports in the bloc.Theentry-exit system (EES), which was due to come into force in full on 6 September, has been delayed multiple times to avoid visitor congestion around large events, including the Olympics in 2024.Now nine countries, including the holiday hotspots France, Greece, Portugal and Italy, have told Brussels they need more time. Germany, Malta, the Netherlands,Switzerlandand Belgium have also sought extra time. Spain, which had teething problems, is implementing the EES fully.‘Pretty shambolic’: new EU border checks cause stress for UK travellersRead moreThe EES, which was first adopted by the EU in 2017, was officially launched last October and was due to become fully operational in April but early problems, particularly in Greece andPortugal, led to a further reprieve for member states.EU sources say the system is considered a success with about 200m registrations and 70,000 people stopped from entering the Schengen area, up from 43,700 in June.These include people without visas, those who have overstayed their 180-day allowance or Britons who have overstayed their 90-day allowance.Criminals using forged passports or ID documents have also been apprehended with fingerprint and facial image records exposing the use of different passports by individuals.View image in fullscreenEES machines at St Pancras International in London, where passengers board the Eurostar to the continent.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty ImagesThe delays in those nine member states are not countrywide. Fingerprinting has started at the Eurostar terminal in Brussels and Antwerp port but not in all airports.Large airports, such as Frankfurt and Schiphol – two of Europe’s busiest international hubs, are also taking biometrics but small airports may not be fully up to speed.Sources say just 12 airports out of 1,500 border crossing points are still having issues.France has also not introduced checks in the Port of Dover where French police are in the unique position to do border controls in a non-EU country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTechnically those that do not capture fingerprints and facial images are now in breach of the EU regulation, which ended any right to suspend the EES, but sources in Brussels have confirmed they will not be prosecuted.Earlier this summer, the EU noted that one of the airports was a small regional facility where 3,000 passengers could arrive in an hour in the peak holiday period, but could not be assessed because there were only four booths for biometric capture.The International Air Transport Associationhad demanded a full suspension in Julycomplaining that passengers were missing connections in Spain, Italy, Greece and Belgium, while Ryanair warned of “queue chaos” in airports including Málaga and Palma.The pre-authorisation app, Travel to Europe, which allows passengers to register their facial image and passport details before travelling, will shortly be working for seven countries, sources say.So far, it is showing as only operational in Sweden and Portugal.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionEuropeFranceFacial recognitionGreecePortugalItalyShareReuse this content

title: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds
Content: Aliko Dangote speaks at the Nigerian stock exchange in Lagos to launch the Dangote refinery IPO.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersView image in fullscreenAliko Dangote speaks at the Nigerian stock exchange in Lagos to launch the Dangote refinery IPO.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersNigeriaAfrica’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPOPublic offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirdsEromo Egbejulein Abidjan and agenciesMon 14 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery inNigerialisted publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October.The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors.‘There is nowhere to fish any more’: life in the shadow of Nigeria’s biggest industrial complexRead moreResponding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.”Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas.His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries.The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran.The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrelon Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security.“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.Explore more on these topicsNigeriaOilOil and gas companiesIPOsAfricaEnergy industryCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Davies admits to drawing on ‘stimulating’ Made in Chelsea for Jane Austen adaptation | Jane Austen | The Guardian
description: Screenwriter points to parallels between two worlds while academic says some of author’s characters ‘would make perfect reality show contestants’
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Screenwriter points to parallels between two worlds while academic says some of author’s characters ‘would make perfect reality show contestants’
Content: Some of the cast from Made  in Chelsea in 2021.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenSome of the cast from Made  in Chelsea in 2021.Photograph: Channel 4Jane AustenAndrew Davies admits to drawing on ‘stimulating’ Made in Chelsea for Jane Austen adaptationScreenwriter points to parallels between two worlds while academic says some of author’s characters ‘would make perfect reality show contestants’Nadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Jane Austen’s novels run on closed social worlds, courtship rituals, status anxiety, gossip and relentless scrutiny of who’s coupling with who, it follows that the obvious contemporary equivalent would be reality television.That’s according toAndrew Davies, the writer who has spent decades modernising British period dramas.Speaking on Radio 4’s Today programme on Monday, Davies revealed that he had been watching Made in Chelsea while working on an adaptation of Austen’s unfinished novel The Watsons.“It’s stimulating really for relationships and ideas,” he said of the Channel 4 series, which follows the relationship dramas and social rivalries of affluent young residents of west London. “These young men and women in The Watsons, for example, are very analogous to Made in Chelsea.”View image in fullscreenAndrew Davies said the young men and women in The Watsons were ‘very analogous’ to the characters of the Made in Chelsea reality show.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianDavies, whose memoir An Unsuitable Boy: A Life in Scripts is out this week, is responsible for the legendary image of Colin Firth as Mr Darcy emerging from a lake in a wet shirt in his 1995 BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, which went some way to injecting Austen into Bridget Jones, written by Helen Fielding around the time it aired. His approach, he said, had been about “bringing out the sex that’s inherent in Austen”.He has previously described his 2019 adaptation of Sanditon as “Love Island” in Austen’s world andtalked aboutwhether Charlotte would “friend-zone” someone or experience a “fanny flutter”. Meanwhile Rose Williams, who starred in the series,said she believed“Austen would probably write something satirical about Love Island if she were alive today”.Joe Bray, an Austen scholar and professor of English at the University of Sheffield, said of the author: “Jane Austen was a shrewd observer of the fashionable manners and fads adopted by the young … and the plots of most of her novels are driven by sexual attraction and/or secret liaisons and engagements.”The Steele sisters in Sense and Sensibility, he suggested, “would make perfect reality show contestants”.Austen also pioneered a way of representing the unspoken thoughts and feelings of her female characters that can be difficult to translate to screen. But Bray noted that Austen herself loved gossiping about neighbours and acquaintances in letters to her sister Cassandra. “I can’t say for certain whether or not she would be a viewer of Made in Chelsea or Love Island,” he said, “but … she would be interested at least!”An academic essay on Made in Chelseadescribed the programme as a “kind of homage” to Austen, arguing that its subject was the “courtship rituals” of young people with money and property, and compared its social world to Pride and Prejudice and Emma.View image in fullscreenAusten scholar Joe Bray suggested that the author would have at least been interested in the likes of Made in Chelsea and Love Island.Photograph: Stock Montage/Getty ImagesThere is indeed a human link between Made in Chelsea and Netflix’s forthcoming Pride and Prejudice: the latter’s writer and executive producer, Dolly Alderton, began her career as a story producer on the reality show – where, she has said, her job involved turning the romantic entanglements of wealthy young Londoners into “a four-part comedy drama”.It remains to be seen whether the Netflix series draws any inspiration from Made in Chelsea, but Reddit users havepreviously theorisedabout whether Alderton took inspiration from the reality show, or her TV adaptation of her memoir Everything I Know About Love. “Who do we think the character ‘Kyle’ is based off? I’m getting Spencer Matthews and Jamie Laing [both Made in Chelsea cast members],” one wrote.In her 2016 modernisation of Pride and Prejudice, Eligible, novelist Curtis Sittenfeld’s transplanted the Bennets to contemporary Cincinnati and made Chip Bingley a former reality-TV star who had appeared on The Bachelor.“Reality dating shows are so formulaic, and courtship in Austen’s time was rigid and proscriptive,”Sittenfeld said. In other words, reality TV provided a modern equivalent for Austen’s world of carefully prescribed romantic encounters; in place of the wealthy unmarried man arriving in the neighbourhood, there is the reality-TV bachelor whose romantic availability is already a matter of public interest.That may explain the extraordinary portability of Austen, from Clueless, which transplanted Emma to 1990s LA, and Bridget Jones’s Diary to Fire Island, Persuasion and the forthcoming Sense and Sensibility.John Mullan, a literature professor at University College London and historical and dialogue consultant on Bridgerton, identified another parallel.“In Austen’s fiction, courtship mostly takes place under the eyes of others,” he said. “Young women and men who might fancy each other are very rarely alone.”But, he added, there is a crucial difference: “What about propriety, restraint, repression? These are also key to Austen’s stories and characters.”Explore more on these topicsJane AustenAndrew DaviesReality TVTelevisionDramaE4newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve never been more terrified!’ Carly Rae Jepsen on motherhood, stardom and her horniest album ever | Carly Rae Jepsen | The Guardian
description: Call Me Maybe made the singer-songwriter famous – but also confused. Who was she? Who was her music for? Fourteen years later, about to release the double album Day and Night, she finally has some answers
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: Call Me Maybe made the singer-songwriter famous – but also confused. Who was she? Who was her music for? Fourteen years later, about to release the double album Day and Night, she finally has some answers
Content: ‘At this stage in my life, I feel much more comfortable with the parts that I don’t have full control over’ … Carly Rae Jepsen.Photograph: Vince AungView image in fullscreen‘At this stage in my life, I feel much more comfortable with the parts that I don’t have full control over’ … Carly Rae Jepsen.Photograph: Vince AungThe big interviewCarly Rae Jepsen‘I’ve never been more terrified!’ Carly Rae Jepsen on motherhood, stardom and her horniest album everCall Me Maybe made the singer-songwriter famous – but also confused. Who was she? Who was her music for? Fourteen years later, about to release the double album Day and Night, she finally has some answersJuan A RamírezMon 14 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarly Rae Jepsen is as bubbly as ever as she comes down for breakfast at Manhattan’s Hotel Chelsea. She’s one of those pop princesses, like Kylie Minogue, whose voice and demeanour remain unchanged whatever the situation.
