And she feels at home at this New York landmark where, last year, she married the musician and producer Cole MGN. That a wedding at the Chelsea would need to be kept to about 100 people was an immediate selling point. “I loved that it was smaller,” she says. “It felt big to me! I didn’t even get time with all the people that were there.”Slow jams, smash hits and Popeye samples: Carly Rae Jepsen’s 20 best songs – ranked!Read moreWe’re here to talk about her new album, though, which comes out 14 years after the song that made her world-famous. Born and raised in the city of Mission in British Columbia, Jepsen had come third on Canadian Idol in 2007, and then released a low-key folk album called Tug of War in 2008, before dropping Call Me Maybe four years later. It became the bestselling global single of 2012; her second album, Kiss, came out in the same year. Now, at the age of 40, she has six more studio albums under her belt. The latest, Day and Night, is her take on marriage and motherhood. And, in its own way – which is to say, a bit coy, a bit breathy – it might also be Jepsen’s horniest album to date.“I’m gonna spit my tea out,” she says when I suggest this, laughing while steadying the cup in her hand. It turns out I’m not the first to broach the subject. During a session with King Princess, Jepsen’s fellow singer-songwriter called her a “very horny writer”.Jepsen thought she’d been subtle about it. “I don’t love it to be aggressively there,” she says. “However, I think that longing is really sexy – knowing what you want and being not afraid to say it out loud. I’ve always found a real thrill in being the person who’s advancing the thing; who’s a couple steps ahead of the person they’re chasing.”As far back as Call Me Maybe, she points out, her music has contained a thread of exhilaration about being the pursuer. If lust is so prominent in Day and Night, it’s because Jepsen and her husband fell in love during the album’s creation. “‘Don’t kiss the producer’ was a rule of mine,” she says – and yet she did.And it’s not the only time she’s broken rules or confounded expectations. Say what you will about Call Me Maybe – and it’s easier to appreciate the track when it’s not blaring out from every storefront – but it demonstrated Jepsen’s mastery of pure pop: melodic, catchy, with fiendishly clever lyrics Abba would be proud of: “I get lovingly told that I’m part Canadian, part Swedish,” she says, delightedly.It sold more than 18m copies, reached No 1 in 19 countries, and won Jepsen a worldwide recording contract. It also helped Kiss, the album on which it appeared, reach the Top 10 in Australia, the UK, Canada and the US. Its follow-up, 2015’s Emotion, was ecstatically reviewed.View image in fullscreenJepsen lets rip at the 2024 Governors Ball in Queens, New York City.Photograph: Nina Westervelt/Billboard/Getty ImagesIn virtually any other era, Jepsen might be filling stadiums. But changing tastes aside, the music scene has fragmented thanks to streaming and social media, and the charts can be topped by a song thatmany have never heard. The one-time “megastar” is now more likely to be described as an “indie darling”. How does she feel about her industry?“There’s a little bit that I don’t totally know or understand, or stay checked into,” she says, “and I don’t know if that aloofness just comes from the fact that it’s not super interesting to me.” Maybe it’s a survival tactic, she adds, “but the reality is, long ago I became aware of what my strategy would be, and I’ve stuck to it. I knew around the time that I made Emotion that I was more excited about having a strong, small-but-mighty group, than I was about trying to be confused and feed the masses.”Now she knows who she is and who her fans are, but that knowledge didn’t come overnight. “I needed to take a second to figure out what it was that I liked about pop music to begin with, and what it was that I thought I had to contribute to it,” she says. “That’s why I went and did Cinderella, which was a really weird left turn.”View image in fullscreenJepsen prepares for her lead turn in Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Cinderella, 2014.Photograph: Bruce Glikas/FilmMagicIn 2014, less than a year after winning three Canadian Juno awards for Call Me Maybe and Kiss, Jepsen made herBroadwaydebut in a production of the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical. “I think everyone in the industry around me at the time was like: ‘What is she doing?’,” she says. But ticket sales were good, her stint on Cinderella was extended (“I love theatre, so it was like getting my cake and eating it”), and the experience reconnected her to her craft: “It was more of an artistic choice than a strategy, I guess.”“I think what I feel about pop music is not that I love all of it, but I have a really strong opinion about it,” Jepsen says. “I don’t know that I can define it, but I was excited about trying to figure out the thing that makes me feel like I did with Rufus, where you know a stranger.” “Rufus” is Rufus Wainwright, whose moody 2001 song Poses first inspired her to “take a run at this music thing”. That unknowability is what still excites her about pop: “The idea that comes across, hopefully, in this album, is that you can play with so many different genres as ingredients and it can still be the thing.”double quotation markI needed to take a second to figure out what I liked about pop music, and what I had to contributeIt was Jepsen’s former A&R representative, John Ehmann, who fostered that playfulness when he encouraged her to release a “B-side” follow-up to Emotion, knowing she had written far more songs than she had released. Initially hesitant, and worried that the songs weren’t up to par, Jepsen was convinced by the lower-stakes connotation of the B-side concept, and the fact that the record would only be an EP. She particularly liked the idea “that it was a bit more like showing the inside process”. Fans loved it and, from there, these projects became increasingly official. After 2016’s Emotion: Side B came 2020’s Dedicated Side B – a full album – and then 2023’s The Loveliest Time, a companion to the previous year’s The Loneliest Time, salvaged from the “100 or so” tracks she’d written for the album but then culled.“It ended up being such a weird door that opened for my life,” this notorious overwriter says. “I’ve so enjoyed this permission to not only get more experimental but, because I write so much, have this other place for things to live. So even when I was creating Dedicated [in 2019], I was already allotting things to this other idea of: ‘Maybe not everyone will get it, but I’ll have some fun.’”From Dedicated onwards, Jepsen felt she was “expanding and exploring, excited about the vastness of what a pop song could be”. But for Day and Night, her goal was cohesion: “something that felt like it lived in a home; a pure world.”View image in fullscreenContemplating the vastness of pop … Jepsen.Photograph: Vince AungSonically, she’d found herself drawn to sunshine through the soul singer Minnie Riperton and jazz vocalist Blossom Dearie, and then the “darker scents” of house music and chillwave producer Bullion, with whom she collaborated on the 2024 single Rare (which appeared on his album Affection, released on Ghostly International). A visit to the Abba Voyage hologram concert, meanwhile, reinvigorated her appreciation for “a tight melody, with updated production”.Then her longtime guitarist, Tavish Crowe, suggested a thought experiment: a musical walk through a house party that included stops by the stoners, the ravers, the couple fighting in a locked room. They landed on the idea of a double album that could sustain all of these ideas. “The challenge became making sure that each of those albums was expansive enough,” she says. “I wanted cohesiveness, but I also didn’t want 12 songs that felt like you were listening to the same song on repeat.” There’s more delving into her thought process, then she stops herself: “Sorry, I sound so nerdy when I talk about this.”Nerdiness is not what comes across on Day and Night, though. There’s that aforementioned sexiness, in lyrics that are less about getting someone into bed than about the difficulty of making it out the next morning. And there’s domestic bliss. Jepsen became a mother in March, which she “didn’t always think was on the cards”.View image in fullscreenA new-mother post on Jepsen’s Instagram.Photograph: @carlyraejepsen / InstagramShe remembers working in a Vancouver coffee shop 20-odd years ago, seeing young kids and thinking: “I would love to hold that cute baby.” But, she says, “I always had this very clear vision for my life; that I was on a mission to make music, and that was, for a very long time, my priority. Similar with getting married.” There was never a bridal Pinterest board for Jepsen, hardly even the thought of a husband. “All of these things were nice, hypothetical ideas that belonged to other people. Maybe I almost romanticise this idea that, as an artist, it was more my job to be an observer of life than to wildly participate.”Now she’s left being a bystander behind. “At this stage in my life, I feel much more comfortable with the parts that I don’t have full control over,” she says. “There is nothing more vulnerable than having a child. It’s this whole heartbeat that breathes outside you. I’ve never been happier and more terrified – but I feel very, very alive.”After Day and Night, Jepsen’s focus will be on the result of a phone call with the theatrical producer Mike Bosner, five years ago. Having heard that she was interested in writing for Broadway, Bosner rang Jepsen and said: “Lena Dunham, 10 Things I Hate About You.” She slaps her palms on the table and mimes an awestruck face.View image in fullscreenJepsen performs at the 2024 Bonnaroo Music and Arts festival.Photograph: Douglas Mason/WireImageJepsen had wanted to work with Dunham for years, having met her through their shared friend and collaborator Jack Antonoff. “She’s been a support from the beginning, always so sweet about certain songs,” Jepsen says, recalling the Girls creator’s love of Guitar String/Wedding Ring, from Kiss. (Dunham used a key line from the song – “If you cut a piece of guitar string / I would wear it like it’s a wedding ring” – as an epigraph for the “Falling in Love” chapter of her 2014 autobiography, Not That Kind of Girl.) “I’ve always thought – and I think everyone feels this way – that the way she puts words together is hilarious and brilliant,” says Jepsen.View image in fullscreenHeath Ledger and Julia Stiles in 1999’s 10 Things I Hate About You.Photograph: Touchstone Pictures/AllstarTheir adaptation of Gil Junger’s 1999 teen comedy 10 Things I Hate About You – a collaboration with co-composer Ethan Gruska and playwright Jessica Huang – is due to open next August. The task of scoring an existing story, let alone one that’s a spin on Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, with a lead character to whose “anger and passion” Jepsen thinks every woman relates, “is a completely different energy of approaching music. You want to honour the 90s and really do it justice.”Having caught a workshop presentation of the production earlier this year, I tell Jepsen how I heard her voice throughout the cast’s. “That is the best part,” she beams, adding that she has enjoyed the challenge of writing for different characters, particularly men. But, she adds: “I do believe if you haven’t felt it you can’t write it – you have to really feel them in order to have anything for them to say.“When you’re singing on Broadway, when you think about the reason one would need to sing in real life, the emotion has to be so potent that words are no longer doing it,” Jepsen says. “There’s only a song when the feeling erupts.”Day and Night is released via Schoolboy and Interscope on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsCarly Rae JepsenThe big interviewBroadwayfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Barrio Triste review – raw and dynamic portrait of anarchic slum life in 1980s Medellín | Movies | The Guardian
description: Bad Bunny collaborator Stillz’s debut feature shot using Betacam focuses on vibes over plot
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Bad Bunny collaborator Stillz’s debut feature shot using Betacam focuses on vibes over plot
Content: Barrio Triste.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenBarrio Triste.Photograph: PRMoviesReviewBarrio Triste review – raw and dynamic portrait of anarchic slum life in 1980s MedellínBad Bunny collaborator Stillz’s debut feature shot using Betacam focuses on vibes over plotPhuong LeMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBest known as the creative mind behind the music videos of Puerto Rican rapper and singer Bad Bunny, Stillz has risen to the top of the industry as an in-demand director and photographer. Interestingly, for his feature-film debut, Stillz has turned away from the glitz and glamour of celebrity to fix his lens on the underdog. Shot on Betacam video and set in the crime-ridden neighbourhoods of 1980s Medellín, Barrio Triste opens with an unexpected act of rebellion: having snatched a camera from a television crew, a group of young men head out on an anarchic joyride and film their exploits in the process. Previously rendered invisible by the system, they have inserted themselves into a tool of mainstream media.There are moments of crisis here and there – the restless band of youths attempt a robbery and even kill a hostage – yet the primary focus seems to be on vibes rather than plot. The ever-roving camera not only channels the agitated psyche of the main characters but also drums up the chaotic pace of Medellín’s underbelly. One particularly memorable sequence moves from the peculiar sight of a punk duo practising on a rooftop to the garbage-strewn streets, during which seemingly benign interactions can quickly escalate into heated altercations. Echoing the handheld cinematography, life in the slums is unmoored and precarious, as if the ground might give way at any second.These moments of visual and emotional rawness are undermined by creative choices that err on the side of superfluousness. Arca’s electronic score is stunning, with scattering beats that resemble gunshots, yet its omnipresence in the film overwhelms the dynamism of the camerawork. Also intrusive are asinine sequences where one of the kids answers vague questions about his hopes and dreams, asked by an unseen presence. Though produced by Harmony Korine’s company EDGLRD, the film doesn’t quite measure up to classic portraits of wasted youth, offering little substance behind its propulsive style.Barrio Triste is in UK cinemas from 18 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsColombiaAmericasreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Route to Cappyness review – capybara boosterism is an ode to the internet’s favourite rodent | Movies | The Guardian
description: From a cappy-cafe owner in Japan to an escaped capybara in the UK, this homespun film takes the temperature of an international obsession
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: From a cappy-cafe owner in Japan to an escaped capybara in the UK, this homespun film takes the temperature of an international obsession
Content: Charming effort … The Route to Cappyness.Photograph: Darkwings WildlifeView image in fullscreenCharming effort … The Route to Cappyness.Photograph: Darkwings WildlifeMoviesReviewThe Route to Cappyness review – capybara boosterism is an ode to the internet’s favourite rodentFrom a cappy-cafe owner in Japan to an escaped capybara in the UK, this homespun film takes the temperature of an international obsessionLeslie FelperinMon 14 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Midlands-based film-maker Sharon Walia’s previous works wasThe Keepers of the Pigs, proudly described on her production company’s website as “the first ever documentary about guinea pigs”. So it makes zoological sense that her latest film takes on capybaras, guinea pigs’ ridiculously cute semi-aquatic cousins that are indigenous to Latin America, andrelatively recently became ubiquitouson social media in memes and short films alike. As glimpsed here, there was even a capybara in the recentAcademy Award-winning animated feature Flow, some pro-cappy boosterism that captured the creatures’ chill vibe and snuffly sweetness.Walia’s celebration of the species stays on script, rejoicing in the animals’ natural geniality, friendliness to other species in their natural habitat, and their compelling, remunerative charm that seems to have bolstered the fortunes of several animal attractions around the world.Equipped with a fairly basic camera, a drone and her five-year-old son for company, Walia visits a variety of venues offering capybara-centric attractions, starting in the species’ home turf in Brazil; there she meets Luciano Mochinski, whose smartphone-shot footage of himselfsitting under an umbrella with an large inquisitive male cappywent viral. (In fact, having achieved virality is often cited as a measure of success for several people here, which is little sad but that’s the times we live in.)Other interlocutors include a cappy-cafe owner in Japan who’s found a great way to get out of the rat race doing what he loves and makes no claims to expertise on the creatures. By contrast, American cappy shillers love to reel off factoids and anecdotes and all sound like they’ve had media training should a camera crew or schoolbus full of kids pull up to the gates. The British cappy-keepers are endearingly more amateur, yet noticeably a little defensive, especially the owners of the park from where Cinnamon, a young female capybara, escaped andmade the newsand, once again, social media.Indeed, the film-making here sometimes resembles the amateur efforts you’d see on social media, especially YouTube; the abrupt music transitions and off-the-shelf graphics look a little more naff than if you were watching this for free. But the homemade quality is part of The Route to Cappyness’s charm, along with the cuddly giant rodent stars themselves.The Route to Cappyness is in UK cinemas from 17 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsAnimalsSocial mediaDigital mediaYouTubereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Prima Facie review – fiery one-woman play is flattened into a bland movie | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Cynthia Erivo takes on the role Jodie Comer made famous for a pointless adaptation of a story about rape and retribution that loses the power it once had
Author: Richard Lawson
Headline: Cynthia Erivo takes on the role Jodie Comer made famous for a pointless adaptation of a story about rape and retribution that loses the power it once had
Content: Cynthia Erivo as Tessa in Prima Facie, ‘an Olivier-winning play somehow reduced to Law & Order blandness’.Photograph: Nicola Dove/Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenCynthia Erivo as Tessa in Prima Facie, ‘an Olivier-winning play somehow reduced to Law & Order blandness’.Photograph: Nicola Dove/Toronto film festivalFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewPrima Facie review – fiery one-woman play is flattened into a bland movieToronto film festival:Cynthia Erivo takes on the role Jodie Comer made famous for a pointless adaptation of a story about rape and retribution that loses the power it once hadRichard Lawsonin TorontoMon 14 Sep 2026 00.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuzie Miller’s award-winning2019 play Prima Facieemploys a familiar narrative device: a hotshot London barrister finds herself on the other side of the bar, subject to the very legal tactics she once so ruthlessly employed. Not as a defendant, but as the accuser in a rape case.We’ve seen versions of this before – a powerful figure suddenly caught in a struggle against a system they helped perpetuate – but Miller’s play distinguishes itself by putting the onus on to one actor.The wonder of Prima Facie is not really its narrative acuity nor its urgent point-making but the breathless and prodigious effort of its performer – most famouslya magnificent, tireless Jodie Comerin London and New York.How could a traditional film hold its focus on one monologuing person for nearly two hours? A rare few have tried that but most financiers and producers seem to think that it might be a good idea to have a few more cast members.And thus the fate of Prima Facie, which Miller and the director, Susanna White, have turned into a cinematic vehicle forCynthia Erivo. Unlike Comer, Erivo has to share the space with other people and must perform in real time what was, on stage, only recollection. In doing so, much of the exciting punch of Prima Facie has been washed away; what remains is a fairly conventional treatise on a pervasive societal ill.The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd review – Amanda Seyfried compels in wrenching prison dramaRead moreErivo plays Tessa, a criminal defense lawyer who is quickly gaining a reputation around the Old Bailey for her wily cunning in pleading her clients’ innocence. She is assigned a lot of sex crimes cases because, as a colleague glumly sums up, it looks good for a man accused of rape to have a female attorney arguing on his behalf.Tessa doesn’t seem to mind; she is simply providing the defense to which everyone is entitled. Morality has no place in the equation, she coolly figures.Tessa is perhaps especially driven because she is trying to transcend humble beginnings. Her mother, June (Noma Dumezweni), works as a cleaner, while her younger brother, Johnny (Toheeb Jimoh), is in construction. Tessa was clever enough to get a scholarship to Cambridge and now lives a flashy, important life in London, stylish Thames-adjacent apartment and all.All of that momentum is horribly disrupted when Tessa is raped by a colleague and lover, Julian (Daniel Ings), a terrible, frightening violation that punctuates what had been a lovely “are we getting serious?” date. Tessa reports to the police and thus sets herself on course for a trial, during which her motives and character will be intensely scrutinized on the way to a likely acquittal. That is just the way things tend to work, a fact Tessa understands all too well. But she goes ahead anyway, trying to rescue some sense of justice from this awful mess.In the play, the actor playing Tessa gets to wax long and rhapsodic on what she loves about the law, describing with relish the minute strategies of cross-examination and reveling in the sport of it all. That actor also has ample time to explicate what is happening inside Tessa’s head: the agonizing doubt, the anger, the fear, the bewilderment that she has become the figure she once easily dismantled in court.Miller and White throw in a little of that internal monologue but sparingly enough that it comes across as merely a half-hearted gimmick. We never get too deep with Tessa, which turns her story into something far more generic than I think the film-makers intended.It does not help matters that White films everything so flatly, with only the occasional attempt to add some visual texture to the proceedings.Erivo approaches the role with a focused rigor and yet she oddly doesn’t have all that much to play. Perhaps part of the problem is that the film makes a three-year time jump from the police report to the trial, which means we’ve no time to sit in the long fallout of the incident, to watch Erivo evolve her characterization as Tessa passes through the crucible of processing what has happened to her. The film becomes quite procedural, slowing down for a long recounting of what we just saw; an Olivier-winning play somehow reduced to Law & Order blandness.Of course, the film’s messaging – about the boggling frequency of sexual assault, about the vexing and myriad struggles of bringing perpetrators to justice – is well worth issuing out. And yet, White delivers all that in far too blunt a fashion. One sorely misses the darkly engrossing journey of the play’s performance, its energetic peaks, its shattering valleys, its spiky humor. All that has been bowdlerized in favor of something far more straightforward and thin.In expanding its view beyond one woman and the fire of her personal testimony, Prima Facie makes itself not universal but frustratingly anodyne.Prima Facie is premiering at theToronto film festivaland is seeking distributionExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalCynthia ErivoDrama filmsFestivalsJodie ComerRape and sexual assaultreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I never pass up a rewatch’: why Valley Girl is my feelgood movie | Nicolas Cage | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films brings us back to 1980s LA
Author: Annie Zaleski
Headline: The latest in our series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films brings us back to 1980s LA
Content: Nicolas Cage and Deborah Foreman in Valley Girl.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenNicolas Cage and Deborah Foreman in Valley Girl.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyMy feelgood movieNicolas Cage‘I never pass up a rewatch’: why Valley Girl is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films brings us back to 1980s LAAnnie ZaleskiMon 14 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a teenager growing up in the 1990s, I was deeply obsessed with all things 1980s pop culture. Chalk it up to nostalgia for my Care Bears-filled childhood – or a stubborn adolescent desire to separate myself from the Dave Matthews Band-loving, khaki-wearing kids at my high school. (Mission accomplished: it’s safe to say I was the only person I knew rocking a bandana tied around my pants leg or a Wild Boys-eraDuran Duranshirt.)‘Swiftly enchanted’: why Bedknobs and Broomsticks is my feelgood movieRead moreBack then, I was especially drawn to 1980s teen movies. In my own life, I was having zero luck finding a New Romantic Romeo; instead, I pined after artsy, sensitive boys who didn’t know I existed. But throughout these films, even the most awkward characters managed to find a happy ending, with the ultimate examples being Samantha (Molly Ringwald) in Sixteen Candles landing hunky Jake Ryan or Stacy (Jennifer Jason Leigh) linking up with Rat (Brian Backer) in Fast Times at Ridgemont High.Out of these teen movies, 1983’s Valley Girl emerged as my hands-down favorite, a permanent feelgood film I never pass up for a rewatch. It’s best described as a new wave Romeo and Juliet. The film focuses on wholesome Julie (Deborah Foreman), the child of two ageing, laid-back hippies who run a health food store and restaurant. Although her parents embarrass her, they give Julie the freedom to find her authentic self. That extends to her romantic life, especially after she connects with Randy (a chiseledNicolas Cage, in one of his first film roles) at a party.They’re polar opposites – he’s a scruffy punk who hangs out in dingy clubs, she’s often found gossiping in a mall food court – but fall head over heels. This causes issues with Julie’s friends, who are uncomfortable that Randyseemsso different from them; in fact, they encourage her to take back her boorish boyfriend, Tommy, with whom she broke up with at the film’s start. Julie is hesitant, for good reason. Randy is actually quite tender despite his edgy exterior. And Tommy’s loutish post-split behavior involved secretly seducing one of Julie’s good friends to use as extortion fodder and, separately, publicly assaulting Randy at a party.After caving in to peer pressure and agreeing to go to prom with Tommy, Julie eventually realizes she’s made a huge mistake. Luckily, Randy hasn’t given up on their relationship – and, like all the best teen movies, Valley Girl culminates in a dramatic prom scene in which he goes to great lengths (and sparks a major food fight) to win her back.The movie arrived not long after Frank Zappa’s 1982 hit song Valley Girl, which satirized a very specific teenage California subculture. (Zappa wasn’t thrilled about the film; he evensued the producers, who subsequently denied the movie had anything to do with the song.) But the movie doesn’t mock the valley girl trend.Instead, Valley Girl meets these teenagers where they are: going shopping, hanging out and eating junk food, and attending house parties with then-novel foods like sushi. They’re shockingly normal, not exaggerated caricatures or curiosities. That’s probably why, years later, I still related to Julie and her friends. The scene of them flipping through racks of colorful clothes reminded me of my own 1990s teenage mall excursions.Chalk up this endurance to Valley Girl director Martha Coolidge, who had a background in documentary film-making and brought an observant eye to the movie. More than once, we see Julie absolutely awed by scenes of gritty 1980s Los Angeles: movie theater marquees, flashy neon signs, and famous locations such as Grauman’s Chinese Theater, the Roxy and the Rainbow Bar & Grill. I recognized her reaction: I had the exact same mind-expanding experience when I finally visited bigger cities and saw things I had only glimpsed in movies.I was also envious of the music in Valley Girl. Julie and Randy go to a cool underground club to watch powerpop legends the Plimsouls rip through an urgent set. Elsewhere, the teens dance to Sparks and the Flirts at a house party, or have a prom where the musical entertainment comes from new wave cult figure Josie Cotton. You felt cool by association because of the soundtrack.When a Valley Girl remake was released in 2020, I couldn’t bring myself to watch it. The magic of the original film was how unselfconscious it was. The movie used a very specific era and location to illustrate something timeless about growing up and navigating complicated relationships. I was a goody two-shoes who grew up in a super-preppy town, so I related to having a sheltered life exploded by new experiences. As an adult, the idea of being bold, meeting new people and going to exciting places continues to inspire me. As much as the Valley Girl plot centered on romance, the movie was also a story about self-discovery and being brave enough to carve out your own offbeat path.Valley Girl is available to watch on Amazon Prime in the US, the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsNicolas CageMy feelgood movieComedy filmsRomance filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A great time with Uncle Junior from the Sopranos: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Fans of the show will not want to miss this revealing new series with Dominic Chianese and his son. Plus, a political drama that’s as thrilling as a Bourne novel
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Fans of the show will not want to miss this revealing new series with Dominic Chianese and his son. Plus, a political drama that’s as thrilling as a Bourne novel
Content: Dominic Chianese presents Dominic & Junior podcast.Photograph: Pacific Press Media Production Corp./AlamyView image in fullscreenDominic Chianese presents Dominic & Junior podcast.Photograph: Pacific Press Media Production Corp./AlamyBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioA great time with Uncle Junior from the Sopranos: best podcasts of the weekFans of the show will not want to miss this revealing new series with Dominic Chianese and his son. Plus, a political drama that’s as thrilling as a Bourne novelHannah J DaviesandHollie RichardsonMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDominic & JuniorThe Sopranos star Dominic Chianese (95) and his son Dominic Chianese Jr (62) helm this new series – a cosy father-soncatchup, and all the better for it. Choice cuts include Chianese Sr’s admission that he thought the show was a spoof at first, playing his first scene as crime boss Junior for laughs. As for “Jimmy” Gandolfini, he was “in the same stratosphere as Al Pacino ... acting with him was so easy because he was so real and so believable”. Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyBear HuntThe Rest Is … stable has form inaudio drama. This new one – an action-heavy political thriller about beef between Britain and Russia – is described by its creators as “a British Bourne”. The dramatic writing and input of real-life defence experts makes for an atmospheric listen that blurs the lines between fiction and present reality. HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyUnderGround Zero: 9/11 & The MobView image in fullscreenMichael Imperioli.Photograph: Deadline/Getty ImagesMore Sopranos-adjacent podcasting, with Michael Imperioli and Steve Schirripa in thisnew dramaabout how the mafia exploited the chaos caused by 9/11. Drawing on true events, it is a solid gangland drama elevated by a strong cast – not least Imperioli as brave cop Frank Sturiano. HJDWidely available, all episodes out nowA Matter of FatRose Stokes is a journalist who has always had issues with her weight. Prof Giles Yeo is an obesity scientist. In this nuancedseries, they exchange views and facts on how the age of GLP-1s has disrupted our relationship with weight and bodies. They unpick the issues from all angles, from how these drugs work to the marketing of them and their own experiences of using them. Hollie RichardsonWidely available, weekly from Tuesday 15 SeptemberLight BoxMark Henry Phillips has spent 20 years composing music for podcasts such as Serial and This American Life. But how might AI music change his job? From copyright issues to the uncanny valley quality of much AI output, Phillips’sseriesis straight-talking – but not overly doomy – as it centres on the insights of those affected by this huge tech shift. title: End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor review – the fightback starts here | Naomi Klein | The Guardian
description: A sharp analysis of the damage wrought by the reckless super-rich, and a progressive toolkit for repairing it
Author: Daniel Trilling
Headline: A sharp analysis of the damage wrought by the reckless super-rich, and a progressive toolkit for repairing it
Content: Demonstrators in New York City.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemonstrators in New York City.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesBook of the dayNaomi KleinReviewEnd Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor review – the fightback starts hereA sharp analysis of the damage wrought by the reckless super-rich, and a progressive toolkit for repairing itDaniel TrillingMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe more power the radical rightwing nationalists of our age accrue, the greater the risk that their destructive brand of politics becomes normalised. We should not, for instance, regard it as normal that the man in charge of one of the world’s largest nuclear arsenals casually promises “a whole civilisation will die tonight”. We should not accept that history’s first trillionaire is allowed to spread racist conspiracy theories to a hitherto unimaginable extent. We should be alarmed that, here in the UK, a party tipped to lead a potential future government is trying to cruise to power in the slipstream of this international movement.In fact, we shouldn’t just be alarmed by such developments: we should stop them and urgently repair the damage already done. But how? And what is the nature of that damage? This bold, clarifying intervention fromNaomi Kleinand Astra Taylor provides some of the answers. “End times fascism” is their term for a convergence of interests that can broadly be understood as a response to the climate crisis. Faced with a world coming under unprecedented strain from environmental shocks and an unequal, resource-hungry economic system, today’s reactionaries are effectively saying: bring it on.“The most powerful people in the world are preparing for the end of the world, an end they themselves are frenetically accelerating,” Klein and Taylor write, describing a loose alliance of three principal factions rooted in US political and business elites. First are the religious fanatics who see each new disaster as a welcome sign we are entering the end of days, but find common ground with secular demagogues who promise a glorious, prosperous future on the ruins of our present. Think, for instance, of the mirage of a “New Gaza”, a property developers’ fever dream that the Trump administration – heavily influenced by Christian Zionists – claims will arise from the wreckage of Israel’s US-backed genocide.Next are the new tech barons, who preach that only the AI “arms race”, as Klein and Taylor put it, can save humanity – even as its demand for water and electricity scorches the planet – while they themselves dream of sitting out societal breakdown in remote, fortified enclaves. Last come the political entrepreneurs who transform visions of disaster into votes by promising to turn their nations into bunkered garrison states. Migration draws most of the attention, but you can also see this logic at work in an increasingly aggressive global scramble for natural resources: “supersized prepping at the level of the nation-state”, in Klein and Taylor’s words.This is nothing less than a revival of fascism, the authors argue – but only if we understand “fascism” as something broader and more persistent than the uniformed mass movements that once brought Europe to the brink of destruction. In their definition, it is a recurring tendency among elites that manifests when capitalism no longer works the way they would like it to, and they feel their positions are threatened. “Fascism,” write the authors, who draw on a range of theorists including Walter Benjamin and WEB Du Bois, “is capitalism with bared teeth.”There have been endless academic disputes over whether such a broad definition of fascism is useful. Personally, I think we shouldn’t get too hung up on terminology – the important thing is to write in a way that makes people alive to problems around them and leaves them feeling empowered to respond. The authors succeed on both counts: Klein has spent almost three decades outlining the connections between unrestrained capitalism and violent, anti-democratic tendencies, while Taylor, a Canadian-American film-maker, writer and activist, is a veteran of movements for social justice.They set out how our economic system, “built on limitless growth, and on limitless wealth for the winners”, has collided with the reality that life on this planet is becoming harder to sustain. As a psychological balm, reactionaries offer “bursts of sadistic satisfaction summoned by footage of immigrants in supermax prisons, or soldiers marching through the streets” that only lead to demands for even more extreme measures. At the same time, the right is prone to splits and overreach, making it vulnerable to challenge by progressives whose ultimate goal must be to dismantle the concentration of wealth and power that got us into this mess in the first place.Klein and Taylor draw particular inspiration from Zohran Mamdani, whose successful run for the New York mayoralty showed it was possible to build a winning coalition by focusing on people’s material concerns – and by celebrating difference rather than trying to deny or apologise for it. They also point to other, creative forms of resistance in the US and elsewhere as the seeds of a new politics “rooted in an expansive, open-armed sense of neighbourliness” that can counter the right’s dystopian visions of the future. The wayVenetians challengedJeff Bezos’s attempt to use their city as a backdrop for his grotesque display of wealth disguised as a wedding, for instance. Or how Minnesotans looked out for one another as their state was bombarded with ICE raids. For the authors, the leftwing, diasporic Jewish idea ofdoikayt, or “hereness” – fighting for justice and equality wherever you may live – is a guiding principle, but only one of a multiplicity of cultural and political traditions that can be drawn on.Here, the account falters a little. End Times Fascism has due regard for the global context, but this is largely a book about the US. That’s not a problem in itself: the US is still (just about) the global hegemonic power. But it does raise questions about where the best lessons can be learned. Is the rest of the world expected to take its cue from American progressives? Or is there more we could discover, say, in parts of the world where reactionary, authoritarian politics has prevailed for longer – and where people might have developed longer-term strategies?It’s not Klein and Taylor’s job to answer these questions comprehensively, though. Their valuable contribution is to map out the frightening new territory in which we find ourselves, and point to an escape.Daniel Trilling is the author of If We Tolerate This: How the British Establishment Made the Far Right Respectable (Picador). End Times Fascism And the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor is published byAllen Lane (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.This article was amended on 14 September 2026. An earlier version said the US has the world’s largest nuclear arsenal. In fact it has the second largest, after Russia.Explore more on these topicsNaomi KleinBook of the dayClimate crisisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Farewell to Eden by Sebastian Faulks review – conflict and compromise, from a veteran of the genre | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A returning British soldier is haunted by his time in Palestine in this panoramic epic set after the second world war
Author: Michael Donkor
Headline: A returning British soldier is haunted by his time in Palestine in this panoramic epic set after the second world war
Content: Sebastian Faulks ‘is deft in the management of his ample material’.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyView image in fullscreenSebastian Faulks ‘is deft in the management of his ample material’.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyFictionReviewFarewell to Eden by Sebastian Faulks review – conflict and compromise, from a veteran of the genreA returning British soldier is haunted by his time in Palestine in this panoramic epic set after the second world warMichael DonkorMon 14 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSebastian Faulks’s latest book focuses on the most irreconcilable geopolitical struggle of our age, the Israel-Palestine conflict. While “the sound of mortar and machine gun, the collision of flesh and metal” are integral to Faulks’s best known works, such as Birdsong, in his 17th novel the military presence is a peacekeeping one. It’s 1946 and infantry officer Philip Deval, who saw action in Normandy, is deployed to the Holy Land to take part in maintaining Britain’s mandate in Palestine. Initially Philip is second in command of a battalion overseeing febrile relationships between Jewish and Arab communities. Britain’s profound failures and manipulation in the region, and the imminence of its disastrous departure from the territory, come under scrutiny.While able to drum up motivation and cheer for the men in his battalions, privately Philip wrestles with inner melancholy. He is “shrouded” in a “loneliness … that insulates him from the world”. Experiences on the battlefield and other, slowly elucidated tragedies have led to his pessimistic bent. Much of what Philip observes in the Middle East, and his “foreboding” sense of its intractable problems, only confirms his despairing sense of human nature. It also underlines his ambivalence towards notions of divine benevolence.double quotation markThe lamenting tone of the title reflects a work mourning seeming certaintiesIn Jerusalem, Philip and some of his men find themselves in a raucous bar. They jostle along among multicultural crowds, those “with yarmulkes, tarbushes … barehead Armenians and Greeks … [all] playing dice and cards in a mix of tongues”. Philip knows that “soon they would [all] be killing each other … Humans had worked out the movements of the planets and prised apart the indivisible atom; they cured mysterious diseases and found a new way, by trade, of making themselves richer than the sum of their possessions … But a group of closely related people in a fertile landscape couldn’t find a way to coexist.”This inability to coexist does, indeed, frequently erupt into shocking violence and inevitable reprisals. Faulks captures these with his typically steady and unblinking attention, in scenes where both the seriousness of his research and his instinct for affecting fictive detail is clear. Not long after Philip’s arrival in the region, Zionist paramilitaries bomb the King David Hotel, location of the headquarters of the Palestine police and the British administration. While helping to rescue survivors from the debris, “in a Remington [typewriter] that Philip lifted clear, there were three severed female fingers jammed between the keys”.Faulks’s plots often cultivate friendships formed in duress. Here, Matthew Kilvert, a priest attached to the peacekeeping mission, has a “genial energy”. He’s fantastically enthusiastic about staging a Christmas production, cast with officers and locals of all backgrounds, of The Importance of Being Earnest. His uproarious Lady Bracknell becomes the talk of the town. Matthew forms an enduring closeness with Philip; their dialogue often glitters with an easy, youthful humour and they are able to share opposing views of what it means to have faith with an instructive conviviality and curiosity. There is a beautiful, strangely rendered moment when Matthew thinks he has had a vision of Christ. Philip listens to Matthew’s retelling of the encounter with quiet interest.A different friendship also shapes Philip’s progress in the novel. With postwar employment opportunities limited, after demobbing Philip retrains as a French teacher and takes up a post at a girls’ boarding school where he and music mistress Frances Darwood – as stiff as Philip is wont to be – strike up a delicate and important confidence. Over evenings listening to recordings of Ravel and Bach, the two gradually share stories of their pasts and the historical forces that have shaped them. This process proves especially harrowing for Frances. Alongside Philip’s detailed recounting of his time in the Holy Land and the desolate realities of weary postwar Britain, Frances’s horrific wartime recollections contribute to the panoramic ambitions of the novel. Faulks is deft in the management of his ample material, throwing in the odd, energising shift in narrative perspective too – an echo of the more sustained polyphony ofA Week in December. There is a lightness and unpredictability in the movement between stories and periods, a kind of deliberate structural restiveness that is of a piece with Philip’s psychic disquiet. This mobility in the organisation of the story culminates in some thrillingly clever late-stage plot developments that are every bit as dramatic as the concluding sections of Faulks’s 2007 novel,Engleby.While characteristically expansive in its scope, at its core Farewell to Eden is about disillusionment and morally compromised nations, peoples and individuals. The lamenting tone of the title – and indeed of the text at large – reflects a work mourning seeming certainties or easy categorical distinctions. It is a novel that asks us what we might do when unavoidably faced with our own imperfection and fallibility, and is wise and sober in its refusal to trumpet answers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
