title: Royal Ballet: The McRae/Vassilev Project review – an encounter between two masterful ROH performers | Dance | The Guardian
description: Directed by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, this is an evening of many parts that sometimes feels bolted together
Author: Sanjoy Roy
Headline: Directed by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, this is an evening of many parts that sometimes feels bolted together
Content: Spellbinding … Vasko Vassilev and Steven McRae in The McRae/Vassilev Project.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSpellbinding … Vasko Vassilev and Steven McRae in The McRae/Vassilev Project.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewRoyal Ballet: The McRae/Vassilev Project review – an encounter between two masterful ROH performersLinbury theatre, LondonDirected by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, this is an evening of many parts that sometimes feels bolted togetherSanjoy RoyMon 14 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s an evening of two halves and many, many parts, some that dovetail snugly, others more clunkily bolted together. And perhaps that’s because The McRae/Vassilev Project is just that: a project more than a piece.Directed by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, it is essentially an encounter between two masterful performers with long careers at the Royal Opera House, dancerSteven McRaeand violinist Vasko Vassilev, entwined with the near mythical figure of another virtuoso artist, Niccolò Paganini.The first half opens with Vassilev centre stage playing Bach (for some reason); he backs off to cede space for a luxurious pas de deux by McRae and partner Sarah Lamb, all exquisite lines, spins and lifts. From this “front stage” scene, the set switches to a backstage studio, artists McRae, Vassilev, Lamb and pianist Pamela Tan Nicholson entering as if for rehearsal. The rest of this section is a light-touch show-and-tell of McRae and Vassilev’s backstories – one a homespun Australian who happened upon dance as a child, the other a Bulgarian prodigy hothoused within a musical family – illustrated with old photos and videos, supplemented by comments from Lamb and Nicholson, and interspersed with consummate yet seemingly off-the-cuff demonstrations of their skills in music and dance.View image in fullscreenL-r: Vasko Vassilev , Pamela Tan Nicholson, Steven McRae and Sarah Lamb in The McRae/Vassilev Project.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe scene is at once charming – personalising the figure of the professional performer – and contrived: even as you warm to the characters you feel the joins in the script (voice acting is not their forte) and the jolts between the attempted naturalism of their conversation and the executed artifices of classical performance.The second half is a complete change of tack. Everyone returns as devilish Paganinis in tailcoats and cummerbunds, hair dyed dark and tastefully tousled. As well as flourishing a violin bow like a baton, sword or spear, McRae uses his tap dance training in fiendish zapateado and brilliant Cossack spins, sometimes melding his commanding footwork in partnership with Lamb’s airy pointe-work and lean lines. Still, it’s perhaps Vassilev who holds the stage most, simply by putting his body into playing Paganini; the laser focus is spellbinding.Shame, then, that there are so many distracting effects, from back-projected dancers to billowing smoke and glaring lights, and a busy abstract animation that visualises the musical dynamics. With performers like these, it’s enough for them to just do their thing.At theLinbury theatre, London, until 19 September.Explore more on these topicsDancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after ‘free Palestine’ speech | Macklemore | The Guardian
description: The American rapper will no longer support Sheeran’s US leg of Loop tour after comments at MetLife Stadium show
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The American rapper will no longer support Sheeran’s US leg of Loop tour after comments at MetLife Stadium show
Content: Macklemore performing on stage at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts on 3o August.Photograph: Arnaud Finistre/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMacklemore performing on stage at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts on 3o August.Photograph: Arnaud Finistre/AFP/Getty ImagesMacklemoreMacklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after ‘free Palestine’ speechThe American rapper will no longer support Sheeran’s US leg of Loop tour after comments at MetLife Stadium showAdrian HortonMon 14 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMacklemorehas been dropped from the remainder of the US leg ofEd Sheeran’s Loop tour, after the American rapper drew headlines for saying “free Palestine” on stage at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.In a brief speech between songs on 4 September, the Grammy-winning artist told the audience he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, prompting apetitionfrom the Israeli American Council demanding his removal from the tour.Messina Touring Group, the promoter of the US leg of Sheeran’s tour,toldRolling Stone: “As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s US Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming US tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans. After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” Sheeran did not immediately reply to requests for comment.The Seattle-bred rapper was slated to open for Sheeran at eight of the remaining 10 shows of his US Loop tour, which will resume on 19 September in Philadelphia. The venues that allegedly objected to Macklemore’s return include stadiums in that city as well as outside Boston, Atlanta, Charlotte, Indianapolis, Dallas and Tampa.Macklemore, long anoutspokensupporterof the rights of Palestinians and those in Gaza, delivered the remarks at his first appearance on the Loop tour on 4 September. “A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: ‘Free Palestine,’” he said in atwo-minute speech. “I said: ‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.”Alluding to possible controversy, he added that not “speaking my heart in order to keep my own comfort, and the audience’s comfort … is the day that I no longer deserve to be on stage”, and called US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) a “terrorist organization”. He also showed images of the devastation from Israeli military attacks in Gaza during his protest anthem Hind’s Hall, which celebrated protesters’ occupation of a building they named in honor ofHind Rajab, a six-year-oldkilled by the Israeli militaryin 2024.The comments spurred the group StopAntisemitism to accuse the musician of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda” in an Instagram post that was amplified by the singer Pink. In another post, Pinkexplainedthat she did not object to Macklemore saying “free Palestine” but added: “I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I’m not asking now. I don’t need anyone fired, and I don’t need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, ‘that scared me, and it scared people I love,’ without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I’m somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?”The Israeli American Council also called for Macklemore to be removed from the tour, claiming his statements raised the question of “where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda”.At the second of his appearances at MetLife on 5 September, Macklemore reiterated his support forPalestineand addressed Jewish members of the audience: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”In a lengthyInstagram poston Monday morning, Macklemore confirmed that Sheeran and his team had decided to remove him from the tour, but noted that he, Sheeran and Pink were not victims. “We have careers, money, opportunities, safety and audiences around the world,” he wrote. “Whatever consequences any of us face for what we say, we get to go home to our families.“The victims are the Palestinian people. The men, women and children who have been killed, starved, displaced and forced to live through unimaginable violence,” he added,citingthe more than 20,000 children killed in Gaza by the Israeli military since the 7 October 2023 terrorist attacks by Hamas.Macklemore explained that the decision came after a week of “difficult conversations” with Sheeran, a friend of 13 years whom he considers a “brother”, though “as I told Ed multiple times on the phone, our friendship can’t change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened.” According to Macklemore, Sheeran was under pressure from stadium owners rallied by Robert Kraft – the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and their Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, where Sheeran was next slated to play – to drop Macklemore from the tour, lest the English singer be barred from their venues. “Ed was in a fucked up position,” the rapper wrote. “He knew it. His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it had never been before.“What I said at MetLife I have been saying on stages around the world for almost three years,” he added. “So why is it an issue now? Because now I’m sharing the stage with one of the biggest artists in the world, in some of the biggest stages in America.”Macklemore ended his multi-page post by reiterating his call to “free Palestine”: “If those words cost me the stage, while turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I’ve ever been on.”In a statement provided toNBC News, Kraft said the decision to bar Macklemore from Gillette Stadium, which is intended to be “a welcoming environment for all guests”, was made after the comments at the MetLife shows and “a broader history of rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same – peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” he added. He also blamed Hamas for actions that “have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike”.“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” he said. Kraft, who is Jewish, created the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, now known as the Blue Square Alliance Against Hate, in 2019. He is a longtimesupporterof the state of Israelas well as its allyin the White House, Donald Trump.The North American leg of Sheeran’s tour will conclude in November at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which earlier this year hosted two shows by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, who has ahistoryofantisemiticstatements. Tour openers Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe are set to take the stage as planned.Explore more on these topicsMacklemoreEd SheeranIsrael-Gaza warPalestinePop and rockGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: Jack Thorne warns some fellow scriptwriters are using AI ‘to cheat’ | Jack Thorne | The Guardian
description: Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate scripts
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate scripts
Content: ‘If publishers, studios, streamers, can point to the writer as the problem, that gives them the excuse to behave however they’d like with content,’ Thorne said.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/WireImageView image in fullscreen‘If publishers, studios, streamers, can point to the writer as the problem, that gives them the excuse to behave however they’d like with content,’ Thorne said.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/WireImageJack ThorneJack Thorne warns some fellow scriptwriters are using AI ‘to cheat’Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate scriptsMichael SavageMedia editorMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 04.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Thorne, one of Britain’s most successful screen and stage writers, has warned that some people in his profession are using AI “to cheat”, as he called for laws banning the secret use of the technology to generate scripts.Thorne, who co-wrote the hit Netflix dramaAdolescenceand wrote the stage play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, said that “writers need to be squeaky clean” in the face of AI models that “steal” the creative industry’s work.In a wide-ranging speech in London, Thorne attacked government inaction over the AI industry’s mass-scraping of material to train their models. He said Keir Starmer’s government had been “a bit dazzled by tech” and lamented a failure to protect the copyright of writers.However, he also said he had heard worrying stories about the misuse of AI among writers that risked undermining the profession.“I have spoken to a number of execs and studio heads about their use of AI, and got hugely different responses, but what I did hear from them – and what anecdotally I’ve heard from a few writers close to me – is that some in my profession are using AI to cheat,” he said.“What I’m not talking about here is using AI to help – to discuss things with, to check for spelling errors or help with layout. I’m talking about using AI as a replacement for endeavour, as a replacement for writing at all. Using prompts instead of writing words.“That is, simply put, failing to write, they’re cheating their employers in doing so, and they’re cheating their fellow writers.”Thorne, who is the president of the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain, warned that “if publishers, studios, streamers, can point to the writer as the problem, that gives them the excuse to behave however they’d like with content”.He added: “Passing AI work off as your own needs to be unlawful. If you use AI to generate content and you do not declare it as such, then that is fraud and the companies you do it to should be entitled to prosecute you.“To discourage it, the impact should be sizeable, and that requires laws but also us as an industry responding. Just as it should get you threatened with expulsion at university if you use it for essays, so it should have some professional impact on your career if you use it for text.”Thorne said broadcasters such as the BBC and Channel 4 should threaten sanctions against those found to have used AI to generate their work.“To protect the most vulnerable, it is essential,” he said. “As writers, what we are is what we make, and both the law and our industry should be absolutely crystal clear on that.”Thorne also said AI must not be allowed to impersonate actors, directors and writers.He criticised inaction by the government to protect the intellectual property of writers from AI models and said the way ministers acted in the next five years “will define what the next hundred years looks like for every writer in this country”.Last year, Starmer’s governmentabandoned a proposalthat would have required artists and copyright holders to actively opt out of having their material fed into AI systems,after a backlash. Ministers instead held a consultation on the issue.“There are so many things the government could be doing,” Thorne said. “Crucially, observation without intervention for fear of upsetting their apple cart could be replaced by observationwithintervention for fear of upsettingourapple cart.“The pieces of AI we use cannot be built using thievery. Cannot be built on a copyright crime. That’s what government is there for, to set lines in an argument. While adaptation is probably necessary, legislating so that you are protecting us from the worst excesses is essential.”He added: “This requires government leadership. In fact, it requires our government to take global leadership.”A government spokesperson said: “Copyright laws must protect the UK’s position as a creative powerhouse while unlocking the extraordinary potential of AI-driven innovation. We are doing the work that’s required to get the right outcomes so both the creative and technical sectors can flourish in this country.”Explore more on these topicsJack ThorneAI (artificial intelligence)Television industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: We Are Family: photography from Images Vevey 2026 – picture essay | Photography | The Guardian
description: We visited the idyllic Swiss lakeside town of Vevey for its 10th Biennale of photography. Global head of photography Fiona Shields picks out some of her favourite projects on display
Author: Fiona Shields
Headline: We visited the idyllic Swiss lakeside town of Vevey for its 10th Biennale of photography. Global head of photography Fiona Shields picks out some of her favourite projects on display
Content: One of Sian Davey’s The Garden images of Martin Parr on display. Photograph: Laetitia GesslerWe visited the idyllic Swiss lakeside town of Vevey for its 10th Biennale of photography. Global head of photography Fiona Shields picks out some of her favourite projects on displayDiscover the 50 artworks on display at the 10th edition of theBiennale Images Vevey, 5-27 September 2026ByFiona ShieldsMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 08.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery two years, on the shores of Lake Geneva at the foot of the Swiss Alps, the town of Vevey transforms its public spaces and buildings with 50 installations of artistic projects from 21 countries, which are free and open to the public. With such a breathtaking natural setting as its backdrop, the photography displayed at Images Vevey has to strike its own particular note of magnificence to hold the gaze.Rising six storeys high, Sian Davey’s portrait of the renowned photographer Martin Parr, who died at the end of last year, sets the tone for this year’s festival. Taken in a splendid garden that seems to have flourished straight from Eden, the monumental portrait overlooks the town.Martin was a significant and much-loved member of the Images Vevey family, having exhibited his own work here on a number of occasions. It is fitting then, that he should embody this year’s theme, “We Are Family”.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenWhen Martin arrived to visit Sian he had recently received a terminal cancer diagnosis but Sian recalls the serenity he experienced in the garden. That sense of peace radiates from the portrait as he watches over the town in a fitting tribute.The creation of the garden itself was a labour of love for Sian and her son Luke. As you can see in the portrait of Martin and in the other photographs in the display, it’s also the playground of Sian’s daughter, Alice, making this in every sense a family affair.View image in fullscreenAlice from The GardenMany of this year’s family-themed projects are a study of love and loss, connection and separation. In Barbara Davatz’s series As Time Goes By the starting point is the relationship between couples who visited her studio from 1982 onwards. Over the course of three decades, she charts their changing relationships creating a fascinating kind of family tree.View image in fullscreenPrints by Barbara Davatz in the central squareUncomplicated by props or elaborate staging, her subjects are presented in their purest form, inviting us to contemplate the course of their lives and the shifting nature of family bonds over time.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenBarbara, Aniko, Sascha – 1997. Barbara + Béla – 2014View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenCarlos + Aniko – 2014, Barbara + Sascha – 1982One of the most joyful series on display is Martina Bacigalupo’s Showing How Big the Sky Is, a project that charts 10 years of personal correspondence and amusing snapshots exchanged via WhatsApp and Skype with her former nanny, Chiou Taur Wu, who she affectionately describes as “auntie”.View image in fullscreenOne of Martina Bacigalupo’s prints on display at the festival“I love being barefoot. Because when your feet are not tied you are free.” Chiou told Martina, offering a glimpse into the context of her life.Born into poverty inTaiwanin 1948 and deprived of an education, Chiou left the country to marry an Italian sailor and began new life with him in Rapallo. But her hopes for a brighter future were dashed when she discovered he had mounting gambling debts which she then spent decades paying off.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenChiou Taur Wu (45, and 46)One of the jobs she took on was caring for Martina and her brother, Tomaso. In all she spent 32 years with the family until retiring back to Taiwan. There, at the age of 70 she resolved to live on her own terms. She returned to education, took dance classes and began an adventure travelling around Asia.Now she is playing and sharing her enchantment with the world with Martina. These vibrant and witty photographs tell of the love and the lasting bond between the two.When Karolina Wojtas was a little girl, she was perfectly content as an only child. The very idea of a sibling filled her with dark thoughts. “I’ll kill them and eat them,” she told her parents when the subject was raised. So when her little brother arrived when she was 13, turbulence was perhaps inevitable.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenWe can’t live – without each other © Karolina WojtasHer project bravely delves into the complex territory of sibling rivalry. The scenes she creates with her brother are infused with humour, tenderness, and at times, a touch of cruelty – decorating him with frankfurters or vegetables for example. Presented at the festival in an anarchic, staged playroom, the images confront us with the messy, funny and sometimes uncomfortable truth of growing up together.View image in fullscreenWe can’t live – without each other © Karolina WojtasThe chains of generations of oppression and poverty link together the story of the Appalachian people explored by the photojournalist Stacy Kranitz, winner of the Images Vevey book award 2025/2026 for her photobook project Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down.View image in fullscreenFamily standing in front of cabin, near Mt. Sterling, North Carolina © Great Smoky Mountains National Park ArchiveDrawing on archive photographs dating back more than a century, alongside newspaper reports charting the heroic early pioneers’ descent into poverty and isolation, the work examines the purpose of photography: is it to bear witness or a tool of propaganda?Stacy tells the story of how these once proud and courageous people made their way to the mountain ranges of the easternUnited States, only to be exploited by mining companies who left them economically impoverished and socially isolated.View image in fullscreenMiner standing at a drift mouth with a coal cart he loaded by hand © William O. Trevey Glass Slide Collection, Radford University 1895-1925During the 1960s, the American author and historian Harry M. Caudill further stigmatised the Appalachian people by arguing that their circumstances couldn’t be fixed. In film footage unearthed by Stacy, Caudill claims that genetic deficiencies had amplified their plight, a theory later echoed in JD Vance’s memoir Hillbilly Elegy,which traces his own family’s Appalachian roots.View image in fullscreenThe exhibition Ain’t no grave gonna hold me down by Stacy Kranitz at Images Vevey 2026Fast forward to the present and, in the photographs Stacy has made of Pat Greene and his friends and family, we see a cycle of deprivation that remains unbroken. Through this project, Stacy challenges stereotypes and assumptions that allow a single image to define people and their circumstances. She draws attention to a system stacked against those who need help most.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenPat with his daughter Vicky on her birthday. Untitled, possibly related to ‘The Blizzard family’, Kempton, West Virginia, 1939 © John Vachon, Farm Security Administration, Stacy Kranitz.View image in fullscreenWest Columbia, West Virginia, 2013Fiona Shields attended Images Vevey atits invitationExplore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayPhotographySwitzerlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In an age of superhero fatigue, Marvel’s best shot is to think small – and outside the box | Movies | The Guardian
description: Sebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green light
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Sebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green light
Content: Sebastian Stan as Winter Soldier AKA Bucky Barnes, with Anthony Mackie, in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier on Disney+Photograph: Julie VrabelováView image in fullscreenSebastian Stan as Winter Soldier AKA Bucky Barnes, with Anthony Mackie, in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier on Disney+Photograph: Julie VrabelováWeek in geekMoviesIn an age of superhero fatigue, Marvel’s best shot is to think small – and outside the boxBen ChildSebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green lightMon 14 Sep 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTShareBlink a little and you might think we are back in 2019. The latest Spider-Man film, Brand New Day, has just passed $2.4bn at the global box office, to become the third-highest grossing film of all time behind Avatar and Avengers: Endgame. Meanwhile Avengers: Doomsday is reported to have already earned more than $50m in US ticket presales alone, despite the fact that it doesn’t come out until December. Clearly we are in the middle of a superhero renaissance.And yet it doesn’t really feel like it, largely because it is something of a turnaround forMarvel, after a pretty disappointing 2025 in which all three of the studio’s releases underperformed. Captain America: Brave New World took $415m worldwide, Thunderbolts* managed $382m and even the well-reviewed The Fantastic Four: First Steps stalled at $521m, against a reported $200m budget. These are hardly Madame Web numbers but they do suggest there is still a problem about what to do with all those superheroes who cannot sustain a $300m multiversal extravaganza.double quotation markMarvel hasn’t really known what to do with the Winter Soldier since the Wakandans removed his Hydra programmingEnter Sebastian Stan, AKA Marvel’s Winter Soldier, who this week suggested the solution might be to place them in cheaper genre films instead. Speaking to New York Magazine,the actor revealedthat he had pitched Marvel boss Kevin Feige a new, “Sicario-esque”” approach for Bucky Barnes’ next adventure. “We keep a real small budget,” he said. “It’s about a guy who thinks he recog­nises someone from his past that had something to do with when, you know, he was brain­washed, and he gets obsessed with this per­son. He goes on a whole jour­ney to try to fig­ure out who this per­son is. It’s a thriller.”In any other period, this might feel like just another example of an actor trying to do his producer’s job for him. But Stan is on something of a career high, having earned his first Oscar nomination forThe Apprenticeand won a Golden Globe forA Different Man. And the idea of dropping the Winter Soldier into a murky, Sicario-style conspiracy thriller almost feels custom-designed to offset superhero fatigue. Stan was perfectly fine in last year’s Thunderbolts*, but the reality is that he could easily have been replaced by Shang-Chi, Ms Marvel or one of the Eternals without anyone really noticing.View image in fullscreenMaking up the numbers … from left, Danai Gurira, Chadwick Boseman, Chris Evans, Scarlet Johansson and Stan in Avengers: Infinity War.Photograph: Chuck Zlotnick/APMarvel hasn’t really known what to do with the Winter Soldier since the Wakandans removed his Hydra programming somewhere between Civil War and Infinity War. We know he’ll be in Doomsday but do we really need him making up the numbers while the better-known Avengers prevent reality from collapsing all over again? Wouldn’t it be better to put him in a grimy $50m thriller in which the fate of one damaged man’s mind matters more than the continued existence of the entire spacetime continuum?This could end up being a whole new thing. Give Ghost a stripped-back heist movie in which her ability to walk through walls is used to break into an actual building. Put Red Guardian into a cold war spy comedy about the increasingly implausible missions he claims to have undertaken against Captain America. Have Wong in an occult detective story involving one cursed object, three suspicious magicians and no portals to other dimensions.View image in fullscreenAn unhinged character study … Joaquin Phoenix as Arthur Fleck in Joker (2019).Photograph: DC Comics/Warner Bros/AllstarThere are also precedents suggesting that these kinds of superhero films can work, even if they are from outside the MCU. Logan was really an elegiac western with Wolverine as an ageing gunslinger ferrying a child across a hostile frontier. Joker sat far closer to the sort of unhinged urban character studies Martin Scorsese made in the 1970s and early 80s than it did to anything involving capes. Between them, these two films earned almost $1.7bn worldwide. It is also arguable that Marvel itself once made these kinds of movies. Captain America: The Winter Soldier was framed as a 1970s-style conspiracy thriller, Ant-Man was configured as a heist movie, and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, thanks to Sam Raimi’s distinctly Evil Dead II-style camera work, ended up with notable horror leanings. All were better movies than the lukewarm ensemble pieces that Marvel seems to have favoured in the past half-decade.No one is arguing that Marvel should stop building towards crescendos involving the entire Avengers gang teaming up to halt the latest threat to the known universe. But there are surely more interesting ways to build interest in the lesser-known heroes who spend most of such films lurking in the background. So why not let Bucky have his $50m breakdown? He can always go back to standing behind Thor when the multiverse explodes afterwards.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekSuperhero moviesSebastian StanMarvelSicariocommentShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Polly, the golden retriever who saved my husband’s life | Dogs | The Guardian
description: We got her as a puppy and she became particularly close to Adam – a blessing when he went into cardiac arrest in the middle of the night
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: We got her as a puppy and she became particularly close to Adam – a blessing when he went into cardiac arrest in the middle of the night
Content: Lifesaver … Hannah and Adam Cooke with Polly in 2025.Photograph: John McVitty/BHFView image in fullscreenLifesaver … Hannah and Adam Cooke with Polly in 2025.Photograph: John McVitty/BHFThe pet I'll never forgetDogsThe pet I’ll never forget: Polly, the golden retriever who saved my husband’s lifeWe got her as a puppy and she became particularly close to Adam – a blessing when he went into cardiac arrest in the middle of the nightHannah Cooke, as told toSinéad CampbellMon 14 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy husband, Adam, and I had always planned to have a big family and that journey began when we got our dog, Polly, five years ago. I’ve loved golden retrievers since I was a child because I grew up with one. We got Polly as a puppy and she was everything we’d hoped for: loving and smart.She immediately connected with both of us, but became inseparable from Adam. They would go for morning runs together; Polly could always be found wagging her tail by his side. This bond proved to be lifesaving.It was a normal Monday night in March 2024 at our home in County Fermanagh. Adam and I had put our one-year-old son, Alfie, to sleep, Polly was resting in her bed in the utility room directly below our bedroom, and we went up to sleep. At around half past one, I was woken up by the sound of Polly barking. I was startled and confused – it was unusual for her to bark so loudly in the middle of the night. I turned to look at Adam, who was lying beside me, and I noticed that he was breathing strangely; he looked as if he was choking. I jumped on top of him to try to wake him but he wasn’t responding – he was unconscious.View image in fullscreenPolly as a puppy: ‘She was everything we’d hoped for.’Photograph: Courtesy of Hannah and Adam CookePanic-stricken, I rang 999 and the paramedics talked me through what I should do. I got Adam out of the bed and on to the floor and began to perform CPR for seven or eight minutes. He was in cardiac arrest. The whole thing was like a horror movie. I didn’t know what to do but I knew I had to act quickly.Adam was taken to hospital and spent the next three weeks in intensive care. Polly was whimpering the entire time he was away, aware that something odd was going on.It was Polly who saved Adam’s life that night. If she hadn’t woken me up as quickly as she did, I dread to think what would have happened. She’s always been acutely in tune with her environment – I think that’s why she was able to sense that Adam was in trouble. After he recovered, Adam nominated Polly and me for a Heart Hero award, organised by the British Heart Foundation, and Polly won the annual award for CPR hero.The fame hasn’t completely gone to Polly’s head. She is still the same as she ever was: a lovable dog who’s as much involved in our family life as any member of our household. Adam is in recovery and has to take it easy these days. He’s still exercise buddies with Polly, but now they just go for walks instead of a morning run.Explore more on these topicsDogsThe pet I'll never forgetPetsHeart attackAnimal behaviourfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt | Lamb | The Guardian
description: Intimidated by the thought of midweek entertaining? Three simple rules make it simple…
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Intimidated by the thought of midweek entertaining? Three simple rules make it simple…
Content: Rosie Mackean’s lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenRosie Mackean’s lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.Quick and easyLambRosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurtIntimidated by the thought of midweek entertaining? Three simple rules make it simple…Rosie MackeanMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEntertaining midweek can feel daunting, but if you employ a couple of tricks, things can very quickly go from mayhem to magic. First, choose a dish that goes perfectly with good bread, so your carb is covered. Second, choose a protein that is quick to cook and great for sharing – little lamb chops are perfect for this, while also being a treat. And, finally, use other ingredients that don’t need much help. Here, the walnuts just get cooked in butter and the lamb juices, the courgettes are simply boiled and dressed, and the yoghurt is, well, yoghurt. Suddenly you’ve conjured up a masterpiece ready for many hands to dig in.Lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurtPrep10 minCook30 minServes4For the chops800g french-trimmed lamb chops(ie, 12-14 chops from 2 lamb racks – I like small, leaner ones)1½ tbsp flaky salt1 tsp black pepper1 tspground cumin1 tspground coriander½ tsp ground cinnamon2 tbspvegetable oil90g saltedbutter2 garlic cloves, unpeeled and bashed1 banana shallot, peeled and sliced100g walnuts½ tsp smoked paprikaJuice of ½lemonFor the courgettes1 generous pinchflaky sea salt, plus fine salt for the boiling water1kg courgettes, cut into roughly 1½cm-thick slices75g extra-virgin olive oilZest of 1 unwaxed lemon1garlic clove, peeled and grated1 big handfulfresh mint, leaves pickedTo serve500ggreek yoghurtFlatbreadsIf the chops are in the shape of a rack, use a sharp knife to separate them. Sprinkle the salt and spices all over the chops, then rub in and leave to sit at room temperature for a few minutes.Meanwhile, bring a large pan of water to a boil and season it generously with salt. Tip in the courgettes and simmer for seven minutes, until just tender. Combine the olive oil, lemon zest and garlic in a large bowl and use a slotted spoon to transfer the cooked courgettes straight into it. Stir, season with salt and leave to sit while you cook the chops.Put a cast-iron (or nonstick) pan on a high heat. Add the oil and the chops, taking care to render any thicker bits of fat before searing them on their flat sides for two minutes each. You may need to do this in batches; pop any seared chops on a rack while you finish the rest.Return all the chops to the pan with about half the butter and the bashed garlic cloves, then let the butter foam and bubble while you gently spoon it over the lamb for another minute. Lift out the chops and set aside to rest.Add the remaining butter to the pan with the shallot, walnuts and smoked paprika, turn down the heat to medium and let the butter foam and brown as the walnuts toast for about six minutes. Add a squeeze of lemon juice to stop the butter cooking further, then take the pan off the heat.Stir the mint into the courgettes, then scoop the yoghurt on to plates. Pile the courgettes around it, then lay the chops on top. Pour over the walnuts and their smoky butter and serve with plenty of flatbread for smooshing and sandwiching.Good Time Cooking: Show-Stopping Menus for Easy Entertaining, by Rosie Mackean, is published by Pavilion Books at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, visitguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsLambQuick and easyFoodMeatMain courseVegetablesHerbs and spicesNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Autumn vibes, summer temps: six ways to get cosy while it’s still warm | Autumn | The Guardian
description: Craving cosiness, but too warm for blankets and baths? Try our autumn cheat sheet
Author: Lily Smith
Headline: Craving cosiness, but too warm for blankets and baths? Try our autumn cheat sheet
Content: Soft landing: ease into autumn before the temperature catches up.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenSoft landing: ease into autumn before the temperature catches up.Photograph: GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterAutumnAutumn vibes, summer temps: six ways to get cosy while it’s still warmCraving cosiness, but too warm for blankets and baths? Try our autumn cheat sheetDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereLily SmithMon 14 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter arecord-breaking summer of heat, temperatures aren’t set to drop enough for hot baths, warm tights and roast dinners just yet. But if the darker evenings and falling leaves have got you craving cosiness, here’s our recipe for achieving that comforting autumnal vibe while it’s still unseasonably warm out.Tidy upView image in fullscreenDry run: swap fresh flowers for something more autumnal.Photograph: Anna Blazhuk/GettyWe did some research, and one of the main things people said made their home feel cosy was keeping it tidy. Clean before an evening in to create a relaxing environment (if you need supplies, the FilterlovesSeep’s 12-month supply of plastic-free sponges). Instead of a vase filled with fresh flowers, opt forbeautiful dried ones– they feel more seasonal and last for ever. Or make your own from the garden: dried poppy seed heads are strikingly sculptural.Fake it till it’s chillyDesperate to dig out your autumn wardrobe but don’t want to overheat? Try a knee-length skirt without the tights: we’re already anticipating Claudia Winkleman’s magnificent Highlands wardrobe in The Celebrity Traitors with this Albarayblack kilt skirt, which we can report hangs beautifully (a checked version has already sold out at Marks & Spencer). If your legs are a little summer-dry, slather them in moisturiser: Garnier’s affordablevitamin C body creamwas rated thebest budget moisturiserin our test.Create atmosphereView image in fullscreenGlow up: candlelight brings the cosy factor before the cold sets in.Photograph: Alexandr Kolesnikov/GettyCandles are a cheat code for instant hygge, but this transitional period feels too soon for cloying pumpkin spice scents. Memree is known for its niche fragrances, including its viraljam-on-toast candle, which has notes of toasted bread, butter and strawberry jam. Alternatively,Daylesford Organic’s log fire candlechannels charred birch logs, incense and leather (and its fragrance fills a room).Portable lamps are also perfect for plonking down wherever you need a vibe boost.Dusk’s rechargeable bobbin lampis super cute, affordable and comes in a tasteful olive green or plum.Snug-but-not-too-hot pyjamasWhile temperatures are still unseasonably high,go for short pyjamas in a soft material that still gives that snug feeling. This Chelsea Peers women’spyjama top and shorts setis made from a breathable, silky modal blend. For men, thisM&S cotton pyjama shorts setis just the right amount of cosy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPamper yourselfView image in fullscreenFace time: a sheet mask brings the spa feeling home.Photograph: Andrii Lysenko/GettyThere’s no doubt that autumn and pampering go hand in hand. If it’s too hot for a bath, try adding more luxury to your shower. TheseSmug steamersdissolve at the edge of the water stream, releasing fragrance. Or try a shower gel with a spa-like scent to help you unwind, such asMethod’s affordable Daily Zen body washwith green tea and cucumber.If you fancy a skincare treatment, opt for a cooling one.Sali Hughes saysthisHada Labo Tokyo sheet maskis a “huge drink of water for a frazzled face”. Or tackle hard heels from a summer of sandal-wearing withmoisturising socks.Create the perfect night inCurling up with a new TV show is much easier when it’s dark at 8.30pm (check our culture team’s guide tothe best autumn TV shows); pair it withM&S’s peanut butter and jelly munch tin, a Filter favourite.Explore more on these topicsAutumnThe FilterInteriorsAccessoriesHomesBeautyChristmasbest ofShareReuse this content

title: Hot and sour, vegetarian mapo and in spicy sauce: Fuchsia Dunlop’s tofu recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Wobblesome, firm or silken, tofu is a star ingredient in Chinese cooking. These dishes show why
Author: Fuchsia Dunlop
Headline: Wobblesome, firm or silken, tofu is a star ingredient in Chinese cooking. These dishes show why
Content: Fuschia Dunlop’s juicy tofu in a spicy sauce.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenFuschia Dunlop’s juicy tofu in a spicy sauce.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.FoodHot and sour, vegetarian mapo and in spicy sauce: Fuchsia Dunlop’s tofu recipesWobblesome, firm or silken, tofu is a star ingredient in Chinese cooking. These dishes show whyFuchsia DunlopMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the west, tofu is often viewed as a substitute for meat, which may explain why firmer types that can be cut into chunks and fried or grilled like meat have become so ubiquitous. In China, however, where tofu has been eaten for at least 1,000 years, it isn’t a substitute for anything; it’s simply a protein-rich ingredient that forms part of most people’s diets, can be cooked with meat and fish, and comes in myriad forms, from the tender, wobbly tofu used to make Sichuanese mapo tofu to firm smoked tofu, sheets of tofu “skin” and the silken tofu that can be as soft as creme caramel. Many Chinese tofu recipes are so delicious that habitual meat-eaters will devour them as keenly as vegetarians.Juicy tofu in a spicy sauceIn Yunnan, eating tofu is a social activity. All over the south of the province, people gather around grills tended by cooks who slowly toast chunks of cured tofu until they are crisp and golden on the outside, soft and slightly juicy within, and customers help themselves, dipping the tofu pieces into soy sauce, chilli, garlic and herbs. Aside from the ubiquitous tofu grills, there are many delicious local tofu recipes, including this one. In Yunnan, they make it with slices of fresh tofu soaked in an alkaline solution, which makes the texture particularly custardy after frying: a sort of artisanal molecular gastronomy (such tofu is described as “enclosing milkiness”). At home, however, I use tofu that is very tender but just holds its shape and is similarly sumptuous when bathed in a spicy sauce with minced pork (to make this vegetarian, simply omit the pork). The tofu can be deep-fried a few hours ahead and chilled until you wish to finish cooking. I use a combination of Sichuan chilli bean paste and sambal oelek instead of Yunnan fermented sauces, which are hard to find outside China.Prep10 minCook20 minServes4 with rice and 2-3 other dishes600g tender plain white tofuCooking oil, for deep-frying, plus 3 tbsp extra for the wok100g minced pork1 tbspShaoxing wine2 tbsp Sichuan chilli bean paste1 small red onion(about 50g), peeled and finely chopped1½ tbsp finely chopped garlic1 tbsp finely chopped ginger2 tbsp finely chopped red chilli1 tbspsambal oelekA few pinches of ground white pepper, to taste1 tsp potato starch mixed with 1 tbsp cold water3 tbsp finely sliced spring onions, green parts onlyCut the tofu into even, 1-1½cm-thick bite-size pieces, then gently pat dry with kitchen paper.Heat oil for deep-frying to 180C. Working in batches, fry the tofu for about five minutes, until golden brown, then drain on kitchen paper. You can do this step a few hours in advance.Put three tablespoons of oil in a seasoned wok on a high heat. Add the pork and stir-fry, breaking up the meat, then, when it turns pale, add the Shaoxing wine. When the meat is a little golden, turn down the heat to medium, add the chilli bean paste and stir until the oil reddens. Add the onion, fry until it smells delicious, then do the same with the garlic, ginger and chilli. Finally, stir in the sambal oelek. You should have a rubbly mass of utter deliciousness.Pour in 250ml water and add a little white pepper to taste. Drop in the fried tofu, nudge the pieces into the sauce, then return to a boil and simmer for a minute or so, to “send the flavours in”. Give the starch mixture a stir and, in a couple of stages, add just enough to thicken the sauce to a lazy gravy. Stir in the spring onion greens and serve.Mushroom mapo tofuView image in fullscreenFuchsia Dunlop’s mushroom mapo tofu.People often ask me how to make mapo tofu vegetarian and, to be honest, I normally just omit the beef from the classic recipe. If you miss the mouthfeel of the meat, this version, made with mushroom mince, is highly satisfying (you can also make the mince a day in advance, if you like). Do finish the dish with a scattering of freshly roasted and ground Sichuan pepper, which is one of the signatures of real mapo tofu. To make the perfect mapo tofu, use the tenderest, silkiest tofu that will hold its shape – as the Sichuanese chef Yu Bo puts it, you want the edges of the cubes to look as if they are straining to contain its voluptuousness. The more wobblesome the tofu, the greater the joy! It’s best to buy fresh tofu in water from Chinese shops; supermarket versions tend to be drier and nubblier. The same mince makes a fabulous pork substitute in dan dan noodles or anywhere, really, where you want to replace mince with something meatless. (Perhaps in lasagne or moussaka, for example.)Prep10 minCook25 minServes4 with rice and 2-3 other dishesFor the mushroom mince200g chestnut mushrooms, or other mushrooms3 tbsp cooking oil2 tsp finely chopped garlic2 tsp finely chopped ginger1 tsp dark soy sauceSaltFor the dish500g tender plain white tofu2 baby leeks, or spring onions, green parts only3 tbsp cooking oil2½ tbsp Sichuan chilli bean paste1 tbsp fermented black beans, rinsed2 tsp ground chillies1 tbsp finely chopped garlic1 tbsp finely chopped ginger¼ tsp ground white pepper1 tbsp potato starch mixed with 2½ tbsp cold water¼-1 tsp ground roasted Sichuan pepper, to toastCut off and discard the dry ends of the mushroom stalks, cut the stems and caps into roughly 5mm-thick slices, then cut into 5mm cubes. Put the oil in a seasoned wok on a high heat, then cook the mushroom cubes for two to three minutes, until greatly reduced in volume and tinged with gold. Add the garlic and ginger, stir briefly until you can smell them, then add the soy sauce and salt to taste. When it’s all sizzly and delicious, take off the heat.Cut the tofu into 2cm cubes and leave it to steep in very hot, lightly salted water while you prepare the other ingredients. Cut the leeks into 2cm lengths.Put the oil in a seasoned wok on a medium heat. Add the chilli bean paste, stir-fry until the oil turns red, then add the black beans and chillies, and stir-fry until they smell delicious. Do the same for the garlic and ginger, taking care not to burn them, then pour in 175ml water. Use a slotted spoon to transfer the tofu from its soaking water to the hot wok, then add the mushroom mince and white pepper, and bring to a boil. Simmer for a couple of minutes, so the tofu absorbs the flavours. If you’re using baby leeks, stir them in and cook for a few moments (if you’re using spring onions instead, add them later). In a few stages, stir in just enough of the starch mixture to thicken the sauce so it clings to the tofu (if using spring onion greens, stir them in now).Pour everything into a deep serving bowl, sprinkle with the ground roasted Sichuan pepper to taste and serve.Sour-and-hot silken tofuView image in fullscreenFuchsia Dunlop’s sour-and-hot silken tofu.The soft wobbliness of “flower tofu”, otherwise known as “tofu brain” or silken tofu, is soothing at any time of day, but I particularly love it for breakfast. It is as satisfying and comforting as porridge, but lighter. You can eat it sweet, with a drizzle of brown sugar syrup or even fruit salad, but I prefer mine with savoury seasonings. There are countless ways to serve silken tofu. In the north, including Beijing, they bathe it in a kind of gravy, thick with morsels of dried lily, mushrooms and wisps of egg. In the Jiangnan region around Shanghai, on the other hand, the adornments are more delicate: tiny dried shrimps and seaweed, preserved vegetables and sliced spring onions. In Sichuan, of course, they like a bit of spice. This recipe, which serves one or two people, depending on appetite, is inspired by the exquisite version dreamed up by Chengdu chef Lu Ziqiang atBirds of a Feather in Brooklyn, New York. I’ve substituted the traditional deep-fried soya beans and noodles for Bombay mix, which is similar in appearance and crunchiness.Prep10 minCook5 minServes1-2300g silken tofu2 tsp Chinese sesame paste1 tspChinkiang vinegar2 tsp light soy sauce1 tsp white sugar1½ tbsp chilli oil, plus ½–1 tbsp chilli sediment½ tsp red or green Sichuan pepper oil2 tbsp finely chopped Sichuan preserved vegetables2 tbsp finely sliced spring onions, green parts only1 small handful Bombay mixTip the silken tofu into a saucepan of boiling water and simmer gently for a few minutes, until heated through. Gently break it up into large, cloud-like clumps, but don’t stir or it will disintegrate.Meanwhile, put the sesame paste in a small bowl and smooth it with the back of a spoon. Gradually stir in the vinegar and soy sauce to create a satiny emulsion, then add the sugar. Stir in the chilli oil and sediment, and the Sichuan pepper oil.When the tofu is ready, gently lift it from the water and transfer to a bowl. Pour the sauce over the top, then sprinkle over the other ingredients. Mix well before eating.These recipes are edited extracts from Five Tastes: The Magic of Flavour in a Chinese Kitchen, by Fuchsia Dunlop, published by Particular Books at £30.
