title: UK credit scores: should you worry about a big shake-up? | Borrowing & debt | The Guardian
description: Your rating is vital when taking on debt, but you could be in for a surprise as a big player changes its rules
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: Your rating is vital when taking on debt, but you could be in for a surprise as a big player changes its rules
Content: Your credit score hellps determine whether or not you can borrow cash, including for mortgages.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyView image in fullscreenYour credit score hellps determine whether or not you can borrow cash, including for mortgages.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyBorrowing & debtUK credit scores: should you worry about a big shake-up?Your rating is vital when taking on debt, but you could be in for a surprise as a big player changes its rulesZoe WoodMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 04.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYour credit score is the magic number that helps lenders decide whether or not to approve a mortgage, loan or credit card application.Typically, the higher the number, the better your borrowing prospects. But a shake-up of the scoring system at TransUnion, one of the UK’s three main credit reference agencies, could mean a shock next time you log in.Previously, TransUnion’s top score was 710, but later this month it will start rolling out a wider range, rating you out of 999.And while the change means tens of thousands of people will be promoted to a higher band (bands are colour-coded like traffic lights, with “excellent” at the top and “very low” at the bottom), others will be demoted and find they have slipped down a rung.The good news, though, is that even if your “score banding” changes, the underlying information held on your credit file will remain the same, and that is what lenders use to decide the outcome of an application – so credit decisions and approvals will not be affected, says the company.In the UK there is no “universal credit score” that is used by lenders or credit reference agencies (CRAs). Each CRA has its own system: the other two main ones in the UK are Equifax and Experian. At Equifax your credit score is between 0 and 1,000, and at Experian it’s 0 to 1,250.View image in fullscreenIn the UK there is no ‘universal credit score used by lenders or credit reference agencies.Photograph: Izel Photography/RFC1/AlamyWhat is my score?It is a number calculated based on your credit history. That is, it’s a measure of how likely you are to repay your debts on time.Before you can take on any kind of debt – and for other purposes, too – banks, mobile phone companies and other businesses will check your creditworthiness with any of the three CRAs. They all use slightly different models, but rely on similar data, such as your history of paying bills, to calculate the score. Those in the top bands are considered a more reliable prospect for lenders, with your score also affecting how much you can borrow and the rate of interest charged.What is TransUnion doing?Previously, its top mark was 710, but this month it will start rolling out the new system that scores you from 0 to 999.TransUnion says the overhaul gives consumers a “clearer and more detailed view of their credit health”.It claims it is “more than a new number range” as it combines how consumers use credit over time, with a “moment-in-time view to provide a more considered picture of how consumers manage credit day-to-day”.View image in fullscreenTransUnion has changed its credit score rankings. Its previous top mark was 710, not its 999.Photograph: SOPA Images Limited/AlamyThe new score draws on more data, including how account balances have changed over time, and how credit cards are used.The company has also changed some of its terminology. The bottom two bands used to be called “poor” and “very poor” but have been renamed “low” and “very low”.TransUnion says most people (58%) will remain in the same score band, while 36% will be boosted to a higher bracket, and 6% will move down a bracket.Madhu Kejriwal at TransUnion says its new score is “clearer, more transparent, informative and better aligned with how lenders view consumers today”.TransUnion credit scoring tableThe new system is being rolled out in stages between late September and June 2027. As a result, some consumers may briefly see two different scores, depending on the app or provider they use, and when it adopts the new model.Even if your score ends up looking worse, TransUnion says that nothing about your underlying credit report will have changed – only the number that you see.View image in fullscreenTom Eyre, the chief executive of credit-building platform Loqbox, says don’t fret if a new model moves you into a lower credit band – ‘it doesn’t mean you have become less creditworthy overnight’.Photograph: Panther Media GmbH/AlamyTransUnion says: “The information shared with organisations about an individual’s credit history will remain unchanged.“As a result, the presence of different scores during the transition will not impact or influence lenders’ decisions on credit applications.”Tom Eyre, the chief executive of the credit-building platform Loqbox, says the changes to scoring systems are not something to worry about. “If a new model moves someone into a lower band, it doesn’t mean they have become less creditworthy overnight. Their behaviour and their history are the same. What’s changed is how the credit rating agency calculates or presents their score.”Eyre adds: “It’s far more important to understand what’s in your report and what shapes it, rather than a specific band or number, as it’s those pieces of information that credit providers actually look at, alongside their own criteria, when making a decision.”What about Experian and Equifax?Experianrejigged its scoring systemlast year, increasing the top of its range from 999 to 1,250, and factoring in items such as rental payments for the first time.Equifax changed its score range from 0-700 to 0-1,000 in 2021 and is not thought to be planning another change any time soon.View image in fullscreenExperian has also upped its highest score, from 999 to 1,250.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyExperian says its new system “better reflects more of the everyday financial behaviours that matter – like paying rent or reducing overdraft use”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt also gives people a “more personalised view of how they’re doing financially, and more practical ways to improve their score”, the company says.Experian also got rid of the “poor” and “very poor” labels, as well as the use of the colour red. Its bands are now called “excellent”, “very good”, “good”, fair” and “low”.After the change, Experian says 42% of people saw their score band improve, and a similar number recorded a drop, while 14% registered no change.View image in fullscreenExperian has got rid of its ‘poor’ and ‘very poor labels.Photograph: Samantha Craddock/AlamyWhat if my score falls?Small movements are not unusual – they can be caused by things such as the fact you’ve used a bit more of your credit card credit limit – and a slight dip is unlikely to affect your ability to borrow.Also, remember that a “low” or “very low” score does not block access to credit. It may make it harder to obtain, though, and the available options may come with a higher interest rate.John Webb at Experian says that, generally, there is “no need to worry” about small changes.“Your credit score can change regularly as the information on your credit report is updated,” he adds.View image in fullscreenEquifax says paying back what you owe in full and on time shows lenders you are able to manage your finances, which supports your overall credit health.Photograph: M4OS Photos/AlamyIt is worth keeping an eye on the direction of travel, and there are lots of free, and paid-for, ways to check your score – many high street banks include the feature in their apps.Eyre says each agency works out its own score from the information it holds, but “it’s the credit file that gives you the detail behind it, such as your accounts, payments and searches”.He explains: “Every credit reference agency is legally required to give you your statutory credit report at no charge, and services such as ClearScore, Credit Karma and the Experian app will show a score, and often basic credit report insights, for free, although you might need to pay to access some additional features.”A steep drop in your credit score is a red flag and you should investigate. It could be something straightforward such as the closure of an account after paying off a longstanding credit card bill, or something more serious, such as a missed payment or identity fraud.How can I improve my credit score?Start by checking that the information in your credit report is accurate.You need to check all three credit reference agencies as Loqbox chief executive Tom Eyre says no single one gives you the whole picture. “They don’t all hold exactly the same information about a person, because lenders and other providers may report to one, two or all three – and some lenders lean on a particular agency when assessing applications.”Experian’s guide toimproving your credit scoreadvises using 30% of your credit card limit, registering on the electoral roll (this helps lenders verify your identity), avoiding new applications for credit unless needed, and keeping up to date with minimum payments.View image in fullscreenUsing 30% of your credit card limit can help boost your credit score, says Experian.Photograph: Realimage/AlamyCraig Tebbutt at Equifax says it is important to “make full repayments on time. Missed payments go on your credit report. Paying back what you owe in full and on time shows lenders you are able to manage your finances, which supports your overall credit health.”Tebbutt says that if you already have a lot of credit available – for example, several credit cards or a large overdraft – lenders may take this into account.Also think about closing accounts you do not use.You should also “be careful when applying for credit”, says Tebbutt. “Every time you formally apply for credit, it leaves a ‘hard search’ on your credit report. Try to space out your applications, and only apply for credit you need.”Finally, review your financial associations: if you have a joint bank account or mortgage with someone, you are “financially associated” with them. If their credit history isn’t great, it could affect your own application.Explore more on these topicsBorrowing & debtConsumer affairsFinancial sectorPersonal loansMortgagesBankingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, Italy | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: It’s the birthplace of the popular cheese, but the Barletta-Andria-Trani province in southern Italy has an array of local delicacies – from olive oil and yellow tomatoes to goat prosciutto
Author: Liz Boulter
Headline: It’s the birthplace of the popular cheese, but the Barletta-Andria-Trani province in southern Italy has an array of local delicacies – from olive oil and yellow tomatoes to goat prosciutto
Content: The Norman cathedral in Barletta.Photograph: Giovanni Ruggiero/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Norman cathedral in Barletta.Photograph: Giovanni Ruggiero/AlamyItaly holidaysBurrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, ItalyIt’s the birthplace of the popular cheese, but the Barletta-Andria-Trani province in southern Italy has an array of local delicacies – from olive oil and yellow tomatoes to goat prosciuttoLiz BoulterMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Idon’t eat mozzarella outside Puglia,” says our friend Savio. “It’s not the same.” Savio is a very opinionated foodie, so I take his words with a pinch of good Puglian sea salt (see below). He was adamant about the superiority of the stretched-curd cheese from his home turf.Puglia is also the birthplace of ingredientdu jourburrata, which originated in Andria, a few miles from Savio’s home town of Barletta. Andria forms one part of the triangular Barletta-Andria-Trani (BAT) province, but despite the cheese connection and Barletta having miles of palm-backed, sandy beaches, it is often passed over for better-known parts of Puglia. So I asked Savio’s company,Unexpected Italy, an app that calls itself the antidote to overtourism, to organise a trip to the area.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsAbout a century ago, in the hills outside Andria, farmer Lorenzo Bianchino was snowed in and couldn’t get his milk to market. To save what he could, he revived an old technique for preserving butter (burro, hence burrata), stuffing cream mixed with mozzarella scraps (stracciatella) in a casing of the stretched-curd cheese.There are now several burrata makers in Andria, the most famous beingCaseificio Olanda, which offers demos, tastings and a museum. Late one morning, we watch Riccardo “Dino” Olanda, son of the founders, work his magic. He adds almost-boiling water to the curds, then mixes with hands red from doing this every day. As he stretches and massages the curds, a smooth velvety mass forms. “See how it’s shiny?” he says. “Means it’s ready.” Working quickly, he squeezes out round lumps between thumb and forefinger into the familiar mozzarella balls. This action ismozzare, hence the name.He also makes little knots and plaits before moving on to burrata. Taking a warm mozzarella ball, he works it into a hollow bag with his fingers then fills it with cream andstracciatellabefore tying the top with string.View image in fullscreenRiccardo Olanda making burrataAfterwards, a dairy-heavy meal totally worth the cholesterol and calories: mozzarella and burrata to start, then bread with chunks ofcaciocavallo(a stretched-curd cheese), and a dessert of heart-shaped fresh ricotta with strawberry jam or cocoa.And, I have to say, Savio is right. The mozzarella and burrata have a juicy, elastic texture and a gorgeous cheesy, umami flavour; the salt and flavour leached out by the whey the cheeses later sit in. How will I ever settle for Tesco Finest after this?double quotation markThe mozzarella and burrata have a juicy, elastic texture and a cheesy, umami flavourOver the next few days, eating our way around the province’s restaurants and food producers, I wonder whether it’s because the ingredients are so good that this area has so many food obsessives, or the other way round.Barletta sees few foreign tourists, but it is full of Italian life. There are lots of independent shops, a Norman castle and cathedral to visit, and every evening people pour into the bars, clubs andgelaterieof thesette strade, seven parallel streets in the old town.Down the coast, Trani, with its sea-facing romanesque cathedral and pretty harbour, attracts some tourists, but they are not in evidence at 7am when the fishing boats return. The men complain of rough seas and a poor catch, but from the back of the boats they’re soon selling mullet, octopus, skate, fat sea snails, monkfish andpalombo(small shark) to restaurateurs and fishmongers. Thirtysomething Nicola says he went out at midday and got back at 3am. When does he sleep? “Never.” A fifth-generation fisher, he began helping on the boats aged six.View image in fullscreenFish straight off the boat at Trani docks.Photograph: Vittorio Sciosia/AlamyWe’ll eat fish later, but today is for pizza.Portentoin Barletta is run by food nut Luigi Lacerenza. He has us try so many local products asantipasti–caprinogoat’s cheese tasting of green mountains, grilledcaciocavallo from an old couple who make just six a week and small-batch salami – that we’re almost too full for pizzas. But they are wonderful: one with sausage, olives, oyster mushrooms and yellow tomatoes; another with aubergines and gratedcacioricotta.‘It’s like bringing the kitchen into the piazza’: seven of the best Italian village food festivalsRead moreIn Cerignola, west of Barletta, Rosario Didonna used the money he won on a TV standup competition to turn his family’s deli into a cosy, wood- panelled restaurant,U’ Vulèsce(dialect for “peckish”). Rosario knows fishers by name, works with small farmers and wine producers, and invitesnonnefrom all over southern Italy to demonstrate recipes in his kitchens.double quotation markI wonder whether it’s because the ingredients are so good that this area has so many food obsessives, or the other way roundWe start with tasty goat prosciutto and plum-sized local olives calledbella di Cerignola. Then an unforgettable prawn tartare served in sea urchin shells, hairy crab spaghetti (“the juice is better than lobster”), octopus with bean puree, and sea bass with orange mayo. He waves away our thanks: “I’m doing the best job in the world!”Nicola Barbera atMasseria Barbera, a farm restaurant in the Alta Murgia national park, is equally inspired, but rather by what grows on the estate founded by his great-great-great-great-grandfather Riccardo, who fought with Garibaldi.Exuberantly bouncing us around the farm – it produces 90% of what the 100-cover restaurant needs – he shows us olives and vines, but also the “weeds” growing around them. “They’re eatable,” he says, grabbing handfuls of peppery rocket, and bitter but delicate wild chicory. From the abundant kitchen garden, he makes eight varieties of tomato sauce.View image in fullscreenMasseria Barbera farm restaurantWe tuck into a lot of this for lunch: a pie with white onions, anchovy and sultanas; courgettes with mint and garlic; spaghetti with yellow tomatoes. (“I call it bastard sauce,” says Nicola. “Those tomatoes take three times as long to pick.”) Then, something I never thought I’d eat: grilled donkey fillet. I feel bad about the patient, mild-tempered beasts, but this is healthy, low-fat food, never intensively farmed. It’s also the best meat I’ve ever tasted.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGood food is made better by good olive oil, and producers here includeMuraglia, known for organic oil in hand-painted, rainbow-stripe ceramic bottles, andSabino Leone, offering tours of its ancient groves and oil mill for €15, plus tastings.View image in fullscreenSabino Leone olive oilThis area also offers plenty to do between meals. Barletta was the home of Italian painter Giuseppe De Nittis, who hung out with Degas and Manet, and took part in the first impressionist exhibition in Paris, in 1874. Over 200 of his works are now displayed in the 16th-centuryPalazzodella Marra(€6).At Europe’s biggest salt pan,Salina Margherita di Savoia, there’s an expanse of peaceful ponds with a snow-white salt mountain to climb. Another day, an exhilarating ebike ride in the Alta Murgia with Filippo Tito ofCycling ’n’ Trek, through dense forest to peer with awe into an old bauxite mine that resembles a mini grand canyon. We get back ravenous, but in this corner of northern Puglia, that’s a blessing.Where to stayUntil this century, Barletta had little tourist accommodation. Pick of the few B&Bs isAntica Dimora(doubles from €97), a restored 17th-century palazzo run by Lilly and Riccardo Manna. There are three smart bedrooms with lots of plants and breakfast features different local specialities each day.Lama di Luna(doubles from €230) is an organic farm in deep countryside, with six rooms set around an 18th-century stone courtyard. A well and solar panels make it energy and water self-sufficient; half of its 200 hectares are left wild, the rest are planted with olives, vines, almonds and cherries. There’s a cinema, a library and a large pool shaded by 600-year-old olive trees.Where (else) to eatView image in fullscreenThe view from A Sud dell’Anima restaurant, MinervinoBarletta’s 60-year-oldMosébakery is revered for itskrapfenfilled doughnuts and sourdough croissants. There are also chocolates, ice-cream and cakes, all housemade, and great coffee.Puglia has hundreds ofgelateriebut experts rateScoopin Canosa (which is called Puglia’s “Little Rome” for its catacombs, temple ruins and Roman bridge). Francesco Di Nunno makes ice-cream with local seasonal ingredients: raspberry and strawberry sorbets are available only in early summer; percoca yellow peach until mid-August.There’s affordable fine dining at chef Luciano Matera’sIl Turraccioloin central Andria. Highlights for me are broad bean and chicory “meatballs”, bright green inside; a “hidden mushroom” under baked eggy topping; and pasta discs with whole and pureed green beans and peas.AtA Sud dell’Anima, chef Nadia Tamburrano uses modern techniques and hyper-local ingredients to make food of astonishing quality for a small hilltop town (Minervino, population under 8,000). Her antipasti explode with flavour thanks to house-cured capers and homemade mustard, syrups and purees. A main of sweetbreads wrapped in intestines feels a bit out-there, but is delicious, the intestines crispy as crackling.The trip was organised byUnexpected Italy, which offers personaliseditineraries for Barlettaand the surrounding areaExplore more on these topicsItaly holidaysFood and drinkEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: I was terrified of the dentist – until I found a very special one | Life and style | The Guardian
description: After an agonising experience, I avoided checkups for four years. But a practice that assured a stress-free process for scared patients was transformative
Author: Robin Craig
Headline: After an agonising experience, I avoided checkups for four years. But a practice that assured a stress-free process for scared patients was transformative
Content: No longer gritting his teeth … Robin Craig at the Modern Dentist, London.Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNo longer gritting his teeth … Robin Craig at the Modern Dentist, London.Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianThe one change that workedLife and styleThe one change that worked: I was terrified of the dentist – until I found a very special oneAfter an agonising experience, I avoided checkups for four years. But a practice that assured a stress-free process for scared patients was transformativeRobin CraigMon 14 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhaven’t always been afraid of the dentist. If you had asked me a decade ago whether sitting in the dentist’s chair filled me with dread or made me break out in a cold sweat, I would have laughed and said no – what is there to be afraid of? It was only in 2021, after I had a filling without being properly numbed, that I understood why people are afraid of dental work. Despite telling him I was in excruciating pain, the dentist carried on with the procedure anyway, and I was left with a newfound and deep-seated fear.At first, this was easily managed. I simply binned the reminders to book checkups, avoided their calls and carried on with my life. After a year, I told myself I’d see the dentist soon – just not yet. I firmly shoved the problem to the back of my mind.However, as time passed, I began to feel a creeping sense of shame. I bristled each time a friend talked about a dentist visit, convinced that they could sense I had not been in several years. I kept my dentist-dodging a secret and became increasingly ashamed of myself – I felt weak and childlike, incapable of a normal adult responsibility. But no matter how hard I tried, I could not bring myself to go.My avoidance came to a head one day in 2025. I noticed that whenever I ate something sweet, I had a sudden toothache. After a few weeks of panicking, I finally admitted my fears to a friend. They recommended a private practice in Shoreditch, London, that had helped them with dental anxiety. After reading its webpage, which assured a stress-free process for scared patients, I nervously booked an appointment.View image in fullscreenOpen wide …Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianWhen I arrived at the clinic a few days later, my hands were clammy and my forehead was covered in a sheen of cold sweat. By the time I went into my appointment, my legs felt like jelly. Before I even sat in the dentist’s chair, I launched into a confession that it had been four years since my last visit and how scared I was of another procedure going wrong.Instead of telling me off, he immediately understood why I was afraid and reassured me that avoidance was a common response to bad dental work. He explained that his practice had a desensitisation process for anxious patients: instead of starting with invasive treatments, they begin with low-stress procedures, such as cleaning, to build confidence and restore my sense of safety. He also told me that if I ever felt pain during an appointment, he would stop immediately, and that I had nothing to be ashamed of – he was just glad that I had come for a checkup at all.After examining my teeth, he said that the pain I felt was likely due to a buildup of plaque and I didn’t need a filling. I did need to have my wisdom teeth removed, but as promised, we would build up to that over a year or more to ensure I was comfortable and ready.We decided to start with a hygienist session where I could pause the cleaning whenever I needed by raising my hand. It felt completely different from the rushed appointments with my previous dentist, who had rarely stopped to ask if I was OK or tell me what he was doing in my mouth. For the first time, I felt in control.Afterwards, my deep sense of shame about dental care finally started to lift. I began speaking to friends about my fear, and found that some of them secretly avoided dental appointments, too. Many of them told me the same thing – that their embarrassment also made it harder to ask for help.I now go to the dentist regularly for checkups and hygiene visits, and am beginning to think about wisdom teeth extraction – something that would have been unimaginable a few years ago. I only wish that the desensitisation approach for anxious patients was more readily available in NHS clinics, but for me, overcoming my fear has been worth the cost.I’ve learned that the time I spent avoiding the dentist wasn’t a personal failure, but a completely natural reaction to a traumatic experience – one that, with the right support, could be overcome.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Can you futureproof your career by choosing an AI-resistant degree? | Higher education | The Guardian
description: Humans will have to compete with AI-powered virtual employees in the near future. Here are our tips for the last human holdouts
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: Humans will have to compete with AI-powered virtual employees in the near future. Here are our tips for the last human holdouts
Content: Stem subjects (science, technology, engineering and maths) have long been associated with good careers.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStem subjects (science, technology, engineering and maths) have long been associated with good careers.Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesUniversity Guide 2027Higher educationCan you futureproof your career by choosing an AI-resistant degree?Humans will have to compete with AI-powered virtual employees in the near future. Here are our tips for the last human holdoutsSally WealeMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFutureproofing your career with an AI-resistant degree is a tough ask, says Charlie Ball, an expert on graduate employment for Jisc, the UK’s higher education digital, data and technology agency.“What you’re trying to do is futureproof a 45-year career in a time of rapid technological change – and that’s really quite hard to do. What’s likely is that jobs that hinge a lot on human, face-to-face interaction are unlikely to be replaced.”He warns however that the discussion should focus less on identifying specific vocational paths that are safe from AI, and more on how to equip young people with a suite of skills that allow them to adapt rapidly to labour market change.But if pushed, areas of work that might offer more protection from AI than others include the following.Research and developmentDegrees in Stem subjects (science, technology, engineering and maths) have long been associated with good careers. Although AI will inevitably affect entry-level lab work, “the creativity and imaginative work will have to be done by humans,” says Ball. “The whole point of R&D is to find out new things, and AI can only really compare against stuff that it’s already got in its database.”EngineeringWe may see AI increasingly embedded in design and modelling, but human engineers will still be required to operate in physical, real-world environments that will continue to require human oversight. “Much of engineering is going to be hard to replace by AI,” Ball says. “We are likely still to need engineers to do the big stuff like civil engineering – building bridges and buildings. Those areas are likely to be OK.”Creative arts and entertainment“Although AI can produce creative art, people generally don’t like it very much,” is Ball’s verdict. He thinks we will get better at spotting its handiwork. “There will always be demand for human-led creativity. Everything AI currently produces is a remix of things that already exist. AI can’t create things. You’ll never get a distinctive new voice emerging. It can’t do that.”Medicine“We will still have doctors in 50 years’ time,” says Ball. “Their jobs will change somewhat. But people will want humans to deliver their health news, particularly the more difficult news. And no matter how good automation gets, when your kids are poorly, you will want to take them to a human GP.” AI can be helpful with diagnoses in some cases, “but it will still make mistakes. Where you will need someone to take responsibility for decisions, they will all have to be human.”Nursing and midwifery“AI and tech will get injected into many health roles, and on balance that’s probably quite a good thing, because at the moment we have nowhere near enough people doing these jobs,” says Ball. “But people will want humans to care for them when they are sick. People will want humans to look after them when they are old. I cannot envisage a situation where there will ever be a robot midwife.”Education“Nor are we going to get robot teachers,” he adds, despite theongoing shortageof teachers in England. “There is already a role for technology in facilitating the delivery of education. But we will still want human educators to make this stuff relatable, and also for the pastoral side of student support. That will remain important.”Explore more on these topicsHigher educationUniversity Guide 2027AI (artificial intelligence)EmployabilityWork & careersUniversitiesStudentsYoung peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Did you solve it? Do you have the brain of an engineer? | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: The answers to today’s puzzles
Author: Alex Bellos
Headline: The answers to today’s puzzles
Content: Photograph: Andrew Soundarajan/AlamyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andrew Soundarajan/AlamyAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleMathematicsDid you solve it? Do you have the brain of an engineer?The answers to today’s puzzlesAlex BellosMon 14 Sep 2026 11.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier today I set four engineering puzzles. Here they are again with solutions. (Do check outthe hundreds of great commentsposted below the line in the original story.)The cranberriesIn a cranberry sorting facility, thousands of cranberries are dropped every minute onto a board. Good cranberries are firm, and bounce, while bad cranberries are soft, and don’t bounce.What simple trick allows sorters to catch all of the good ones and none of the bad?SolutionThe board is at an angle. Good berries bounce off onto a conveyor belt. Bad ones fall down into a discard box.Caps offIn the US, medicine bottle caps are designed to be secure against only 85 per cent of children under five.Why is this percentage not higher? Eighty-five seems quite low.SolutionIf the child-resistance rate was 100 per cent, the mechanism would also be hard for weak or arthritic hands. If the bottle is too hard for an elderly person to open, they may leave the cap off entirely, which is more dangerous than the small percentage of clever or strong kids who’d have taken it off anyway.The standard isn’t “as safe as possible” — it’s tuned to the point where making itsaferfor kids would make itlesssafe overall.Slats entertainmentIn 2020, engineers replaced the pedestrian handrail on the Golden Gate Bridge. The old handrail rested on metal balusters in the shape of an H, so the support looked like “HHHH…” where the H’s horizontal section was 10cm wide. The new handrail was supported only by thin vertical slats, making it look like “IIII…” and where each slat was only 0.6cm wide.The aim of the new handrail was to make it less resistant to wind, and hence safer during high winds. But it brought two serious unintended consequences.What were they?Solution1) The wind level on the bridge was much higher, to the great annoyance of cyclists.2) During certain winds, the whole bridge began to make anunbearable whistling noisethat could be heard for miles. Essentially, the new slats behaved like reeds, and the bridge turned into in a gigantic harmonica.Under pressureCabin air pressure in a plane is controlled to a level that is comfortable to humans. When a plane flies, the air pressure outside the plane drops to much lower than this level, causing the air pressure in the cabin to push outwards against the frame with great force.In the early 1950s, there were some major plane crashes when the fuselage was ripped apart mid flight.UK manufacturer de Havilland found a way to pressure test its plane, the Comet, the world’s first commercial jet, without the plane leaving the ground.What did they do?SolutionEngineers at Farnborough built a giant water tank at and submerged the plane in it. Filling the cabin with water and increasing the pressure let engineers safely find the limit at which the structure would fail. Air at that same pressure would have exploded destructively, destroying the evidence along with the plane.Here’s a picture of the water tankfrom 1954, with the Comet’s wings sticking out.Today’s puzzles were adapted fromHow to Keep a Plane in the Sky, by Alex Davies. The book tells fascinating stories about test engineers – those geniuses whose work underpins our trust that objects do not crack, break or explode. You can buy the book at theGuardian Bookshopand other retailers.I hope you had fun. I’ll be back in two weeks.I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one,email me.Explore more on these topicsMathematicsAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleEngineeringEngineering generalShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … having a hot drink will cool you down? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A warm cup of tea can trigger sweating and lower your body temperature, but only if you’re in an airy space
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: A warm cup of tea can trigger sweating and lower your body temperature, but only if you’re in an airy space
Content: Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …Life and styleIs it true that … having a hot drink will cool you down?A warm cup of tea can trigger sweating and lower your body temperature, but only if you’re in an airy spaceKate LloydMon 14 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCould a warm cup of tea really be the key to cooling down in hot weather? Or is that just something caffeine fiends tell themselves when they’re still working through a pot of coffee as the temperature hits 30C?Prof John Tregoning, the author ofLive Forever? A Curious Scientist’s Guide to Wellness, Ageing and Death,says it depends on the circumstances. He points to the work of Australian scientist Prof Ollie Jay, who is a world leader in researching heat and how it balances out in your body.When it comes to drinking a hot beverage, there are two effects on your body. “You’ve got the heat that the drink gives you, and then the amount that you sweat as a result of it,” Tregoning says.While you’re consuming the warm drink, its high temperature will cause your body temperature to rise. That elevated temperature will trigger you to sweat more.double quotation markThe key message is to take on fluids, whatever their temperature, especially in hot weatherThis is where things become complicated. Sweat cools down the body when it evaporates. When water on the skin turns to gas, it takes heat energy away from the body.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it true that … it’s harder for women to do pull-ups?Read moreOnly some environments are conducive to this process, however. In breezy spaces, the sweat evaporates efficiently, but in places with high humidity or poor ventilation sweat will run off the body instead. “That’s inefficient,” says Tregoning. “When you drink a hot drink in that environment, you get hotter rather than cooler.”Essentially: drinking a hot drink to cool down after a windy coastal walk? Good. Drinking a hot drink to cool down in a tropical rainforest? Bad.Tregoning says: “I think the key is to take on fluids, whatever their temperature, especially in hot weather. There isn’t a massive advantage in hot or cold drinks. It’s down to personal preference.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleIs it true that …Health & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The desecration of DC: from a giant arch to a nuke-proof bunker, Trump’s legacy-building blingfest is an architectural atrocity | Architecture | The Guardian
description: A bloated ballroom, a six-storey military HQ, a helipad-cum-cocktail patio, a gilded angel on a giant arch honouring himself … our architecture critic deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of Washington
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: A bloated ballroom, a six-storey military HQ, a helipad-cum-cocktail patio, a gilded angel on a giant arch honouring himself … our architecture critic deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of Washington
Content: A lust for supersizing … the plan for Trump’s triumphal arch.Illustration: US Commission on Fine Arts/ReutersView image in fullscreenA lust for supersizing … the plan for Trump’s triumphal arch.Illustration: US Commission on Fine Arts/ReutersArchitectureThe desecration of DC: from a giant arch to a nuke-proof bunker, Trump’s legacy-building blingfest is an architectural atrocityA bloated ballroom, a six-storey military HQ, a helipad-cum-cocktail patio, a gilded angel on a giant arch honouring himself … our architecture critic deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of WashingtonOliver WainwrightMon 14 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen you have a developer as US president, you might expect some zhooshing up of the capital. A few buildings renovated, maybe some parks replanted. But when you have a megalomaniac builder in charge, things can get out of hand. A decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected,I askedwhat it might mean for the US to be led by a real estate tycoon whose career had left a trail of broken promises, angry buyers and endless lawsuits, with rules flouted,heritage trampledand the world pockmarked by a fleet of aspirational towers clad with a flimsy veneer of luxury. The answer is worse than I could have imagined.With the air of a nightmarish Hollywood sequel, Trump 2 has seen the president’s true architectural ambitions unleashed: The Blingpire Strikes Back. As America’s self-styled decorator-in-chief, Trump has not only overseen the gilded mutilation of the White House, but embarked on the Mar-a-Lagofication of Washington DC itself, applying his gold paintbrush to statuary, daubing ponds with flaking pool liner, and brewing plans for a colossal triumphal arch – all procured in ablizzard of no-bid contracts. And, in true dodgy salesman style, this programme of bauble-building is turning out to be a high-profile decoy for deeper damage being wrought elsewhere.double quotation markIf the government wants to bulldoze the Statue of Liberty, nothing can be doneThe bloated White House ballroom is the most emblematic project of Trump’s reign so far, a chandelier-bedecked warehouse conceived on a scale that would make Ceaușescu blush. Standing like an overly iced wedding cake atop a multilevel concrete bunker, it is a swaggering confection that masks deep-rooted paranoia: a decadently wrapped panic room, where a besieged dictator might hole themselves up.View image in fullscreenWhat lies beneath … the ballroom hides a full-scale military complex, including a hospital.Illustration: McCrery Architects/White House“It won’t interfere with the current building,”Trump promised last July, when he announced the plans. “Not touching it.” It would seat 650 guests and cost $200m, funded by private donations. Less than three months later, without waiting for congressional approval, he tore down the historic East Wing, anddumped the rubble on a nearby public golf course(which he also plans to redevelop). The ballroom ballooned, as if injected with rapid weight-gain formula, to seat 1,000 in a building three times the volume of the White House. The price has also tripled to $600m, at least half of which will now be picked up by the taxpayer.Trump boasted that his ballroom will be “more beautiful” than Versailles, but it looks like something thrown together from the classical off-cuts bin, without any regard to how the pieces fit. “It has all the kneejerk gestures of classicism,” a former Commission of Fine Arts (CFA) official told me, “but they are not integrated in a way that makes any sense.”A sweeping ceremonial staircase leads to nowhere. A grand pedimented entrance is shunted to one end of the east facade. The portico columns run four rows deep (“The supreme court is three deep,”Trump noted. “No other building has it, and I did it because it’s incredible.”) The ballroom’s proportions are so out of whack, it will make the White House look like a lopsided fiddler crab, the swollen appendage vastly dwarfing the original building.View image in fullscreenNot exactly flag blue … the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/ReutersThe inflated scale was too much to bear for its architect, the bowtie-wearingJames McCrery II, who protested at the increasingly Frankenstein nature of the classical details being applied. Enter Shalom Baranes, whoseDC firmhas handled multibillion dollar federal contracts, including the renovation of the Pentagon after the 9/11 attacks.Baranes’s experience with fortified facilities has come in handy, given that the project has evolved into what Trump now calls “the Magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex”. The party hall, the presidentconfirmed in March, “essentially becomes a shed for what’s being built under” – namely a six-storey military-grade bunker, replete with a command and emergency operations centre, a full-scale military hospital, secure telecommunications hubs and situation rooms, all serviced by specialised air-handling and filtration networks to protect against biological, chemical and radiological threats. “It’s meant for if there’s a nuclear attack,” Trump has boasted. “The concrete is so hard, I’m not sure you could take it down.”Behind the overblown cornice, the ballroom’s roof will be home to a military drone port and air-defence missile system. Images show it looking like an aircraft carrier parked next to the White House. In typically Trumpian newspeak, the project has gone from being a space to entertain dignitaries to a “desperately needed National Security structure” that must be completed at all costs.After court rulings halted construction, the supreme court recentlyweighed in to allow it to resume– although, tellingly, the ruling made no comment on the project’s legality. But questions in the courts have revealed just how far Trump’s aides see his absolutist rule extending. “If the government decides, very quickly, to bulldoze the Statue of Liberty,”one judge asked, “nothing can be done?” A lawyer for the administration responded: “I think that’s right, yes.”View image in fullscreenDrinks all round … construction continues on a helipad-cum-cocktail patio on the south lawn of the White House.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APSimilarly bullish efforts are being made to force through the president’s second flagship vanity project, the elephantine triumphal arch. It was casually announced last October, with 3D-printed models displayed like tacky souvenirs in the Oval Office. It is planned to tower 250ft above Memorial Circle, a vast roundabout on Columbia Island in DC’s Potomac River – 1ft for every year of US independence. But there has been no ambiguity about what the looming edifice is really there to honour. When asked, Trump simply replied: “Me.”It “will be the GREATEST and MOST BEAUTIFUL Triumphal Arch,” he boasted on social media, “anywhere in the World”. He has cited Roman precedents and “the one in Paris”, adding that his version “will surpass it in every way”. Oddly, given his fondness for the North Korean regime, he has neglected to mentionPyongyang’s Arch of Triumph, built in 1982 to mark Kim Il Sung’s 70th birthday. Clad with 25,500 blocks of sparkling white granite, one for each day of Kim’s life, its crowning stone slab rises 10m taller than Trump’s (although his is topped with a statue for an extra 25m of vanity height).Hitler’s Triumphbogen, also unmentioned, would have been twice the size.To aid his Napoleonic cosplay, the president has hired Harrison Design,purveyors of gaudy McMansionsfrom Atlanta to LA, with the arch project led by Nicolas Charbonneau, principal of the firm’s Sacred Architecture Studio. Charbonneau first sketched the idea to illustrate an April 2025 essay by conservative critic Catesby Leigh, titledWashington Needs an Arch. It proposed a modest structure of 60ft. Trump got hold of the idea and, with his irrepressible lust for supersizing, pumped it up fourfold.View image in fullscreenDwarfing the White House … the ballroom will have a drone port on its roof.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersAs with the ballroom-bunker, the arch has become larger and more encrusted with gilded ornament – in a word, more Trumpian – as it has progressed. The final design, unveiled this April, features a 60ft golden-winged Lady Liberty sprouting from its summit like an oversized cake-topper, flanked by two plump eagles. Even Trump’s allies have suggested the design could be toned down. At a CFA review, McCrery, the first ballroom architect, advised removing four golden lions from the base of the arch. “They’re noble, they’re courageous, and they’re strong,” he noted. But “they’re not of this continent”. The arch must celebrate American triumphs only – and that goes for the animals too.Trump’s reflecting pool saga: a timeline of failure and finger-pointingRead moreThe National Park Servicehas determinedthe project will “adversely affect” dozens of historic sites around DC, while a group of Vietnam veterans has filed a lawsuit, arguing the arch will be an unwelcome “expression of domination”, with its observation deck looming over Arlington National Cemetery. Neither of these are proving to be obstacles,with excavation set to begin soon.Preliminary works do not augur well. A mockup of the arch was erected for the Great American State Fair in July, made of plywood wrapped with white vinyl. It buckled in the heat, its surfaces warping and peeling, while globules of expanding foamoozed from its wonky cornice. It was instantly dubbed the Temu arch – a fitting moniker, given that Trump’s Oval Office swags appear to have beensourced from the fellow Chinese online marketplace Alibaba.The ballroom and the arch received tens of thousands of objections from the public, but both projects were fast-tracked through the system. As the former CFA official told me, it was “highly unusual” that the initial concept schemes were granted final approval without details being resolved. The ballroom took just 12 minutes of deliberation. And it has set the tone of things to come. There’s nothing a developer hates more than red tape, and Trump has vowed to streamline regulations across the board. Beyond speeding up his DC follies, the proposed changes will lubricate drilling, pipe-laying and datacentre building, in the name of “reclaiming America’s proud heritage as a nation of builders”.View image in fullscreenGold, gold, everywhere … Trump in the Oval Office.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesObscured by all the controversy around these trophy projects is the fact that the administration has moved to weaken protections on historic buildings and landscapes drastically, unleashing the steamroller of development across the country. The changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act would narrow the definition of historic places, exclude consideration of the “visual, atmospheric or audible” consequences of projects on historic sites, and reduce requirements for consulting Indigenous tribes and the public. As Brent Leggs, president of the National Trust for Historic Preservation,remarked, it would “eviscerate the preservation of our shared civic and cultural heritage in the United States”.The irony couldn’t be clearer. Trump bloviates about continuing America’s tradition of monument building, while weakening the very mechanisms that exist to protect the country’s heritage. Still, by slashing these protections, at least he is paving the way for his own additions to be toppled just as hastily as they were erected.‘Dictator-for-life vibes’: our architecture critic on Trump’s bulletproof ballroom blingRead moreGiven the construction quality so far, future topplers might not need much help. The Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has now been drained for a second time, after the coating used in the first $15m renovation began peeling offwithin days of its completion. Despite a new filtration system intended to keep the water a pristine shade of “American Flag Blue”, massive algae blooms quickly turned it a swampy green. While Trump blamed vandals, justice department legal filings eventually conceded the failure was due to the “hasty and botched” renovation. “I have a guy who’s unbelievable at doing swimming pools,” Trump boasted, before awarding the no-bid contract toa companythat had worked on his Virginia golf course.Elsewhere around the capital, the “Safe and Beautiful” initiative has seen $76m spent on fountains, $5m on gilding a pair of equestrian statues of The Arts of War and The Arts of Peace, $500,000 on a single statue pedestal to display a statue of a prominent slave owner, which had been removed from Delaware amid Black Lives Matter protests, and countless other acts of cosmetic surgery in the name of cleaning up the “cesspool” of DC.View image in fullscreenNewly covered in gold leaf … the Arts of War statues.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOne of the crowning trinkets will be theNational Garden of American Heroes, for which $40m has been ringfenced. According to Executive Order 13978, this park of 250 statues will “reflect the awesome splendour of our country’s timeless exceptionalism” in the face of the “reckless attempt to erase our heroes, values and entire way of life”. The list of figures to be commemorated includes slave owners and others whose statues were toppled in the wake of George Floyd’s murder. Sculpture expertsdescribedthe proposed timeline as “completely unworkable” and likely to produce “slapdash and uninspired” work, suggesting the only place with foundries capable of realising a project on this scale and speed would be China. Alibaba prepare!Trump’s construction mania is all-consuming. He uses press conferences to show off his latest renovations andhas spokenof how building is the “fun” thing he does to relax, in between kidnapping South American presidents, bombing the Middle East and bullying Greenland. But White House insiders say his therapeutic hobby has become the policy priority, a massive drain on the administration’s energies and resources.The Resolute desk has never seen so many samples and swatches – whether marble for the Lincoln bathroom, golden drapes for the East Room, or the “million-year lifespan” pavers for the driveway – a White House shopping list that now tops $900m. The Oval Office looks like a developer’s showroom, most recently displaying a two-metre model ofTrump’s $22bn makeover of Dulles airport, boasting gold-mirrored ceilings and “the largest garage in the world”.The closer autocrats come to their end, the more frenziedly do they build. Nero embarked on a golden palace before he was driven to suicide. Marie Antoinette built a model hamlet before she was beheaded. Hitler pored over architectural plans in his bunker during his final days. Trump is buried in catalogues of fixtures and fittings, busy inspecting the workmanship of his helipad-cum-cocktail patio, as the country crumbles around him.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureDonald TrumpUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re not going to back down’: tiny Dorset B&B stands up to Airbnb’s legal bid to ‘monopolise’ letters ‘bnb’ | Airbnb | The Guardian
description: Three little letters - bnb-side’s name is a play on the local b-side arts festival, but Silicon Valley colossus sees threat to global brand
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Three little letters - bnb-side’s name is a play on the local b-side arts festival, but Silicon Valley colossus sees threat to global brand
Content: ‘We do things differently here in Portland’: Rocca Holly-Nambi, director of b-side, and Cat Wightman, manager of the bnb-side guesthouse.Photograph: Pete MillsonView image in fullscreen‘We do things differently here in Portland’: Rocca Holly-Nambi, director of b-side, and Cat Wightman, manager of the bnb-side guesthouse.Photograph: Pete MillsonAirbnb‘We’re not going to back down’: tiny Dorset B&B stands up to Airbnb’s legal bid to ‘monopolise’ letters ‘bnb’Three little letters - bnb-side’s name is a play on the local b-side arts festival, but Silicon Valley colossus sees threat to global brandAmelia HillMon 14 Sep 2026 04.27 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn one corner is bnb-side, a six-room bed and breakfast on the Isle of Portland – a tiny wedge of limestone tied by a narrow ribbon of shingle to theDorsetcoast – that was created to help secure the future of the rock’s much-loved arts festival, b-side.On the other isAirbnb, the San Francisco-based booking colossus. The battle between them is over the three little letters they share.View image in fullscreenbnb-side, a six-room B&B on the Isle of Portland, has received legal letters from booking titan Airbnb.Photograph: Pete Millsonb-side says the “bnb” in bnb-side means what it has always meant: bed and breakfast. But lawyers for theSilicon Valleytitan say the name of the guesthouse, perched on an outcrop just 4 miles long by 1.5 miles wide, threatens the global brand of the $100bn heavyweight.“We thought the name was both really obvious and really cool,” said Rocca Holly-Nambi, director of b-side. “b-side was founded almost 20 years ago, so when we set up our BnB in 2024 to raise money for the festival, we just popped the ‘bn’ in front because it’s a universally recognised description of what we’re offering.”Airbnb doesn’t agree. In May, it sent the first of three legal letters to the tiny social enterprise to demand it cease its attempt to register the B&B using the name it had used since it opened its doors.“They won’t let us compromise by using a different case, an ampersand or an ‘and’,” said Holly-Nambi. “According to Airbnb, we can’t describe our BnB as a BnB at all.”View image in fullscreenA creative retreat held at bnb-side – the social enterprise was set up in 2024 to raise money for the b-side festival.Photograph: HandoutFor bnb-side, losing the argument could mean more than abandoning a clever name. It would mean replacing signage and rewriting websites, social media and all other material referencing and advertising the B&B.“That’s not just a huge waste of money – of which we don’t have much – and of the equally valuable time of our volunteers, but it would throw b-side’s core income stream into chaos,” said Holly-Nambi. “We’d have to painstakingly build our reputation and brand back up from scratch all over again.”Raina Summerson, chair of b-side, is fuming and incredulous. “We opened bnb-side because we were completely dependent on public funding and wanted to be more financially secure,” she said. “bnb-side now generates almost half the festival’s annual £250,000 turnover. If it loses its name, we risk having to establish it all over again.”Short-stay Street: in some parts of Sydney, Airbnb guests outnumber residentsRead moreAirbnb has opposed the name on three separate legal grounds: that consumers will confuse the two brands, that bnb-side could benefit from or damage Airbnb’s reputation, and that bnb-side will financially profit by misrepresenting itself as an official Airbnb service.b-side is asking the Intellectual Property Office to reject Airbnb’s opposition in full, with costs awarded in their favour. The case is still under way, with no ruling having yet been made.View image in fullscreen‘It’s pretty bitter,’ said Cat Wightman, pictured at bnb-side, describing the legal battle with Airbnb, a company that has ‘conquered’ Portland.Photograph: Handout: bnb-side, PortlandAirbnb’s claim has hit a nerve on the proud, windswept outcrop. Cat Wightman, manager of bnb-side, said: “It’s pretty bitter. We’ve watched other small, local hospitality businesses go under, and local people unable to afford homes here, who have been negatively affected by the force with which the Airbnb market has conquered Portland. One person owns eight properties on the island, all of which are rented out on Airbnb.”b-side obtained pro bono advice and is working with the law firm Stevens Hewlett & Perkins to defend them, but the process is still intimidating. “It’s terrifying but we’re not going to back down,” said Holly-Nambi. “We do things differently here in Portland.”EU to regulate short-term rentals in plan to tackle affordable homes shortageRead moreCraig Beaumont, a trademark attorney and senior associate at Barker Brettell, a law firm that specialises in intellectual property, said that for all Airbnb’s might, this would not be an easy or straightforward win for them.“This feels like an uphill battle they’re embarking on,” he said. “BnB has long been widely understood as shorthand for a descriptive phrase, and descriptive phrases are available for the public to use.”bnb-side are not the only company who agree with Beaumont: Companies House records show that in the past decade 14 accommodation companies with “bnb” in their name successfully registered their businesses.View image in fullscreenThe Airbnb logo on display at its San Francisco HQ – the colossus may be facing an ‘uphill battle’ as it seeks to stake a claim to the letters ‘bnb’.Photograph: Gabrielle Lurie/ReutersDarren Meale, a partner and trademark litigation specialist at Simmons & Simmons, said it was no surprise the term was used so often. “It’s quite punchy of Airbnb to say they’re so well-known that they can monopolise a term that they only incorporated into their name in the first place because it was a descriptive one that everyone immediately understood, and then say that someone else using the term is going to confuse customers and damage them.”Lee Curtis, a partner and chartered trademark attorney at IP law firm HGF, agreed that Airbnb “may be testing the limits” of the law. But he pointed to another risk for the lodging colossus.“There’s a public relations angle to take into account,” he said. “Some companies may welcome getting a reputation for aggressive enforcement but that can backfire when the target is a community organisation, like this one.”Airbnb has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsAirbnbHospitality industryDorsetFestivalsIntellectual propertyHouse pricesSilicon ValleyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade | Slavery | The Guardian
description: St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans
Author: Morgan Ofori
Headline: St Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved Africans
Content: Animation: Alexander Purcell. Illustrations by Diana EjaitaEnslaving nationSlaveryThe London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave tradeSt Barts is one of many UK institutions whose benefactors were involved in the trafficking of enslaved AfricansWritten byMorgan OforiandDavid Conn; Animation by Alexander Purcell; Photography by Wayne CrichlowMon 14 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.03 EDTShareInside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includesbiographical data on every known investorin Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.It reveals howwealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to St Barts who are directly linked to this history.Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.View image in fullscreenThe grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOrnate boards adorn the walls of the Great Hall in St Barts, where governors recorded their philanthropic donations, many while investing in the companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe church of St Bartholomew the Less, in the grounds of St Barts hospital.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA portrait of King Henry VIII in the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, surrounded by the boards commemorating the hospital’s benefactors.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianPhillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.View image in fullscreenA diagram of a ship showing the cramped conditions in which enslaved Africans were trafficked.Composite: GuardianThe 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.Others commemorated at St Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of St Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington,has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statueat the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.Slavery was not a footnote to British history. It helped shape the nationRead moreThese connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including St Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to St Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.View image in fullscreenSeveral leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at St Barts.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAfter the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans formalised to become a lucrative source of funds for merchants.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Great Hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message. Its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – are tied to themes of healthcare.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored last year and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda.Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The GuardianThe private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to St Barts after his death in 1688.Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, St Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.St Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

title: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Public offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirds
Content: Aliko Dangote speaks at the Nigerian stock exchange in Lagos to launch the Dangote refinery IPO.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersView image in fullscreenAliko Dangote speaks at the Nigerian stock exchange in Lagos to launch the Dangote refinery IPO.Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/ReutersNigeriaAfrica’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPOPublic offering of Aliko Dangote’s Nigerian oil refinery business could swell his net wealth by two-thirdsEromo Egbejulein Abidjan and agenciesMon 14 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery inNigerialisted publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October.The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors.‘There is nowhere to fish any more’: life in the shadow of Nigeria’s biggest industrial complexRead moreResponding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.”Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas.His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries.The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran.The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrelon Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security.“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.Explore more on these topicsNigeriaOilOil and gas companiesIPOsAfricaEnergy industryCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to power | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Neck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbing
Content: Presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APView image in fullscreenPresidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro.Photograph: Bruna Prado/APBrazil‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to powerNeck-and-neck with Lula in polls, Flávio Bolsonaro fires up his base in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais – starting at the scene of his father’s stabbingTom Phillipsin Juiz de ForaMon 14 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgiant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former presidentJair Bolsonarofluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.“Brazil is rudderless.Brazilhas no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.View image in fullscreenBolsonaro supporters float a giant balloon depicting the US president, Donald Trump, holding Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty ImagesBolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands ofa radical rightwing movementthat tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.Last September,Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentencefor spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.View image in fullscreenBrazil’s president Lula at a reelection campaign rally in Curitiba on Saturday.Photograph: Rodolfo Bührer/ReutersNearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation!
