Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused oftrying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favourthrough economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, thatJair Bolsonaro was stabbedin the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.View image in fullscreenDavi Frederico at the airport in Juiz de Fora.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianBolsonaro’sshock winushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part ofa plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.View image in fullscreenStreet hawkers at Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign event pay tribute to the US connection.Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’sattempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.View image in fullscreenSupporters gather to greet Flávio Bolsonaro at Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianMinas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, withone recent pollputting him ahead there.“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro addresses supporters at the spot where Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in Juiz de Fora during the 2018 presidential campaign.Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty ImagesFor progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminalshis father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.View image in fullscreenLennon César: ‘Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.’Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianLennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’shostility to minorities.César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.View image in fullscreenGraffiti on Flávio Bolsonaro’s headquarters in the city of Juiz de Fora.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Content: Shares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ developmentDonald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’Lauren AlmeidaMon 14 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 03.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for aslowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day.The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to“slow down”.However,Donald Trumpdismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”.In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!”The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”.OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fearsRead more“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote.Trump offered a similar assessment when he called Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, while the executive was on stage at an AI conference in California on Monday.“It’s a hoax,” Trumpsaid via speaker phoneto the audience. “The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That’s not going to happen.”The UN security council, meanwhile, is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week as international concern rises, Agence France-Pressereportedon Monday.Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer ofOpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chipmakers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.Shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%.In Europe, shares in the Dutch tech manufacturer ASML, Europe’s biggest company by value and an important supplier for the semiconductor industry, slumped by 6%.There was, however, a rally in shares that have been threatened by the rise of AI, including the advertising group WPP, which rose by 5% in London, and the analytics business Relx, which was also up 5%. The latter had suffered a sharp fall earlier this year after Anthropic launched a suite of new data and automation tools.Amodei has said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.His claims have beendisputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support forAmodei’s essayon slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder,toldthe BBC an AI “kill switch” that could be triggered by a third party may be necessary to prevent catastrophe.Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of UK MPs and peersidentified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them.Meanwhile, China’s top intelligence official warned that the use of AI by adversaries could pose a risk to the country’s political and social security.Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced US models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to Beijing’s critical information ​infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?Read moreDespite such concern about the risks around AI, Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares tolist on the US stock marketthis year.OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing tosafety concerns with the technology.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Stock marketsAsia PacificComputingTechnology sectorDatacentresDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indonesian police investigate deaths of Australian man and two children in Bali as suspected murder-suicide  | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Police in Bali believe the two young children died as a result of violence, while a 57-year-old man is believed to have taken his own life
Author: Caitlin Cassidy
Headline: Police in Bali believe the two young children died as a result of violence, while a 57-year-old man is believed to have taken his own life
Content: Police officers are investigating the deaths of a 57-year-old Australian man and two children aged seven and four.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice officers are investigating the deaths of a 57-year-old Australian man and two children aged seven and four.Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/ReutersIndonesiaIndonesian police investigate deaths of Australian man and two children in Bali as suspected murder-suicidePolice in Bali believe the two young children died as a result of violence, while a 57-year-old man is believed to have taken his own lifeCaitlin CassidyMon 14 Sep 2026 04.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndonesian police are investigating the deaths of three Australians who died in Bali over the weekend, with initial reports suggesting a father killed his two young children before taking his own life.The man, 57, and his two children, seven and four, who are also Indonesian citizens, were discovered deceased in a bungalow in Kuta on Sunday morning.According to Denpasar police, a witness, 51-year-old Nur Khamid, received a phone call from someone claiming to be the victim’s wife at about 8.30am on Sunday. She was in Jakarta, and asked Khamid to check on the condition of her husband and family, who she had been unable to reach.Khamid went to their bungalow and tried to look inside through a window, but “no activity or people were visible inside”, Denpasar police said in its statement.The witness then met the bungalow owner and both returned to perform a check before contacting the “neighbourhood head”, Kelian Lingkungan. Residents “knocked and pounded” on the door before it was forcibly opened, and the three bodies were located.“Police officers arriving at the scene conducted a crime scene investigation and preliminary examination alongside the Denpasar Police Identification Team,” the statement read.“From the initial external examination of the three victims, it is suspected that the two children died as a result of acts of violence, while [the father] is suspected to have died by hanging.”The bodies are at Prof Dr IGNG Ngoerah Central general hospital for further examination and handling.The Denpasar police chief, senior commissioner Leonardo D Simatupang, said Kuta police officers were investigating the incident.“Investigators are still conducting inquiries, including crime scene processing, examining CCTV footage at the scene, and questioning witnesses – including the victim’s wife – to determine the cause of death,” he said.Simatupang said Kuta police had taken a statement from the man’s wife and reviewed CCTV footage. They had also coordinated with the Australian consulate.A spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade confirmed it was providing consular assistance to the family of the three Australians.“We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time. Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment,” they said in a statement.In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is on 13 11 14 and the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and the domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247. In the US, the suicide prevention lifeline is 988 and the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines can be found via www.befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaBaliAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s dependence on gas generation during evening energy peak falls by almost 70% | Energy | The Guardian
description: Batteries now meet almost half of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during hours of highest demand
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: Batteries now meet almost half of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during hours of highest demand
Content: Batteries met 49% of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during the evening in August 2026, up from 0.4% in 2020.Photograph: Juan Algar/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBatteries met 49% of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during the evening in August 2026, up from 0.4% in 2020.Photograph: Juan Algar/Getty ImagesEnergyAustralia’s dependence on gas generation during evening energy peak falls by almost 70%Batteries now meet almost half of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during hours of highest demandFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPetra StockMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s dependence on gas for power during the evening, when the grid is under the most pressure, has fallen by almost nearly 70% over the past year as batteries surged in,replacing the fossil fuel.Gas generation during the busy early evening, between 5pm and 8pm, fell by 67% in the year to August, as large-scale batteries continued to come online and 500,000home batteries were installedunder the government’s subsidy program, analysis by consultancy EnergyEdge found.The company’s managing director, Josh Stabler, said batteries big and small recorded their highest peak output on record, off the back of rapid uptake.“The rate of installation of batteries in Australia is the fastest uptake of any electricity asset ever – faster than solar, faster than wind,” he said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailAccording to the EnergyEdge report: “batteries have taken the evening peak, and they’re not giving it back”. Batteries met 49% of the grid’s dispatchable power needs during the evening in August 2026, up from 0.4% in 2020. In contrast, gas fell from 65.9% to 20.6% over the same period.Wholesale electricity prices fell in response – a win for households – but potentially a problem for future investment in new dispatchable power.Recent quarterly data (April to June) from the Australian Energy Market Operatorhighlighteda similar pattern, with gas generation recording its lowest Q2 on average in more than two decades. Gas power declined in all regions, the AEMO said, with the fall “most evident” during the evening peak.The Grattan Institute’s energy and climate change program director, Alison Reeve, said utility scale batteries were increasingly mopping up surplus renewable energy in the middle of the day and displacing the role of gas during the peak.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionElectric car owners could save hundreds of dollars a year under the solar sharer scheme. Here’s howRead more“Overall, this is super good news. What you actually end up doing is flattening out the load curve over the day,” she said, and that reduced volatility in the system.In the longer term, less gas and lower volatility should be good for prices, she said. Although the declining demand and added uncertainty could make gas more expensive and less profitable at those times when it was needed – in those few dark, still and cold weeks in winter.“That’s kind of the challenge that is coming for gas,” she said. “We know that gas generators are going to be important, because they’re going to be the backup when you get those two weeks in winter where solar, wind and batteries can’t carry you through.”AEMO’s 20-yearroadmap, the Integrated System Plan, anticipated gas would play “a more strategic, back-up role, with flexible generators that can also provide system security service” in future. “This is more likely to be in winter, especially in the southern states, when shorter days reduce solar output, and when more electricity is needed for longer and colder nights.“Gas is going through a transition and its whole role is going to change,” Reeve said, a shift that would affect the amount of gas needed, the number of generators and the running costs. “The sooner that we actually grasp that the future for gas generators is going to look nothing like the past, the better we will be at managing that whole process and making sure it doesn’t end up costing people a lot of money.”Explore more on these topicsEnergyEnergy storageFossil fuelsGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cloudy with a chance of rainbow: iridescent clouds brighten the sky over parts of Victoria | Australia weather | The Guardian
description: Rainbow clouds are not uncommon in Australia but rarely photographed, and experts say they get their colours when light is diffracted around ice crystals
Author: Jack Larkin
Headline: Rainbow clouds are not uncommon in Australia but rarely photographed, and experts say they get their colours when light is diffracted around ice crystals
Content: Iridescent clouds over Mount Waverley, Melbourne.Photograph: Amruta WazalwarView image in fullscreenIridescent clouds over Mount Waverley, Melbourne.Photograph: Amruta WazalwarAustralia weatherCloudy with a chance of rainbow: iridescent clouds brighten the sky over parts of VictoriaRainbow clouds are not uncommon in Australia but rarely photographed, and experts say they get their colours when light is diffracted around ice crystalsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJack LarkinMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRainbow clouds shone over parts ofVictoriaover the weekend, in an unusual visual phenomenon known as iridescent clouds.Photographs of the spectacle were taken by onlookers in theMelbournesuburbs of Mount Waverley and Caroline Springs.Sarah Scully, a senior meteorologist at the Bureau ofMeteorology, said the visual phenomenon was not uncommon in Australia but was rarely captured.“People don’t often notice them, as they’re really fleeting,” she said.Blankets of colour: Western Australia’s wildflower season bursts into life – in picturesRead moreIridescent clouds often form from cirrus clouds, which were seen over Victoria on the weekend. Cirrus clouds are made up of ice crystals and are commonly found in the higher levels of the troposphere – the level of the atmosphere where most weather occurs – where the temperatures are coldest.The clouds get their rainbow appearance when light is diffracted – bent – around ice crystals. The phenomenon often occurs in newly formed clouds where the ice crystals are the same size.View image in fullscreenRainbow clouds often form from cirrus clouds.Photograph: Amruta WazalwarThe smaller the cloud, the more rays of sunlight can pass through and be diffracted by a single ice droplet, according to the BoM.Iridescent clouds gain their appearance from the diffraction of sunlight, which causes the colours to spread into rings or waves.They differ from rainbows, in which both the refraction (bending) and reflection (bouncing back) of sunlight result in colours in a specific order with neater bands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIridescent clouds are sometimes mistaken for sun dogs, another type of visual phenomenon with similar characteristics.“Sun dogs are a different type of optical phenomenon,” Scully said. “They occur almost like a pillar of light that’s either on both sides of the sun or just on one side of the sun.“That is due … to water crystals being in the atmosphere and … it sits at low levels of the horizon. You need it to sit even lower [than an iridescent cloud].”Explore more on these topicsAustralia weatherMeteorologyVictoriaMelbournenewsShareReuse this content

title: Gonorrhoea and syphilis rise by more than 50% in Australia with ‘concerning’ rise in cases in women | Health | The Guardian
description: Newly collated data also shows Indigenous Australians experiencing disproportionally high rates of infection
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: Newly collated data also shows Indigenous Australians experiencing disproportionally high rates of infection
Content: Australia’s Indigenous population is diagnosed with gonorrhoea at more than four times the rate of non-Indigenous Australians. Image shows CGI gonorrhoea bacteria.Photograph: Science Photo Library/AlamyView image in fullscreenAustralia’s Indigenous population is diagnosed with gonorrhoea at more than four times the rate of non-Indigenous Australians. Image shows CGI gonorrhoea bacteria.Photograph: Science Photo Library/AlamyHealthGonorrhoea and syphilis rise by more than 50% in Australia with ‘concerning’ rise in cases in womenNewly collated data also shows Indigenous Australians experiencing disproportionally high rates of infectionFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAchol ArokMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 17.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRates of reportedgonorrhoeaand infectious syphilis have increased by more than 50% across Australia over the past decade, with experts warning of concerning rises among women.Newly collated sexual health data from the University of New South Wales’ Kirby Institute shows 42,393 gonorrhoea notifications and 5,986 infectious syphilis notifications were recorded in 2025. The figures represent 10-year increases of 57% and 56%, respectively.Syphilis and gonorrhoea are bacterial infections that can cause serious health complications if left untreated. Both are curable when detected early.Men accounted for the majority of cases last year, making up 73% of gonorrhoea notifications and 78% of infectious syphilis notifications, with the report suggesting a significant proportion of transmission continues to occur through male-to-male sexual contact among gay and bisexual men.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe new data also flagged a “concerning increase in syphilis among women”. Syphilis notification rates increased by 167% among women, compared with 39% among men. Experts said the figures reflected “an increase in heterosexual transmission”.Dr Skye McGregor, an epidemiologist at the Kirby Institute, said the trend is “an urgent priority” because of the risks posed by syphilis during pregnancy.“It’s really concerning because the rise among women has contributed to syphilis in pregnancy, which can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, congenital syphilis and infant deaths,” McGregor said. “These are really substantial impacts on infants, but also the community as a whole. Across that same 10-year reporting period, there were 113 congenital syphilis cases and, tragically, 40 of those infants died.”About half of those congenital syphilis cases involved Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander infants.“[It was] a really terrible outcome, which is entirely preventable with early testing and treatment during pregnancy,” McGregor said.Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians also remain a priority group, experiencing disproportionately high sexually transmitted infection (STI) rates. Compared with non-Indigenous Australians, the Indigenous population is diagnosed with gonorrhoea at more than four times the rate and syphilis at more than six times the rate.McGregor said the disparity highlighted the need for sustained investment in culturally safe sexual health services and improved access to timely testing and treatment, particularly in regional and remote areas.“We know how hard it can be to get an appointment in an urban setting with a GP, particularly if you want a preferred provider by gender or cultural background,” she said. “And that’s even more exacerbated in regional and remote settings.”McGregor said social determinants of health also contributed to the disparity, including income, education, employment, job security and food insecurity.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt-home STI test pulled from Australian shelves after failing to detect infectionsRead moreShe stressed the importance of culturally safe sexual health testing services and community-led programs supported by the National Aboriginal Community ControlledHealthOrganisation and governments.“Modelling has predicted that without that enhanced response, actually the rates of syphilis would have been far higher … this amazing community-driven response has actually ensured that the rates do stay lower than they could have been across that time period,” McGregor said.McGregor said the new data should serve as a public health reminder of the importance of testing and treatment, raising concerns that reduced testing could be an unwanted hangover from the Covid-19 pandemic.“We saw a decrease during that time period, but we really need to make sure everyone’s resuming their pre-Covid screening so that sexual health is just a part of good health overall,” she said.UNSW’s 2019 National Debrief Survey looking into sexual health attitude revealed that almost two-thirds of young people who had five or more casual partners in the past 12 months did not use condoms. But McGregor said reducing STI rates required a holistic approach.“Condoms are still an important prevention approach, and yes, people should be using condoms with new sexual partners … but also, this is about comprehensive prevention,” she said. “Early testing ensures people know their status, they can be treated, prevent onward transmission.”McGregor also stressed the importance of “post-diagnosis care”, retesting and regular engagement with a healthcare provider, as “we do know that one infection then risks a repeat infection”.Explore more on these topicsHealthSexual healthIndigenous AustraliansGonorrhoeaWomen's healthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Queensland homeless man shot with Taser after being given move-on order to make way for kite festival | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Advocate says homeless clearances should be halted after man is hospitalised during confrontation in Brisbane park
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Advocate says homeless clearances should be halted after man is hospitalised during confrontation in Brisbane park
Content: A spokesperson for the Queensland police said its officers had attempted to de-escalate the situation and disarm Martin, but were unsuccessful.Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA spokesperson for the Queensland police said its officers had attempted to de-escalate the situation and disarm Martin, but were unsuccessful.Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The GuardianAustralia newsQueensland homeless man shot with Taser after being given move-on order to make way for kite festivalExclusive:Advocate says homeless clearances should be halted after man is hospitalised during confrontation in Brisbane parkFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA homeless man was shot with a Taser by police after attempting to take his own life during a tent city clearance, sparking calls for mental health considerations when dealing with move-on orders amid Queensland’s homelessness crisis.On 1 September, Moreton Bay city council rangers gave six homeless residents 24 hours to leave Pelican Park north of Brisbane, where Martin* had been living in a camper trailer, tomake way for a kite festivalthis weekend.The 48-year-old said he was unable to comply with the move-on order because he had lost his driver licence due to a drink-driving conviction.“I was under the understanding that they were coming to basically take my shit,” he told the Guardian. “In times gone past, I’ve complied.“This time I can’t, and they told me that basically they’re going to impound everything.”The homeless man, who has prostate cancer, told the rangers he would rather die than lose his few possessions.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“I said, ‘All right, well, if this is what you wish to do, then not a problem. Bring an ambulance and a body bag for me,’” Martin said.He then stabbed himself in the neck with a knife. Moments later he was shot with a Taser at least twice by police.He said he had not threatened anyone else before injuring himself.A spokesperson for the Queensland police said its officers had attempted to de-escalate the situation and disarm Martin, but were unsuccessful.NSW government paid for homeless man to be sent back to New Zealand instead of offering housingRead more“Immediate first aid was applied by officers to the man, who had sustained a serious self-inflicted injury,” they said.“The QPS remains committed to providing officers with mental health training, focusing on an informed awareness of different categories of mental illness and the application of appropriate strategies to safely respond to persons experiencing mental health distress.”Local homeless advocate Beau Haywood, founder of charity Nourish Street, said the incident showedwhat can go wrongif councils continued their enforcement-led approach to the state’s homelessness crisis. He said Moreton Bayshould halt homeless clearancesuntil they could show they were both safe and legal.Snapping pointMartin, whose camp is part of a small tent city of about a dozen residents near the waterfront in Clontarf, is a former security guard who lost his job during the pandemic. He has lived homeless in the Moreton Bay area for more than three years, and is on the social housing waiting list.He’s not alone: Moreton Bay has thestate’s longest social housing waiting list– 5,146at last countin 2025 – and a major rough sleeping problem. Several tent cities in the area house hundreds of people.He said after it happened he woke up in an ambulance on the way to the RoyalBrisbaneand Women’s hospital. He had surgery to patch up his injuries, saw a mental health worker, and asked to be discharged so he could get back to his camper trailer to protect his belongings.The next day, the hospital booked him a taxi back to the park.He had not been seen by any health professional since his discharge, he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson for the Metro North health service said it was “unable to comment on the specific details of a patient’s situation to respect their privacy and confidentiality”.View image in fullscreenMoreton Bay has Queensland’slongest social housing waiting list, with several tent cities in the area housing hundreds of people.Photograph: Andrew Messenger/The GuardianMoreton Bay was the first of many councils across the country toturn to enforcement as the solution to Australia’s worsening homelessness crisis. It made national headlines when it bulldozed a tent city in Lawnton, which the Queensland supreme court ruled aviolation of the state’s Human Rights Act.Haywood said the council had halted clearances during and after the court case, but had recently restarted them after announcingit would designate a park for the homeless.State-owned land is Luke Quinn’s final refuge from council patrols — but soon even that meagre safety could disappearRead moreHaywood said during clearances, homeless people like Martin could feel backed into a corner and it was inevitable that people would eventually snap.“I’ve seen it time and time again. Every move brings [someone’s mental health] down even further . And I think for that gentleman, he reached his point,” he said.“I think that if council were aware of his mental health and physical health, that maybe some more precautions should be taken. Some mental health treatment should have been offered at the time.”Haywood said the clearances should be halted until they could be done safely.Martin said he loved old movies, motorcycles and a long chat. He has refused treatment for his prostate cancer. He said before he died he wanted to see friends in Townsville and South Australia. He said one of his greatest joys was to cook for his homeless friends.Since the confrontation, Martin’s circumstances have not changed. He has not been offered housing, or an alternative place to stay.There are 44,294 Queenslanders on the social housing waiting list.A homeless service hopes to tow his vehicle to a different park this week.*Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsAustralia newsBrisbaneQueenslandHomelessnessHousing (Society)Housing (Australia news)newsShareReuse this content

title: Member of British armed forces killed in Ukraine crash, says MoD | Military | The Guardian
description: Ministry of Defence says person, who has yet to be identified, died in road traffic incident not believed to be result of hostile action
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Ministry of Defence says person, who has yet to be identified, died in road traffic incident not believed to be result of hostile action
Content: A small number of British military personnel in Ukraine provide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PAView image in fullscreenA small number of British military personnel in Ukraine provide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces.Photograph: Tim Ireland/PAMilitaryMember of British armed forces killed in Ukraine crash, says MoDMinistry of Defence says person, who has yet to be identified, died in road traffic incident not believed to be result of hostile actionPriya Bharadiaand agencyMon 14 Sep 2026 15.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA member of the UK armed forces has been killed in a crash in Ukraine, theMinistry of Defencesaid.The person, who has not yet been named, died in a road traffic incident on Saturday. It is understood the incident was not a result of hostile action.The person’s family has been informed and has asked for some time before more details are made public.“Our thoughts and our sympathies are with the individual’s loved ones at this difficult time,” an MoD spokesperson said.The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said on X: “This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our Armed Forces.“My deepest condolences go to them all.”The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, said on X he was “saddened to hear this news” and offered his condolences to the person’s family and friends.A small number of British personnel inUkraineprovide security to diplomats and support the country’s armed forces.British paratrooper George Hooley, 28, was killed in Ukraine in December while watching Ukrainian forces testing defensive capability.‘He served with honour’: Starmer pays tribute to British soldier killed in UkraineRead moreThe MoD described his death as a “tragic accident” that occurred “away from the frontlines”.Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine is in its fifth year and the conflict continues with fresh strikes on Ukraine, including an attack on a gasworks and a drone attack on a train station on Sunday.The attack hit a train at Yahodyn station, on the Polish border, shortly after a train carrying Boris Johnson had left ahead of schedule.Ukraine’s railway operator said the attack may have been aimed at the train carrying the former prime minister, among other dignitaries.Johnson had been returning from a major conference in Kyiv along with former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt and a number of European security advisers.According to a translation from Ukrainian, rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia said in a post on Telegram it was “quite possible” the drone had been aimed at Johnson’s train.Explore more on these topicsMilitaryMinistry of DefenceUkraineEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe must build own AI or risk getting cut off by US or China, says ECB’s Lagarde | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Central bank chief says continent’s AI dependency could give trade partners unprecedented leverage in negotiations
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Central bank chief says continent’s AI dependency could give trade partners unprecedented leverage in negotiations
Content: Christine Lagarde spoke in Vienna about Europe and AI on Monday.Photograph: Hans Klaus Techt/APA/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChristine Lagarde spoke in Vienna about Europe and AI on Monday.Photograph: Hans Klaus Techt/APA/AFP/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Europe must build own AI or risk getting cut off by US or China, says ECB’s LagardeCentral bank chief says continent’s AI dependency could give trade partners unprecedented leverage in negotiationsDan Milmoand agencyMon 14 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China, according to the president of theEuropean Central Bank.Christine Lagarde said the continent needed AI models – the technology that powers AI tools such as chatbots – that were “good enough” to carry out most tasks and run from domestic datacentres. If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force”.AI is being built elsewhere, the ECB boss said in a speech in Vienna, with the US producing 59 notable models last year and China 35, whileFranceand the UK produced one each. She added that the US hosts 75% of the world’s AI computing capacity – produced by datacentres – and Europe just 5%.Datacentres are growing target of global climate-related legal cases, report findsRead moreLagarde saidEuropefaced “an awkward choice”. “Either it holds back on adopting, because it cannot protect its data, and forgoes the growth. Or it adopts AI quickly, becomes highly dependent, and risks losing the freedom to organise its economy according to its own values.”Cutting Europe off from AI or changing the terms of its access would have a widespread and immediate economic impact, she said.View image in fullscreenDatacentre run by French company OVHcloud in Roubaix – Lagarde wants Europe to have more domestic capacity.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images“Within a few years it will be screening goods at the border, deciding which tax returns are audited, dispatching trains, watching patients on wards and clearing payments at banks. A withdrawal of access, or a change in its terms, would then reach every sector at once,” she said.Lagarde said this represented leverage that “no trade partner has ever held over Europe, and it could be ‌used in any negotiation, on tariffs or on digital taxes, for example”.While the EU and the US remain key allies, the Trump administration has shaken that trust in a range of episodes including the imposition of tariffs, demands to take overGreenland– a largely autonomous territory that is part of the Danish commonwealth – and the withdrawal of US troops from Europe over political disagreements.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump, pictured at an event in the White House last year, has shaken trust with his new tariff regime.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesIf adopted quickly, AI could lift the level of productivity – a measure of economic performance – by up to 4% over a decade, which would be ​transformative for public finances, Lagarde said.Urging Europe to build more computing capacity, she said: “Europe already has too little datacentre capacity to meet its own demand, and on current trends, that gap is projected to grow more than sixfold within a decade.”US ​technology firms’ investment ‌needs are so ​large that they are ​doing some of their borrowing in Europe, pushing up costs for everyone else as they crowd out others in the debt market. European pension funds also invest heavily in US tech stocks, so any market correction would affect European savings, she added.Reuters contributed to this report.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)EuropeChristine LagardeEuropean Central BankDonald TrumpComputingChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief says | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mark Rutte says attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus shows Vladimir Putin’s desperation
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Mark Rutte says attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus shows Vladimir Putin’s desperation
Content: 0:50Russian drone strike hits train near Poland-Ukraine border – videoUkraineRussian strike on passenger train will not deter Ukraine’s backers, Nato chief saysMark Rutte says attack that narrowly missed Boris Johnson and David Petraeus shows Vladimir Putin’s desperationJennifer Rankinin Brussels andCharlotte HigginsandAmy Hawkinsin KyivMon 14 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of Nato has said a Russian drone attack on a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland would not deter Kyiv’s western backers.Mark Rutte said the strike on a passenger train showed how desperate Vladimir Putin had become. “He thinks that he can stops us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong. Our answer is to increase support,” the Nato general secretary said.European leaders have condemned the strike in which a Russian drone hit a passenger train on Ukraine’s border withPolandon Sunday shortly after a convoy of high-level diplomats and former leaders had passed through.The earlier train, which was carrying the former UK prime minister Boris Johnson was running ahead of schedule,may have been the target of the Russian drone strike, Ukrainian Railways has said.A spokesperson forthe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, struck a similar note to Rutte, saying the attack “was a futile attempt byRussiato undermine our support for Ukraine. It will not deter us.”View image in fullscreenMark Rutte, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, said Ukraine’s western backers would answer the drone strike by increasing support.Photograph: APThe French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, said the goal of the attacks was “to intimidate Europeans, discourage and above all divide them”.The EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy, Kaja Kallas, said the strike “was clearly a message to the western world”. Speaking on the sidelines of an Arctic conference in Finland, she said: “I think the question for us is what do we take from that message? I think we should act the opposite. We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off, because otherwise, you know, Russia will just achieve what they want, which is the submission of Ukraine.”A spokesperson for Kallas added: “We strongly condemn the latest Russian strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border, including the attack against the passenger train,” and referenced a recent EU decision to approve a €6.1bn tranche of the €90bn loan for Ukraine. “We are acting on the front to equip Ukraine better to defend itself, and we will continue to stand firmly with Ukraine and its right to defend itself against Russian aggression,” the spokesperson said.Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.View image in fullscreenKaja Kallas: ‘We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared off.’Photograph: Petras Malūkas/AFP/Getty ImagesWestern Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.The strikes, which prompted air raid warnings in Poland, came as EU diplomats met in Brussels on Monday for last-ditch talks on the rollover of the bloc’s sanctions against more than 2,600 Russian individuals and entities involved in supporting Vladimir Putin’s war. The sanctions are due to expire on Tuesday but their prolongation is being held up by a dispute about whether to remove an individual from the list.Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram on Sunday: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries as well as Johnson and the former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.The diplomatic train, Ukrainian Railways said, had left ahead of schedule and could have been the target of the Russian drone. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at Yahodyn station when the drone struck, according to the rail operator.View image in fullscreenDonald Tusk said Poland had been tipped off by its security services and allied intelligence agencies that an attack such as this was likely.Photograph: Piotr Nowak/EPAThe Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.This article was amended on 14 September 2026 to clarify that David Petraeus was on a separate train to Boris Johnson.Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropean UnionRussiaEuropePolandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine and Russia have agreed not to hit energy targets, Trump claims – as it happened | World news | The Guardian
description: US president blames conflict, and ‘not Iran;, for spike in US diesel prices
Author: Tom Ambrose
Headline: US president blames conflict, and ‘not Iran;, for spike in US diesel prices
Content: 11.22 EDTTrump claims Ukraine and Russia have agreed not to hit energy targetsDonald Trump has said Ukraine and Russia have agreed not to hit one another’s energy targets.In a post on his own Truth Social platform, the US president claimed that the world’s diesel price rise is “mostly caused by the Russia-Ukraine war, not Iran”.He wrote:double quotation markUkraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise! The World’s Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran.Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage.He spoke after diesel prices in the US hit a record on Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average.Ukraine has for months been targeting Russia’s oil and gas industry with long-range strikes, prompting fuel rationing across the country and causing Moscow to ban diesel exports in July, removing supplies from the already tight global market.Share

title: Sweden’s political parties launch coalition talks as both blocs try to secure power | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Centre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battle
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Centre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battle
Content: The Social Democrats’ party leader, Magdalena Andersson, has started a long and difficult process of trying to form a new government.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Social Democrats’ party leader, Magdalena Andersson, has started a long and difficult process of trying to form a new government.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPASwedenSweden’s political parties launch coalition talks as both blocs try to secure powerCentre-left bloc led by Social Democrats has narrow lead with 95% of vote counted, but faces internal policy battleMiranda BryantNordic correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSweden’s political parties have launched coalition negotiations as the Social Democrats leader, Magdalena Andersson, started the long and difficult process of trying to form a new government.Full results from Sunday’s election are not expected until after overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, but with 95% of the votes counted, the Social Democrats and the centre-left bloc had a narrow but growing lead of 176 seats to the right-leaning parties’ 173.The far right’s march to power in Sweden has been halted, but its influence remainsRead moreAfter losing support for the first time since they were founded, the far-right Sweden Democrats, who were hoping to enter government for the first time, appear to be out of the picture. But many of its policy ideas – on immigration laws, integration and crime – have become mainstream, including in the centre-left.Both Andersson and the outgoing centre-right prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, of the Moderates have each said they want to explore possible coalition options to secure power.View image in fullscreenSweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, leader of the conservative Moderates, has said he wants to explore possible coalitions to secure power for another term.Photograph: Christine Olsson/TT/TT News Agency/AFP/Getty ImagesAfter a long election night during which there was just one seat between the two blocs, Social Democrat leaders met Andersson on Monday morning at the party’s Stockholm headquarters.Questions remain as to whether the bloc is willing to work with the Left party (Vänsterpartiet), which the Centre party has previously ruled out.The Social Democrats press secretary, Tobias Baudin, said he had been in contact with colleagues from opposition parties and called for the resignation of Kristersson, who led the rightwing Tidö coalition government with the support of the Sweden Democrats.“Now the voters have had their say and they have given him a failing grade for himself and his government,” Baudin told the Swedish broadcaster SVT, adding: “He should resign himself. In fact it doesn’t matter, if he doesn’t resign he will be removed. How he does it is up to him.The Centre party said that in talks with the Social Democrats it would be seeking a government with a “desire for political stability” and a “clear centre-right character” with no “fringe politics”.The Social Democrat Morgan Johansson, who under the last Social Democrat-led government was deputy prime minister, said the Centre party’s announcement was a positive development and that overall there were “good prospects”.All of the left-leaning parties want a change of government, he said. “That is the starting point. I don’t think anyone wants us to end up in a situation where blockages lead to a new election.”Meanwhile, Kristersson appears to be keeping his options open.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Sunday night he said the result could lead to a “complicated government formation, where it ends remains to be seen”. On Monday, before a meeting with his fellow Tidö coalition leaders, he declined to elaborate, saying he would wait for a full result before having conversations. “If all the red lines remain then Sweden won’t have a government at all,” he added. “I plan to pursue a number of possibilities that may exist.”The Liberals and Christian Democrats have both said they will not work with the Social Democrats.After the overseas votes are counted on Wednesday, the final election results are not expected until the weekend.The new parliament will meet for the first time on 28 September and the earliest date that the speaker can suggest a prime minister is 29 September, but talks could take considerably longer. If, when parliament votes for a prime minister candidate, more than half say no, then the speaker must find a new candidate. If there are four failed votes there will automatically be a new election.After the 2022 election, it took 37 days to form a government; in 2018 it took 134 days to form a new coalition.Fredrik Furtenbach, the senior political correspondent at Sveriges Radio (Radio Sweden), said: “I think it will end with either the Left or Centre party having to give way. It might take several failed prime minister votes first.” But he does not believe the Social Democrats and Moderates, who he describes as “traditional archenemies”, will end up working together. “You cannot share the position of prime minister.”Explore more on these topicsSwedenEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: US borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-off | US economy | The Guardian
description: Soaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fears
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Soaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fears
Content: The US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenThe US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAUS economyUS borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-offSoaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fearsRichard PartingtonandLauren AlmeidaMon 14 Sep 2026 12.48 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 04.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS government borrowing costs have risen to 5% for the first time since 2023 as soaring oil prices fuelled by the war in the Middle East trigger an intensifying sell-off in the global bond market.The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year US Treasury bonds hit the psychologically important threshold on Monday, on a day of renewed selling pressure on Wall Street as the global oil price reached $108 a barrel.With traders awaiting a crunch US Federal Reserve interest rate decision on Wednesday, the benchmark rate has steadily climbed from a low this year of 4% before the outbreak of the US-Israeli war onIranin late February. The yield was last above 5% in October 2023.Saudi Arabia shuts down key oil pipeline, blaming drones from IraqRead moreIt comes as the rising global oil price stokes inflation fears, with the latest move prompted by aseries of drone attacksthat have forced Saudi Arabia to close a vital east-west crude pipeline as the fallout from the war mounts.Bond market chartBrent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, surged to more than $108.5 a barrel on Monday – a 3.7% increase on the day.The spike came after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia andcaptured the strategic island of Perimin the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway.The rise was also fuelled by the Gulf states postponing a meeting with Tehran to discuss creating a temporary shipping lane through the strait of Hormuz, a vital channel through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.Oil price chartTraders in the kingdom have warned itwill run out of oil stocks for exportif it does not reopen the east-west pipeline within days.Gas prices also climbed higher on Monday, with the UK benchmark rising by 5% to 208.73p a therm – its highest level since December 2022.It came despite Donald Trump on Monday announcing a deal between Ukraine and Russia not to hit each other’s energy targets, while insisting that he believed a politically sensitive rise in US diesel fuel prices was being driven by the conflict in Europe rather than the war in Iran.Map of Houthi territorial gains in YemenWith fears mounting as the Middle East war escalates, bond markets have come under intense selling pressure. The US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets, meaning a jump in borrowing costs for Washington has consequences for countries, businesses and households worldwide.Borrowing costs also rose across Europe on Monday, including a rise in 30-year UK government yields to the highest level since March 1998.UK bond chartThe moves come as traders awaitdecisions on interest ratesfrom the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of England on Thursday after the European Central Bankraised borrowing costs last week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith investors anticipating an increase from the Fed and a hold decision from Threadneedle Street amid mounting inflationary pressures, analysts said global bond markets could face another week of renewed volatility.Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “Markets are starting the week on a defensive footing, with the combination of another escalation in the Middle East and increasingly hawkish central-bank expectations weighing on risk appetite.”With wholesale energy prices on the rise, the cost of petrol and diesel hit new Iran war highs on Monday, according to the RAC, with the average cost of petrol climbing to 169.68p and diesel hitting 191.68p.The US-Israeli war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East this year, sending the oil price soaring from its prewar level of about $72 a barrel topeak at $126in April.Brent crude later fell back over the summer amid hopes of a lasting ceasefire, before starting to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart.After a recent stepping-up of hostilities the benchmark againrose above the $100 a barrel thresholdlast week for the first time since July.Chris Beauchamp, of the broker IG, said a “move back to the spring highs” looked increasingly likely. “Oil markets are being subjected to their worst fears all at once – attacks on energy infrastructure, the closure of Hormuz and a breakdown in attempts to restart negotiations,” he said.Map showing location of pipeline hit by drone strikes in Saudi Arabia“The risk of further disruption is also spreading beyond the Gulf, with the threat of renewed Houthi attacks on shipping adding another layer of uncertainty around key energy and trade routes.“The major surprise is how calm markets remain in the face of all this, but if prices breach the March highs, things could get ugly very quickly.”Oil output fromSaudi Arabiahad been under pressure before the attacks on its major pipeline. Riyadh told the Opec oil cartel recently that its crude production in August was at its lowest level since 1990, according to Bloomberg.Explore more on these topicsUS economyOilOil and gas companiesCommoditiesGlobal economyEconomicsEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says he will consider releasing more 9/11 records after families’ request | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: Families have asked Trump to declassify records that could shed light on Saudi Arabia’s alleged role in the 2001 attacks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Families have asked Trump to declassify records that could shed light on Saudi Arabia’s alleged role in the 2001 attacks
Content: Terry Strada, national chair of 9/11 Families United, speaks during a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in New York City on 11 September 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersView image in fullscreenTerry Strada, national chair of 9/11 Families United, speaks during a ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in New York City on 11 September 2026.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersSeptember 11 2001Trump says he will consider releasing more 9/11 records after families’ requestFamilies have asked Trump to declassify records that could shed light on Saudi Arabia’s alleged role in the 2001 attacksAssociated PressMon 14 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpsaid on Sunday that he will look into requests from families of9/11victims to release records that could shed light on Saudi Arabia’s alleged role in the attacks 25 years ago.Several families have long alleged that a group of extremist religious leaders inSaudi Arabiagained influence in the kingdom’s government and aided the hijackers. Fifteen of the 19 hijackers were Saudis, but the Saudi government has long denied any involvement in the attacks.The families have asked Trump to declassify and release the relevant records. Asked about it on Sunday during his trip to Ireland, the president said he would consider it.“I’m going to look at it when I get back,” Trump said just before boarding Air Force One to return to Washington after a weekend in Ireland. “I know they asked me Friday.”The relatives of 9/11 victims have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle against the Saudis. One of them,Terry Strada, called on Trump during a remembrance in New York City on Friday to “tell the Saudis to stop lying”.Strada, who lost her husband, Tom, on 9/11, said US presidents had chosen “to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families”.Strada, who was one of the 9/11 family members who read aloud the names of victims at the remembrance on the 25th anniversary of the attacks, added that the current administration should “stand with the families, stand with the survivors”.“It has been one betrayal after another,” she said. “President Trump can still change that.”Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001Donald TrumpUS politicsSaudi ArabiaTrump administrationMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZA  | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’
Content: NAZA directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor at the Venice film festival. There are now calls to strip them of their Israeli citizenship.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNAZA directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor at the Venice film festival. There are now calls to strip them of their Israeli citizenship.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesNAZAIsraeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZAMiki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceSian Cain,Lorenzo Tondoin Jerusalem and agenciesMon 14 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli directors ofNAZA, a documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship, accusing them of “treason against the state”.NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.In the film, the Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spoke to 24 Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombardGazathat have killed tens of thousands of civilians. In one interview, a source claims that approval had been given to kill 500 NAZA in order to kill one Hamas member.The 80-minute documentarywon a special jury prizeat this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receivinga 25-minute standing ovation– a festival record.0:50NAZA director says ‘it’s important Israelis watch this film’ after win at Venice festival – videoOn Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.On Monday, Zohar expanded on these comments, issuing a statement saying: “This morning, I wrote to the director general of the Population and Immigration Authority and the director general of the interior ministry, asking them to examine the possibility of revoking the Israeli citizenship of the creators of the anti-Israel film NZA [sic] for breach of loyalty to the state and collaboration with the enemy.“I also asked them to investigate how the materials used in the film were obtained, who was responsible for obtaining them, and whether any actions carried out in acquiring or disseminating them could amount to assisting the enemy during wartime.“Freedom of expression is not a licence to betray the state. Anyone who acts against Israel during a war must know that there will be a price to pay.”The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, condemned the film. “It’s shocking. We ⁠are fighting global antisemitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” he said in a video posted on social media. “And ‌now two Israeli directors portraying ‌the IDF as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”Other Israeli ministers also took aim at the directors, who won an Oscar in 2025 for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead more“You are a disgrace and an embarrassment to the entire people of Israel. Go away!” the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said on X.“I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms.”On Monday, the chief of general staff of the Israeli military claimed the film was “based on blood libels, deliberate distortions of reality and grave, false accusations against IDF soldiers and commanders”.Eyal Zamir said military lawyers were examining “possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it”.The former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman called Abraham and Szor “haters of Israel”, while the former prime minister Naftali Bennett described it as “a horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters”.The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, although it is rarely applied. In 2022 the supreme court confirmed that the state may strip people of their nationality if they have failed to show “loyalty”, for example by committing acts of espionage or treason. The law was also expanded in 2023 to apply to people convicted of “terrorism”. The law requires the interior minister to submit the revocation request, the justice minister to approve it and judges to validate it.Abraham’s family home wastargeted by a rightwing mobafter the world premiere of 2024’s No Other Land, which focused on the destruction of Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank.“We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic,” hetold the Guardian, adding: “For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons.“Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”The Israeli military initially responded toNAZAby saying it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary and criticised the use of anonymous testimonies, saying the identities of the whistleblowers “cannot be verified”. In a later response, the military said “the allegations required a detailed, evidence-based response rather than a blanket dismissal”.Some figures on the Israeli left praised the film and its directors. The former lawmaker Yousef Jabareen, chair of the leftwing Hadash party, congratulated the directors on the award, thanking them for bringing “these horrific crimes and the brutal reality in Gaza” before millions of people.Anat Saragusti, the head of press freedom at the Union of Journalists in Israel, said: “The Israeli public has not received anything close to adequate coverage in Hebrew of what has happened in Gaza. For much of the war, Israeli media barely showed the Palestinian side of the story – the civilian casualties, the children killed, the destruction. People could find that information elsewhere if they actively looked for it, but they were not seeing it in the mainstream Hebrew-language media.”In an editorial, the Haaretz newspaper urged Israelis to confront what it described as the reality of Israel’s actions in Gaza. “By screening their film at the Venice film festival,Abrahamand Szor are trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that there’s a black stain on the way Israel is conducting war in Gaza, to put it mildly,” Haaretz wrote.The Palestinian militant group Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Hamas militants also took 251 hostages to Gaza.The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the subsequent three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties.A Guardian News & Media spokesperson said: “The Guardian is disturbed to see the authoritarian response toNAZAin Israel.“Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are brave journalists and film-makers. The attacks against them come from people who have not yet seen the film.“NAZA is based on more than three years of investigative journalism. The testimonies it contains are true and we believe they deserve to be heard. The interviews were given by confidential journalistic sources.“We will robustly defend NAZA – and the team behind it – from any attacks or attempts at censorship.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaGazaPalestineIsrael-Gaza warnewsShareReuse this content

title: US airman recounts Iran rescue in 60 Minutes segment branded propaganda | CBS | The Guardian
description: Critics say segment about airman’s rescue was made to boost public perception of Trump’s unpopular war
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Critics say segment about airman’s rescue was made to boost public perception of Trump’s unpopular war
Content: Wreckage is seen from what Iranian authorities say is a US military helicopter that crashed during a mission to rescue the missing American pilot of an F-15E that was downed earlier this week, in a handout image provided on 5 April 2026 in an unspecified location in Iran.Photograph: Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWreckage is seen from what Iranian authorities say is a US military helicopter that crashed during a mission to rescue the missing American pilot of an F-15E that was downed earlier this week, in a handout image provided on 5 April 2026 in an unspecified location in Iran.Photograph: Iran's Ministry of Culture and Islamic Guidance via Getty ImagesCBSUS airman recounts Iran rescue in 60 Minutes segment branded propagandaCritics say segment about airman’s rescue was made to boost public perception of Trump’s unpopular warRichard LuscombeMon 14 Sep 2026 10.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US airman has spoken of climbing a 7,000ft ridge with a broken back, arm and shoulder afterhe was shot down in Iran– and of being rescued by a team of American special forces as hostile locals closed in on him.The air force colonel, identified only by his codename Bravo, appeared on camera Sunday night on CBS’s 60 Minutes in a segment some critics have labelled Pentagonpropagandato boost public perception of Donald Trump’sunpopular war.Pete Hegseth, the president’s defense secretary;
