Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff; and Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command; all appeared on the show to talk about the rescue operation. “Alpha”, the co-pilot of the downed F-15 fighter jet, declined to take part, despite reportedpressurefrom the Trump administration to do so.The airmen were recovered in April in an operation involving thousands of military personnel, including the elite Army Delta Force, Navy Seal Team Six, and a CIA decoy operation to distract and deceive Iranians chasing a bounty for their capture, the 60 Minutes segment said.Bravo, who was reportedly also initially hesitant to take part,toldinterviewer Norah O’Donnell that his aircraft was struck by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile – and he realized his parachute was damaged after he and his co-pilot ejected.“When I looked up and saw no parachute, that was the most terrifying thing I’ve ever seen,” the weapons system operator said. “So I paused, right then. And I prayed: ‘Lord, your will be done. But if I’m getting through this, I need help.’”Bravo said he was unable to fully untangle his chute and hit the ground hard.“Based on my description and the injuries that I had, the professionals think I hit the ground, going somewhere between 70 and 100 mph,” he said.In addition to the broken bones, Bravo said he also sustained a sprained ankle in the hard landing, and serious wounds to his head and face.“I had injuries, but we all train to adapt and overcome the things that we’re faced with,” he said. “I moved as quickly as I could, despite the injuries, away from the place that I landed.”Bravo said he managed to hike and climb up the 7,000ft ridge with only a pistol, a communication device and a tracking beacon.Declassified video broadcast by 60 Minutes showed a “risky” daytime raid by US forces to rescue Alpha, who landed about 5 miles away from his colleague. More than 20 helicopters took part in that operation – and the video showed two of them under fire.“It was a gun fight all the way in and all the way out,” Hegseth told O’Donnell. “But they got Alpha back. And then we began to, immediately, I mean you’re celebrating that Alpha’s back, but you realize the job’s only half done.”While Alpha was retrieved about six hours after they were shot down, Bravo’s ordeal lasted about 50 hours.“As soon as I found a spot that I felt provided some concealment, I started working toward communication,” he said. “When I got to the moment where I could review and think about all that I’d gone through, I sent: ‘God is good,’ as a recognition of all that he had brought me through.”Cooper said a plan to rescue him was accelerated as soon as it was clear he had survived.“There was a: ‘I’m hurt, I’m moving,’ and there was a ‘God is good’ message that came in there,” he said. “Now we knew he was alive. He’s moving. OK, let’s keep planning.”US bombers and drones hitIran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces nearby, according to CBS, which showed separate video of those attacks. Two large search and rescue planes with special forces troops and small helicopters landed on a makeshift desert airstrip several miles from where Bravo was hiding.His first glimpse of the US soldiers was, he said, “one of the greatest moments of my life” – and came with about 1,500 Iranian personnel inside a 10-mile radius, Cooper said.The extraction did not conclude without incident. One rescue plane became lodged in the desert sand, was abandoned and then bombed to avoid it falling into enemy hands.Cooper said more than 90 Americans were involved on the ground, supported by several hundred more in the air, and up to 5,000 people involved overall.“What you need to know is we would have sent more to go get the back-seater,” he said.CNNreportedon Saturday that getting the airmen to appear on television was a priority for Hegseth, who was eager to present a success story in Trump’s ongoing war that has killed 18 US troops, wounded more than 800 and sent oil and gasoline pricessoaring.In a statement to CNN, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell called that story “a complete lie”. He said the decision about whether to participate in the 60 Minutes interview on Sunday “was each pilot’s alone, because it is their story”.“As CNN notes, one pilot decided to participate and one did not,” Parnell’s statement said. “Additionally, the [Pentagon] took great care to ensure operational security, sources, and methods were protected. To suggest otherwise is to denigrate every member of our military who participated in and supported the interview.”CNN further reportedBari Weiss, CBS News’s editor-in-chief, who has been criticized for perceived favoritism towards the Trump administration, put pressure on Hegseth for exclusive access to the story.A backlash to the airing of the segment wasreported on Mondayby the Daily Beast. One analyst, Zeteo News media commentator Justin Baragona, postedon Xthat a CBS staffer told him: “Norah [was] absolutely willing to play the part of dimwit reporter used as a propaganda tool.”Explore more on these topicsCBSUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpUS militaryPete HegsethUS foreign policyIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Gulf states postpone strait of Hormuz talks with Iran as Yemen conflict intensifies | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Impasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipeline
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Impasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipeline
Content: Houthi armed forces patrol Sana’a over the weekend  as the rebel group swept down the west coast of Yemen and seized the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHouthi armed forces patrol Sana’a over the weekend  as the rebel group swept down the west coast of Yemen and seized the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesStrait of HormuzGulf states postpone strait of Hormuz talks with Iran as Yemen conflict intensifiesImpasse comes amid growing Saudi anger with Tehran over Houthi advances and strikes on airbase and pipelineOil prices rise after drone attacks shut down Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipelinePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 14 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGulf states have postponed a critical meeting with Iran on the future of the strait of Hormuz owing to a lack of Arab consensus and growing Saudi Arabian anger with Tehran for helping the Houthis loosen Riyadh’s grip in Yemen.The stalemate over the vital waterway came as Houthi rebels launched a fresh barrage of missile and drone attacks on Saudi military targets. A Houthi military spokesperson claimed its forces had attacked the King Khalid airbase in Khamis Mushait, hitting fighter-jet hangars, radar systems, runways and landing strips, ammunition depots and additional targets.Last week, Tehran-backed militias in Iraq forced Saudi Arabia to close a critical east-west pipeline that had been acting as a means for Riyadh to export oil afterIraneffectively closed the strait of Hormuz.The closure of the pipeline, the postponement of the Hormuz meeting, and the Houthis’ seizure last week of Yemen’s Red Sea coast – which gave the group control over another vital waterway, the Bab al-Mandab strait – combined todrive up oil pricesabove $108 a barrel on Monday.Later in the day, Houthi officials said they had seized the strategic islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish in the southern Red Sea just inside the mouth of the strait, according to the AP.View image in fullscreenA screengrab of video released by the Houthi authorities shows fighters during an offensive in the port city of Mocha, Yemen.Photograph: Houthi Military Media Center Handout/EPAAlso on Monday, the Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, held urgent discussions with the US ⁠Central Command chief ⁠Adm ​Brad Cooper in Jeddah to discuss “the latest developments in the region”, according to Saudi media. Sources told US media last week that the Saudi de facto ruler had sought military assistance ‌from Donald Trump to help fight theHouthis. So far the US has provided only logistical and intelligence backing,Middle East map 14 SeptemberThe Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting was postponed at the last minute, deferring a proposed agreement on a new temporary route for commercial shipping when the strait of Hormuz is reopened.In a statement, Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, said the meeting had been delayed in the interests of consensus. “We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting co-operation in our region,” he wrote on X. He gave no further details.The meeting would not have led to the immediate opening of the strait, since Tehran has set a series of other preconditions: including requiring the US to lift a blockade of Iran’s oil ports, the handing over of many frozen Iranian assets and a ceasefire in Lebanon.But it would have been the first meeting between Iran and the main GCC member countries for two years. The planned agreement on a temporary route for ships to use would have formalised Iran’s control of the strait, since the entry route would have been entirely in Iranian waters.Washington has not expressed publicly an opinion over the proposed deal, and some of Trump’s recent social media posts – claiming full US control of the strait – seemed to bear little relationship with what shipping companies have been reporting.The atmosphere surrounding the meeting, in preparation for weeks, had been rapidly souring because of the advance by the Houthis inYemenand the drone attack on the Saudi pipeline by an Iran-backed Shia militia in Iraq.Vantor Technologies released high-resolution satellite images showing the damage to the east-west pipeline pumping station near Al Mesba’ah, Saudi Arabia. The station appears to be almost completely destroyed.View image in fullscreenA satellite shows damage to a pumping station along the east-west pipeline near Al Mesaba’ah, Saudi Arabia.Photograph: Satellite image ©2026 Vantor/AFP/Getty ImagesIran’s foreign ministry spokesperson denied any Iranian involvement in the pipeline attack, or on events in Yemen.US military bases throughout the Gulf have been attacked by Iran in response to the Iran war.Saudi Arabia, which backs the UN-recognised Yemeni government based in Aden, is trying to regain the initiative after Houthi forces swept down the west coast of Yemen from the port of Hodeidah last week and seized the Bab al-Mandab strait, a narrow waterway that links the Red Sea with Asia and is viewed as second in strategic importance to the strait of Hormuz.It was claimed that a Saudi air bombardment was making it difficult for the Houthis to gain full control of the Yemen waterway or the strategic islands in the Red Sea.View image in fullscreenA commercial vessel anchored off Yemen’s coast at Bab al-Mandab. The Houthis leadership says it is seeking to block only Saudi-linked ships.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe Houthi leadership says is not seeking to block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea but only Saudi-linked ships. It is also offering cut-price fees in the ports it controls on the west coast of Yemen in an effort to lure traffic away from the ports controlled by the Aden-based government in the south.It is widely accepted that Iran backs the Houthis, but the group also operates independently of Tehran. The rebels ultimate aim is to oust Saudi Arabia from the country, and take full control of the territory.Saudi Arabia has tried different tactics in handling the Houthis during the decade-long civil war in Yemen, including making concessions in the hope the highly ideological group would reach a power-sharing deal.The Yemen government said preliminary tolls indicated that 150 civilians had been killed and 200 others injured in the course of the recent Houthi advance. About 85,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzYemenSaudi ArabiaHouthisIranSaudi Arabia drone attacksUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Duke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UK | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Committee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residents
Author: Priya Bharadia
Headline: Committee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residents
Content: Meghan’s risk assessment will be her first since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.Photograph: Kristina Bumphrey/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMeghan’s risk assessment will be her first since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.Photograph: Kristina Bumphrey/Variety/Getty ImagesPrince HarryDuke and Duchess of Sussex granted security review after return to UKCommittee to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s publicly funded police protection now they are full-time residentsPriya BharadiaMon 14 Sep 2026 18.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex will have a review of their publicly funded security following their return to the UK.The royal and VIP executive committee (Ravec), which oversees tax-funded security for royalty and public figures, is to reconsider Harry and Meghan’s level of police protection.The committee met last week to discuss the couple’s case, now they and their children are full-time residents in the UK and not just visitors.It will be the first risk assessment for Meghan since the couple stepped back as working members of the royal family in 2020.Harry was granted a review of his security in July but has yet to receive a decision.The Telegraph has reported that Ravec’s chair informed Harry last week the committee had commissioned a new risk assessment and a separate one for Meghan, in light of their return to the UK.The committee has reportedly asked the couple to provide their schedules and daily routine, including the school run, to inform their decision.Last year, Harry lost a legal challenge against the Home Office after the automatic tax-funded security for him and his family was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals.“The UK is my home,” said Harry in his witness statement. “The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil. I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.”The couple returned to the UK on 26 August. Soon after, a formal letter was issued on behalf of King Charles, reiterating their status as non-working royals.The letter stated the couple were “akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests” and “any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities”.The Sussexes also decided on Monday to switch their children to a new school just two days after they started, reportedly due to security concerns over the long journey and heavy traffic.“The decision for the children to move school was taken following a discussion with the family’s security team about the practicalities of their current arrangements,” a family spokesperson told Hello! magazine.“The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.“This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there.”Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ministers seek law change to make £72m donations to Reform illegal | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Plans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirements
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Plans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirements
Content: Nigel Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNigel Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianParty fundingMinisters seek law change to make £72m donations to Reform illegalPlans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirementsPippa Crerar,Jessica ElgotandKiran StaceyMon 14 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced.In a move that is likely to set off furious complaints from Nigel Farage’s party, the government will table amendments to legislation going through the House of Lords within weeks that puts the legality of Reform’s latest donations in doubt.Senior Labour and union figures had urged ministers to look again at party funding rules after Reform announced at the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who have both previously been based overseas, were each donating £36m to the party.Government sources, however, said the plans to strengthen the representation of the people bill had been under way for weeks, after MPs pushed for further action on domestic donations in the House of Commons.Under the proposals, which are expected to be tabled at the Lords committee stage of the legislation, individual donors will have to prove their ongoing physical presence in the UK, in line with the residence requirements applied to other areas of government policy, such as tax status.graphicThe extraordinary measure will be seen as a sign of the stakes attached to the donations, which would give Reform a vast advantage in organising supporters on the ground before the next election.However, Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors, although the party has said the £72m donations are in line with both current rules and those already voted on by MPs in the bill.The legislation currently restricts donations from expats to £100,000, which would also apply for the first 12 months after they return to the UK – backdated to 25 March this year.Ministers have already brought in a minimum residency requirement of the remainder of the calendar year in which they return, plus a further full year, meaning Reform may not be able to accept the £72m donations until January 2028.Delo has been based in Hong Kong but said in April he would return to the UK to avoid restrictions, while Harborne was based in Thailand but is believed to have registered to vote in Hampshire in June.“Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” Farage told the BBC. When asked if the two billionaires were UK residents as of 25 March, he replied: “All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.”View image in fullscreenLady Taylor told peers that the government was considering how it could strengthen the residency requirements of political donors.Photograph: HoLSharon Taylor, a Labour minister in the Lords, told peers that as well as donors having to demonstrate a “genuine and ongoing connection to the UK”, the government was also looking at further restrictions.“We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy,” Lady Taylor added.However, MPs and peers who have been pushing for a full domestic donations cap are unlikely to be satisfied by the new amendments. Government sources have said they do not want to delay the bill’s progress further by considering such a cap, but are open-minded on further legislation. MPs have voiced anger in internal WhatsApp groups that the chance has been missed to cap domestic donations in this bill while it was in the Commons.Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour.“How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” the communities secretary said.“It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.”Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations.The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed.Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations.Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”.However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day.In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.”The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality.Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps.“The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said.“But we have to ask the question, is this healthy for our democratic process to have more money coming from fewer people in bigger lumps?”MPs who have campaigned for a donations cap are working with peers on a number of amendments to the bill which would tighten it up without having to wait for another act of parliament.They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval.Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister in the Lords, said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling. “Even just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system,” she said.Reform denounced the government’s existing plans, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, describing them on X as “an unprecedented step from a leftwing government to plunge Britain into dictatorship and communism”.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingReform UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: British man accused of drugging and raping wife over two decades admits 60 offences | UK news | The Guardian
description: Man, who cannot be named to protect anonymity of his victim, admits scores of criminal offences
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: Man, who cannot be named to protect anonymity of his victim, admits scores of criminal offences
Content: The man, appearing at Manchester Minshull Street crown court, admitted charges including sharing intimate images of his victim.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenThe man, appearing at Manchester Minshull Street crown court, admitted charges including sharing intimate images of his victim.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAUK newsBritish man accused of drugging and raping wife over two decades admits 60 offencesMan, who cannot be named to protect anonymity of his victim, admits scores of criminal offencesJosh HallidayandHannah Al-OthmanMon 14 Sep 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has pleaded guilty to drugging and sexually assaulting his wife over a period of 20 years as he admitted 60 criminal offences.The man, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim, is in his 60s and before his arrest lived in Stockport, Greater Manchester.He admitted 60 counts, which include 21 counts of rape and sharing intimate images of his victim.His estranged wife sat on the front row of the packed courtroom with other family members as he entered his pleas, occasionally sobbing as he did so.In June, the man pleaded guilty to 15 of the charges against him. On Monday he admitted the final 45 at Manchester’s Minshull Street crown court.The defendant also previously pleaded guilty to sharing intimate photographs or film of his wife, without her consent, for sexual gratification.Twelve co-defendants all deny various allegations involving the same woman.Rick Jackson, an assistant chief constable of Greater Manchester police, said: “Our focus remains on supporting the victim of this horrific campaign of abuse through what is a very complex investigation.“Specialist support continues to be provided to the victim at the centre of this case.“If you are concerned you, or someone you know, may be affected by drug-facilitated sexual abuse, please know that you do not need proof, certainty, or a clear memory to be taken seriously.“You are not expected to understand exactly what has happened or who was involved in order to be taken seriously. If you feel that something has happened, then please report it or ask for help.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Davies admits to drawing on ‘stimulating’ Made in Chelsea for Jane Austen adaptation | Jane Austen | The Guardian
description: Screenwriter points to parallels between two worlds while academic says some of author’s characters ‘would make perfect reality show contestants’
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Screenwriter points to parallels between two worlds while academic says some of author’s characters ‘would make perfect reality show contestants’
Content: Some of the cast from Made  in Chelsea in 2021.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenSome of the cast from Made  in Chelsea in 2021.Photograph: Channel 4Jane AustenAndrew Davies admits to drawing on ‘stimulating’ Made in Chelsea for Jane Austen adaptationScreenwriter points to parallels between two worlds while academic says some of author’s characters ‘would make perfect reality show contestants’Nadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentMon 14 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Jane Austen’s novels run on closed social worlds, courtship rituals, status anxiety, gossip and relentless scrutiny of who’s coupling with who, it follows that the obvious contemporary equivalent would be reality television.That’s according toAndrew Davies, the writer who has spent decades modernising British period dramas.Speaking on Radio 4’s Today programme on Monday, Davies revealed that he had been watching Made in Chelsea while working on an adaptation of Austen’s unfinished novel The Watsons.“It’s stimulating really for relationships and ideas,” he said of the Channel 4 series, which follows the relationship dramas and social rivalries of affluent young residents of west London. “These young men and women in The Watsons, for example, are very analogous to Made in Chelsea.”View image in fullscreenAndrew Davies said the young men and women in The Watsons were ‘very analogous’ to the characters of the Made in Chelsea reality show.Photograph: David Sillitoe/The GuardianDavies, whose memoir An Unsuitable Boy: A Life in Scripts is out this week, is responsible for the legendary image of Colin Firth as Mr Darcy emerging from a lake in a wet shirt in his 1995 BBC adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, which went some way to injecting Austen into Bridget Jones, written by Helen Fielding around the time it aired. His approach, he said, had been about “bringing out the sex that’s inherent in Austen”.He has previously described his 2019 adaptation of Sanditon as “Love Island” in Austen’s world andtalked aboutwhether Charlotte would “friend-zone” someone or experience a “fanny flutter”. Meanwhile Rose Williams, who starred in the series,said she believed“Austen would probably write something satirical about Love Island if she were alive today”.Joe Bray, an Austen scholar and professor of English at the University of Sheffield, said of the author: “Jane Austen was a shrewd observer of the fashionable manners and fads adopted by the young … and the plots of most of her novels are driven by sexual attraction and/or secret liaisons and engagements.”The Steele sisters in Sense and Sensibility, he suggested, “would make perfect reality show contestants”.Austen also pioneered a way of representing the unspoken thoughts and feelings of her female characters that can be difficult to translate to screen. But Bray noted that Austen herself loved gossiping about neighbours and acquaintances in letters to her sister Cassandra. “I can’t say for certain whether or not she would be a viewer of Made in Chelsea or Love Island,” he said, “but … she would be interested at least!”An academic essay on Made in Chelseadescribed the programme as a “kind of homage” to Austen, arguing that its subject was the “courtship rituals” of young people with money and property, and compared its social world to Pride and Prejudice and Emma.View image in fullscreenAusten scholar Joe Bray suggested that the author would have at least been interested in the likes of Made in Chelsea and Love Island.Photograph: Stock Montage/Getty ImagesThere is indeed a human link between Made in Chelsea and Netflix’s forthcoming Pride and Prejudice: the latter’s writer and executive producer, Dolly Alderton, began her career as a story producer on the reality show – where, she has said, her job involved turning the romantic entanglements of wealthy young Londoners into “a four-part comedy drama”.It remains to be seen whether the Netflix series draws any inspiration from Made in Chelsea, but Reddit users havepreviously theorisedabout whether Alderton took inspiration from the reality show, or her TV adaptation of her memoir Everything I Know About Love. “Who do we think the character ‘Kyle’ is based off? I’m getting Spencer Matthews and Jamie Laing [both Made in Chelsea cast members],” one wrote.In her 2016 modernisation of Pride and Prejudice, Eligible, novelist Curtis Sittenfeld’s transplanted the Bennets to contemporary Cincinnati and made Chip Bingley a former reality-TV star who had appeared on The Bachelor.“Reality dating shows are so formulaic, and courtship in Austen’s time was rigid and proscriptive,”Sittenfeld said. In other words, reality TV provided a modern equivalent for Austen’s world of carefully prescribed romantic encounters; in place of the wealthy unmarried man arriving in the neighbourhood, there is the reality-TV bachelor whose romantic availability is already a matter of public interest.That may explain the extraordinary portability of Austen, from Clueless, which transplanted Emma to 1990s LA, and Bridget Jones’s Diary to Fire Island, Persuasion and the forthcoming Sense and Sensibility.John Mullan, a literature professor at University College London and historical and dialogue consultant on Bridgerton, identified another parallel.“In Austen’s fiction, courtship mostly takes place under the eyes of others,” he said. “Young women and men who might fancy each other are very rarely alone.”But, he added, there is a crucial difference: “What about propriety, restraint, repression? These are also key to Austen’s stories and characters.”Explore more on these topicsJane AustenAndrew DaviesReality TVTelevisionDramaE4newsShareReuse this content

title: UK politics: Farage hints that Reform’s £72m donations may not be legal under new elections bill - as it happened | Politics | The Guardian
description: In an interview about the donations, he said they are compliant with the law ‘today’
Author: Andrew Sparrow
Headline: In an interview about the donations, he said they are compliant with the law ‘today’
Content: 09.04 EDTFarage hints £72m donations to Reform UK won't be legal under retrospective measures in elections bill when it becomes lawNigel Faragehas hinted that the donations to Reform UK worth £72m might not be legal under the legislation to tighten elections law currently going through parliament.He made the apparent concession in an interview with the BBC in which he strongly objected to the government’s plan to make a new law banning Britons who live abroad, or who have recently relocated to the UK, from giving more than £100,000 a year to political parties retrospective.It seems likely that the law would apply to Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, the two cryptocurrency billionaires who have each pledged £36m toReform UK.In an interview,Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, asked Farage if he was sure that both donations were compliant with the law now, and “how we expect it soon to be”.Faragereplied:double quotation markBoth these donations are 100% compliant with the law today. Of that there is no question whatsoever.Masonpointed out that Farage was saying “today” and he asked if Delo and Harborne were both resident in the UK on 25 March – after which the retrospective restrictions on donations by new arrivals will kick in when the representation of the people bill becomes law.Faragereplied:double quotation markI’m not going to go into their particular details. All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.Now there is talk, and Angela Rayner was talking about this yesterday, there is talk of them retrospectively declaring donations illegally.Well, that simply cannot be. If a government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There’d be a response the other way. We or the Conservatives would say, right, if you’re going to stop legitimate donors like this, we will then say to the trade unions, you can’t give money. And if you do that, you have collapsed the whole political system.In fact, there has not just been “talk” of making the cap retrospective. The bill legislating for this has gone through the Commons, and MPs debated amendments creating these exact lawson Wednesday 2 September.While laws applying retrospectively are rare, they are not unprecedented. Reform UK wants to pass retrospective legislation itself. For example, it plans to abolish indefinite leave to remain as an immigration status, including for people who already have it.Farage’s position is different from the one adopted by his party over the weekend whenRobert Jenrick, the Treasury spokesperson, said that Reform UK was confident the Delo and Harborne donations were “entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it’s going to be in the future”.ShareUpdated at10.18 EDT

title: AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Content: Shares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ developmentDonald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’Lauren AlmeidaMon 14 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 03.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for aslowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day.The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to“slow down”.However,Donald Trumpdismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”.In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!”The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”.OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fearsRead more“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote.Trump offered a similar assessment when he called Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, while the executive was on stage at an AI conference in California on Monday.“It’s a hoax,” Trumpsaid via speaker phoneto the audience. “The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That’s not going to happen.”The UN security council, meanwhile, is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week as international concern rises, Agence France-Pressereportedon Monday.Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer ofOpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chipmakers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.Shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%.In Europe, shares in the Dutch tech manufacturer ASML, Europe’s biggest company by value and an important supplier for the semiconductor industry, slumped by 6%.There was, however, a rally in shares that have been threatened by the rise of AI, including the advertising group WPP, which rose by 5% in London, and the analytics business Relx, which was also up 5%. The latter had suffered a sharp fall earlier this year after Anthropic launched a suite of new data and automation tools.Amodei has said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.His claims have beendisputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support forAmodei’s essayon slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder,toldthe BBC an AI “kill switch” that could be triggered by a third party may be necessary to prevent catastrophe.Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of UK MPs and peersidentified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them.Meanwhile, China’s top intelligence official warned that the use of AI by adversaries could pose a risk to the country’s political and social security.Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced US models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to Beijing’s critical information ​infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?Read moreDespite such concern about the risks around AI, Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares tolist on the US stock marketthis year.OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing tosafety concerns with the technology.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Stock marketsAsia PacificComputingTechnology sectorDatacentresDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: US borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-off | US economy | The Guardian
description: Soaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fears
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Soaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fears
Content: The US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenThe US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAUS economyUS borrowing costs hit 5% for first time since 2023 amid bond sell-offSoaring oil prices of above $108 a barrel after Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure stoke inflation fearsRichard PartingtonandLauren AlmeidaMon 14 Sep 2026 12.48 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 04.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS government borrowing costs have risen to 5% for the first time since 2023 as soaring oil prices fuelled by the war in the Middle East trigger an intensifying sell-off in the global bond market.The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year US Treasury bonds hit the psychologically important threshold on Monday, on a day of renewed selling pressure on Wall Street as the global oil price reached $108 a barrel.With traders awaiting a crunch US Federal Reserve interest rate decision on Wednesday, the benchmark rate has steadily climbed from a low this year of 4% before the outbreak of the US-Israeli war onIranin late February. The yield was last above 5% in October 2023.Saudi Arabia shuts down key oil pipeline, blaming drones from IraqRead moreIt comes as the rising global oil price stokes inflation fears, with the latest move prompted by aseries of drone attacksthat have forced Saudi Arabia to close a vital east-west crude pipeline as the fallout from the war mounts.Bond market chartBrent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, surged to more than $108.5 a barrel on Monday – a 3.7% increase on the day.The spike came after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia andcaptured the strategic island of Perimin the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway.The rise was also fuelled by the Gulf states postponing a meeting with Tehran to discuss creating a temporary shipping lane through the strait of Hormuz, a vital channel through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.Oil price chartTraders in the kingdom have warned itwill run out of oil stocks for exportif it does not reopen the east-west pipeline within days.Gas prices also climbed higher on Monday, with the UK benchmark rising by 5% to 208.73p a therm – its highest level since December 2022.It came despite Donald Trump on Monday announcing a deal between Ukraine and Russia not to hit each other’s energy targets, while insisting that he believed a politically sensitive rise in US diesel fuel prices was being driven by the conflict in Europe rather than the war in Iran.Map of Houthi territorial gains in YemenWith fears mounting as the Middle East war escalates, bond markets have come under intense selling pressure. The US 10-year Treasury yield is used in global financial markets as a benchmark for pricing other assets, meaning a jump in borrowing costs for Washington has consequences for countries, businesses and households worldwide.Borrowing costs also rose across Europe on Monday, including a rise in 30-year UK government yields to the highest level since March 1998.UK bond chartThe moves come as traders awaitdecisions on interest ratesfrom the US Federal Reserve on Wednesday and the Bank of England on Thursday after the European Central Bankraised borrowing costs last week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith investors anticipating an increase from the Fed and a hold decision from Threadneedle Street amid mounting inflationary pressures, analysts said global bond markets could face another week of renewed volatility.Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “Markets are starting the week on a defensive footing, with the combination of another escalation in the Middle East and increasingly hawkish central-bank expectations weighing on risk appetite.”With wholesale energy prices on the rise, the cost of petrol and diesel hit new Iran war highs on Monday, according to the RAC, with the average cost of petrol climbing to 169.68p and diesel hitting 191.68p.The US-Israeli war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East this year, sending the oil price soaring from its prewar level of about $72 a barrel topeak at $126in April.Brent crude later fell back over the summer amid hopes of a lasting ceasefire, before starting to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart.After a recent stepping-up of hostilities the benchmark againrose above the $100 a barrel thresholdlast week for the first time since July.Chris Beauchamp, of the broker IG, said a “move back to the spring highs” looked increasingly likely. “Oil markets are being subjected to their worst fears all at once – attacks on energy infrastructure, the closure of Hormuz and a breakdown in attempts to restart negotiations,” he said.Map showing location of pipeline hit by drone strikes in Saudi Arabia“The risk of further disruption is also spreading beyond the Gulf, with the threat of renewed Houthi attacks on shipping adding another layer of uncertainty around key energy and trade routes.“The major surprise is how calm markets remain in the face of all this, but if prices breach the March highs, things could get ugly very quickly.”Oil output fromSaudi Arabiahad been under pressure before the attacks on its major pipeline. Riyadh told the Opec oil cartel recently that its crude production in August was at its lowest level since 1990, according to Bloomberg.Explore more on these topicsUS economyOilOil and gas companiesCommoditiesGlobal economyEconomicsEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: She’s Donald Trump’s least-favorite Fox News host. But Jessica Tarlov remains undeterred | Fox News | The Guardian
description: The 42-year-old liberal commentator regularly co-hosts the network’s 5pm talk show, taking flak from her conservative colleagues and harsh insults from the president.
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: The 42-year-old liberal commentator regularly co-hosts the network’s 5pm talk show, taking flak from her conservative colleagues and harsh insults from the president.
Content: ‘I’m trying to open them up to the notion that there are sane lefties out there, even if I’m a more moderate lefty, and that it isn’t the end of the world – the apocalypse is not coming – if we’re coming into office.’Photograph: Roy Rochlin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I’m trying to open them up to the notion that there are sane lefties out there, even if I’m a more moderate lefty, and that it isn’t the end of the world – the apocalypse is not coming – if we’re coming into office.’Photograph: Roy Rochlin/Getty ImagesBooks interviewFox NewsInterviewShe’s Donald Trump’s least-favorite Fox News host. But Jessica Tarlov remains undeterredJeremy Barrin WashingtonThe 42-year-old liberal commentator regularly co-hosts the network’s 5pm talk show, taking flak from her conservative colleagues and harsh insults from the president.Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJessica Tarlov is the left-leaning Fox News host that some of the network’s most conservative viewers, includingDonald Trump, love to hate.The US president regularly bashes Tarlov on his Truth Social platform, in April calling her “one of the Least Attractive and Talented People on all of Television”, and demanding thatFox“GET HER OFF THE AIR.”But, as a rotating co-host of political talkshow The Five, the 42-year-old former pollster and Democratic strategist has carved out a prominent role for herself as the network’s most capable messenger for the left, regularly doing battle with conservative co-panelists like Jesse Watters and Greg Gutfeld. She also recently signed a new contract, meaning she will be a regular presence on Fox for years to come.Still, some critics have consistently questioned what Tarlov is able to accomplish, considering she is totally outnumbered on the show by conservatives.View image in fullscreenJessica Tarlov’s book ‘I Disagree’Photograph: Random HouseIna new book published Tuesdaycalled I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends, Tarlov lays out how she became Fox’s go-to Democrat – and offers advice for readers on how they can effectively message their own political points in heated environments.“I think the dance can be really complicated and you’re spending a lot of time thinking about the right balance between being friendly and firm, and how you can create connective tissue and olive branches with someone that you disagree with in a way that signals to the audience that you are a part of the conversation and that you’re leading with humanity, but that your point of view is worth tussling with for them,” she said.This interview has been edited for clarity and conciseness.In your book, you write that you initially faced skepticism from those in your circle and professional network about your decision to appear as a Democrat onFox News. Nearly a decade later, do you still face the same kind of pushback?Not really. I think people are pretty clear about who I am and what I’m doing. I have enough experience, also, with the type of debating or disagreeing that I do to know that it isn’t about facilitating a conservative, looking better, or making the truth safe to hear for other people. That there’s real advocacy going on, and a real desire to be in this very important bipartisan arena. And so yeah, I don’t think people feel that way. And also now that I’m a co-host on The Five for four and a half years, and just signed a new deal, that’s where I live – for a while. So I think people understand that it’s something that’s really important to me and part of my identity.Do you sense that the audience likes your presence on the show?In general, yes. I do. I mean, if you look at my Twitter timeline, no, those people do not enjoy my presence. And the ones who are doing petitions on Facebook and email [Fox News chief executive] Suzanne Scott daily about getting me off The Five, especially because there’sa picture of mewith [progressive streamer] Hasan Piker, which apparently means that I’m Hasan Piker’s wife or something like that and condone everything that he’s ever said. But in general, and when I meet fans of The Five out in the wild, they love the dynamic and the personal relationships, especially with Jesse and Greg. With Jesse, it’s very sibling-y, and they like the pointed back-and-forth and how we have relationships, frankly, that mirror what their real lives look like. I think it’s soothing in that way. And a lot of cable news doesn’t have that interplay … Obviously I’m outnumbered, but I’m the genuine article, and they’re the genuine article, and I think people like that.Fox News seems to havea longstanding policyof not taking the bait and responding to Trump’s attacks on its employees. Do you ever worry that Trump’s criticisms will affect your standing at Fox?No. I mean, I think that Suzanne Scott and the entire leadership team know exactly who I am, and that they want me to keep doing what I’m doing. And if it aggravates him – he would just get annoyed at somebody else anyway. If he’s in a bad mood, he’s in a bad mood. And I think that he understands that as well. I’ve never had a conversation with him, but the idea of posting ‘Dear Fox executives, fire Jessica Tarlov’ or calling into The Five and saying the show would be better without her, I don’t think he thinks that means that I’m going to get fired from my job. … But yes, in general, we don’t respond to it, and there’s no reason to, and honestly it just makes it worse.Have you ever asked one of your co-hosts who talks regularly to Trump to ask him to cut it out?They have said stuff like, “Oh, come on, we love her.” But the general feeling is that if you feed the beast, it gets worse, and that it is going to be probably worse for me if somebody goes to the mat about it. I’m pretty sure that [former The Five co-host Jeanine Pirro], when she was on the show, had said something to him about, like, “She’s great.” But I know who I am. I know what my relationship is like with them. I know what their relationships with him are like as well, and I don’t need anybody’s help that way. My skin is thick enough for this hand that I’ve been dealt.Do you think you provide more value by being one of the few left-leaning commentators on Fox rather than being part of a larger group of similarly minded pundits on a network like MS Now or CNN?Yeah, I don’t think that there’s any comparison in terms of the type of conversation or back-and-forth across ideological differences that you’re having, but [also] in sheer size of audience. And it’s not just conservatives. We have moreDemocratsand independents watching too. … And also it’s not that fun talking to people who agree with you all the time. I have that in my personal life. We’re all kind of various denominations of left-leaning, except I have one uncle who voted for Trump on Israel in 2024, which is pretty common now within liberal Jewish families. So I think I have the coolest job in media, definitely for a liberal. I feel that way, even if it’s tough sometimes.You said that you want to be known as “a partisan that is focused on winning elections”. Do you think your role on The Five helps Democrats win elections?I understand that my commentary or a clip of me can affect people in a multitude of ways, but I am in a long-term relationship with my colleagues and the viewers of The Five, where I’m trying to open them up to the notion that there are sane lefties out there, even if I’m a more moderate lefty, and that it isn’t the end of the world – the apocalypse is not coming – if we’re coming into office. And to also point out the places where there is agreement, because I think people are really hungry for that. They want to see the dialogue, and they want to see the friendships because their real life looks like that. And they want to hear about ideas from the other side from somebody that really believes in it too. And I don’t say things I don’t believe in.Explore more on these topicsFox NewsBooks interviewUS politicsDonald TrumpRepublicansDemocratsUS television industryFoxinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Calvert-Lewin shows the way as Leeds thrash limp Newcastle and rise to third | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Leeds romped to 4-1 victory over Newcastle, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin leading the way as Daniel Farke’s side stayed unbeaten
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Leeds romped to 4-1 victory over Newcastle, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin leading the way as Daniel Farke’s side stayed unbeaten
Content: Dominic Calvert-Lewin takes the acclaim from the Leeds supporters after putting Leeds ahead 3-0.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersView image in fullscreenDominic Calvert-Lewin takes the acclaim from the Leeds supporters after putting Leeds ahead 3-0.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersPremier LeagueCalvert-Lewin shows the way as Leeds thrash limp Newcastle and rise to thirdAaron Bowerat Elland RoadMon 14 Sep 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt what stage does a good start become something more significant? Perhaps we are not quite there yet; maybe we are. But as the goals flew in on a chaotic night at Elland Road, it was difficult not to think the boundaries of expectation for Leeds were potentially being redrawn.Ask those close to the action over the summer at Leeds and the feeling was that there was a possibility of something special materialising this season. Having found their feet in thePremier Leaguein the last campaign, the platform had been set and a very good summer transfer window seemed like the catalyst for even brighter days to return to West Yorkshire.VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood downRead moreBut even with that optimism in mind, this night felt significant. Leeds did not just beat a Newcastle side who themselves have started brightly under Matthias Jaissle, they dismantled them. And with the manner of this victory, Daniel Farke’s side sit third in the table.Perhaps, in this world of demanding success overnight, there is a lesson here in patience for both clubs too. As Elland Road’s patrons likely pinched themselves when the outstanding Dominic Calvert-Lewin made it 3-0 before half-time it was easy to forget that, under a year ago, large swathes of supporter were suggesting time was up for Farke.His decision to change to a back three against Manchester City last November saved his job and sparked an upturn in form that saw Leeds secure safety beforestarting this campaign in magnificent fashion. If this start continues with another win over Crystal Palace on Sunday, perhaps this side can do greater things than many first thought.As for Jaissle, this was his first large bump in the road as Newcastle manager and there will possibly be more over the coming months as he imprints his vision on this team. But the decision-making of the Leeds side who vanquished them is evidence enough that patience can often pay off and Jaissle and his team could have no complaints about the scoreline.Leeds were magnificent from start to finish. The opening goal was perhaps a touch fortuitous as Ao Tanaka’s shot bounced off the substitute Sean Steur and Lewis Miley to wrongfoot Lukas Hornicek, but it was the least Leeds deserved. Two minutes later, the lead was doubled when Jayden Bogle headed home a James Justin cross.View image in fullscreenDominic Calvert-Lewin’s header for Leeds’ second was deflected in off Jayden Bogle.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesBogle has quietly been one of Leeds’ standout performers for some time and he is one of a few Leeds players who Thomas Tuchel may find difficult to ignore before naming his latest England squad later this week. The man who slotted home Leeds’ third in first-half stoppage time has perhaps even greater a claim for a call-up.Calvert-Lewin’s latest goal was brilliantly taken; a measured finish that made it 3-0 at half-time.With James Trafford between the sticks, Leeds have a clutch of players who may be fancy their chances of international recognition if they keep this up; a surefire sign of a club trending upwards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey may have a manager in that bracket as well. “There’s never a perfect performance in football but that was top class for more or less the whole game,” Farke said. “We know we have to stay humble; we might not have the best individual quality but we can be an outstanding team.”The prospect of a grand Newcastle comeback appeared unlikely from the moment Sven Botman carelessly gave away possession to Anton Stach shortly after half-time and Stach spurned a glorious chance to make it 4-0. But Leeds did not have to wait long for their fourth goal, as Noah Okafor struck through a crowded penalty box to put the result beyond doubt.Jaissle’s demeanour became more and more exasperated as the evening wore on and unsurprisingly he cut a frustrated figure afterwards. “We couldn’t match the intensity of Leeds and you see how difficult it can be to win a game in the Premier League,” he said. “We’ll have some ups and downs and this was a big down. A tough night.”There was at least a consolation in the final moments as Bazoumana Touré, a bright spark after coming on, capitalised on a rare Leeds error to make it 4-1.But the damage had long since been done – and the party among the home support by this time was already well under way.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueLeeds UnitedNewcastle Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: From influencers to brutal finishes, US Open 2026 was worst grand slam in recent memory | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Despite the drama on the court, the poor condition of Arthur Ashe Stadium was just one problem among many
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Despite the drama on the court, the poor condition of Arthur Ashe Stadium was just one problem among many
Content: Ben Shelton sprawled out on the court during his men’s singles final defeat against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreenBen Shelton sprawled out on the court during his men’s singles final defeat against Alexander Zverev.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026AnalysisFrom influencers to brutal finishes, US Open 2026 was worst grand slam in recent memoryTumaini CarayolDespite the drama on the court, the poor condition of Arthur Ashe Stadium was just one problem among manyMon 14 Sep 2026 15.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareAt the end of another comically late night and early morning in Flushing Meadows, when the remaining spectators were departing, a familiar scene was unfolding on the US Open tournament grounds. A handful of workers had congregated directly beneath a hole in the ceiling inside one of the tournament shops as they tried to stop water from flowing out of a broken pipe and ruining thousands of pounds worth of merchandise below.This was not a surprising sight. Upon entering Arthur Ashe Stadium this year, fans were greeted by some ominous signs: “Pardon our appearance while we write the next chapter of Arthur Ashe Stadium.” The tournament’s appearance, it must be said, was hideous. Inside the corridors and rooms at one of the biggest sporting events in the world, it felt like its main building was falling apart.Dogs, bands and pre-match outfits: best images from the US Open tennis 2026Read moreSeemingly every other day a new leak revealed itself in the media centre, with long plastic sheets attached from the ceiling to buckets on the floor containing the splashing in various parts of the room. In the nearby workers’ restaurant, a dramatic burst of water from the ceiling caused its closure for one day. Throughout the tournament, a colleague joked that most sane human beings would not return every day to work underneath a ceiling that seemed ready to collapse at any time. Elsewhere, numerous photographers reported feeling sick after inhaling fetid fumes from the drains in the photo pit.This was the worst grand slam tournament in recent memory for various reasons. When people look back, 2026 will be remembered as the US Open’s year of the influencers, a group united by their talent for making everything about them. It takes a special level of foolishness to bring ring lights to a tennis match, loudly film TikTok videos in the middle of games and repeatedly stand up to take selfies during points. There is a widespread belief that everyone involved in the sport should help to “grow the game” at all costs. Sometimes, though, gatekeeping is great. Meanwhile, the general conversation on Ashe was so loud at times that even Aryna Sabalenka’s screams were drowned out.Although the 16 hours of tennis between 11.30am on Tuesday and 3.33am on Wednesday provided one of the most spectacular quarter-final days in recent history, with four dramatic final sets in four matches, it is an obvious sign of dysfunction in this sport that tournament organisers still have not prioritised finding a real solution to these early morning finishes.In the heat of battle, though, there was still so much to enjoy. Women’s tennis stole the show again as the entire top six reached the quarter-finals and, for the first time in 51 years, the top four shut out the rest of the tour in the semi-finals.Sabalenka’s comeback victory against Linda Noskova, the 21-year-old Wimbledon champion, was one of the best matches of the year and she will eventually reflect on how well she recovered just to reach the final after such a nightmare summer.View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina’s excellence was a reflection of the high standard of women’s tennis at the tournament, one positive amid the negatives.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/Imagn Images/ReutersElena Rybakina dealt spectacularly with so many obstacles: the No 1 ranking, an achilles injury and one of the toughest possible drawsto win the title. Her level on hard courts over the past year has been incredible and her quiet, reserved nature is the perfect foil to the intense extroversion of Sabalenka.Meanwhile, Zheng Qinwen’s back-to-back comebacks from 0-5 to 7-5 in the third set of her third-round match against Madison Keys, and then in the first set ofher fourth-round match against Iga Swiatek, were astonishing and she greatly deserved her dramatic return to the big stage. Iva Jovic and Alexandra Eala showed relentless competitiveness can sit comfortably with strong friendship as they battled into the night. A year after the pitiful state of her serve reduced her to tears on the court, Coco Gauff’s semi-final run was a reflection of her great progress.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionConversely, 2026 has been a miserable year for men’s tennis, primarily due to the shocking amount of injuries sustained by younger players. The difficulties ofCarlos Alcarazand Jannik Sinner are only the tip of the iceberg: Jack Draper, Holger Rune, Lorenzo Musetti, Arthur Fils and João Fonseca have all missed a significant amount of the past year. Even those who competed in New York are still working through the consequences of missing so much action.The men’s draw still produced one of the memorable sporting moments of the year courtesy of a special champion. At 3.40am on Wednesday, after Ben Shelton’s monumental victory against Alcaraz, the Spaniard finally made his exit from Ashe. He had pushed himself to the limit for 4hr 28min, vomiting repeatedly, only to lose by narrow margins in a fifth set tie-break. However, after being away for four and a half months because of a wrist injury and unsure about how his body would react upon his return, he was finally able to again participate in the sport he loves and he left the court feeling like himself. As Alcaraz walked through the tunnel leading to the locker room, a place that had seen so many tears, his face broke out into a wide, joyful smile.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Aryna SabalenkaCarlos AlcarazUS Open tennisTennisanalysisShareReuse this content

title: VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood down | Video assistant referees (VARs) | The Guardian
description: The VAR officials who failed to disallow Erling Haaland’s winning goal in the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down this weekend
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: The VAR officials who failed to disallow Erling Haaland’s winning goal in the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down this weekend
Content: Erling Haaland’s goal was given even though Enzo Fernández (right) was in an offside position and regarded as likely to have affected the passage of play.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenErling Haaland’s goal was given even though Enzo Fernández (right) was in an offside position and regarded as likely to have affected the passage of play.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty ImagesVideo assistant referees (VARs)VARs who wrongly confirmed Haaland’s goal at Manchester United are stood downMatt Donohue and his assistant not used this weekendPro Ref said allowing winner was ‘error of judgment’Paul MacInnesMon 14 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe video assistant referee officials whoallowed Erling Haaland’s winning goalin the Manchester derby on Sunday have been stood down. Matt Donohue and his assistant, Blake Antrobus, have been told by Pro Ref they have not received appointments for this weekend’s round of Premier League fixtures.Howard Webb, the chief ­refereeing officer, took the decision with his management team after a review of the weekend’s action. Their availa­bility will be reconsidered after the international break.VAR controversy decides Manchester derby as City keep pace with Arsenal: Football Weekly – podcastRead moreDonohue was called on to check Michael Oliver’s decision to ­disallow Haaland’s 60th-minute goal for offside. Using semi-automated ­offside technology, Donohue was able to establish that theManchester Citystriker was onside and he overturned ­Oliver’s call. But he failed to spot Enzo Fernández had ­influenced play from an offside position, an ­infringement which Pro Ref said should have led him to recommend an on-field review.This is the first time officials have been made to stand down this season owing to an error. Donohue, an EFL referee since 2018, has taken charge of three Championship matches this season as well as his VAR work. His EFL profile says he has completed Pro Ref’s “Enhanced VAR ­Training Programme”. ­Antrobus is also an assistant referee in the ­Premier League and ran the line in the first three matchdays.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Pro Ref acknowledged an “error of ­judgment” in the Haaland incident in a statement on Sunday night and is understood to have contacted ­Manchester United to explain the mistake.Explore more on these topicsVideo assistant referees (VARs)RefereesPremier LeagueManchester CityLaws of footballManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Spanish GP plans to change Madring after fierce criticism from F1 drivers | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Discussions are already under way to change the layout of Formula One’s newest circuit after driver condemnation of the Madring during its inaugural Grand Prix
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Discussions are already under way to change the layout of Formula One’s newest circuit after driver condemnation of the Madring during its inaugural Grand Prix
Content: The Spanish Grand Prix race was far from thrilling with drivers largely circulating behind one another.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Spanish Grand Prix race was far from thrilling with drivers largely circulating behind one another.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Spanish GP plans to change Madring after fierce criticism from F1 driversNew track for Spanish GP frustrated drivers and fansMcLaren’s Stella: ‘It’s impossible to attempt overtaking’Giles Richardsin MadridMon 14 Sep 2026 06.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiscussions are already under way to change the layout of Formula One’s newest circuit after driver condemnation of the Madring during its inaugural grand prix. The race in Madridwas won by Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, but it was notable for being a procession with overtakes failing to reach double digits over 57 laps. Drivers were left frustrated and disappointed at an opportunity that had been lost, resulting in a chorus of criticism.“I don’t know how someone looks at this design and goes ‘mint’,” said the defending world champion,Lando Norris, who finished third. “There’s a lot of opportunity. They can make it into a track that’s good for racing and I’m excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes.‘No stopping him’: Hamilton admits defeat as Antonelli charges towards F1 world titleRead more“The fact you have to turn and brake basically defeats the whole object of racing. They can do some simple changes. I hope they do it because then it should be more exciting for everyone.”The race was far from thrilling with drivers largely circulating behind one another, albeit at high speed, but unable to find any opportunity to make a move. Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto dismissively categorised it as uninvigorating to drive in as it had been to watch. “I almost fell asleep as well,” he said.The Madring, a hybrid circuit of part public roads and part purpose-built track, has been constructed in north-east Madrid around a conference centre on the way to the airport. Logistically, it has been a success, with transport to and from the track managed well, despite the huge numbers of fans, which F1 puts at 352,000 for the weekend.The teams enjoyed the facilities and space and it presented a high-speed and spectacular challenge on a narrow, technical circuit many drivers enjoyed over a single lap in qualifying. However, in racing terms, the track, built at a reported cost of approximately £71m, was frustrating.It was designed by the Italian Jarno Zaffelli who said he hoped “people walk away recognising it’s possible to build a street circuit that is not boring”. That was a goal left sorely wanting after the race, with people walking away looking bored.“There are some corners that need to be changed to create more overtaking opportunities because it’s nice over one lap, but in the race you’re just stuck behind,” said Antonelli.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli’s victory gave him a lead of 81 points over his teammate, George Russell.Photograph: David Davies/PAHis feelings were echoed by Max Verstappen who finished second. “If you just drive a little bit in the middle, then you can’t pass,” he said. Verstappen had warned of the poor design from the moment he had first driven the track in a simulator.The Mercedes team principal,Toto Wolff, acknowledged there were discussions about changes taking place even before the race. “The tricky bit [is] doing a track that is spectacular for the drivers and then building it in a way that there is lots of overtaking,” he said. “I had a discussion [on Saturday] with the CEO of the circuit and they are totally open-minded about next year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We’ve had the discussions with the FIA. What is it we should do? How is it that we should lay the track out when it comes to overtaking? There is a constant discussion and they are on it and understand we can tweak it a little bit.”The Madring has a 10-year contract to host the Spanish Grand Prix and theMcLarenteam principal, Andrea Stella, was clear he expected there to be considerations of layout changes. “It’s a shame it’s so difficult. It just requires a large, large lap-time difference to be able to overtake,” he said. “What F1, we’d like to review, is there’s some modifications required in order to introduce an overtaking possibility.“At the moment the straight may be long enough, but there’s absolutely no way the two cars can enter the corner together. It’s basically impossible to attempt overtaking.”Antonelli has a lead of 81 points in the world championship over his teammate George Russell, with nine meetings remaining and the next round at Baku in two weeks.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportLando NorrisKimi AntonelliToto WolffMercedes GPnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Josh Allen rollercoaster is up and running again for the new NFL season | Buffalo Bills | The Guardian
description: The Bills quarterback produced his usual thrills: a galloping touchdown run, a near game-ending mistake and a brilliant throw. Buffalo fans better hold on
Author: Doug Farrar
Headline: The Bills quarterback produced his usual thrills: a galloping touchdown run, a near game-ending mistake and a brilliant throw. Buffalo fans better hold on
