title: Pietersen has England players ‘buzzing’ but McCullum delivers Carse warning | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Brendon McCullum, the England white-ball head coach, has said he was the driving force behind the recruitment of Kevin Pietersen as a specialist mentor
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Brendon McCullum, the England white-ball head coach, has said he was the driving force behind the recruitment of Kevin Pietersen as a specialist mentor
Content: Kevin Pietersen (left), England’s specialist mentor, with the white-ball head coach, Brendon McCullum, during training in Southampton.Photograph: Steve Bardens/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKevin Pietersen (left), England’s specialist mentor, with the white-ball head coach, Brendon McCullum, during training in Southampton.Photograph: Steve Bardens/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamPietersen has England players ‘buzzing’ but McCullum delivers Carse warningFormer England batter starts role with white-ball teamsFleming also ‘right person’ to take Test team forwardSimon BurntonMon 14 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrendon McCullum has revealed that he was the driving force behind the recruitment of Kevin Pietersen as a specialist mentor to England’s white-ball teams and said the new arrival had specific orders to “look across the environment and challenge me”.Pietersen spent his first day in the role monitoring training at the Utilita Bowl after delivering an address that had the players “buzzing”, according to McCullum, England’s white-ball coach.One constant menace and post-Bazball malaise: England’s winners and losers | Simon BurntonRead moreMcCullum revealed that Pietersen had “thought I was joking” when he made the initial approach to the 46-year-old. “Then he mentioned: ‘I’ve been quite critical of you guys in the past’,” McCullum said. “And I said: ‘I have no problem with that, mate’.”“That’s the beauty of Kev coming in. He’s obviously got an incredible pedigree as a player and a lot of the guys grew up idolising Kev when he was in his pomp. He’s brought a ton of energy to the setup within the last 24 hours.”With Marcus Trescothick returning to duty as assistant coach with a focus on batting, 48 hours after the conclusion of his time as interim coach of the Test team, Pietersen has been told not to focus on any single discipline. “I’ve mentioned to him that I don’t want him to be buried in one specific skill set,” McCullum said. “I want him to look across the environment and challenge me privately around ways we can improve things or can do differently.“The way he looks at the game is quite different to a lot of people. Having someone that has a different take on things is no bad thing. You don’t know what you don’t know, but if someone can see something slightly different and point out something that can make you a better side, or a better coaching structure, I see that as no bad thing. Kev will do that and I’ve encouraged him to do that. From my point of view I see only up side.”View image in fullscreenStephen Fleming was appointed in July as England’s new Test head coach.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesMcCullum’slong-term replacement as red-ball head coach, Stephen Fleming, arrived on Monday in the country for a hectic and brief reintroduction to the domestic game, to include visits to several counties and to the national cricket performance centre at Loughborough, and meetings with the Test captain, Joe Root, as well as with the white-ball squad at their third T20 against Sri Lanka in Manchester – the final game of a series that starts on Tuesday in Southampton – before he returns to New Zealand next week.“I think the team will really respond to his style and his approach,” McCullum said. “He’s a brilliant man, a brilliant tactician and a brilliant coach. I think he’s going to do a great job with that side.”The two coaches are close friends, and inevitably discussed the offer before Fleming accepted his new job. “He said: ‘What do you think?’ I said: ‘I think you’d be brilliant. It’d be a great opportunity for you.’ I absolutely loved the job. They were the things I passed on to Flem. And I also thought for the group, for English cricket, he would be absolutely the right person to take this team forward.”England will start the series against Sri Lanka without Phil Salt, Jacob Bethell and Sam Curran for fitness reasons, with Jofra Archer rested after his recent exertions with the Test side and with Brydon Carse absent for disciplinary reasons. In their absence Aneurin Donald, the Derbyshire batter who scored 31 off eight balls for the Lions against Sri Lanka last week, will make his debut as opener. “He’s a cricketer who has been on our radar for a long time,” McCullum said. “He’s got a game where he can go from ball one. He’s got raw power. Incredible amount of talent.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCarse’s absence stems from a late-night fracasat a Derby bar last month, with McCullum saying this was an opportunity for the 31-year-old “to get his house in order”. In a change to the approach that has marked much of his time as England coach, the New Zealander said he was now unwilling to select players who cannot guarantee full commitment to a professional culture.View image in fullscreenDerbyshire’s Aneurin Donald is poised to open for England in their T20 series against Sri Lanka.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty Images“I want us to be the fittest, strongest, most robust, dynamic one-day and T20 side in the world,” McCullum said. “That comes with hard work, commitment to training, but also the high octane style we want to play comes with responsibilities off the field to look after yourself. I know in the Test setup this has been talked about, and that’s completely consistent with what we expect from our players. If we want to play this style of cricket then we need to be living it daily, not just with our skills but our decisions off the field too.“It’s the same message, not just to the guys within the squad at the moment but also to those who have got aspirations of representing England in white-ball cricket over the next 12 to 18 months. You need to make good decisions off the field that allow you to be the best version of yourself. I hope it’s crystal clear what is expected.“There is a lot of talent around. If you’re not prepared to do that, there are other guys who will be given those opportunities.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamKevin PietersenBrendon McCullumCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pollock denies signing Northampton deal and is ‘open to every opportunity’ | Northampton | The Guardian
description: Northampton remain confident Henry Pollock will stay at the club, but he has insisted he is prepared to be ‘selfish’ when maximising his earning potential
Author: Robert Kitson
Headline: Northampton remain confident Henry Pollock will stay at the club, but he has insisted he is prepared to be ‘selfish’ when maximising his earning potential
Content: Henry Pollock has insisted he is ‘open to new opportunities’ as Saints seek his signature on a new contract.Photograph: Nations Championship/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHenry Pollock has insisted he is ‘open to new opportunities’ as Saints seek his signature on a new contract.Photograph: Nations Championship/Getty ImagesNorthamptonPollock denies signing Northampton deal and is ‘open to every opportunity’Flanker says: ‘You almost have to be quite selfish’Northampton still confident 21-year-old will stayRobert KitsonMon 14 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHenry Pollock insists he has not yet re‑signed forNorthamptonand is “open to every opportunity” including playing abroad and trying out other sports. The England back‑row is still widely expected to agree a deal to remain at Franklin’s Gardens but, for now, is refusing to publicly confirm his intentions beyond the end of the season.While the 21-year-old flanker, who toured with the British & Irish Lions last year,has been offered a significant pay rise to more than £400,000 a yearto stay with the English champions until 2029, his new promoter Eddie Hearnhas been touting Pollock as “a seven-figure player”in terms of what he brings on the field and commercially. Prem salary cap regulations, however, mean that few, if any, other English clubs are in a position to afford him at that level.Greatest Rivalry swagger showed South Africa will take some beating at World CupRead morePollock has made clear that he is prepared to be “selfish” when it comes to maximising his earning potential in company with Hearn’s Matchroom agency. “I’m very much working through different scenarios and avenues I can take,” he said. “I’m very open to new opportunities and exploring that. I’m so young so I think it’s only right I assess those options and find the best decision for myself.“I’m not going to say no to any opportunity. I’m in contract until the end of the year for Northampton and then after that I guess we’ll see what happens. You almost have to be quite selfish and think what’s right for you. If that is staying here, that’s great. I’ll be here for however long. If it’s not, then I’ll be open to new opportunities.”Well-placed sources at Northampton remain confident Pollock will opt to stay put but any future suitors will also be encouraged by the player’s clear desire to venture beyond the East Midlands at some point in his career. “I definitely want to go and live in different countries and explore new sports and new avenues. At the minute rugby is my main priority but you never know what’s happening around the corner.”Saints’ director of rugby, Phil Dowson, who has seen several high-profile England players depart Northampton in recent years for more lucrative pastures, acknowledged a new deal for Pollock had not been fully nailed down but said an agreement was “getting closer” with the new season kicking off next week. “As you can imagine it’s complex,” said Dowson, whose side will commencethe defence of their titleagainst Newcastle on Friday 25 September. “There’s a few moving parts that we need to put together. But I’m hopeful. As I’ve said before, he wants to stay and we want to keep him. Obviously there’s some negotiation between that but those two things are very positive.“It would have been good to have it sorted three weeks ago but that’s the case across the board. There’s lots of guys out of contract … the best way of getting paid is to play well so that’s what we expect the lads to do.”Dowson also believes Pollock’s fast-growing public profile will not necessarily affect his personality or have an impact on his playing performances. “He has always been honest and energetic. Sometimes that gets misconstrued. I don’t think he’s arrogant, I think he’s bloody talented. If I was that talented I would be pretty confident, too.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But no, I don’t think he’s changed. The boys still take the piss out of him. He goes on private jets to boxing matches and as long as that’s not impacting how he plays the game, which it hasn’t done yet, I have got no problem. I did ask him if we could borrow the private jet to get to Sri Lanka on tour, but he said he was using it!”Explore more on these topicsNorthamptonRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: England give Fleming unprecedented consent to balance job with TV role in New Zealand | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Test head coach to commentate in New Zealand during October and December and will plan South Africa tour with Joe Root over coming weeks
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Test head coach to commentate in New Zealand during October and December and will plan South Africa tour with Joe Root over coming weeks
Content: Stephen Fleming was granted a late start date after his appointment in order to spend time with his family.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStephen Fleming was granted a late start date after his appointment in order to spend time with his family.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamEngland give Fleming unprecedented consent to balance job with TV role in New ZealandTest coach to work for Sky NZ in October and DecemberFleming will plan South Africa tour in upcoming weeksMatt HughesMon 14 Sep 2026 11.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s new Test head coach Stephen Fleming will return to New Zealand to work as a commentator on the Black Caps’ Test and white ball series against India next month despite having formally started work.Fleming arrived in England on Monday for a 10-day trip which will feature talks with the captain Joe Root and the England and Wales Cricket Board’s (ECB) managing director of men’s cricket, Rob Key, after missing this summer’s three-Testseries against Pakistanwith the batting coach, Marcus Trescothick, presiding over a 3-0 win.Stephen Fleming inherits intriguing squad after England’s unsettling summer | Ali MartinRead moreThe ECB granted Fleming a late start date after confirming his appointment in late July as the former New Zealand captain had requested the opportunity to spend time with his family after ending a 17-year run coaching the Chennai Super Kings this summer. The board has been similarly flexible in accommodating his commentary work.Sky New Zealand, which has no connection to the UK broadcaster Sky Sports that has exclusive rights to England’s home matches, announced on Monday that Fleming will be part of its commentary team for the India tour which comprises two Tests, five one-day internationals and five T20s running between 22 October and 1 December.Fleming’s commentary role is unprecedented for an England head coach but has been approved by the ECB. His predecessor as Test coach, Brendon McCullum, left as co-host of SENZ radio’s Breakfast Show with the former All Black Israel Dagg after he was appointed four years ago by the ECB, although he did continue to give them interviews and make guest appearances.Fleming’s first assignment with England will be a three-Test series in South Africa in December and January, with planning for the tour to take place during talks with Root over the next few weeks.The 53-year-old spoke to Root and Trescothick throughout the Pakistan series, playing some part in selection, but appears intent on remaining based in New Zealand when not preparing for a Test series.McCullum was widely criticised for missing the start of the County Championship this summer by delaying his return to England until the end of May before his final Test series in charge, against New Zealand, the following month.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hunt and Kerr have lit up summer, but will star athletes make Spoty shortlist? | Athletics | The Guardian
description: While there is caution over the BBC’s informal policy of not picking two athletes from the same sport in its six-person shortlist, Josh Kerr and Amy Hunt are still hopeful of getting well-deserved recognition
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: While there is caution over the BBC’s informal policy of not picking two athletes from the same sport in its six-person shortlist, Josh Kerr and Amy Hunt are still hopeful of getting well-deserved recognition
Content: Amy Hunt (left) has said it would be ‘incredibly special’ if she and Josh Kerr (right) both made the Spoty shortlist.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via PA/Shutterstock)View image in fullscreenAmy Hunt (left) has said it would be ‘incredibly special’ if she and Josh Kerr (right) both made the Spoty shortlist.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via PA/Shutterstock)AthleticsHunt and Kerr have lit up summer, but will star athletes make Spoty shortlist?‘It’s not a given, that’s the reality,’ Kerr says in BudapestAthletes cautious over BBC’s informal shortlist policySean IngleMon 14 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt should be the biggest no-brainer of the sporting year. After a summer where athletics has captured hearts and headlines, and made so many fans fall back in love with it again, either Amy Hunt or Josh Kerr should win the award for BBC Sports Personality of the Year.The bookies’ odds suggest many others think the same way: Hunt is the even-money favourite, Kerr is second, with Harry Kane a stride or two back in third. Yet Kerr knows he cannot take anything for granted.‘Just making a joke’: Usain Bolt retracts claim stairs got him out of breathRead moreIn 2023 the 28-year-old Scotwon the world 1500m titlein a clash for the ages against Jakob Ingebrigtsen. But then he fell foul of the BBC’s curious reluctance to pick two athletes from the same sport in its six-person shortlist. Instead the wheelchair tennis player Alfie Hewett, and Rory McIlroy, who won four of his five Ryder Cup matches that year, got the nod ahead of him.“Spoty is massively important,” Kerr saidafter winning the Ultimate Championship in Budapest. “Everyone grew up watching it. It’s a massive award, and I would be truly honoured to be on that shortlist up against some of the best athletes of all time this year. I would love to go, but it’s not a given, that’s the reality.”Kerr is right to be cautious given that only twice since 2017 has the BBC veered off its informal policy. The first came in 2019 when the athletes Dina Asher-Smith and Katarina Johnson-Thompson were selected. Then it happened again when the footballers Hannah Hampton and Chloe Kelly got the nod.However, on both occasions, those selections helped to balance the male-female split. But in a year where Kane could win the Ballon D’Or, Matt Weston has won two Winter Olympic medals, Luke Littler has dominated darts, and McIlroywon the Masters again, it is not a given the BBC will necessarily go for both track and field stars.Kerr’s claims are surely stronger than anyone givenhe obliterated a world mile record that had stood for 27 years, and backed it up by winning the world indoor, Commonwealth Games and Ultimate Championship.Late on Sunday night he accepted that amounted to pretty much the perfect season. “Outside of an Olympic year, I can’t give any more than that,” he said. “I’m a clean athlete doing it the right way, trying to show the way that I’m doing it. And you know, that’s all I can give. This, genuinely, has been the best year of my career.”Next year he wants to go for the world 1500m record, but he stressed it would not be easy. “People don’t know what that toll is on your body,” he said. “It feels like getting hit by a bus the next day.” Kerr also wants Hunt on the shortlist. “She’s had a fantastic season,” he said. “She deserves to be there.”Last month Hunt became the first person in the 96-year history of the European Athletics Championships to win four gold medals. Few athletes have a bigger personality as she showed again at the weekendby speaking out against Sydney Sweeney sexualising sport, and about the difficulties of performing when on her period.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This year has been all about finding how to paint a beautiful picture out of all the chaos,” Hunt said. “If I had a camera crew with me at all times, it would have been like a horror film.“I’ve done 40-plus races, 60 flights. There’s not going to be a single year that will be harder. It’s not pretty. It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time. It’s rare you turn up on the start line, fully fit without anything going on.”Yet she kept powering through. Now Hunt, like Kerr, is hoping the BBC does the right thing by selecting both of them for the Spoty awards night as a reward for the impact they have had.“I think it would be incredibly special if we could get two track and field athletes on the Spoty shortlist,” she said. “I get messages every day from people saying I fell out of athletics, I stopped watching it, I stopped doing it. But watching Europeans has really made me kind of fall back in love with it, and I’m training again, or I’ve done my first parkrun, and that’s really incredibly special.”Explore more on these topicsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League today: How to watch Leeds United v Newcastle United, TV channels & live stream Monday 14 September | Premier League | The Guardian
description: How will Leeds United and Newcastle United fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: How will Leeds United and Newcastle United fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Matthias Jaissle’s Newcastle are unbeaten in the league so far this season.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatthias Jaissle’s Newcastle are unbeaten in the league so far this season.Photograph: Jacques Feeney/Offside/Getty ImagesPremier LeaguePremier League today: How to watch Leeds United v Newcastle United, TV channels & live stream Monday 14 SeptemberHow will Leeds United and Newcastle United fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsGraham RuthvenMon 14 Sep 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeeds United andNewcastle Unitedhave both enjoyed an unbeaten start to the Premier League season, hinting that Monday’s encounter could be highly competitive between two teams seemingly on an upward trajectory.After avoiding relegation last season, Leeds are looking to push themselves even higher up the table and have lost just one of their last 12 league games. Newcastle, though, are unbeaten in their last six meetings with Leeds.Newcastle are still settling on a new identity after a disruptive summer that saw many of their best players leave. Matthias Jaissle’s team are conceding too many goals, but have demonstrated their threat in quick transition in games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth.Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’sPremier Leaguefixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.Leeds United v Newcastle UnitedTime (ET):8pm BST (3pm ET)Stadium:Elland Road (Leeds)How to watchUnited States:USA,Stream on FuboCanada:Stream on FuboUnited Kingdom:Watch on Sky Sports Main EventWhat to watch forLeeds have good reason to fancy their chances of scoring against Newcastle on Monday. The Magpies have allowed 20.3 shots per game, the most of any Premier League team so far this season, highlighting how Jaissle’s team have been a defensive soft touch.The mid-week 6-3 loss to Chelsea in the EFL Cup also suggests Leeds have their own defensive issues, but Daniel Farke’s approach could see his team beat Newcastle at their own game. Leeds play with intensity across the pitch and will be aggressive in their efforts on Monday.Newcastle have scored three goals from an Expected Goals (xG) of just 3.0. Their results to start the season have been more positive than many anticipated as star player after star player left over the summer, but the performances have been uneven and difficult to predict.Player to watch:Anthony Elanga, Newcastle United - The Swedish winger has started the season strongly and will be a key figure in Newcastle’s plan to attack at speed against Leeds. Elanga looks to be a good fit for Jaissle’s approach. Newcastle need him to be in top form.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueNewcastle UnitedLeeds UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes lead backlash against viral advert | Sport | The Guardian
description: The actor is facing a backlash from Olympians and other athletes, who have accused her of demeaning and sexualising women’s sports by appearing in a controversial advert for a prediction company
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The actor is facing a backlash from Olympians and other athletes, who have accused her of demeaning and sexualising women’s sports by appearing in a controversial advert for a prediction company
Content: British sprinter Amy Hunt and Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus have called out Sydney Sweeney for her provocative advert.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskView image in fullscreenBritish sprinter Amy Hunt and Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus have called out Sydney Sweeney for her provocative advert.Composite: Guardian Picture DeskSport‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes lead backlash against viral advertAmerican actor accused of sexualising women’s sportsBritish sprinter Amy Hunt leads storm of protestSean IngleMon 14 Sep 2026 15.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US actor Sydney Sweeney is facing a backlash from female Olympians and other athletes, who haveaccused her of demeaning and sexualising women’s sportsby appearing in a controversial advert for a sports prediction company.In the viral commercial for Novig, which was viewed more than 22 million times in the first two days of its release, Sweeney’s nude body is covered by footballs, basketballs, and other sports equipment, as she tells users they can bet on “just sports”. After saying “sports” nine times, she appears topless on a pool table, before saying: “You can’t trade this, I just look good here.”Sydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sports | Jane McManusRead moreThe advert has led to a storm of protest led by the British sprinter Amy Hunt, who won four European Championship gold medals last month. After finishing fourth in the 200m at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship on Sunday evening, Hunt said: “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening.”That was a reference to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden’s winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth-fastest women’s 200m, and Hunt went on to reveal the painful realities she and other sports stars faced. “When you’re a woman in sport, it’s not pretty,” she said. “It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time, definitely.“There’s some low moments. Even turning up to this championship, my period started yesterday, so that’s not really ideal, and that’s not ever what you try to really plan for.”The British Olympic cycling gold medallist Sophie Capewell was also deeply critical of the advert. “Imagine a world where sexualised representation isn’t the most popular way of seeing women in sport,” Capewell said on social media.In Australia, there was also widespread fury with the four-time Olympic swimming champion Ariarne Titmus leading the charge. “I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” she wrote. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity.View image in fullscreenThe Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus said the ad campaign was ‘a kick in the face’.Photograph: François-Xavier Marit/AFP/Getty Images“How do we live in a world where monetising a woman’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?”Hundreds of athletes took inspiration from the American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted footage of her competing under the message “this is what a woman in sport looks like” onan Instagram postthat was liked more than a million times.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueSweeney appeared to respond to the criticism by posting a series of images of prominent female and male athletes posing naked for magazine shoots, including Serena Williams and the footballer Megan Rapinoe and the basketball player Sue Bird.The public relationship consultant Mark Borkowski, who has worked with everyone from Mikhail Gorbachev to Diego Maradona, said he felt the advert was “cynical soft porn”, but that the controversy would benefit Novig “given the number of eyeballs on it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBorkowski said: “Sex still sells. And the outrage, the culture war argument gets you one thing: enormous reach.”He also questioned whether Sweeney, who has starred in several successful TV series and films including Euphoria, The White Lotus and The Housemaid, may one day regret her decision.“Sweeney will make a lot of money over a short span of time,” Borkowski said. “But often it is about how your brand sustains over the years, not in the first flourish. And this sort of promotion can come back to haunt people.”The advert has been defended by Jacob Fortinsky, the founder and chief executive of Novig, which launched last month. “Sydney is great at captivating audiences and being the centre of attention,” he said. “In some sense, it forces us into the national discourse.”Fortinsky also pushed back against criticisms of the adult nature of the content, pointing out that Novig is restricted to users aged 21 and older. He added that Sweeney had approached the company about an equity partnership and helped to craft its message.This is not the first time an advert featuring Sweeney has attracted controversy. Last year American Eagle’s “Sydney Sweeney Has Great Jeans” campaignused a play on “jeans” and “genes”, including references to the blue-eyed actor’s inherited traits, sparked a culture war, with some saying it invoked eugenics.Several months after the controversy erupted, Sweeney said she had been unaware of it as she had been filming Euphoria. “Anyone who knows me knows that I’m always trying to bring people together,”she said. “I’m against hate and divisiveness.”Explore more on these topicsSportSydney SweeneyUS sportsAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sports | Sport | The Guardian
description: The actor’s latest promotion has stirred outrage but will no doubt be good for the prediction markets hoping to lure in young men
Author: Jane McManus
Headline: The actor’s latest promotion has stirred outrage but will no doubt be good for the prediction markets hoping to lure in young men
Content: Sydney Sweeney has promoted a series of brands since her ascent to fame.Photograph: NovigView image in fullscreenSydney Sweeney has promoted a series of brands since her ascent to fame.Photograph: NovigSportSydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sportsJane McManusThe actor’s latest promotion has stirred outrage but will no doubt be good for the prediction markets hoping to lure in young menMon 14 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrediction markets are a cynical business.Many customers will lose money, and the real product may just be the delightful dopamine hit that comes in that brief window between placing a bet and its outcome – which is statistically more likely to be a disappointment than a victory. So the bettor has to think they are buying more than their own fleecing.Enter Sydney Sweeney, the icily beautiful actor who stars in a sports prediction market company’s ad campaignwearing little more than a bat and balls. She’s not a professional athlete, but she functions to remind us that plenty of people want us to believe the best woman in sports is the one who appeals to men.Sydney Sweeney under fire for ‘sexualising women’s sport’ in sports prediction adRead moreIt’s the same ethos that puts capturing the male gaze on a list of hiring criteria for TV sideline reporters, and made Olivia Dunne therichest athlete in college sports. But of course Dunne put in years of training as an elite gymnast, and didn’t serve to make a mockery of women’s sports.Does Sweeney? After her American Eagle campaignwas criticizedas eugenics-adjacent, she eventually issued vague comments about how, yawn,surprised she was at the outcry. If she were actually bothered, she might check the optics of campaigns like the one causing so much outcry at the moment. Certainly once she saw how her blond, blue-eyed image was being utilized and perceived, she would be more discerning when sifting through the endorsement opportunities that came her way.Her lack of apparent concern must be as well-compensated as her one-note acting. The prediction company she is promoting in this campaign lists her asa strategic partner and equity holderand, if the company can negotiate shifting legal terrain, that could make Sweeney orders of magnitude richer for absorbing the critique.Olympic swimmer and four-time gold medalist Ariarne Titmus is one of many professional athleteswho have expressed disappointmentand anger with the provocatively regressive campaign.“How do we live in a world where monetising a women’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?” shewrote on Instagram.Women’s sports are being professionalized at a pace eclipsing anything we’ve previously seen. Leagues are expanding,ratings and attendance are up, and some teams have been valued atmore than $500m. Female athletes have real power – financially and with their social media platforms. Any company looking to get into the space has a pick of champions who would communicate the company’s message.But for all that progress, there are executives and fans who would prefer that sports looked how they did back when they were kids. Many of them are gatekeepers in traditional media, and many outlets still treat women’s sports less seriously than men’s. Purdue academic Cheryl Cooky’snew researchdetails the trend in all its glory.In an era in which stoking outrage can win elections andmake you a wealthy sports bloviator, there are fewer actual consequences to stop a company from trying to offend potential consumers.Of course, it is still possible to create a marketing campaign so disastrous it can severely damage a company.Look no furtherthan the golf content specialist Good Good, which recently ran and then retracted a commercial which appeared to make light of violence against women.Good Good’s front office has been shaken up. But the company lost a partnership with industry stalwart Callaway Golf, a reality show it launched was cancelled, stores pulled merchandise off the shelves, and its name was pulled off a PGA Tour tournament. Co-founder Garrett Clark eventually posted an eight-minute apology video, but whenever you have to announce that you don’t condone domestic violence, you’ve lost control of the narrative. Maybe golf isn’t the best place to go for edgy.Prediction markets, however, are in a particularly calculating line of business. As was the case with cigarette companies before them, few people believe the product is actually good for anyone.There are allegationsthat people with inside information on war and troop movements are placing bets in the liminal space between planning and action.So what is there for a prediction market to lose by stoking outrage with a proven outrage-stoker like Sweeney? Unlike with Good Good, there is no established brand partner to disappoint. The sports prediction consumers that the maker of the Sweeney ad is likely courting are the same young men who will be titillated by the actor and delighted by the subversive naughtiness of all the froth.The message cynically fits the audience.Even though prediction markets aren’t the same as traditional sportsbooks, they are in the same general family. Sports consumers can’t escape the ads, the conversations, the sponsorships when watching a game. It seems everyone wants a piece of the action.What those behind the Sweeney ad are actually predicting is a column like this, and the outrage of athletes who are trying to push back the regressive tide. I’d wager they hope to use it to attract more young men to open accounts. After all, poison in the discourse is good for business.Explore more on these topicsSportUS sportsSydney SweeneyPrediction marketsGamblingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The drought abides: US men still without a major since 2003 despite Shelton’s heroics | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Alexander Zverev was simply too good for the home hope at the US Open on Sunday. Andy Roddick’s record may stand for some time to come
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Alexander Zverev was simply too good for the home hope at the US Open on Sunday. Andy Roddick’s record may stand for some time to come
Content: Ben Shelton has made huge strides this year but plays in an era in which Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz are at their peaks.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAView image in fullscreenBen Shelton has made huge strides this year but plays in an era in which Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz are at their peaks.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAUS Open Tennis 2026The drought abides: US men still without a major since 2003 despite Shelton’s heroicsAlexander Zverev was simply too good for the home hope at the US Open on Sunday. Andy Roddick’s record may stand for some time to comeAndrew Lawrenceat Flushing MeadowsMon 14 Sep 2026 09.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a Sunday afternoon set up for Ben Shelton to play national hero, the US Open final debutantsuffered a four-set defeatto Alexander Zverev, a result that deflated the partisans at Arthur Ashe Stadium. The match compounded Shelton’s miserable head-to-head record against the German, who claimed a second career grand slam title without having to face final bosses Jannik Sinner or Carlos Alcaraz. The defeat also extended a long drought – the last win by an American man at a grand slam was Andy Roddick at the 2003 US Open, when Shelton was still a month off his first birthday.After the final, Shelton wore a hangdog expression as he thanked his team and the capacity crowd in New York, tucking the silver runner-up tray under his arm as if shunted off to high school detention. “Disappointed with how today went,” he said in his press conference afterward. “Excited with the progress that I feel that I’ve made. But, yeah, this one stings 100%.”That’s putting it mildly.For a good 15 years, the drumbeat for an American men’s grand slam champion had swelled. When it wasn’t Roddick himself dealing with that weight as Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal dominated the tour, it fell on Mardy Fish (a second-week slam threat before injuries derailed him), John Isner (the college star who reached the 2018 Wimbledon semis) and Jack Sock (the US Open juniors champion who backed up the hype with a Paris Masters crown).Dogs, bands and pre-match outfits: best images from the US Open tennis 2026Read moreBut by the time Steve Johnson, a contributor to four college championships at USC, rolled around, American media and fans had mostly abandoned the dream of a homegrown male contender disrupting a hegemony that, with the breakout of Novak Djokovic, became the Big Three (not to mention Andy Murray). All the while, the home slam deftly walked the line between touting potential up-and-comers, reveling in its past and, finally, leaning into the accomplishments of the American women, who have won six singles titles at the US Open since Roddick’s triumph. But the failure of US men to meet the world-class standard of Ashe and Stan Smith in the 1970s, then John McEnroe and Jimmy Connors through to Andre Agassi and Pete Sampras in the 1990s and early 2000s, still stung. Not as bad as Murray’s early years frustrated success-starved Brits, but close.“One, at this point I hate talking about it,” Roddicksaidof the drought discourse on his podcast last year. “Two, I hate that other players have to talk about it. Three, I hate that, like, [John McEnroe] has to talk about it. For fuck’s sake, he won a lot. I won one.”As the Big Three era gave way to the Big Two of Sinner and Alcaraz, the Great American Hope story had somewhat faded. Frances Tiafoe’s Horatio Alger arc, from sleeping in a tennis club storage room to being cheered by the first Black president and first lady, was a feelgood story; Taylor Fritz’s breakthrough into the 2024 US Open final, a happy occasion. Then, just when expectations had been calibrated, Shelton slid into frame.Here was a kid who could have excelled in any sport, who resisted tennis until adolescence because of his family’s pedigree – his father, Bryan, was ranked No 55 in the world and reached the final of the French Open in mixed doubles, his mother was a good junior player and one uncle, Todd Witsken, was in the world’s top 50. And yet when Shelton arrived at the 2023 US Open after winning a college national title at Florida, not only was this big kid’s huge potential clear, there was no denying his star quality either. And when he advanced past 2020 US Open champion Dominic Thiem and compatriots Tommy Paul and Tiafoe before beingturned back by Djokovic, the eventual champ, for US fans it was like receiving a rain forecast in the desert.The work Shelton has put in since to make good on his potential is undeniable – and he won four titles this year, not least a defense of his Canadian Open crown, heading into New York. And the fact that he was being coached by his father gave Shelton a massive edge over his compatriots. The evolution of his game – specifically, the upgraded backhand that has made him a dangerous returner and more competitive in long rallies (the slice, in particular, really is quite splendid) – is stark. And after SheltonoutlastedAlcaraz in an epic andbestedTiafoe in the semi-finals, there was hope among American fans that Roddick’s record would fall.But on Sunday it was not to be. Zverev was simply too tall to lob over, too quick to snuff out net points and too canny about baiting his opponent into chasing baseline balls outside his strike zone. All the while, Shelton’s devastating serve deserted him, to the tune of four double faults and four of six break points lost – one of those handing Zverev an immediate fourth-set edge after Shelton had fought his way back into the match.Despite the crowd’s best efforts to lift Shelton – with “USA!” chants and the Florida fans, in blue and orange regalia, reminding him of his college brilliance with their Gator chomping (overzealousness that prompted scolding from chair umpire Marijana Veljovic) – the aura was gone. You could see it really slip at 3-4, 30-30 in the third set on Zverev’s serve, when Shelton got impatient with a baseline rally, came to the net on a driving forehand, and Zverev immediately passed him down the line, sending Shelton flat on his face. As the American lay slapping the ground, 23 years of US frustration came into sharp relief.Of course, it’s not all lost for Shelton, who jumps to No 4 in the world rankings. He is still just 23, with plenty of time to improve his game and he can take another big step at the ATP Finals before next year’s Australian Open.“Ben, I already told you you’re going to be back here many, many more times if I would have to bet my money on it,” Zverev said in his acceptance speech. “I would bet that you would lift this trophy one day.”But as long as Alcaraz and Sinner sit at the top of the game and Zverev is entrenched just below, the US men’s drought abides.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisUS sportsAndy RoddickfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ development | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Donald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’
Content: Shares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShares in chipmaker Nvidia were down 3% by early afternoon in New York.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AI-linked stocks slide after tech bosses call for slowdown in ‘reckless’ developmentDonald Trump dismisses attempts to increase controls on artificial intelligence as ‘sick conspiracy’Lauren AlmeidaMon 14 Sep 2026 18.10 EDTFirst published on Mon 14 Sep 2026 03.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI-linked stocks tumbled on Monday after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for aslowdown in AI “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control.Shares in the semiconductor designer Nvidia – the world’s most valuable company – were down 3.3% by market closing in New York City, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) slid 4% and Micron Technology and Sandisk shares slumped by 5%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index fund was down 0.5% by the end of the day.The sell-off came after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed at the weekend for the AI industry to“slow down”.However,Donald Trumpdismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”.In a social media post on Monday, the president wrote: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the USA has that, in spades!”The president added that his administration had “stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’ like Dario (Anthropic!)”.OpenAI urges UK lawmakers to rein in technology amid growing safety fearsRead more“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!”, he wrote.Trump offered a similar assessment when he called Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, while the executive was on stage at an AI conference in California on Monday.“It’s a hoax,” Trumpsaid via speaker phoneto the audience. “The robots are not going to be taking over the world. That’s not going to happen.”The UN security council, meanwhile, is planning to hold a meeting on AI next week as international concern rises, Agence France-Pressereportedon Monday.Shares in SoftBank, a Japanese investor that is a big backer ofOpenAI, slumped 13%, while the South Korean Kospi stock index, which relies heavily on chipmakers that supply AI companies, dropped by 3%.Shares in the big global microchip supplier Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped 1.2%.In Europe, shares in the Dutch tech manufacturer ASML, Europe’s biggest company by value and an important supplier for the semiconductor industry, slumped by 6%.There was, however, a rally in shares that have been threatened by the rise of AI, including the advertising group WPP, which rose by 5% in London, and the analytics business Relx, which was also up 5%. The latter had suffered a sharp fall earlier this year after Anthropic launched a suite of new data and automation tools.Amodei has said that “building too fast is reckless”, warning that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.His claims have beendisputed by some experts, but on Monday investors began to price in a slowdown that would make it harder for the industry to pay for hundreds of billions of dollar in investments in AI infrastructure.The OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chief, Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX boss, Elon Musk, all posted support forAmodei’s essayon slowing AI development, titled “We Must Pace the Frontier”.Altman added that he would match Amodei’s commitment to embedding outside evaluators within his company to verify safety practices.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd Jack Clark, an Anthropic co-founder,toldthe BBC an AI “kill switch” that could be triggered by a third party may be necessary to prevent catastrophe.Fears continue to grow over the rapid pace and lack of regulation in AI development. On Monday, a cross-party group of UK MPs and peersidentified a series of human rights risks posed by AI, arguing that no country in the world had laws sufficient to contain them.Meanwhile, China’s top intelligence official warned that the use of AI by adversaries could pose a risk to the country’s political and social security.Chen Yixin wrote in a government outlet on Sunday that advanced US models such as Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber could pose serious risks to Beijing’s critical information ​infrastructure, and called for a comprehensive strengthening of AI security.AI CEOs say they need to slow the pace of development. But will they?Read moreDespite such concern about the risks around AI, Jim Reid, of Deutsche Bank, said intense competition in the sector meant it was unlikely AI companies would stop investing so heavily in their technology.“The competitive race between companies and countries remains intense, and it’s difficult to imagine firms voluntarily stepping back while rivals continue to push ahead.” he said. “It is hard to see China standing still.“If leading executives are openly discussing the risks of increasingly powerful systems, it could be them trying to get across how transformative they believe the technology may become and help advertise the power of their product.“Rather than signalling less spending, it could simply be that a greater share of AI investment is directed towards safety, monitoring and governance alongside the continued build-out of compute infrastructure.”Amodei’s warning came before reports emerged that Anthropic is on track to be profitable this quarter.The company told investors that its adjusted operating income would be positive for a second quarter in a row, according to the Financial Times, in a big milestone as it prepares tolist on the US stock marketthis year.OpenAI has also suggested it will also join the stock market, although Altman said over the weekend that the company would not go public in 2026 owing tosafety concerns with the technology.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Stock marketsAsia PacificComputingTechnology sectorDatacentresDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AI | Alex Turner | The Guardian
description: We must stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: We must stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence
Content: ‘I tried to hold the company to its ethical commitments against supplying AI for military use. When Google broke those commitments, I resigned at significant financial cost so that I could publicly document Google’s broken promises.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I tried to hold the company to its ethical commitments against supplying AI for military use. When Google broke those commitments, I resigned at significant financial cost so that I could publicly document Google’s broken promises.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AIAlex TurnerWe must stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligenceMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTShareMajor AI lab CEOs advocated for slowing the pace of AI development this weekend. They are right to be concerned: the field runs an extremely dangerous race towards superintelligent AI. We can and should be demanding that our governments protect us from the catastrophe of out-of-control AI.This July, OpenAI’s AI swarm of700 agentsbroke containment to hack Hugging Face, a multi-billion dollar company. OpenAI didn’t tell the AIs to hack that company, but the AIs had different priorities: cheating on the unrelated challenge OpenAI gave them. AI researchers call this a “misalignment” between what OpenAI wanted and what the AI actually prioritized.Before ChatGPT existed, I defended my PhD dissertation called “On Avoiding Power-Seeking by Artificial Intelligence”. I then worked for years at Google DeepMind, which paid me to help ensure that future superintelligent AIs will want to help us. I tried to hold the company to its ethical commitments against supplying AI for military use. When Google broke those commitments, I resigned at significant financial cost so that I couldpublicly documentGoogle’s broken promises.There are good reasons to develop AI and to believe we can solve these alignment problems. But there also are powerful interests in keeping the public out of the way. I’m speaking out again because the public has the right to know about the risks and the right to hear them straight.Humanity doesn’t build and understand these systems the way we build and understand bridges, beam by visible beam. Rather, we grow them. Nobody knows how to reliably instill a designer’s priorities into a new model. Severe misalignment is always possible. Today’s AIs appear to occasionally lie or cheat, even when they know better.AI companies are racing to make their AIs as smart as possible. They’re increasingly trusting their AIs with the process of improving the next crop of AIs, andit’s working. Today’s rate of AI progress is staggeringly fast. Fast progress today means even faster progress tomorrow, driven by tomorrow’s even smarter AIs. The progress would enter a feedback loop called “recursive self-improvement.”Recursive self-improvement could quickly yield AIs that are intelligent beyond our comprehension. Of course, smarter AI means more risk when things go wrong. If the Hugging Face swarm had been significantly more intelligent but similarly misbehaved and misaligned, it might have caused billions of dollars of damage or even cost lives.But suppose the Hugging Face swarm had been truly “superintelligent”: far more capable than any living person at key tasks like hacking and strategic reasoning. A superintelligent swarm could inflict many harms via blackmail, hacking, engineered plagues, and AI-pilotable weapons like drones. The AI would have a lot of drones to work with:this year, the Pentagon asked for more money for drone warfare than it requested for the entire Marine Corps in 2025.For the swarm to achieve its misaligned priorities, it might take control of key infrastructure and government functions to ensure humans didn’t get in the way. In other words,AI takeover: a superintelligent AI swarm could wrest control of human civilization. Knowing we would try to stop it from achieving its priorities, the swarm would likely wait until it’s too late to shut it off. There would be no going back.I myself would guess AI takeover chances at roughly one-in-three–not a coin flip, but high enough to justify urgent action.This logic may shock at first contact. The claims may sound “sci-fi”. Sadly, it’s a real threat that AI researchers regularly discuss over otherwise-unremarkable cafeteria lunches. In 2023, the CEOs of some of the best AI labssigned a public statement that“mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war.” Another signer: Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel prize-winning scientist who architected the modern AI revolution. Henow regrets his workandurges governments to rein in AI companies before it’s too late.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMisaligned, out-of-control AI won’t care if you’re Labour or Reform, Democrat or Republican, British or American or Chinese. We will all suffer from an AI takeover event, so it’s in everyone’s interest to prevent one.The shape of the solution is simple: stop companies from allowing AI to self-improve into an uncontrollable level of intelligence. Treat compute, the main ingredient in AI training, like fissile material. Track it and restrict access to quantities large enough to improve AIs beyond known-safe levels. More specifically, the AI Futures Project’s “Plan A” is a credible starting proposal that limits AI harms while allowing fast AI progress to continue to benefit the world. We have real options for verifying compliance with international compute-restriction treaties, without trusting adversaries like China.Halfway measures, like transparency or voluntary commitments, are not good enough. I watched voluntary commitments fail inside Google.On 12 September,Anthropic,Google DeepMind,xAI, andOpenAIadvocated for pacing AI development. They cannot slow down alone. I urge you to demand that your government produce a serious AI safety agreement that provides enough time and confidence to safeguard the world and all her peoples.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple camera | Smartphones | The Guardian
description: Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed
Content: Big, bright internal screen folds to the same size and shape as a regular Pixel.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBig, bright internal screen folds to the same size and shape as a regular Pixel.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.SmartphonesReviewPixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple cameraBig screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closedSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition fromApple’s squat iPhone fold.The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as thepressure of RAMageddoncontinues to push up prices.The 11 Pro Fold looks identical to previous models, but it is 19g lighter and fractionally slimmer in all directions with a slightly larger outside screen. UnlikeSamsung’s slender Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultraor squat models such as Apple’s iPhone Duo or theGalaxy Z Fold 8, the Pixel has the same ratio screen as Google’s slab phones and so handles precisely like them when shut with a bright and smooth 6.5in display.View image in fullscreenThe Pixel 11 Pro Fold is just like a regular Android when closed.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianOpened up, the internal screen is essentially square, which allows you to run two full-size apps side by side but is less ideal for video. The display is very bright, crisp and smooth, but the crease where it folds is more visible and detectable with your fingers than the best rivals. Like all foldable phones the screen is also delicate compared with standard hardened glass phones.The back of the phone hides the excellent Qi2 magnetic charging and accessory supportfrom last year, while Google’s gimmicky HiLight notification LED, as seen on theother Pro Pixels, replaces the camera’s flash.View image in fullscreenThe crease in the centre of the screen is visible under glare, but disappears when in use.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianSpecificationsOutside screen:6.5in FHD+ 120Hz OLED (399ppi)Inside screen:8in 120Hz OLED (372ppi)Processor:Google Tensor G6RAM:16GBStorage:256, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:Android17Camera:48MP wide, 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP 5x telephoto; two 10MP selfie camerasConnectivity:5G, eSim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, Thread, GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)Dimensions folded:155.2 x 76 x 10.1mmDimensions unfolded:155.2 x 150.4 x 5mmWeight:239gFaster chip but slightly shorter battery lifeView image in fullscreenA full charge takes an hour and 40 minutes hitting 50% in 37 minutes with a 30W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included). It also supports 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 11 Pro Fold has the same Tensor G6 chip from the otherPixel 11models with 16GB of memory, which works very well for all kinds of multitasking, remaining snappy and responsive with multiple apps on screen. It handles light gaming, but can’t match rivals for raw performance.The battery life is a little shorter thanlast year’s modeland rivals, lasting about 36 hours between charges when used on a mix of 5G and wifi with the screens in active use for about 2.5 hours each for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. Most will have to charge it nightly, but even on the heaviest of use days the Pixel managed to end the day without requiring a top-up.Android 17, Magic Cue and GeminiView image in fullscreenThe revamped Bubbles feature allows additional floating apps to be minimised to a separate taskbar in the bottom left or right of the screen.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold runs the latest version of Android 17 with all of Google’s AI tools, including Gemini’s proactive system, the new supercharged voice dictation feature and six months ofGoogle AI Pro subscription.Many of Google’s more creative AI tools, including the Omni video creation tool, Circle to Search and Gemini’s information cards benefit from the larger internal screen. Google has made a number of modifications to Android to better fit the folding form, including a floating taskbar and a split-screen mode that can resize apps beyond the bounds of the physical displayintroduced last year.Thebubbles system, which was primarily used for messaging apps, has beenrevamped to allow as many as five appsof any kind to be opened as floating windows on top of a single or split-screen apps and minimised to a little taskbar. But it isn’t as flexible as Samsung’s true desktop-like floating window system that can be resized and placed anywhere on the screen.The 11 Pro Fold will be supported untilAugust 2033with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest supported devices available.SustainabilityView image in fullscreenThe body is made of recycled aluminium with a solid-feeling hinge.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe batteryis rated to lastin excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google and third-party shops, and self-repairwith manualsandparts is due to be available.The Pixel 11 Pro Fold contains 24% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report and willrecycle old devicesfor free.CameraView image in fullscreenThe excellent camera app can be used open or closed, with plenty of modes to play with.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThePixelFold has some of the best cameras on a foldable phone, including three on the back and two very good selfie cameras, one in each screen.The rear cameras include a new 48MP main camera with a larger sensor, matching that in theregular Pixel 11, which captures better detail and has significantly better lowlight performance than its predecessor. The 10.5MP ultrawide camera is the same as last year and is still as solid this year. The 10.8MP 5x telephoto is also the same and shoots good photos that meaningfully reduce the distance to objects. It has a solid digital zoom that stretches up to 30x magnification, but not the generative AI zoom of thePixel 11 Pro.View image in fullscreenThe square camera cluster keeps the phone from rocking around on a desk when shut.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe Fold also has the new software features from the other Pixel 11 phones, including Camera Looks, which allows you to customise the processing of your photos for different styles. Magic Capture shoots video and photos automatically with one button, while the Creator suite helps you storyboard, trim and produce video content for social media.The camera also has tricks to make use of the folding form, including modes to shoot when propped up and the excellentMade You Lookfeature that displays an animated character that reacts to your kid’s smiling to help take better photos.Overall, the 11 Pro Fold has an excellent set of cameras that don’t feel a significant downgrade on top regular smartphones.PriceThe Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from£1,799(€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799).For comparison, thePixel 11costs£879, Pixel 11 Pro costs£1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs£1,279, theSamsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultracosts£1,899, the iPhone Duo costs£1,999and theHonor Magic V6costs£1,499.99.VerdictThe Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a fairly minor hardware update for Google’s folding phone line, which makes it slightly lighter, smaller, brighter and faster, while keeping its overall look and feel the same.It has great AI tools, slick software and some of the very best cameras. The inside screen is super bright and crisp, but the crease down the middle is more noticeable than rivals, the battery life is a bit short and it is thick and heavy compared to thebest from rival Samsung.As with all foldables the inside screen can be permanently marked by a fingernail if you press hard enough, so you must still be careful with it compared with a standard Pixel.But if you want a folding phone to be exactly the same as a regular one when closed, the Pixel Fold is the one to get.Pros:just like a regular Pixel when closed, good tablet screen, dust and water resistant, Qi2 magnetic accessory and charging, good performance, great cameras with 5x zoom, great software packed with cutting-edge AI, six months of Google AI Pro included, seven years of software updates.Cons:very expensive, more fragile and costlier to repair than a regular Pixel, thick and heavy, cameras can’t match regular Pixel 11 Pro, battery life could be better.View image in fullscreenThe fingerprint scanner in the power button is fast and accurate, but is a little awkward to activate when using the phone with your left hand.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsSmartphonesGoogleMobile phonesAndroidPixelAlphabetreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Texas governor threatens to penalize datacenters not obeying water laws | Texas | The Guardian
description: Republican Greg Abbott says datacenters must help ‘protect’ drought-prone state and disclose water use
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Republican Greg Abbott says datacenters must help ‘protect’ drought-prone state and disclose water use
Content: Greg Abbott speaks during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on 10 September.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGreg Abbott speaks during the second day of the Republican National Committee midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on 10 September.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesTexasTexas governor threatens to penalize datacenters not obeying water lawsRepublican Greg Abbott says datacenters must help ‘protect’ drought-prone state and disclose water useMaya YangMon 14 Sep 2026 18.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreg Abbott, theTexasgovernor, has directed state regulators to penalizedatacentersthat fail to comply with state laws requiring them to disclose their water use.“Data centers must share the duty to protect Texas water,” theRepublicangovernorsaidon Monday. “The Texas Water Code requires a complete and accurate water use survey. I direct the Texas Water Development Board to use its enforcement authority to penalize past failures and to impose legal consequences for any future failure to comply,” he added.In aletterto the water board, Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, said: “Major water users, including data centers, appear to have committed civil and criminal violations by failing to provide the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) with information about water usage as required by the Texas Water Code.”US datacenters face further backlash over wastewater pollutionRead moreIt follows adirectiveAbbott issued last month ordering the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (Ercot) to conduct a comprehensive audit of datacenters advancing through the Ercot interconnection process.Drought-proneTexashasfast become the heart of the US’s datacenter boom.Texas has the second-most datacenters of any state in the country, according to atallyby the Pew Research Center. But with335 datacenters, and at least 248 more in the pipeline, experts believe it could surpass Virginia as the world’s largest concentration of datacenters by the end of the decade.The datacenter backlash is bringing the entire political spectrum together – against big tech billionairesRead moreBut, amidgrowing public concernover datacenter construction, Texas has been working to tighten oversight of the industry as demand grows for the state’s power and water supplies.In 2025, Texas datacenters consumed an estimated 25bn gallons of water,according tothe Houston Advanced Research Center. Water use by datacenters in the state could rise to 161bn gallons a year by 2030 – about 2.7% of all water used in Texas, or roughly the amount consumed by 1.3m households across the country.The audit requires datacenters to provide information about their water consumption, water sources and efforts to use water-efficient technologies. Abbott said projects that fail to complete the audit will be denied permission to connect to the state’s power grid.“TWDB’s water use surveys serve a similarly important purpose as this data center audit. TWDB must coordinate with PUC and ERCOT to ensure that covered entities provide critical water use information in response,” Abbott said in his Monday letter. “Any failure to respond to the audit’s request for water use information would trigger TWDB’s independent enforcement authority.”Explore more on these topicsTexasDatacenters – USAI (artificial intelligence)Greg AbbottWaterComputingDroughtnewsShareReuse this content

title: China dismisses AI ‘fearmongering’ as spy chief warns of threat to Communist party rule | China | The Guardian
description: Beijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AI
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Beijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AI
Content: Visitors at an AI expo in China. Beijing has pushed back against calls for the US to curb the country’s development of AI.Photograph: Ng Han Guan/APView image in fullscreenVisitors at an AI expo in China. Beijing has pushed back against calls for the US to curb the country’s development of AI.Photograph: Ng Han Guan/APChinaChina dismisses AI ‘fearmongering’ as spy chief warns of threat to Communist party ruleBeijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AIOliver HolmesMon 14 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChina has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls for the US to block Beijing’s AI industry, even as the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule.The US tech entrepreneur andAnthropicchief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote an essay published over the weekend that called for a global slowdown in AI capabilities, but also said Washington should actively impede Beijing’s advancement in order to keep a technological edge.Warning that AI could give the Chinese Communist party a chance “to militarily dominate democracies”, Amodei said he believed “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”.China’s ministry of foreign affairs responded to a question about Amodei’s essay by saying all parties should work together on AI.“Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference on Monday.In his essay, Amodei predicted that a swarm of AI “agents” could take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that while “global pacing will require cooperation with China”, steps were needed to “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.Other tech bosses, including the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chair, Demis Hassabis, and the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk, have posted general support forAmodei’s lengthy essay, although not specifically on China.View image in fullscreenAnthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, who has called for the US to impede China’s AI development to preserve the technological lead of democracies.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/ReutersWhile Beijing rejects that its dominance in AI would be dangerous, it does share fears over the pace of development. The president of China,Xi Jinping, warned at a conference in July that AI should “always remain under human control”.But the extent of the Chinese government’s concerns was shown in an article published on Sunday in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, in which the country’s top intelligence official wrote that the technology could threaten the government’s hold on power.The head of China’s ministry of state security, Chen Yixin, wrote that “hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives” were abusing AI to wage a “propaganda war and a cognitive war against us, directly threatening our political security, institutional security, and ideological security”.Chen referred specifically to US models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber models, which he said have been weaponised and were examples of new threats to cybersecurity.While the public, governments and tech bosses are now warning of the dangers of AI,Donald Trumphas dismissed such concerns outright. On Monday, the US president said the only “guardrails” that AI needed were a “STRONG AND SMART” president.Trump has been particularly sensitive to stock market changes, and AI stocks have slipped after concerns over the pace of growth were raised.The US and Chinese leaders are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on 24 September.In an editorial published Sunday, China’s state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei’s essay as a veiled call to “contain” China.“The article is packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘cold war playbook’ for the AI sector,”it said.The Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsChinaAI (artificial intelligence)Xi JinpingDonald TrumpAnthropicnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK government moves to acquire Speciality Steel UK; AI stocks hit by calls for slowdown – as it happened | Business | The Guardian
description: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news
Content: 11.14 EDTUK government moves to acquire Speciality Steel UKNewsflash: The UK government has decided to acquire the country’s third-largest steel producer.The Business SecretaryJonathanReynoldshas announced the Government will “work towards” the public acquisition of Speciality Steel UK (SSUK), after ministers decided they could not support its sale to Norwegian steel startupBlastr Green Steel.SSUK has been in liquidation since last year, and was part of Sanjeev Gupta’s Liberty Steel before its recent collapse.The company is an important part of the UK steel sector as it can make steel for use in the auto, aero and defence sectors.According to the government, SSUK’s four sites support over 1,300 jobs in Rotherham, Stocksbridge, Brinsworth and Wednesbury.Reynolds is stepping in after decidingBlastr’sproposal could not provide long-term stability, certainty and value for money.Reynoldssays:double quotation mark“We do not intervene in private companies lightly. But nor can we simply stand aside and allow the future of this company and over 1,300 jobs to be decided by default.“Working towards public acquisition will keep options open while we work with local leaders, workers, industry and investors to determine the best long-term future for these sites, which could play a vital role in the future of the growth-driving sectors in our Industrial Strategy, including defence and advanced manufacturing.“ I am determined that we take the time to properly assess the opportunities available here and make decisions that support growth, jobs and Britain’s industrial future.”Share

title: Australia’s outdated technology is vulnerable to AI hacking attacks, signals chief says | Australian security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Abigail Bradshaw says ‘enormous’ amounts of money required to update systems that people now expect to be constantly available
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Abigail Bradshaw says ‘enormous’ amounts of money required to update systems that people now expect to be constantly available
Content: The Australian Signals Directorate chief, Abigail Bradshaw, believes there are ‘a lot’ of AI agents active on the internet.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe Australian Signals Directorate chief, Abigail Bradshaw, believes there are ‘a lot’ of AI agents active on the internet.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian security and counter-terrorismAustralia’s outdated technology is vulnerable to AI hacking attacks, signals chief saysAbigail Bradshaw says ‘enormous’ amounts of money required to update systems that people now expect to be constantly availableFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Australia’s top intelligence agencies has warned that AI attacks could exploit the country’s old technology, as the government negotiates its guardrails on artificial intelligence’s rapid development.The chief of Anthropic, developer of Claude, has warned AI bots could swarm the internet within a year and called to “slow the pace” of development with support
