To access them, we wade daily through brain-rotting media we would otherwise choose to avoid.The price we pay for connection is our own minds.An $18bn settlement – and Zuckerberg barely blinked. The tech titans must be stripped of their power, and soon | Jonathan FreedlandRead moreIn its most recent legal settlement, Meta agreed to pay $17bn and make design modifications to better protect 13- to 17-year-olds: a two-hour daily cap across Facebook and Instagram; a lockout between midnight and 6am, with notifications silenced from 10pm; hidden “like” counts; a ban on cosmetic-surgery filters; and the option to return to an un-optimized-for-your-attention news feed.The settlement doesn’t include rationales or any admissions of culpability. But implicit in the changes is the idea that short-form video, lack of choice, and passive, mindless consumption are the main culprits. Direct messages with personal contacts and long-form content are excluded – the things users both want and that we know are relatively safe.Though the settlement is only geared towards protecting a subset of adolescents, what research we have suggests social media’s cognitive risks affect teenagers and adults equally. We all have grounds for wanting greater control over our digital environment.It may be just a matter of time before cognitive research can do for social media what decades of epidemiology did for lead in the 1960s, 70s and 80s: allow concerned citizens to push for corporate changes that make the worldsafer for everyone.Science and litigation will continue to lag behind the relentless pace of big tech. Knowing this, perhaps the safest way to approach the digital world, where we now spend most of our time, is to listen to our own minds and bodies. The science is telling us that teens – and their grandmothers – knew intuitively that something was wrong, even if research will take years to prove exactly what it was.Caty Enders is a journalist and researcher exploring our relationship to technology. She writes the newsletterStanding in the CurrentExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionMetaTikTokInstagramDigital mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Forget the bombing: the Trump administration keeps insisting this isn’t a war. But it’s not just a matter of semantics
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Forget the bombing: the Trump administration keeps insisting this isn’t a war. But it’s not just a matter of semantics
Content: ‘The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it?’Photograph: Eric Lee/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreen‘The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it?’Photograph: Eric Lee/Pool Reuters/APOpinionTrump administrationThe situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a warArwa MahdawiForget the bombing: the Trump administration keeps insisting this isn’t a war. But it’s not just a matter of semanticsMon 14 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTShare“Iwill not send you to fight and die in stupid foreign wars that never end,” Donald Trumppromiseda crowd in Pennsylvania in 2024. While the disastrous conflict in Iran, which has escalated in recent days, may make it seem like the president has reneged on that promise, that’s inaccurate. It would be wrong to say that the president has dragged the US into yet another disastrous forever war in the Middle East because, as government officials keep insisting, what’s happening in Iran isn’t actually a war.“I wouldn’t call it a war,” JD Vance told reportersearly this month, for example, after being asked whether the fighting in Iran might be over by the November midterms. “Right now, there is no active shooting.”Maybe not, but there has been quite a bit of active bombing. Earlier this month, a US missile strikehit a weddingat a private home in southern Iran, killing at least four people, including a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old. That’s fairly restrained compared to the massacre inMarchwhen a US precision-guided missile hit an elementary school in Iran,killing 150 people, including 120 children, but it’s still something I would personally file under “possible war crimes”.Trump’s repeated threats to ‘wipe out’ Iran are normalizing mass violence | Mohamad BazziRead moreBut not only does the Trump administration keep insisting this isn’t a real war, they’re also adamant there aren’t any real crimes being committed: the vice-president would like to stress that you shouldn’t believe your eyes or ears when it comes to the civilian deaths being reported. Despite a weapons expert and avisual analysisby the New York Times concluding that the bomb that hit the wedding party in a residential area of the country was American, Vance has a hunch the whole thing might have been made up by some untrustworthy brown people.“The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,”Vance saidat that same press briefing, in relation to the wedding massacre. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.”The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it? A little skirmish? An interminable series of special military operations? A very bloody screw-up? Trump himself has called it a war on several occasions. Last Wednesday,for example, he said: “The war is going to end immediately after the election.” However, rather confusing matters, he also recently suggested he agreed with Vance that it wasn’t a full-fledged war. “I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,”Trump saidlast month. Those are some very expensive potatoes: the not-a-war already has a price tag oftens of billions. Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, has roughly estimated that it has cost the typical US household $1,200. And then of course there’s the human cost: thethousandsof lives that have been lost.What we call this “military conflict” isn’t just semantics, it matters greatly. Not least because the constitution is very clear that a president can’t unilaterally start an official war on a whim; only Congress has the power to declare a war. Trumpisn’tthe first president to launch major military action without going to Congress for a declaration: Harry Truman classified the Korean conflict as a “police action” to bypass Congress and presidents since have engaged in similar semantic sleights-of-hand. But, as the historian and foreign relations expert Fredrik Logevall noted in aninterviewwith the Harvard Kennedy School: “What’s extraordinary about President Trump in the current context is that he has not really bothered to even consult with Congress, never mind seek the approval of Congress.” In other words, he’s acting like a dictator.Trump, to be fair, has been clear that he’s exploiting the Truman Playbook. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say if you use the word ‘war,’ that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” Trumpsaidat a fundraising dinner in March. “They don’t like the word ‘war’ because you’re supposed to get approval. So, I’ll use the word ‘military operation’, which is really what it is. It’s a military decimation.”Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreAvoiding a formal declaration of war might also help the US government bypass certain “wartime” obligations to its service members and their families. Libby Klinner, the widow of an airman killed in combat operations againstIranin March, recently posted on Instagram that she wasn’t receiving certain benefits because the US wasn’t technically at war.“The Air Force recently told me that because we haven’t officially declared war, my kids and I aren’t eligible for some benefits,”Klinner wrote. “So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we’re left with are being dictated by semantics and public perceptions.”After this post went viral, it seems the government has stepped in smooth things over. Vance recently said the administration would ensure Klinner receives “what she is entitled to.” He added: “We will certainly work that on the back end.”The government might be able to fix Klinner’s benefits, but they’re going to have a hard time remedying the economic and political damage this not-a-war is inflicting. Trump’s popularity is plummeting, and amajorityof Americans arefed upwith this “small potatoes” conflict that has been going on for six months and making everyday life more dangerous and expensive. According to an estimate from Brown University last week, the conflict has cost Americans$100bnin extra energy costs. That bill is going up by $1m every two minutes. This week oil prices also climbed over$100 a barrelfor the first time since July.Meanwhile, with hostilities escalating and no off-ramp in sight, it looks like Trump is out of options. All he has left is empty promises. The president has insisted that energy priceswill tumble“right after the election” and, in a sign he is completely desperate, promised every American adult$5,000if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. The Trump administration can call the war whatever they like, but future generations will define it as a disastrous act of hubris.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionJD VanceUS-Israel war on IranDonald TrumpIranMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: The US right still paints Muslims as the ‘enemy’. But they are fighting for a brighter future for Americans | Nesrine Malik | The Guardian
description: Progressive politicians such as Zohran Mamdani offer answers to the bitter post-9/11 legacy of failures at home and abroad, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: Progressive politicians such as Zohran Mamdani offer answers to the bitter post-9/11 legacy of failures at home and abroad, says Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik
Content: Zohran Mamdani after the ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11 2001 attacks in New York, 11 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Gray/ReutersView image in fullscreenZohran Mamdani after the ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11 2001 attacks in New York, 11 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Gray/ReutersOpinionSeptember 11 2001The US right still paints Muslims as the ‘enemy’. But they are fighting for a brighter future for AmericansNesrine MalikProgressive politicians such as Zohran Mamdani offer answers to the bitter post-9/11 legacy of failures at home and abroadMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.12 EDTShareTwenty-five years after 9/11, two pieces of journalism, describing two different phenomena in contemporary New York, tell us a great deal about a city, and indeed a world, caught between two eras. In one, New York Magazine dives into “Habibi City”, a New York where a “cultural shift is underway, led by a generation of New Yorkers coming into its own”. This new generation is labelled as originating in “SWANA” – south-west Asia and north Africa, a region that “includes countries from Palestine to Iran to Sudan”. In the other, Vanity Fairdescribescalls for Zohran Mamdani to not attend the 9/11 memorial ceremony as partly founded in “inchoate, emotional” impulses, that see “the city’s first Muslim mayor as a stand-in for the 19 Muslims who hijacked four planes and turned them into deadly weapons, part of the ‘them’ who attacked ‘us’.”Together they capture what has changed over a generation, and what remains stubbornly the same. Members of a diaspora of Muslim background are indeed breaking through and accumulating, asNew YorkMagazine says, “clout”. They are no longer simply a fixture of bodegas and halal carts, but of Saturday Night Live, upmarket dining, entertainment and politics too. Mamdani is both the expression of that cohort and the catalyst of its recognition as an emerging force. They care deeply for their local communities but also for those in Gaza and beyond.I use the descriptor “of Muslim background” rather than “Muslim” because this diasporic identity is a diverse one that is rooted in a religion but expands to encompass everyone from the practising to those for whomIslamis a cultural totem.The capaciousness of this heritage is demonstrable in its integration – without compromise – into mainstream American society. Mamdani and the Democratic Senate nominee for Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, recuse themselves from the rote fealty to American glory and dare to point out both US support for Israel and the calamitous outcomes of the “war on terror” in the Middle East.This is the result of this new generation of Americans coming from an immigrant background that has cultivated a less parochial and supremacist view of the US. There is something historically inevitable in this. Immigration from countries and backgrounds against which the US has waged military and ideological war eventually yields not a cowed assimilation, but a sort of political cosmopolitanism – kryptonite for American exceptionalism.39:2125 years after 9/11, is Islamophobia in the US at an all-time high? — Stateside with Kai and CarterGrowing up in the shadow of Islamophobia is another formative experience that ironically forced many to identify in terms of religious background rather than race or national origin. “In a way,” said American comedian Ramy Youssef, in a now legendary standup comedysegment, “9/11 made me more Muslim. Cos I was told it was my fault.” This is a profoundly recognisable story for many, including myself, for whom a casual religious identity became a sharp political one during the “war on terror” years.At the same time as this new generation found their political and social power, the Islamophobia that began in 2001 has only further burrowed into the fabric of American society. Pew researchfoundthat, a quarter of a century after 9/11, “public attitudes toward Islam have become more ‘negative’ and more ‘partisan’” than they were in the wake of the attack. In March 2002, 25% of US adults believed that Islam “is more likely than other religions to encourage violence”. Today that figure has doubled to 51%. That is why Mamdani can be seen as a representative of hijackers (despite the fact that he was nine years old on 9/11) and El-Sayed can be called a “terrorist” by Senator Tommy Tuberville. Congresswoman Nancy Mace said that “every single Muslim holding public office in America” is a “threat to both national security and our republic”. “Jihadists”, said Donald Trump, were “being elected all over the place”.Rozina Ali, the author ofSeasons of Fury, a study of the history of Islamophobia in the US, tells me that contemporary Islamophobia cannot be separated from a wider failure of American politics at home and abroad. The “war on terror” turned into a foreign quagmire. At home, a financial crisis saw millions of people lose their homes and savings. One of the reasons Islamophobia has been used by the right is that “a lot of these things can be explained by so called invasions from foreigners or a foreign culture like Islam”. The right, she said, simply “doesn’t have an effective vision for this country that can actually solve a lot of the ills”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think | Moustafa BayoumiRead moreThe problem for this approach is not only that Muslims are no longer keeping their heads down, but that they represent a broader progressive politics. Political candidates as well as cultural figures are mobilising large blocks of voters and backersbecausetheir worldview has been informed by profound marginalisation. They can root their politics in material concerns about standards of living as well as unpopular foreign policy, in addition tohumanisingthe toll of the political backlash against Muslims and making it a part of the American story. They can unite a broad coalition of people because they too experience being on the losing side against a political establishment.Despite all the vitriol from the right, anti-Muslim propaganda has not prevented these connections being formed. At the 9/11 commemorative ceremony this past weekend, Mamdani soberly and graciouslyshookthe hand of Rudy Giuliani, the man who was mayor of New York on 9/11, and who hadcalledfor Mamdani not to attend. One man was the past, and the other was the future.Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: As Reform celebrates £72m in donations, tell me this: are you ready to see two rich men buy our democracy? | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: It’s not just that Nigel Farage claimed his movement abhorred the super-rich. It’s also the obscenity of individuals seeking so much sway over who runs the country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: It’s not just that Nigel Farage claimed his movement abhorred the super-rich. It’s also the obscenity of individuals seeking so much sway over who runs the country, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Nigel Farage after his closing speech at Reform UK’s annual conference in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenNigel Farage after his closing speech at Reform UK’s annual conference in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionReform UKAs Reform celebrates £72m in donations, tell me this: are you ready to see two rich men buy our democracy?Owen JonesIt’s not just that Nigel Farage claimed his movement abhorred the super-rich. It’s also the obscenity of individuals seeking so much sway over who runs the countryMon 14 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTShareAs£72m in donationsmakes its way to Reform UK’s bank accounts, consider what Nigel Faragesaidon the eve of Britain’s vote to leave the European Union a decade ago. “This referendum is the people versus the establishment,” he declared. “It is the vested interest, it’s the rich, it’s the big business.”Just two years ago,Farage assailed“an unholy alliance of big business, big banks and big government”. He is also the same man who, when he debated with the then Liberal Democrat leader, Nick Clegg, in 2014,claimed to“represent the mercantile, trading, entrepreneurial end of society”, while his opponent “represents big banks, big government and big business”.To be clear, Farage’s political outfit isbeing bankrolledby two cryptobillionaires. One of them is Ben Delo, who once developed high-frequency trading systems for JP Morgan.That investment bank was a particular bete noire of Farage: when it backed the Remain campaign,he savaged“the unholy alliance of big banks and big politics”. The other is the Thailand-based cryptobillionaire Christopher Harborne, who gave Farage hispre-election £5m giftand provided two-thirds of Reform’s funding – until now, that is.Neither of them is the plucky small merchant evoked by Farage’s rhetoric. The man who denounced banks buying political influence is now dependent on two wealthy figures from the world of finance. Predictably, Reform says its benefactors want “nothing” in return for their colossal donations. Yet the two businessmen who have just coughed up the biggest donations in British political history will surely be delighted with Reform’s plans to slash taxes on crypto assets and set up a “bitcoin reserve”.The political fraud that is rightwing “populism” is quite something to behold. These movements claim to champion the little guy against the elites. Whether embodied by wealthy tycoon Donald Trump, whose relatives and friends are making a killing from his administration, or the privately educated millionaire ex-City broker Farage, the formula is straightforward. Dupe struggling people into believing their problems are caused by migrants, refugees and minorities – while championing the interests of the mega-rich who actually hold the power.Sure, British democracy has always come with heavy caveats. Political parties and politicians have always received hefty donations from an economic elite that, to be clear, does not give money away without expecting a return. They can also rely on powerful lobbyists to advance their interests. Then there’s the “revolving door” through which politicians and civil servants leave public office for lucrative jobs with companies in the very industries they were previously responsible for overseeing and regulating. And there’s a British newspaper industry mostly owned by rich moguls with a vested interest in defending a status quo they profit from.View image in fullscreenA protest placard near the Houses of Parliament in London on 9 September.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersBut these latest donations take the corruption of our democracy to a whole new level. That two donations to Reform in a single weekend now eclipse the total amount spent by all political parties at the last general election tells its own story. Indeed, these donations amount to about14 timesthe total spent by Farage’s party at the last election – when, it should be noted, it won more than 4m votes, or one in seven votes cast.The party can now pay for hundreds of full-time staff, build local political hubs and massively expand its polling and research infrastructure. Crucially, it can throw vast sums at digital advertising, which can be uniquely tailored to the interests and concerns of individual voters. We know fromresearch in the USthat digital ads can shift voting intention. The more money a political party has, the more it can afford to experiment until it finds the ads that work.Indeed, all the evidence suggests that money wins votes. A recentpeer-reviewed studyexamined every British general election between 1857 and 2017, and found a strong relationship between relative campaign spending and votes. Rich donors really do shower political parties with money for a reason. Reform’s mega-donations underline that democracy is for sale.But could this spectacularly backfire? Reform is, after all, already embroiled in multiple controversies over gifts and donations from wealthy donors, andits ratingshave taken a bad beating.Polling earlier this yearfound that 83% of Brits believe that “wealthy individuals use political donations to influence the government to further their own personal interests”. That figure was only four points lower among Reform voters, who were also nearly 10 times as likely to say they would view a party more favourably if it promised to cap donations as to view it less favourably.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFarage hints that Reform’s £72m donations may not be legal under new elections bill - UK politics liveRead moreIt would be naive, alas, to believe that this will finally burst the gilded Reform bubble. What it does do depends on what the national political conversation is about. Labour has had long enough in government to change the law to block such donations, and tragicallyAndy Burnham has retreatedfrom his stated desire to cap them at £500,000.But that would mean a Labour party that was determined to confront wealthy vested interests. Because Starmerism had no desire to replace an economic order rigged in favour of elites, it was unable to redirect anger away from the scapegoating of migrants. Instead, it simply replicated Farage’s xenophobia, which only ever legitimises the arguments of the anti-migrant right.A different approach, based on redistributing wealth and power, would force a different conversation. So far, thanks to pressure from Zack Polanski’s Green party, Burnham has shifted some of the rhetoric. But if Labour were to, say, hike taxes on wealth in order to invest in crumbling services, it could pair that with a sustained attack on Farage as the plaything of wealthy vested interests.Otherwise, the outrage over these donations will fade. The old poison will remain – and this time it comes with £72m behind it.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is released in October. title: Canada should become an EU state in all but name. Here’s how to make that a reality | Fabian Zuleeg | The Guardian
description: From the UK to Japan, so many countries need to quickly be brought inside the European tent without the rigours of full membership, says economist Fabian Zuleeg
Author: Fabian Zuleeg
Headline: From the UK to Japan, so many countries need to quickly be brought inside the European tent without the rigours of full membership, says economist Fabian Zuleeg
Content: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and European Council president Antonio Costa in Brussels in June 2025.Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPAView image in fullscreenEuropean Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney and European Council president Antonio Costa in Brussels in June 2025.Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPAOpinionEuropean UnionCanada should become an EU state in all but name. Here’s how to make that a realityFabian ZuleegFrom the UK to Japan, so many countries need to quickly be brought inside the European tent without the rigours of full membershipMon 14 Sep 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 13.42 EDTShareThe worst conclusion to draw from Iceland’sEU referendum resultlast month would be that the country, apparently nowon Donald Trump’s imperial mapalong with Canada and Greenland, wanted to distance itself from Europe. Rather, the decision to refuse the reopening of EU accession talks shows that asking voters to choose between membership of the 27-nation bloc and staying outside the club is too binary. Some countries want to be inside the European tent without necessarily becoming members. The EU needs a new status for them.There are existing models of close cooperation. Iceland and Norway, for example, participate in much of the single market through theEuropean Economic Area (EEA). A range of other partial, gradual or associated membership options for candidate countries is being debated.What I am proposing is different from any of them. It is not about setting up a stepping stone to accession, nor is it primarily about access to the single market. Instead, it is about letting like-minded countries combine with the EU when geopolitical and geo-economic necessities demand it, without them having to sign up to a predetermined constitutional outcome.The main criterion for the novel status I call “integrated partnership” would be geopolitical rather than geographical. A country would not have to aspire to EU membership to qualify. It would not even have to be situated in Europe.Iceland, the UK and Norway are obvious potential candidates, but so are Canada, Japan and South Korea.These countries would be inside the tent wherever legally and politically possible, pooling sovereignty across specific policy areas. This relationship could ultimately amount to quasi-membership, with corresponding rights and obligations. Unlike membership of the EEA, however, it would extend beyond the economy. Defence, security, economic security and foreign policy would be as fundamental to the relationship as trade and the single market.Countries already seeking full EU membership, of which there are nine at the moment, will continue to prioritise that end goal. But the EU will struggle to deliver on its promises to all of those in the queue within a reasonable timeframe. Political resistance to the union’s expansion beyond the 27 existing members could intensify ifkey national elections next yearcreate a shift in the EU’s majority political outlook. Already, internal reforms, budgetary concerns and the complexities of accession could leave some countries waiting for years.All sides would benefit from giving these queueing nations another option. Ukraine or the western Balkan countries should not remain stranded in a geopolitical waiting room simply because the EU lacks the political will or administrative bandwidth to admit them. Of course, safeguards are essential: this kind of advanced partnership must be a bridge to membership for those seeking it, not a car park that allows governments of existing EU nations to renege on promises if they become electorally unpopular.The defining test for partners must be genuine like-mindedness around democratic values: a sustained commitment to liberal democracy, the rule of law, political sovereignty and an international order based on rules.Canada should be among the first candidates. TheEU-Canada summit in Octobershould go beyond another list of worthy deliverables and start the process of establishing a special status so deep that the country could eventually become the equivalent of an EU member state in all but name. Ursula von der Leyen should announce as much in her annual state of the union address this week. With Canada’s relationship with the USon the ropes, Brussels has an eager partner in Mark Carney, who said on Sunday that he wants a “unique alliance” with the EU.But that would require clear commitments from Ottawa as well as Brussels. Integrated partners should not get a free ticket to the benefits of EU policies without corresponding obligations and costs.The case for this is becoming easier to make. Democracies face increasingly aggressive behaviour from authoritarian powers. Middle powers risk being isolated, divided and picked off individually.As Carneyhas argued, they must act together in response to the rupture of the old international order. Integrated partnership could help operationalise Carney’s argument.There is also a more uncomfortable reason for new geopolitical architecture. It cannot be assumed that countries, even those supposedly joined at the hip through the EU, will always continue on a like-minded path. France or Germany could in the future be governed by illiberal anti-European forces unwilling to defend the principles on which European integration rests.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA network encompassing democratic EU members and their close partners could then become a political counterweight, helping to preserve collective action when consensus inside the EU becomes impossible. This should not become an alternative EU. But Europe cannot base its geopolitical strategy on the assumption that every one of its governments will remain committed to European integration or even liberal democracy.The European project emerged from the ruins of the second world war. Now, in a very different geopolitical context, we need ambitious mechanisms for bringing like-minded democracies together. But full EU membership cannot be the only route to deep integration. Maximum integration without a predetermined end point should now become the objective.Iceland’s vote, driven by concerns over fisheries and other totemic national issues, shows why new thinking and geopolitical ambition are needed. Geography should no more determine who can be inside Europe’s tent than the time it takes to conduct painstaking enlargement negotiations. Increasingly, the decisive question is whether Europe can club together with all countries that are prepared to defend democratic principles together.Fabian Zuleeg is chief executive and chief economist at the European Policy CentreExplore more on these topicsEuropean UnionOpinionCanadaMark CarneyIcelandInternational tradeGlobal economyEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: The right is wrong about digital duty of care. It promises Australians more freedom, not less | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: Labor’s law would allow choice for social media users and build accountability into the internet rather than allow the tech industry to operate with impunity
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: Labor’s law would allow choice for social media users and build accountability into the internet rather than allow the tech industry to operate with impunity
Content: Prime minister Anthony Albanese. The government’s long-awaited digital duty of care legislation was condemned by both the Coalition and One Nation.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenPrime minister Anthony Albanese. The government’s long-awaited digital duty of care legislation was condemned by both the Coalition and One Nation.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionSocial mediaThe right is wrong about digital duty of care. It promises Australians more freedom, not lessPeter LewisLabor’s law would allow choice for social media users and build accountability into the internet rather than allow the tech industry to operate with impunityMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.23 EDTShareWhen you hear them cry “freedom”, you know a culture war is brewing. And so it was last week that a bid to make tech companies address the harmful impacts of their products became a piece of political performance theatre.The Coalition and One Nation tripped over each other to condemn the government’s long-awaited digital duty of care legislation. To Angus Taylor it is “a blank cheque for political censorship”; for Pauline Hanson it’s “Communist China”.For their fracturing base, it’s another reason to hate on the government.Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithmsRead moreLet’s be clear what the political right is really saying: that in the name of “freedom” we reject laws that would hold the most powerful companies on earth accountable for their products.At its heart is the confused and contradictory binary of safety and freedom; a false trade-off that has actively fuelled the very toxic online world these laws seek to purify. Un-muddling this is critical if we are to build an internet that actually works for people.We canpartly explainthis political response as a self-interested attempt to protect the very algorithms that are driving the rise of the populist right. But there is also a legitimate debate to be had over the degree to which the state exercises its control over us all.In the 25 years since 9/11, the powers the state has amassed over us have grown year on year until we have found ourselves living under a sophisticated surveillance apparatus created in the name of homeland security.Frombuilding backdoorsto monitor our phones and internet usage, to facial recognition cameras inpublic spaces, to sophisticated data-matching by companiessuch as Palantir, to the routine extension of police powers like theNSW government’s brazen bidto extract data from citizens’ phones without a warrant, our digital freedoms have eroded until they barely exist.double quotation markThis is not some academic argument – online harms are realOver those 25 years, the right has been willing backers of this erosion of personal freedoms.Privacybecame nostalgia, civil liberties conditional and the idea that our online activity could be captured and exploited normalised.These capabilities were commercialised by the nascent social media companies. First Google and then Facebook developed models to render and extract our online activity into the personalised advertising models thatShoshana Zuboff dubbed “surveillance capitalism”.It is the real-world impact of this model, the companies it spawned and the capabilities it drove that thedigital duty of carebill seeks to address.This is not some academic argument – online harms are real: children are being exploited in horrendous ways, teenagers are taking their own lives, girls are driven to eating disorders, young men are being recruited into an exploitative sphere, communities are dividing and the common anchors of truth are being eroded.The principle is simple: if you are offering an online product you need to be awake to its impact and take steps to make it safe. Whether you are producing a car, a financial service or a toy, that’s what is expected of you in the real world: that it will be safe.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow much control should we have over the algorithm? - podcastRead moreAt the tip of the legislative spear is the right for us to choose how our feeds operate, whether we want our feed full of paid recommendations or to simply to follow our friends and chosen interests. This seems the very expression of freedom of choice.The focus of the freedom warriors’ outrage appears to be the codification of specific harms covered by the laws and the minister’s discretion to add rapidly emerging risks (think nudify apps) to a list of specific areas where the duty of care should apply. This has been conflated into a government grab for power.If attempting to codify these limits of government power has the perverse effect of giving the freedom warriors a focal point to attack, a better approach might be to establish a more general duty of care to be shaped by the courts reflecting evolving community expectations.A general duty of care is not a novel concept; it underpins workplace safety laws. All employers must take reasonable and practicable steps to provide a safe place of work, which is why fewer people die on the job.This has also driven broader public health advances; the reason we don’t have smoking indoors is not a legislative prohibition (cry freedom!) but an enforcement of the employer’s safety obligations to co-workers and public-facing staff.So where to from here? Rather than being forced into this phoney freedom war, maybe it is time to reset the discussion by starting with what we all should be able to agree on.Should we do all we can to keep kids safe? Yes. Should the laws of the land apply in digital spaces? Yes. Should people have control over their feeds? Yes. Should there be lines of accountability for damage caused by a commercial product? Well, it happens in the offline world so why would it be different?If we can agree on the basic principle that online services should carry the onus of making their products safe then we can have a sensible debate about not if but how these platforms should be held to account.Because that’s what these laws are actually about: not safety or freedom or any crude trade-offs but our sovereign freedom as a nation to build accountability into the internet rather than continuing to allow the tech industry to operate with impunity.Alongside privacy laws also before parliament, this is significant structural reform to reset the way the internet works: enforceable standards on the collection of your data (fair and reasonable) and how it is used and deployed against us (digital duty of care).Embedding these rights for Australian citizens doesn’t solve everything about the toxic environment these corporations have created but it could give us a fighting chance to make the internet great again. That’s a culture war worth waging.Peter Lewis is non-executive chair of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host ofBurning Platforms, a weekly podcast focusing on the politics of technology. His columns are accreditedProudly HumanExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionAustralian politicsPrivacyInternet safetycommentShareReuse this content

title: There’s a surprisingly simple reason for England’s high antidepressant use: lots of people need them | Dean Burnett | The Guardian
description: The idea that GPs are ignoring guidelines and ‘overprescribing’ doesn’t hold water. Instead, look to our social and economic crises, says doctor of neuroscience Dean Burnett
Author: Dean Burnett
Headline: The idea that GPs are ignoring guidelines and ‘overprescribing’ doesn’t hold water. Instead, look to our social and economic crises, says doctor of neuroscience Dean Burnett
Content: Illustration: Nash Weerasekera/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nash Weerasekera/The GuardianOpinionMental healthThere’s a surprisingly simple reason for England’s high antidepressant use: lots of people need themDean BurnettThe idea that GPs are ignoring guidelines and ‘overprescribing’ doesn’t hold water. Instead, look to our social and economic crisesDean Burnett is a doctor of neuroscienceMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTShareAnew NHSreporthas revealed the highest ever levels of antidepressant use recorded in England, with roughly one in seven people prescribed an antidepressant item in 2025-26. This has resulted in a swathe of media coverage expressing alarm over the increase, with questions about what could, or should, be done to reverse the trend.Such a high level of antidepressant use should, of course, prompt concern and reflection. But the popular claim that has taken hold is that antidepressant use is too high because of “overprescribing”, as Dr John Read, a professor of clinical psychology, says in the Daily Mail. This is the idea that patients are being prescribed antidepressants when they shouldn’t be, or when better, safer alternatives are available.This idea is worth challenging – but first it’s important to consider how we got here. The increase in antidepressant use is strongly correlated with a rise in diagnoses in common disorders including depression and anxiety. Much of this is the afterlife of the Covid-19 pandemic and its associated lockdowns: according to ONS data, across Britain, the rate of depressive symptoms in adultsdoubledduring the crisis to almost one in five. As of April 2025, the figuresremain almost as high. This surge has particularly affectedyoung people in England, with one in four having a mental health condition, according to NHS data.So with this rise, an increase in antidepressant use is predictable. Lockdown, however necessary for public health, has had lasting implications for the country’s wellbeing.But it’s not only the consequences of the pandemic. What this data also indicates is that persistent regional inequalities have a worsening effect on mental health outcomes, and therefore antidepressant use. The most dramatic increases in antidepressant use are found in themost impoverishedregions of England, while more affluent regions report modest levels of antidepressant use.The highest rate of antidepressant use was seen in patients treated under the North East and North Cumbria integrated care board, with 200 in every 1,000 people prescribed antidepressant medication. Consider that this ICB contains some of the country’smost deprived areas, which have “faced longstanding inequalities and poor health for decades”, and you have further proof of something that has long been clear: poverty isinextricably linkedto poorer mental health outcomes. One key element that underpins many cases of depression, anxiety and related disorders ischronic stress. It’sour brain’s achilles heel. And a guaranteed source of chronic stress is a life of constant poverty.The argument presented against wide antidepressant prescription, as laid out in the Daily Mail, is that “doctors [are] increasingly being expected to treat wider social and life problems with medication”. Such a position assumes that a neat division can be drawn between these social problems and the mental health conditions they produce.These socioeconomic factors also explain why antidepressants are used more and more as a first-line treatment. It’s all well and good to argue that less severe cases of depression should be treated with talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, but these involve regular one-one-one sessions with trained counsellors, andthe wait for such interventionson the NHS regularly lasts months, if not years.In the most deprived areas,access to such servicesis even more difficult, whereas for the most part, antidepressants are accessible straight away. It should also be said that GPs followstrict clinical guidelinesfor prescribing antidepressants, as set out by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. These state that practitioners should “not routinely offer antidepressant medication as first-line treatment for less severe depression unless that is the person’s preference”. So it is clear that GPs are not simply handing out pills, but rather responding to legitimate patient demand.Of course, antidepressants can’t be a magic bullet – mental health services are evidently in need of deep reform and increased funding. We have already heard pledges to improve services, including with the government’s announcement in May this year of anew mental health strategyin England to drive a shift from crisis intervention to preventive care. And there are already technological interventions being recommended, includingdigital therapiesfor depression and anxiety that “could free up thousands of NHS therapist hours”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe government’s callout for frontline workers, clinicians and mental health experts to share views on transforming mental health care shows that there are likely several creative solutions to tackle this crisis, without the need for medication. Still, there should be no doubt about the simple reality: more people than ever are taking antidepressants because they genuinely need them.So the point here is not that the record rates of antidepressant use in England isn’t a problem. It undoubtedly is. But to determine that this is due to “overprescription” is to mistake a symptom for a much deeper social and economic crisis as its cause.Dean Burnett is a doctor of neuroscience and the author of The Idiot Brain and Emotional IgnoranceExplore more on these topicsMental healthOpinionDepressionPovertyHealth policyNHSAnxietyHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Islamophobia is rising – and Britain’s politicians have been dangerously complacent in tackling it | Arun Kundnani | The Guardian
description: Mainstream figures have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties, says Arun Kundnani, editorial director of Monthly Review Press
Author: Arun Kundnani
Headline: Mainstream figures have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties, says Arun Kundnani, editorial director of Monthly Review Press
Content: Anti-Islamophobia protest outside Conservative party headquarters in London, 29 February 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenAnti-Islamophobia protest outside Conservative party headquarters in London, 29 February 2024.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAOpinionIslamophobiaIslamophobia is rising – and Britain’s politicians have been dangerously complacent in tackling itArun KundnaniMainstream figures have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political partiesMon 14 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.10 EDTShareFive years ago, many Muslims wondered if the prejudices they faced were set to fade away. The “war on terror” was dwindling in prominence, and new enemies such as Russia seemed to be displacing fears of Islamic terrorism. Yet Britain’s Islamophobia has only intensified since then. A poll published in July found thattwo out of five Britons believe Muslims cannot integrateinto British society. Earlier in the summer, it was reported thatmore than half of Muslims in Britain had personally experienced anti-Islam prejudicein the last year, and a quarter in a public place.The evidence of a worsening climatefor Muslims has been mounting since two summers ago, when racist riots erupted across the UK, targeting mosques and asylum hostels. Watchingvideos of those events,I was disturbed by the parents who brought their young children to watch while mobs attempted, with apparently murderous intent, to break into the buildings.It was not only hardened far-right activists but a much broader cross-section of British societythat was willing to participate in racist violence directed at Muslims or asylum seekers assumed to be Muslim.But it is the widespread indifference to anti-Muslim racist violence that is most distressing. Last October,a white man raped a Sikh womanin her Walsall home while shouting Islamophobic abuse, believing her to be Muslim, and telling her he was a “British master”. The case attracted little public comment, despite seeming to be part of apattern of racist sexual crimesin the region. Likewise, there was only modest coverage of therampaging knife attackthat began at an Edinburgh mosque in June that left a number of men injured.To understand why Islamophobia is so pervasive, we need to grasp the deeper forces that enable it. The first is a bedrock of anti-Islam attitudes set during the 1990s when, with the cold war over, neoconservative intellectuals began to see in Islam a new enemy to replace communism. After Muslim protests against Salman Rushdie’s The Satanic Verses, some liberal commentators also began to declare that Islam was incompatible with western values. That all might have remained a problem of cultural adaptation to be solved through community-building, but during the “war on terror”, anti-Muslim racism was institutionalised in the daily functioning of the British state by the Labour government. Ministers made regular speeches singling out Muslim communities as threats, while under the Prevent policy, thousands of public sector workers were trained to regard ordinary Muslim political and religious behaviours asindicators of extremism.The second has to do with Palestine. The groundswell of opposition to Israel’s genocide in Gaza has been profoundly disconcerting to Britain’s foreign policy establishment. In turn, the hundreds of thousands of people who marched on demonstrations have been depicted as supporters of, or aligned with, Islamic extremism. That has restored a virulent atmosphere of animosity towards Muslims, who are again seen as dangerous and disloyal.We might think, for example, of Keir Starmer’s description ofplannedprotests on 7 October 2025 as“un-British”, his suggestion that further protests could be banned and hiscall for prosecutionagainst demonstrators using contested phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – despiterepeated explanationsthatsuch slogansarenot calls for violence. His comments reflect a widespread belief that ordinary protest – against a genocide! – is actually something else: the importing by Muslims and their allies of dangerous foreign ideologies. But to say that is to demonise the bond of allegiance between Muslims in the west and Muslims in other parts of the world fighting colonial occupations. That community-based international solidarity, of the kind that Britain used to hold up as evidence of its tolerance, should only be welcomed.Third, there are the barriers that make it hard to even raise the issue of anti-Muslim racism in a fruitful way. Talk about Islamophobia in the mainstream of British public life and you will face the ritual demand that you also condemn Islamic extremism and acknowledge antisemitism among Muslims. Of course, an attack on a synagogue is to be condemned as forcefully as an attack on a mosque. But the harder political question is how to create the conditions in which neither one of those attacks is made likely. In this, Jewish communities have the resolute support of the British government. Muslims do not. For decades, they have been on the receiving end of official disdain, and when they attempt to assert a modicum of political representation they areaccused of “family voting”.This matters because racism is about power. Its function is to divide society so that certain groups can be subjected to exceptional forms of exploitation or elimination. It is typically experienced as routine and structured powerlessness: the daily struggle to eke out a living in the face of discriminatory employers, public services riddled with suspicion, oppressive policing, immigration enforcement. Twenty-five years ago, policymakers at least paid lip service to racism as “institutional”, which helped to make visible some of its structural features. But that is no longer true. Racism is nowadays framed mainly as a problem of extremist individuals radicalised by hateful and polarising ideologies.Tackling racism means overcoming that lack of power. But the opposite is happening as governing elites continuously reinforce racist attitudes. A decision, for instance, to allow Ukrainians fleeing warpreferential entry to the UKwhile many Afghans fleeing war have to risk their lives in dangerous sea crossings – a policy of racial segregation that is as absolute and violent as those of the Jim Crow south of the US – is also a form of public messaging. Policymakers can hardly be surprised when ordinary people take their cue from such policies and decide that non-white immigrants must indeed be a threat to national identity. Racism applied at the border inevitably seeps into other areas of public life.Then there is the other response to talking about Islamophobia: to switch the conversation to a victimhood competition, the never-ending game of fighting over whose oppression is greater, as if there were some way to rank Black people, Jews and Muslims by the scale of horrors they have experienced. What this misses is that the fate of Muslims is inseparable from the fate of all people of colour in the UK. What Britain does to Muslims today it is likely to do to Black people tomorrow, and vice versa. And if a future government of Britain decided to carry out the mass deportation of Muslims from the country, I have no doubt it would decide soon afterwards to do the same to Jews. When supporters of Israel promoteIslamophobia, they are playing with fascist fires that will end up engulfing us all.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor decades, Britain’s mainstream political leaders have been enabling anti-Muslim racism, creating the ideal conditions for the rise of hard-right political parties. They continue to do so, sleepwalking to social disaster with an unconscionable recklessness and complacency. It is high time they woke up.Arun Kundnani is editorial director of Monthly Review PressDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsIslamophobiaOpinionIslamReligionJudaismRacecommentShareReuse this content

title: One Nation’s immigration policy deserves serious discussion – but not for the reason you might think | Alan Gamlen | The Guardian
description: Its proposal to regulate the size and composition of the temporary migrant population has merit, but other aspects are blunt and punitive
Author: Alan Gamlen
Headline: Its proposal to regulate the size and composition of the temporary migrant population has merit, but other aspects are blunt and punitive
Content: ‘Australia last recorded negative net overseas migration during the Covid border closure. Businesses failed, the economy contracted sharply and governments spent massively to cushion the shock.’Photograph: @ Didier Marti/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Australia last recorded negative net overseas migration during the Covid border closure. Businesses failed, the economy contracted sharply and governments spent massively to cushion the shock.’Photograph: @ Didier Marti/Getty ImagesOpinionOne NationOne Nation’s immigration policy deserves serious discussion – but not for the reason you might thinkAlan GamlenIts proposal to regulate the size and composition of the temporary migrant population has merit, but other aspects are blunt and punitiveMon 14 Sep 2026 04.21 EDTShareThe surprising thing aboutOne Nation’s new immigration policyis not that it contains extreme ideas. It is that parts of it deserve serious discussion.The best part is its pledge to regulate the size and composition of the temporary migrant population.This is the right number to target because it links directly to problems people care about, including poor planning, obstacles to integration and migrant worker exploitation.It is also feasible to contain. Its size is determined by two flows a government can control: the net intake of people on temporary visas, and the number who convert to permanent status.If these flows are kept equal, the temporary population stabilises. This is not a theory or forecast. It is a mathematical fact.By contrast, recent political debate has focused on net overseas migration (Nom): the difference between migrant arrivals and departures.Populist One Nation’s latest victory points to a thirst for unity. But there are better ways to feel connected | Peter LewisRead moreNom provides a rough measure of all migration. So to claim Nom is the problem supports the false conclusion that all migration is problematic.It is not. Some parts cannot and should not be regulated, such as movements of Australian citizens. Others, such as permanent migration, are already well regulated. Temporary migration, by contrast, was deregulated 25 years ago and now needs reviewing.Regulating temporary migration means controlling how many temporary migrants arrive, how long they stay, how many leave and how many become permanent residents. This is all possible under existing legislation. What is changing is the political consensus about whether it is desirable.Following Canada’s lead in regulating the temporary migrant population could help Australia avoid the problems of previous “guest worker” programs.One Nationdeserves credit for putting this on the table.Beyond this, however, its policy jumps from real problems to blunt, kneejerk cuts that would do more harm than good.First, it proposes reducing the temporary migrant population by 750,000 over three years by pushing net overseas migration into negative territory.That is extraordinarily radical. We tried it recently – and it went badly.Australia last recorded negative net overseas migration during the Covid border closure.Businesses failed, the economy contracted sharplyand governments spent massively to cushion the shock. Deliberately recreating that outcome makes little sense.double quotation markMigration is too important to be governed by slogans, arbitrary numbers or scapegoatsSecond, One Nation’s approach to departures is too punitive. Australia has the right to enforce its immigration laws, and people without a lawful basis to remain have to leave.But a three-month deadline backed by aggressive enforcement and lifetime re-entry bans raises questions about proportionality and due process. Families, children, long residence and legal processes make cases more complicated than a blanket rule allows.A migration system must be enforceable, fair and humane. The one-off Covid cohort requires a mix of conversion to permanence for some, extended temporariness for others and, for a few, incentives to depart once visas expire. The objective should be harm minimisation, not an arbitrary net migration target.Third, there is a racial dimension that cannot be ignored.One Nation has a long history of framing migration through racial and cultural division. That does not make every question it raises illegitimate. It is reasonable to argue migration is too high or temporary migration needs tighter regulation.10:29One Nation wants to restrict migration. A town in Barnaby Joyce's electorate welcomes it – videoBut blaming particular ethnic or religious communities for housing shortages, pressure on services, falling living standards, crime or security threats is analytically weak and socially corrosive. There is a crucial distinction between debating migration policy and blaming migrants.A better policy would stabilise the system after Covid and tackle the long-term imbalance between permanent and temporary migration. Both require governing the temporary population deliberately.We should collectively decide how large it should be, what purposes it serves, and where pathways should end. People should either leave when their temporary purpose has ended or, where Australia’s need and their connection have become permanent, have a realistic pathway to permanence.Australia once led the world in migration research and policymaking,but that capability has eroded. It needs an independent national migration research institute to produce authoritative data, model competing proposals and test political claims against evidence.Migration is too important to be governed by slogans, arbitrary numbers or scapegoats. If Australia wants a system that commands public confidence, it needs a better-informed debate about what migration is for and how it should be governed.Alan Gamlen is a professor at the School of Regulation and Global Governance at the Australian National University and director of the ANU Migration HubExplore more on these topicsOne NationOpinionMigrationAustralian immigration and asylumAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Phone coverage across the London tube? That’s sent me hurtling down a tunnel of despair | Lucy Pasha-Robinson | The Guardian
description: Going deep underground used to offer a refuge from the pressure to be constantly connected. That’s soon to change – and I’m not happy, says Guardian assistant Opinion editor Lucy Pasha-Robinson
Author: Lucy Pasha-Robinson
Headline: Going deep underground used to offer a refuge from the pressure to be constantly connected. That’s soon to change – and I’m not happy, says Guardian assistant Opinion editor Lucy Pasha-Robinson
Content: ‘Who has the self-discipline not to doom scroll all the way down the Central line? Not me, that’s for sure.’Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/PAView image in fullscreen‘Who has the self-discipline not to doom scroll all the way down the Central line? Not me, that’s for sure.’Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/PAOpinionLondon UndergroundPhone coverage across the London tube? That’s sent me hurtling down a tunnel of despairLucy Pasha-RobinsonGoing deep underground used to offer a refuge from the pressure to be constantly connected. That’s soon to change – and I’m not happyMon 14 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.49 EDTShareRejoice! For by the end of 2026, 4G and 5G mobile coverage is expected acrossthe whole London underground network. After months of delays and setbacks, 121 subterranean tube stations will be dragged kicking and screaming into the 21st century, joining Paris and Berlin in perma-connectivity bliss. But should we really be so happy about the rollout?Going deep underground was once a way of escaping the incessant communications of this exhausting modern life. Emails to respond to? WhatsApp messages piling up? The tube used to be one of the last remaining bastions of resistance against the constant expectation to do. To optimise. A simpler place where you could justifiably and believably ignore messages and reply later with a “sorry, I was on the tube”.I see the economic arguments for being better connected. Of course it’s good for business for us to be “on” all the time. And yes, I’ll admit, it is stressful when you get stuck in a tunnel and can’t let your boss know you’re running late. The rollout will also host the new Emergency Services Network (ESN), which will allow first responders to access vital information in an emergency – you can’t argue with that. And, credit where credit is due, the project inarguably representsa remarkable feat of engineering, involving 700 staff and the rollout of hundreds of miles of fibre cabling in the tube’s ancient tunnels.But on an individual level, what good comes from permanent online connectedness? Studies have shown it’sreally badfor our health. Perhaps you’ll be able to leave the office earlier if you’ve got ahead with your work during your morning commute. But it horrifies me that if clients want an instant response, or a bad boss is contacting you out of hours, there’ll soon be nowhere to plausibly hide. I know, I know, lots of people are already living in this brave new world. The tube has 60% connectivity as it is, and lots of commuters who use train networks outside London are used to tethering to a phone or connecting to the train wifi to get ahead on work during their journey. But wasn’t our inability to do the same once a huge point in Londoners’ favour? Yes, the tube is a sweaty sardine can but at least you could lose yourself in a (pre-downloaded) podcast or a book for half an hour, instead of fielding Slack messages from your colleagues.I can’t understand why we aren’t all more perturbed by this frightening normalisation of being always on. We should be railing against it with all our might. Why must every minute of our time be accounted for?Boredom and daydreamingare good for our brains – we should all be doing more of that.I’m aware that I sound like a luddite. And I know lots of people find it exceedingly useful being able to work through their to-do list in those idle minutes between leaving the house and arriving somewhere else. But it’s becoming abundantly clear with everynew alarmist studythat we need saving from ourselves when it comes to our phone addiction. After a day at work and one too many soul-sucking conversations with colleagues, who has the self-discipline not to doom scroll all the way down the Central line? Not me, that’s for sure.And people can’t be trusted to use this newfound perma-connectivity politely either. My colleagueDan Hancox has recently been bemoaningthe “astonishing number of grown adults who think it’s OK to surf the slopwave without headphones” – a phenomenon that has become noticeably and obnoxiously worse since the tube got internet. And don’t get me started on the number of people talking on the phone on loudspeaker these days. Must we all be made to listen to everyone’s personal conversations on the tube now too? Is this the future?Give it up, I hear you say. That ship has already sailed. Maybe. But I don’t have to be pleased about it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLucy Pasha-Robinson is a Guardian assistant Opinion editorExplore more on these topicsLondon UndergroundOpinionMobile phonesPublic transportLondonHealth & wellbeingInfrastructureTelecomscommentShareReuse this content

title: We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism? | Brigid Delaney | The Guardian
description: There are several answers, and none of them will be provided by tech. One thing we must do is identify the ingredients for human flourishing
Author: Brigid Delaney
Headline: There are several answers, and none of them will be provided by tech. One thing we must do is identify the ingredients for human flourishing
Content: ‘Flourishing is having a direct relationship with the natural world – not the world through a screen, or the natural world itself destroyed and degraded to create more capacity for screen-based existence.’Photograph: Martyn Williams/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Flourishing is having a direct relationship with the natural world – not the world through a screen, or the natural world itself destroyed and degraded to create more capacity for screen-based existence.’Photograph: Martyn Williams/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism?Brigid DelaneyThere are several answers, and none of them will be provided by tech. One thing we must do is identify the ingredients for human flourishingSun 13 Sep 2026 23.49 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 14.05 EDTShareImagining the future as almost entirely bleak has somehow crept into the collective consciousness this year.Last week I was having coffee with an old friend. He was telling me about what his kids wanted to study when they went to university, when he suddenly broke off, stared into the middle distance and said, “I wish I’d never had children.”He’d been a father for 20 years and I’d never heard him say that.“Oh my god, why?”He loves his kids beyond measure, but right at that moment, he looked desolate.“AI,” he replied.“What about it?”It could have been anything AI-related at this point in time. Was it that AI was going to take all the jobs his kids would have done, rendering their lives impoverished and without purpose or meaning? Or was it environmental, with all the water and energy AI consumes that is going to create further stress on the climate and make the planet uninhabitable? Or was it the news that week that AI could “kill all humans” within the next 10 years?It was the latter. We talked listlessly about the “killing all humans” thing for a bit, then moved on. But the shadow had fallen and I started wondering: is the polycrisis that we are facing so overwhelming that we don’t even have the capacity to talk about it with urgency any more? Instead it’s just there, in the air, ambient, like pollution, each particle containing its own particular doomsday scenario – and the only way to be in this atmosphere is to be numb to it.‘Too little, too late’: critics perplexed and suspicious of AI leaders’ call for a slowdownRead moreCurrently, for so many, all our past and future decisions are being refracted through this strange and dark moment.If you’re middle-aged, it looks like my friend, wishing (for a moment) you’d never brought kids into the world. Or it might be wondering if it’s worth continuing to work, if you’re not going to be able to enjoy a normal retirement.If you’re young, it looks like being unable to pick a university degree or vocation because you don’t know what professions or trades will be obsolete in a few years. Or wondering if it’s worth sacrificing and saving for an enormous house deposit, if you won’t have a proper job or future to service a 30-year mortgage.And if you’re older, it’s being grateful that you won’t be around to see it all unravel.There are several answers, or ways out of this nihilism we now face – and none of them will be provided by tech.The first is to wake up. Usually if someone wasactuallytrying to kill you – if they broke into your house and tried to murder you – you would fight back.Yet we greet the news that AI could cause human extinction with a glazed indifference.It’s worth remembering that no one actually asked for AI, and yet here it suddenly is trying to kill us. And even if that’s averted, it’s embedding itself in our workplaces and in our emotional lives (ChatGPT may be thelargest provider of mental health servicesin the US), robbing us of the capacity for critical thinking, and threatening economic and social stability.Why are we so numb in the face of what is – currently – a preventable threat?This numbness could be the result of almost 20 years of smartphones and social media where, addicted to entertainment, our attention spans have been shortened, and through our individualised algorithms, our capacity for organisation and collective action have been diminished.Or it could be the huge political power tech companies have that means all of us – including governments – feel powerless.It could be that the tide of this thing – this progress, theLast Invention– feels inevitable, and like the Luddites storming the factories, any resistance is ultimately useless.The next solution, after we wake up, is to return to first principles. What are the ingredients for human flourishing? Once we can articulate that, it’s like a rope that can guide us back to where we should be.Human flourishing is not having a machine to do your critical thinking for you – rather, it’s to engage in the pleasure and the pain of working things out for yourself.Flourishing is human-to-human relationships where we care for and nurture each other. It’s not talking to an LLM for 18 hours a day about our personal problems.Flourishing is having a direct relationship with the natural world – not the world through a screen, or the natural world itself destroyed and degraded to create more capacity for screen-based existence.These are all things worth fighting for. There is a place for technology in our world, it’s just that when we start hearing that it could destroy our world, we should wake up, shake off that numb feeling and start fighting back.Brigid Delaney is the author of five books, including The Seeker and the SageExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘A double entendre in every crevice’: what, beyond near-naked tennis, is Sydney Sweeney’s game? | Television | The Guardian
description: With her new, semi-nude advert for sports site Novig, the actor cements her reputation as the anti-woke poster girl. But is it real – or just provocation with a soft porn gaze?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: With her new, semi-nude advert for sports site Novig, the actor cements her reputation as the anti-woke poster girl. But is it real – or just provocation with a soft porn gaze?
Content: ‘A kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to sport’ … Sweeney in one of the images for the ad campaign.Photograph: NovigView image in fullscreen‘A kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to sport’ … Sweeney in one of the images for the ad campaign.Photograph: NovigAdvert reviewTelevisionReview‘A double entendre in every crevice’: what, beyond near-naked tennis, is Sydney Sweeney’s game?With her new, semi-nude advert for sports site Novig, the actor cements her reputation as the anti-woke poster girl. But is it real – or just provocation with a soft porn gaze?Zoe WilliamsMon 14 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBear with me here, but I’m beginning to suspectSydney Sweeneyis a very fine actor. It’s a skill she has been recognised for in the past, of course, winning nominations for Emmys for Euphoria and The White Lotus, but I mean it in a deeper sense, related to her work in advertising rather than drama – can she do more than play a role? Can she make you feel what she’s feeling?In her “controversial” new ad for the sports prediction site Novig (the scare quotes are because, when you’re begging for controversy this hard, you shouldn’t just be handed it on a plate), she adopts the garb of various sports. Her face, body, aspect, gait and mien are all carefully configured to amp up the erotic overtones to the maximum degree, and yet the feeling that beams out of each image is: “This is really going to piss people off, and I couldn’t be more delighted.” Her expression is so speechful that you cannot help but share in some of her hellion joy.‘Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like’: female athletes spark backlash against viral advertRead moreIn brief: the proposition of the betting site is that it’s only for betting on sports – no wars, no deaths, no politics, just sports. Even the captions, absent the Sweeney, are a red rag to a bull, since betting on wars and death is a disgusting and inhumane thing to do – the surge in people trying to spin cash out ofdeaths in Iran, in Ukraine, says something profound about where we’ve got to in late capitalism. Whatever that profound thing is, it’s definitely not funny.However, we are where we are, and that’s not Sweeney’s concern. She is there to wrinkle out the double entendre from every conceivable crevice. Do spherical things remind you of breasts? What if I get these two American footballs and put them in front of my actual breasts? Would it help if I was naked to the waist? Ah, better still if I were wearing no clothes at all and only the footballs stood between me and my modesty? The age-old tennis shot, immortalised by the80s Athena posterin which the viewer is invited to consider just how nearly they can see a player’s butt – well, that’s here, only this time minus the skirt.View image in fullscreenSweeney in another shot for the ad campaign.Photograph: NovigSweeney’s facial expressions are like a WikiHow gallery, “how to: soft-porn” – they often feel quite old-fashioned, pert or faux naive, more like 70s graphic novel erotica than modern, up-to-the-minute pornography. Yet, throughout, there is a layer of knowingness: “I know exactly how much I’m going to drive you mad, and why.”Truthfully, it’s hard (as a card-carrying member of the wokerati, just out here in the world, trying to keep up) to figure out what the fundamental provocation is. Sweeney famously last made headlines with the “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” ad for American Eagle Outfitters. It was taken by many to be a call back to Donald Trump’s “You have great genes, you know that?” speech, which itself was taken as a densely layered challenge to the world, that his supporters were better human specimens than everyone else. Was the speech white supremacist or simply Trumpian-supremacist? You couldn’t really stick anything on him because, as ever, it was only atmospherically decipherable. Sweeney, however – with her very blondness, her unarguable whiteness – people did stick a white-supremacist agenda on, one she soon decried, saying she was against “divisiveness”.11:05Sydney Sweeney naked sports ad controversy: what’s she playing at? - The LatestEver since, Sweeney has been taken as an anti-woke poster-girl, though since nobody can agree what “woke” means, still less what “anti-” it entails, this poster is more confusing than an avant garde typographer’s ball. She seems to want to kick that hornet’s nest with this Novig ad, but is it by inviting her own objectification? Or is there a complicated message in there about femaleness in elite sport, which has become such a lightning rod for anti-trans activism? Or are we supposed to disapprove of the pornification of the visual realm?None of the above! Ariarne Titmus, four-time Olympic gold medal-winning swimmer, explained on Instagram: it’s “a kick in the face to every woman who had dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity”. And now she says it, yes, that makes perfect sense. What Sydney Sweeney’s game is, beyond almost-naked tennis, is anyone’s guess.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionAdvert reviewSydney SweeneyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying’: how we made cave horror classic The Descent | Movies | The Guardian
