description: ‘The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower’
Author: Alex Deller
Headline: ‘The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower’
Content: ‘I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked’ … Shauna Macdonald in the 2005 horror.Photograph: 1996-98 AccuSoft Inc., All rights reserved/PatheView image in fullscreen‘I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked’ … Shauna Macdonald in the 2005 horror.Photograph: 1996-98 AccuSoft Inc., All rights reserved/PatheHow we madeMovies‘The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying’: how we made cave horror classic The Descent‘The child crawler whose head I crush with my boot was only 11, bless him. It was actually me stamping on a cauliflower’Interviews byAlex DellerMon 14 Sep 2026 10.23 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 18.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeil Marshall, writer/directorI was introduced to Christian Colson at Celador Films off the back of [2002 horror film] Dog Soldiers, and I pitched them a project – actually a feature-length version of my student graduation film – about zombies on an oil rig. They liked it but said it was too expensive, so on the train back to Newcastle I was asking myself what would make a really scary horror film that could be contained and so made on a budget. I was thinking of things set in the dark and was like, well …caves. At the back of my mind was a school trip to a lead mine where the guide had said, “OK, everybody, turn your lights off” and, for the first time, I experienced a darkness that I just couldn’t fathom.We wanted the film to feel as realistic as possible: when you’re caving, the only lights you have are what you take with you. There are no beautiful shafts of light making everything look pretty. It meant having huge portions of the screen in total darkness, so only when a character turns around and shines a light you finally see what’s in the shadows.double quotation markAlex said her lines with an ice pick through her neck. Then I caved her head in with a stoneDarkness was definitely my friend, but it did mean a lot of planning because each character had to have something they could light the scene with, even if it was just a box of matches. Sam McCurdy, the director of photography, and I discussed lighting sources that we could potentially use, and I structured the film around who had which light at which time. This gave us a lighting scheme: if you’re with the fire, it’s Sarah. If it’s a torch, it’s Juno.There isn’t a single real cave in the whole film. It was a mixture of amazing sets by Simon Bowles, a couple of matte paintings and a miniature set built by Leigh Took – the water pouring down the waterfall wasn’t water, it’s salt.For the crawlers, I wanted something very basic-looking, not too many lines or details. The challenge was how to make them scary but keep them human, because the notion is that these are the cavemen who stayed in the cave rather than those who left the dark and started building cabins in the open. Visually they were a hybrid of Nosferatu and Iggy Pop, but movement-wise I thought we should make them like spiders – the way they’ll stop and be perfectly still before suddenly going off at 100 miles an hour and then stopping again.I conceptualised the film as Sarah’s descent into being this primal savage: her undergoing a rebirth in order to survive, even though you’re not sure she’s going to be able to go back to society afterwards.View image in fullscreen‘I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked’ … a crawler in The Descent.Photograph: PatheShauna Macdonald, played SarahThis was the era of FHM, Loaded and all those lads’ mags, so I initially thought it was going to be girls looking sexy in tight spaces covered in blood and gunge. I wasn’t interested in that. When I read the script, though, it was excellent. It was about a grieving mother and I also needed to be physically strong and brave. I thought, “I have to do this part because I don’t know if I’ll be able to pull it off.”We weren’t allowed to see the crawlers or even any pictures of them. I was the first to see one because we were shooting chronologically once we got into the caves. The others were all asking “what does it look like?!” but I didn’treallyknow because it was quite far away. I just knew it was grey or white and slimy, and it looked a bit like Gollum.I think Neil was right to keep us apart, because when we were faced with them, I was being leapt at by a really scary man, basically naked, who’d been training for months and months – that really focuses the mind. When we came to fight them, they were so animalistic it was really unnerving. The actors had figured out how the crawlers’ system worked and their different characteristics. You felt like you were fighting a pack with all its dynamics, and that was pretty intimidating.That whole sequence where Sarah goes into survival mode was great. First I had the dying scene with Alex Reid, who played Beth, just making it look really easy. It was like, “OK, Alex, you’ve had an ice pick through your neck, but it’s really important that you tell these plot points …” And she was, “Yeah, cool, no problem.” And then, of course, I cave her head in with a stone. Then I get leapt on by a child crawler. He was only like 11, bless him, and I crushed his head with my boot, which was actually me stamping on a cauliflower. Then the mother finds out, and we have this fight sequence where one mother has to kill another to survive. The eye-gouging was very, very satisfying. Then another crawler comes along and I bash his head in too. Afterwards I’m submerged in this pool of blood, which was a Jacuzzi that they’d overflowed. This amazing stunt girl had to do the run and jump, because the pool was so shallow they couldn’t insure an actor to do it. All I had to do was emerge and take the glory.In the press, it was all about “girl power”. But we were like: “Have you seen what we do to each other?!” Whatwasvery girl power was how fiercely we actors supported each other and we continue to do that. The only way you can really show love is by turning up for your friends, and the six of us have done that repeatedly for the last 21 years or so. We’ve got a WhatsApp group and still meet regularly. I do wonder, if we’d met on a different project, would the same thing happen? Or was it the film? If you throw a group of people in a cave, maybe you all come out bonded for life.The Descent is available on 4K UHDExplore more on these topicsFilmHow we madeHorror filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Oasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concerts | Oasis | The Guardian
description: After 2025’s wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, and revisit the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumph
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: After 2025’s wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, and revisit the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumph
Content: Liam Gallagher (left) and Noel Gallagher of Oasis, who are to return to Knebworth in 2027.Photograph: Joshua Halling/Oasis/PAView image in fullscreenLiam Gallagher (left) and Noel Gallagher of Oasis, who are to return to Knebworth in 2027.Photograph: Joshua Halling/Oasis/PAOasisOasis announce 2027 tour, including return to Knebworth 30 years after historic concertsAfter 2025’s wildly lucrative reunion, the Gallagher brothers will tour the UK, Ireland and US, and revisit the Hertfordshire site of their greatest live triumphFrom the archive: How did the Guardian cover Oasis at Knebworth 1996? Well … we didn’tLaura SnapesMon 14 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOasis have finally confirmed new tour dates for 2027, including their long-rumoured return to Knebworth for a run of shows 30 years after they played a historic two nights at the Hertfordshire venue in 1996.“Start the celebrations!”, the band said in a statement. “After a period of reflection, The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force in Recent British History” – a quote froma Guardian opinion pieceabout the band – “has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people. Come witness the fitness. It shall be a sight to behold.”Titled Oasis Live 27, the dates encompass the UK, Ireland, mainland Europe and the US, beginning in Glasgow on 21 May, and touring through Manchester, Munich, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome, Boston, Las Vegas and Slane Castle (north of Dublin), ending with four nights at Knebworth in September.The band had teased the news in a massive drone display above Manchester’s Etihad stadium last week, after hinting at the dates on Instagram.The tour follows Oasis’s acclaimed 2025 reunion, which saw them play 41 dates spanning the UK, Europe, North and South America, east Asia and Australia, 16 years after they split in 2009. “You struggle to think of another artist that’s received such a vociferous reception,” wrote Guardian critic Alexis Petridis ina five-star reviewof the first night of the tour in Cardiff.The 2027 tour will be Oasis’s first visit to mainland Europe since their reunion and adds US cities they didn’t visit during that run. Their return to Paris will be particularly poignant, given it was shortly before a 2009 set at the city’s Rock en Seine festival that the band first split up.In the UK, tickets will cost between £71.50 and £266.60. Those hoping to buy them will have a happier experience than those in the same position last year: all pricing information for Oasis Live 27 has been shared in advance after action by the competition watchdog forced Ticketmasterto change how it advertises tickets, including ending “misleading” information about seats, after fan backlash over its handling of the 2025 tour.Last year, the use of “tiered” pricing meant that some fans, expecting to pay £148.50 per ticket, found themselves faced with costs of £350 at the checkout – and only a matter of minutes in which to decide whether to go ahead with their purchases. Now, Ticketmaster must tell fans 24 hours in advance if tiered pricing will be used, which tickets it covers and how the system works. When the sale is live, the price range must be shared and updated as tickets sell out.Anyone wanting a ticket for 2027’s tour mustregisterbetween now and 4pm BST on 17 September. The registration has been introduced “to reduce queuing times and organised ticket touting in order to give genuine fans the best possible chance to buy tickets,” according to organisers.View image in fullscreenOasis pictured at Knebworth in 1996.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyFans had a chance to revisit the 2025 tour – or catch up on what they missed – as a documentary about the reunion,Don’t Look Back in Anger, hit cinemas last week after premiering at the Venice film festival. It earned glowing reviews for its emotional portrait of the band’s fans.The documentary didn’t touch on the furore around ticket prices, other than one onstage comment from Liam Gallagher: after referring to the people in the cheap seats, he added: “Actually there are no cheap seats, sorry about that.”The news that Oasis would return toKnebworth was first teased by an unlikely suspect, the British peer Baroness Taylor of Stevenage. In October 2025, she suggested in the House of Lords that Oasis would be playing five shows “in the fantastic venue of Knebworth House”, just a mile away from her own residence.Don’t Look Back in Anger trailer – videoShe quickly retracted her comments in the chamber,clarifying to the Guardianthat she was “speaking hypothetically following speculation that they would play Knebworth again as they did in August 1996”.In August, it was reported that SJM Concerts managing director Simon Moran had secured an events licence for Knebworth, prompting further speculation about an Oasis appearance. The licence would cover audiences of 125,000 people.At the original 1996 dates, the band played to 250,000 fans – just one tenth of the number who applied for tickets, estimated at the time to be more than 4% of the entire British population. “This is history,” Noel Gallagher told the Knebworth crowd on the second night. The bandrecently started selling replicasof Noel and Liam’s respective outfits on the night.A 2021 documentary, the prosaically titled Oasis Knebworth 1996, positioned the concerts as “the peak of British culture” wrote Guardian music editor Ben Beaumont-Thomas ina four-star review. The film’s voiceovers, he continued, implied that “all live music went downhill afterwards. It’s a lie every generation tells itself.” Liam subsequently headlined the park in June 2022.UK Music estimated that the band’s five nights at Manchester’s Heaton Park last year led to music tourist spending in the north-westrising 16% year on year to £1.4bn. Momentum behind the tour was alsocredited with boostingthe UK’s ongoing vinyl revival.Do you remember the first time? Why Britpop nostalgia just won’t go awayRead moreOasis are also rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027, the festival’s return after a fallow year in 2026.Their reunion poured more fuel on the fire of enduring Britpop nostalgia, sparking acritically panned playdocumenting the rivalry between Oasis and Blur, an album called Britpop by Robbie Williams and evenan embrace of Oasis in the US, a country that had been historically immune to their charms.Oasis Live 27 tour dates in fullCeltic Park, Glasgow: 21, 23, 25, 28, 29 MayEtihad Stadium, Manchester: 4, 6, 8, 11, 12, 15, 18, 19, 22, 25, 26 JuneAllianz Arena, Munich: 2, 3 JulyEstadi Olímpic Lluís Companys, Barcelona: 10, 11 JulyJohan Cruijff Arena, Amsterdam: 16, 17 JulyStade de France, Paris: 23, 24 JulyStadio Olimpico, Rome: 29, 30 JulyGillette Stadium, Boston: 10, 13, 14 AugustAllegiant Stadium, Las Vegas: 20, 21, 24 AugustSlane Castle, Ireland: 4, 5 SeptemberKnebworth, Hertfordshire: 11, 12, 18, 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsOasisNoel GallagherLiam GallagherPop and rockBritpopnewsShareReuse this content

title: The desecration of DC: from a giant arch to a nuke-proof bunker, Trump’s legacy-building blingfest is an architectural atrocity | Architecture | The Guardian
description: A bloated ballroom, a six-storey military HQ, a helipad-cum-cocktail patio, a gilded angel on a giant arch honouring himself … our architecture critic deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of Washington
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: A bloated ballroom, a six-storey military HQ, a helipad-cum-cocktail patio, a gilded angel on a giant arch honouring himself … our architecture critic deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of Washington
Content: A lust for supersizing … the plan for Trump’s triumphal arch.Illustration: US Commission on Fine Arts/ReutersView image in fullscreenA lust for supersizing … the plan for Trump’s triumphal arch.Illustration: US Commission on Fine Arts/ReutersArchitectureThe desecration of DC: from a giant arch to a nuke-proof bunker, Trump’s legacy-building blingfest is an architectural atrocityA bloated ballroom, a six-storey military HQ, a helipad-cum-cocktail patio, a gilded angel on a giant arch honouring himself … our architecture critic deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of WashingtonOliver WainwrightMon 14 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen you have a developer as US president, you might expect some zhooshing up of the capital. A few buildings renovated, maybe some parks replanted. But when you have a megalomaniac builder in charge, things can get out of hand. A decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected,I askedwhat it might mean for the US to be led by a real estate tycoon whose career had left a trail of broken promises, angry buyers and endless lawsuits, with rules flouted,heritage trampledand the world pockmarked by a fleet of aspirational towers clad with a flimsy veneer of luxury. The answer is worse than I could have imagined.With the air of a nightmarish Hollywood sequel, Trump 2 has seen the president’s true architectural ambitions unleashed: The Blingpire Strikes Back. As America’s self-styled decorator-in-chief, Trump has not only overseen the gilded mutilation of the White House, but embarked on the Mar-a-Lagofication of Washington DC itself, applying his gold paintbrush to statuary, daubing ponds with flaking pool liner, and brewing plans for a colossal triumphal arch – all procured in ablizzard of no-bid contracts. And, in true dodgy salesman style, this programme of bauble-building is turning out to be a high-profile decoy for deeper damage being wrought elsewhere.double quotation markIf the government wants to bulldoze the Statue of Liberty, nothing can be doneThe bloated White House ballroom is the most emblematic project of Trump’s reign so far, a chandelier-bedecked warehouse conceived on a scale that would make Ceaușescu blush. Standing like an overly iced wedding cake atop a multilevel concrete bunker, it is a swaggering confection that masks deep-rooted paranoia: a decadently wrapped panic room, where a besieged dictator might hole themselves up.View image in fullscreenWhat lies beneath … the ballroom hides a full-scale military complex, including a hospital.Illustration: McCrery Architects/White House“It won’t interfere with the current building,”Trump promised last July, when he announced the plans. “Not touching it.” It would seat 650 guests and cost $200m, funded by private donations. Less than three months later, without waiting for congressional approval, he tore down the historic East Wing, anddumped the rubble on a nearby public golf course(which he also plans to redevelop). The ballroom ballooned, as if injected with rapid weight-gain formula, to seat 1,000 in a building three times the volume of the White House. The price has also tripled to $600m, at least half of which will now be picked up by the taxpayer.Trump boasted that his ballroom will be “more beautiful” than Versailles, but it looks like something thrown together from the classical off-cuts bin, without any regard to how the pieces fit. “It has all the kneejerk gestures of classicism,” a former Commission of Fine Arts (CFA) official told me, “but they are not integrated in a way that makes any sense.”A sweeping ceremonial staircase leads to nowhere. A grand pedimented entrance is shunted to one end of the east facade. The portico columns run four rows deep (“The supreme court is three deep,”Trump noted. “No other building has it, and I did it because it’s incredible.”) The ballroom’s proportions are so out of whack, it will make the White House look like a lopsided fiddler crab, the swollen appendage vastly dwarfing the original building.View image in fullscreenNot exactly flag blue … the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool.Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/ReutersThe inflated scale was too much to bear for its architect, the bowtie-wearingJames McCrery II, who protested at the increasingly Frankenstein nature of the classical details being applied. Enter Shalom Baranes, whoseDC firmhas handled multibillion dollar federal contracts, including the renovation of the Pentagon after the 9/11 attacks.Baranes’s experience with fortified facilities has come in handy, given that the project has evolved into what Trump now calls “the Magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex”. The party hall, the presidentconfirmed in March, “essentially becomes a shed for what’s being built under” – namely a six-storey military-grade bunker, replete with a command and emergency operations centre, a full-scale military hospital, secure telecommunications hubs and situation rooms, all serviced by specialised air-handling and filtration networks to protect against biological, chemical and radiological threats. “It’s meant for if there’s a nuclear attack,” Trump has boasted. “The concrete is so hard, I’m not sure you could take it down.”Behind the overblown cornice, the ballroom’s roof will be home to a military drone port and air-defence missile system. Images show it looking like an aircraft carrier parked next to the White House. In typically Trumpian newspeak, the project has gone from being a space to entertain dignitaries to a “desperately needed National Security structure” that must be completed at all costs.After court rulings halted construction, the supreme court recentlyweighed in to allow it to resume– although, tellingly, the ruling made no comment on the project’s legality. But questions in the courts have revealed just how far Trump’s aides see his absolutist rule extending. “If the government decides, very quickly, to bulldoze the Statue of Liberty,”one judge asked, “nothing can be done?” A lawyer for the administration responded: “I think that’s right, yes.”View image in fullscreenDrinks all round … construction continues on a helipad-cum-cocktail patio on the south lawn of the White House.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APSimilarly bullish efforts are being made to force through the president’s second flagship vanity project, the elephantine triumphal arch. It was casually announced last October, with 3D-printed models displayed like tacky souvenirs in the Oval Office. It is planned to tower 250ft above Memorial Circle, a vast roundabout on Columbia Island in DC’s Potomac River – 1ft for every year of US independence. But there has been no ambiguity about what the looming edifice is really there to honour. When asked, Trump simply replied: “Me.”It “will be the GREATEST and MOST BEAUTIFUL Triumphal Arch,” he boasted on social media, “anywhere in the World”. He has cited Roman precedents and “the one in Paris”, adding that his version “will surpass it in every way”. Oddly, given his fondness for the North Korean regime, he has neglected to mentionPyongyang’s Arch of Triumph, built in 1982 to mark Kim Il Sung’s 70th birthday. Clad with 25,500 blocks of sparkling white granite, one for each day of Kim’s life, its crowning stone slab rises 10m taller than Trump’s (although his is topped with a statue for an extra 25m of vanity height).Hitler’s Triumphbogen, also unmentioned, would have been twice the size.To aid his Napoleonic cosplay, the president has hired Harrison Design,purveyors of gaudy McMansionsfrom Atlanta to LA, with the arch project led by Nicolas Charbonneau, principal of the firm’s Sacred Architecture Studio. Charbonneau first sketched the idea to illustrate an April 2025 essay by conservative critic Catesby Leigh, titledWashington Needs an Arch. It proposed a modest structure of 60ft. Trump got hold of the idea and, with his irrepressible lust for supersizing, pumped it up fourfold.View image in fullscreenDwarfing the White House … the ballroom will have a drone port on its roof.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersAs with the ballroom-bunker, the arch has become larger and more encrusted with gilded ornament – in a word, more Trumpian – as it has progressed. The final design, unveiled this April, features a 60ft golden-winged Lady Liberty sprouting from its summit like an oversized cake-topper, flanked by two plump eagles. Even Trump’s allies have suggested the design could be toned down. At a CFA review, McCrery, the first ballroom architect, advised removing four golden lions from the base of the arch. “They’re noble, they’re courageous, and they’re strong,” he noted. But “they’re not of this continent”. The arch must celebrate American triumphs only – and that goes for the animals too.Trump’s reflecting pool saga: a timeline of failure and finger-pointingRead moreThe National Park Servicehas determinedthe project will “adversely affect” dozens of historic sites around DC, while a group of Vietnam veterans has filed a lawsuit, arguing the arch will be an unwelcome “expression of domination”, with its observation deck looming over Arlington National Cemetery. Neither of these are proving to be obstacles,with excavation set to begin soon.Preliminary works do not augur well. A mockup of the arch was erected for the Great American State Fair in July, made of plywood wrapped with white vinyl. It buckled in the heat, its surfaces warping and peeling, while globules of expanding foamoozed from its wonky cornice. It was instantly dubbed the Temu arch – a fitting moniker, given that Trump’s Oval Office swags appear to have beensourced from the fellow Chinese online marketplace Alibaba.The ballroom and the arch received tens of thousands of objections from the public, but both projects were fast-tracked through the system. As the former CFA official told me, it was “highly unusual” that the initial concept schemes were granted final approval without details being resolved. The ballroom took just 12 minutes of deliberation. And it has set the tone of things to come. There’s nothing a developer hates more than red tape, and Trump has vowed to streamline regulations across the board. Beyond speeding up his DC follies, the proposed changes will lubricate drilling, pipe-laying and datacentre building, in the name of “reclaiming America’s proud heritage as a nation of builders”.View image in fullscreenGold, gold, everywhere … Trump in the Oval Office.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesObscured by all the controversy around these trophy projects is the fact that the administration has moved to weaken protections on historic buildings and landscapes drastically, unleashing the steamroller of development across the country. The changes to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act would narrow the definition of historic places, exclude consideration of the “visual, atmospheric or audible” consequences of projects on historic sites, and reduce requirements for consulting Indigenous tribes and the public. As Brent Leggs, president of the National Trust for Historic Preservation,remarked, it would “eviscerate the preservation of our shared civic and cultural heritage in the United States”.The irony couldn’t be clearer. Trump bloviates about continuing America’s tradition of monument building, while weakening the very mechanisms that exist to protect the country’s heritage. Still, by slashing these protections, at least he is paving the way for his own additions to be toppled just as hastily as they were erected.‘Dictator-for-life vibes’: our architecture critic on Trump’s bulletproof ballroom blingRead moreGiven the construction quality so far, future topplers might not need much help. The Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool has now been drained for a second time, after the coating used in the first $15m renovation began peeling offwithin days of its completion. Despite a new filtration system intended to keep the water a pristine shade of “American Flag Blue”, massive algae blooms quickly turned it a swampy green. While Trump blamed vandals, justice department legal filings eventually conceded the failure was due to the “hasty and botched” renovation. “I have a guy who’s unbelievable at doing swimming pools,” Trump boasted, before awarding the no-bid contract toa companythat had worked on his Virginia golf course.Elsewhere around the capital, the “Safe and Beautiful” initiative has seen $76m spent on fountains, $5m on gilding a pair of equestrian statues of The Arts of War and The Arts of Peace, $500,000 on a single statue pedestal to display a statue of a prominent slave owner, which had been removed from Delaware amid Black Lives Matter protests, and countless other acts of cosmetic surgery in the name of cleaning up the “cesspool” of DC.View image in fullscreenNewly covered in gold leaf … the Arts of War statues.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOne of the crowning trinkets will be theNational Garden of American Heroes, for which $40m has been ringfenced. According to Executive Order 13978, this park of 250 statues will “reflect the awesome splendour of our country’s timeless exceptionalism” in the face of the “reckless attempt to erase our heroes, values and entire way of life”. The list of figures to be commemorated includes slave owners and others whose statues were toppled in the wake of George Floyd’s murder. Sculpture expertsdescribedthe proposed timeline as “completely unworkable” and likely to produce “slapdash and uninspired” work, suggesting the only place with foundries capable of realising a project on this scale and speed would be China. Alibaba prepare!Trump’s construction mania is all-consuming. He uses press conferences to show off his latest renovations andhas spokenof how building is the “fun” thing he does to relax, in between kidnapping South American presidents, bombing the Middle East and bullying Greenland. But White House insiders say his therapeutic hobby has become the policy priority, a massive drain on the administration’s energies and resources.The Resolute desk has never seen so many samples and swatches – whether marble for the Lincoln bathroom, golden drapes for the East Room, or the “million-year lifespan” pavers for the driveway – a White House shopping list that now tops $900m. The Oval Office looks like a developer’s showroom, most recently displaying a two-metre model ofTrump’s $22bn makeover of Dulles airport, boasting gold-mirrored ceilings and “the largest garage in the world”.The closer autocrats come to their end, the more frenziedly do they build. Nero embarked on a golden palace before he was driven to suicide. Marie Antoinette built a model hamlet before she was beheaded. Hitler pored over architectural plans in his bunker during his final days. Trump is buried in catalogues of fixtures and fittings, busy inspecting the workmanship of his helipad-cum-cocktail patio, as the country crumbles around him.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureDonald TrumpUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Touring can take musicians to isolating, anxious extremes. Access to therapy on the road is a vital support | Music | The Guardian
description: I know from our early days how high-pressure road life can be. While big tours often hire therapists, grassroots acts can’t afford it. I’m pleased to back a new scheme that aims to change that
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I know from our early days how high-pressure road life can be. While big tours often hire therapists, grassroots acts can’t afford it. I’m pleased to back a new scheme that aims to change that
Content: Thom Yorke and Philip Selway of Radiohead performing in 2006.Photograph: Jo Hale/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThom Yorke and Philip Selway of Radiohead performing in 2006.Photograph: Jo Hale/Getty ImagesMusicTouring can take musicians to isolating, anxious extremes. Access to therapy on the road is a vital supportPhilip Selway, RadioheadI know from our early days how high-pressure road life can be. While big tours often hire therapists, grassroots acts can’t afford it. I’m pleased to back a new scheme that aims to change thatMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTShareWhenRadioheadstarted touring, it was hugely exciting, but we got signed when we had been going for five or six years and had only really played in Oxford. Suddenly you’re entering a new world: the first flush of fame, being compared to everyone else, the furnace-like experience when a band takes off and a whole new routine of late nights, bad food and everything else that goes on around live music. Everything is heightened and it can be very isolating.In 1992 we were playing small venues in a van and then suddenly in 1993 we were spending the second half of the year in the US. On our second long tour that year, everything caught up with me. I kind of withdrew into myself. Something about being in the US made me feel “impostor syndrome”. I really did feel a very long way from home. All that anxiety has to come out somewhere – for some it’s drink and drugs – but for me it came out in my playing. There was one particular show where we were opening for Tears for Fears and another band who had [Blondie’s] Clem Burke on drums. Clem was my absolute drummer hero but I just hit peak overwhelm, and my drumming went off a cliff. Every limb seemed to be going at its own speed. The kick drum became like trying to open a heavy door.By the end of the tour it was very noticeable. I was lucky in that I could speak to my wife – this was pre-Zoom or FaceTime, so meant very expensive phone calls! – but after that tour one of our managers asked me to go and have a chat and broached it with me very nicely. Having that space to begin talking about it was absolutely invaluable. Similarly, when we opened for James and then REM, they became kind of mentors: seeing how other people navigate it all was fascinating.On Radiohead’s tour last autumn, with the help of the Music Industry Therapist Collective, we were able to put an initiative in place to support the health and well-being of all tour personnel. The MITC provided introductory sessions during rehearsals and production build, and confidential drop-in therapy sessions were available to anyone in the touring party during the tour if they wanted them. But until now there’s been nothing like that available for bands playing venues like the ones we did when we started.At that level, your margins are nonexistent, your workload is much greater – loading the gear and so on – and you’re driving yourself between shows. You’re expected to get your head down and get on with it, but it can mean times when you’re not necessarily looking after yourself physically and you can feel very isolated. There’s an emotional and geographical displacement in moving from place to place and living on top of each other. There’s the sound check, the gig, meeting people afterwards, anxiety that some people guiding you may not have your best interests at heart. You can feel really vulnerable, and there’s no way of getting off that roundabout until you get home. It’s difficult to talk about because nobody wants to rock the boat, and other people might be going through the same thing, so you don’t want to burden them.‘The working class can’t afford it’: the shocking truth about the money bands make on tourRead moreThat’s why I’m supporting a new project called the Pay It Forward Fund, which has been set up by Tamsin Embleton and the Music Industry Therapist Collective to provide much-needed mental health support for musicians and crews on smaller tours, having grown out of the kind of help MITC already provides to larger tours. If someone is looking to reach out to a therapist, it can be really good to talk to someone who has lived experience in the music industry, so this project will mean people have someone to talk to who understands what they’re going through. I’ve volunteered for the Samaritans since I was a student and know how important it is to talk.I’d have really appreciated something like the Pay It Forward Fund back in Radiohead’s early days, so that’s the kind of space I hope it can provide. Initially £272,000 is being provided to finance 150 tour teams of practitioners over a three-year period, an occupational health, mental health education and pastoral care programme for crews and artists on smaller tours. Hopefully after that it will become an everyday part of touring and make the sort of difference it would have done for me. You might be on the other side of the world, but you can reach out and talk to somebody face to face.Applications for the Pay It Forward Fund are now open. title: Beck: Ride Lonesome review – stunning end to the heartache trilogy of Sea Change and Morning Phase | Beck | The Guardian
description: On his first album in seven years, Beck keeps the quality control extremely high as he surveys mid-50s malaise in the wake of divorce
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: On his first album in seven years, Beck keeps the quality control extremely high as he surveys mid-50s malaise in the wake of divorce
Content: Guess I’m doing fine … Beck.Photograph: Mikai KarlView image in fullscreenGuess I’m doing fine … Beck.Photograph: Mikai KarlBeckReviewBeck: Ride Lonesome review – stunning end to the heartache trilogy of Sea Change and Morning Phase(Iliad/Capitol)On his first album in seven years, Beck keeps the quality control extremely high as he surveys mid-50s malaise in the wake of divorceAlexis PetridisMon 14 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last timeBeckreleased an album it was 2019 and the singer-songwriter found himself in a strange and unenviable position. In some quarters, the arrival of Hyperspace was eagerly anticipated precisely because his personal life was in turmoil. Nine months before its release, his 15-year marriage to actor Marissa Ribisi had ended in divorce, an experience he understandably described as heartbreaking. Unfortunately for him, there exists a pervasive argument that Beck’s greatest work is born out of misery.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Ride Lonesome.Photograph: CapitolHis beloved 2002 album Sea Change featured a set of disconsolate acoustic songs written in the wake of a break-up with his long-term girlfriend Leigh Limon that Beck had initially thought were too personal for public consumption. They were certainly very different from the knowing, postmodern approach with which he’d made his name, but no matter: Sea Change went on to become a huge critical and commercial success. It wasn’t entirely clear what prompted the gloomy mood of 2014’s Morning Phase, but it very much seemed to be cut from similar musical and lyrical cloth. Some critics suggested it was the best album of his career; it subsequently won three Grammys, including album of the year. Given the circumstances, there was much pre-release speculation that Hyperspace would be a companion piece.Instead, Hyperspace was synth-heavy, produced by Pharrell Williams and clearly influenced by vaporwave: its tone was dreamily buoyant and noticeably light on wracked soul-bearing. After its release, Beck seemed to tacitly suggest to fans of Sea Change and Morning Phase that there wouldn’t be any more where they came from. “When I try to shoe-horn my life into a song,” he told the New Yorker, “it gets really ham-fisted.”Seven years on, he appears to have reconsidered. The first thing you hear on Ride Lonesome is a softly strummed acoustic guitar, echoey pedal steel and Beck’s voice. “Walk away, hang your head on the hollow moon,” he sings, as the album’s title track gets under way: should there be any lingering doubt about the mood it’s intent on evoking, it goes on to reference Julie London’s Cry Me a River and Johnny Thunders’ You Can’t Put Your Arms Around a Memory. “It feels like I’ve been here before,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him.He certainly has. There’s an intentionality about the way Ride Lonesome reconvenes the team responsible for Sea Change and Morning Phase – the former’s producer Nigel Godrich is once more behind the mixing desk, the backing musicians who appear on both albums are present and correct, the orchestrations are the work of Beck’s father David Campbell – and about the artists the music here evokes. As on Sea Change’s Round the Bend and Morning Phase’s Heart Is a Drum, the ghosts of Nick Drake and his string arranger Robert Kirby are very clearly summoned up, most noticeably on In the Night. On Run Away, we find Beck exactly where he was on Sea Change’s The Golden Age and Morning Phase’s Unforgiven: alone, behind the wheel of a car in the small hours, aimlessly driving around in an attempt to assuage his unhappiness.Beck’s greatest songs – ranked!Read moreSimilar sound, similar mood, similar lyrical themes: of course, the danger is of diminishing returns. But Ride Lonesome never feels like a pale imitation or a craven attempt to recapture past glories. That’s partly because of the standard of the songwriting. Beck has suggested that one reason the album took so long to make is because of stringent quality control: songs were recorded, then set aside for years, then reconsidered, a huge amount of material was discarded. You can tell: everything here, from the sparse country-rock of Slow Canyon to the lush, harmony-drenched Falling Through My Hands is melodically exquisite; every song has the requisite emotional impact.But it’s also because Ride Lonesome is clearly an album made by a noticeably older artist than either of its predecessors: its mood is marked not just by the collapse of a relationship, but a sense of time passing, of things – to borrow a phrase from Nick Drake – moving just a little too fast. “I don’t know where I’m going,” he sings on Bleed, as strings gently rise and fall around him, “but it feels like I’ve been here before”: a neat capturing of a very mid-50s kind of malaise. An affecting sense of weariness seeps into everything, even the ostensibly optimistic – and utterly lovely – closer Beyond the Light comes filled with evocations of lost “nameless days” and of “the dying of the light”.Unfortunately for Beck, Ride Lonesome does little to dispel the aforementioned theory about his best work being born out of unhappiness. There’ll be consolation in the fact it’s also that rarest of things: a sequel to a sequel that’s every bit as good as its predecessors.Ride Lonesome is released on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsBeckPop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: In an age of superhero fatigue, Marvel’s best shot is to think small – and outside the box | Movies | The Guardian
description: Sebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green light
Author: Ben Child
Headline: Sebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green light
Content: Sebastian Stan as Winter Soldier AKA Bucky Barnes, with Anthony Mackie, in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier on Disney+Photograph: Julie VrabelováView image in fullscreenSebastian Stan as Winter Soldier AKA Bucky Barnes, with Anthony Mackie, in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier on Disney+Photograph: Julie VrabelováWeek in geekMoviesIn an age of superhero fatigue, Marvel’s best shot is to think small – and outside the boxBen ChildSebastian Stan says he pitched Marvel a mid-budget thriller starring his Winter Soldier character. Perhaps the studio should give it – and other modestly scaled vehicles – the green lightMon 14 Sep 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTShareBlink a little and you might think we are back in 2019. The latest Spider-Man film, Brand New Day, has just passed $2.4bn at the global box office, to become the third-highest grossing film of all time behind Avatar and Avengers: Endgame. Meanwhile Avengers: Doomsday is reported to have already earned more than $50m in US ticket presales alone, despite the fact that it doesn’t come out until December. Clearly we are in the middle of a superhero renaissance.And yet it doesn’t really feel like it, largely because it is something of a turnaround forMarvel, after a pretty disappointing 2025 in which all three of the studio’s releases underperformed. Captain America: Brave New World took $415m worldwide, Thunderbolts* managed $382m and even the well-reviewed The Fantastic Four: First Steps stalled at $521m, against a reported $200m budget. These are hardly Madame Web numbers but they do suggest there is still a problem about what to do with all those superheroes who cannot sustain a $300m multiversal extravaganza.double quotation markMarvel hasn’t really known what to do with the Winter Soldier since the Wakandans removed his Hydra programmingEnter Sebastian Stan, AKA Marvel’s Winter Soldier, who this week suggested the solution might be to place them in cheaper genre films instead. Speaking to New York Magazine,the actor revealedthat he had pitched Marvel boss Kevin Feige a new, “Sicario-esque”” approach for Bucky Barnes’ next adventure. “We keep a real small budget,” he said. “It’s about a guy who thinks he recog­nises someone from his past that had something to do with when, you know, he was brain­washed, and he gets obsessed with this per­son. He goes on a whole jour­ney to try to fig­ure out who this per­son is. It’s a thriller.”In any other period, this might feel like just another example of an actor trying to do his producer’s job for him. But Stan is on something of a career high, having earned his first Oscar nomination forThe Apprenticeand won a Golden Globe forA Different Man. And the idea of dropping the Winter Soldier into a murky, Sicario-style conspiracy thriller almost feels custom-designed to offset superhero fatigue. Stan was perfectly fine in last year’s Thunderbolts*, but the reality is that he could easily have been replaced by Shang-Chi, Ms Marvel or one of the Eternals without anyone really noticing.View image in fullscreenMaking up the numbers … from left, Danai Gurira, Chadwick Boseman, Chris Evans, Scarlet Johansson and Stan in Avengers: Infinity War.Photograph: Chuck Zlotnick/APMarvel hasn’t really known what to do with the Winter Soldier since the Wakandans removed his Hydra programming somewhere between Civil War and Infinity War. We know he’ll be in Doomsday but do we really need him making up the numbers while the better-known Avengers prevent reality from collapsing all over again? Wouldn’t it be better to put him in a grimy $50m thriller in which the fate of one damaged man’s mind matters more than the continued existence of the entire spacetime continuum?This could end up being a whole new thing. Give Ghost a stripped-back heist movie in which her ability to walk through walls is used to break into an actual building. Put Red Guardian into a cold war spy comedy about the increasingly implausible missions he claims to have undertaken against Captain America. Have Wong in an occult detective story involving one cursed object, three suspicious magicians and no portals to other dimensions.View image in fullscreenAn unhinged character study … Joaquin Phoenix as Arthur Fleck in Joker (2019).Photograph: DC Comics/Warner Bros/AllstarThere are also precedents suggesting that these kinds of superhero films can work, even if they are from outside the MCU. Logan was really an elegiac western with Wolverine as an ageing gunslinger ferrying a child across a hostile frontier. Joker sat far closer to the sort of unhinged urban character studies Martin Scorsese made in the 1970s and early 80s than it did to anything involving capes. Between them, these two films earned almost $1.7bn worldwide. It is also arguable that Marvel itself once made these kinds of movies. Captain America: The Winter Soldier was framed as a 1970s-style conspiracy thriller, Ant-Man was configured as a heist movie, and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, thanks to Sam Raimi’s distinctly Evil Dead II-style camera work, ended up with notable horror leanings. All were better movies than the lukewarm ensemble pieces that Marvel seems to have favoured in the past half-decade.No one is arguing that Marvel should stop building towards crescendos involving the entire Avengers gang teaming up to halt the latest threat to the known universe. But there are surely more interesting ways to build interest in the lesser-known heroes who spend most of such films lurking in the background. So why not let Bucky have his $50m breakdown? He can always go back to standing behind Thor when the multiverse explodes afterwards.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekSuperhero moviesSebastian StanMarvelSicariocommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve never been more terrified!’ Carly Rae Jepsen on motherhood, stardom and her horniest album ever | Carly Rae Jepsen | The Guardian
description: Call Me Maybe made the singer-songwriter famous – but also confused. Who was she? Who was her music for? Fourteen years later, about to release the double album Day and Night, she finally has some answers
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: Call Me Maybe made the singer-songwriter famous – but also confused. Who was she? Who was her music for? Fourteen years later, about to release the double album Day and Night, she finally has some answers
Content: ‘At this stage in my life, I feel much more comfortable with the parts that I don’t have full control over’ … Carly Rae Jepsen.Photograph: Vince AungView image in fullscreen‘At this stage in my life, I feel much more comfortable with the parts that I don’t have full control over’ … Carly Rae Jepsen.Photograph: Vince AungThe big interviewCarly Rae Jepsen‘I’ve never been more terrified!’ Carly Rae Jepsen on motherhood, stardom and her horniest album everCall Me Maybe made the singer-songwriter famous – but also confused. Who was she? Who was her music for? Fourteen years later, about to release the double album Day and Night, she finally has some answersJuan A RamírezMon 14 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarly Rae Jepsen is as bubbly as ever as she comes down for breakfast at Manhattan’s Hotel Chelsea. She’s one of those pop princesses, like Kylie Minogue, whose voice and demeanour remain unchanged whatever the situation. And she feels at home at this New York landmark where, last year, she married the musician and producer Cole MGN. That a wedding at the Chelsea would need to be kept to about 100 people was an immediate selling point. “I loved that it was smaller,” she says. “It felt big to me! I didn’t even get time with all the people that were there.”Slow jams, smash hits and Popeye samples: Carly Rae Jepsen’s 20 best songs – ranked!Read moreWe’re here to talk about her new album, though, which comes out 14 years after the song that made her world-famous. Born and raised in the city of Mission in British Columbia, Jepsen had come third on Canadian Idol in 2007, and then released a low-key folk album called Tug of War in 2008, before dropping Call Me Maybe four years later. It became the bestselling global single of 2012; her second album, Kiss, came out in the same year. Now, at the age of 40, she has six more studio albums under her belt. The latest, Day and Night, is her take on marriage and motherhood. And, in its own way – which is to say, a bit coy, a bit breathy – it might also be Jepsen’s horniest album to date.“I’m gonna spit my tea out,” she says when I suggest this, laughing while steadying the cup in her hand. It turns out I’m not the first to broach the subject. During a session with King Princess, Jepsen’s fellow singer-songwriter called her a “very horny writer”.Jepsen thought she’d been subtle about it. “I don’t love it to be aggressively there,” she says. “However, I think that longing is really sexy – knowing what you want and being not afraid to say it out loud. I’ve always found a real thrill in being the person who’s advancing the thing; who’s a couple steps ahead of the person they’re chasing.”As far back as Call Me Maybe, she points out, her music has contained a thread of exhilaration about being the pursuer. If lust is so prominent in Day and Night, it’s because Jepsen and her husband fell in love during the album’s creation. “‘Don’t kiss the producer’ was a rule of mine,” she says – and yet she did.And it’s not the only time she’s broken rules or confounded expectations. Say what you will about Call Me Maybe – and it’s easier to appreciate the track when it’s not blaring out from every storefront – but it demonstrated Jepsen’s mastery of pure pop: melodic, catchy, with fiendishly clever lyrics Abba would be proud of: “I get lovingly told that I’m part Canadian, part Swedish,” she says, delightedly.It sold more than 18m copies, reached No 1 in 19 countries, and won Jepsen a worldwide recording contract. It also helped Kiss, the album on which it appeared, reach the Top 10 in Australia, the UK, Canada and the US. Its follow-up, 2015’s Emotion, was ecstatically reviewed.View image in fullscreenJepsen lets rip at the 2024 Governors Ball in Queens, New York City.Photograph: Nina Westervelt/Billboard/Getty ImagesIn virtually any other era, Jepsen might be filling stadiums. But changing tastes aside, the music scene has fragmented thanks to streaming and social media, and the charts can be topped by a song thatmany have never heard. The one-time “megastar” is now more likely to be described as an “indie darling”. How does she feel about her industry?“There’s a little bit that I don’t totally know or understand, or stay checked into,” she says, “and I don’t know if that aloofness just comes from the fact that it’s not super interesting to me.” Maybe it’s a survival tactic, she adds, “but the reality is, long ago I became aware of what my strategy would be, and I’ve stuck to it. I knew around the time that I made Emotion that I was more excited about having a strong, small-but-mighty group, than I was about trying to be confused and feed the masses.”Now she knows who she is and who her fans are, but that knowledge didn’t come overnight. “I needed to take a second to figure out what it was that I liked about pop music to begin with, and what it was that I thought I had to contribute to it,” she says. “That’s why I went and did Cinderella, which was a really weird left turn.”View image in fullscreenJepsen prepares for her lead turn in Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Cinderella, 2014.Photograph: Bruce Glikas/FilmMagicIn 2014, less than a year after winning three Canadian Juno awards for Call Me Maybe and Kiss, Jepsen made herBroadwaydebut in a production of the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical. “I think everyone in the industry around me at the time was like: ‘What is she doing?’,” she says. But ticket sales were good, her stint on Cinderella was extended (“I love theatre, so it was like getting my cake and eating it”), and the experience reconnected her to her craft: “It was more of an artistic choice than a strategy, I guess.”“I think what I feel about pop music is not that I love all of it, but I have a really strong opinion about it,” Jepsen says. “I don’t know that I can define it, but I was excited about trying to figure out the thing that makes me feel like I did with Rufus, where you know a stranger.” “Rufus” is Rufus Wainwright, whose moody 2001 song Poses first inspired her to “take a run at this music thing”. That unknowability is what still excites her about pop: “The idea that comes across, hopefully, in this album, is that you can play with so many different genres as ingredients and it can still be the thing.”double quotation markI needed to take a second to figure out what I liked about pop music, and what I had to contributeIt was Jepsen’s former A&R representative, John Ehmann, who fostered that playfulness when he encouraged her to release a “B-side” follow-up to Emotion, knowing she had written far more songs than she had released. Initially hesitant, and worried that the songs weren’t up to par, Jepsen was convinced by the lower-stakes connotation of the B-side concept, and the fact that the record would only be an EP. She particularly liked the idea “that it was a bit more like showing the inside process”. Fans loved it and, from there, these projects became increasingly official. After 2016’s Emotion: Side B came 2020’s Dedicated Side B – a full album – and then 2023’s The Loveliest Time, a companion to the previous year’s The Loneliest Time, salvaged from the “100 or so” tracks she’d written for the album but then culled.“It ended up being such a weird door that opened for my life,” this notorious overwriter says. “I’ve so enjoyed this permission to not only get more experimental but, because I write so much, have this other place for things to live. So even when I was creating Dedicated [in 2019], I was already allotting things to this other idea of: ‘Maybe not everyone will get it, but I’ll have some fun.’”From Dedicated onwards, Jepsen felt she was “expanding and exploring, excited about the vastness of what a pop song could be”. But for Day and Night, her goal was cohesion: “something that felt like it lived in a home; a pure world.”View image in fullscreenContemplating the vastness of pop … Jepsen.Photograph: Vince AungSonically, she’d found herself drawn to sunshine through the soul singer Minnie Riperton and jazz vocalist Blossom Dearie, and then the “darker scents” of house music and chillwave producer Bullion, with whom she collaborated on the 2024 single Rare (which appeared on his album Affection, released on Ghostly International). A visit to the Abba Voyage hologram concert, meanwhile, reinvigorated her appreciation for “a tight melody, with updated production”.Then her longtime guitarist, Tavish Crowe, suggested a thought experiment: a musical walk through a house party that included stops by the stoners, the ravers, the couple fighting in a locked room. They landed on the idea of a double album that could sustain all of these ideas. “The challenge became making sure that each of those albums was expansive enough,” she says. “I wanted cohesiveness, but I also didn’t want 12 songs that felt like you were listening to the same song on repeat.” There’s more delving into her thought process, then she stops herself: “Sorry, I sound so nerdy when I talk about this.”Nerdiness is not what comes across on Day and Night, though. There’s that aforementioned sexiness, in lyrics that are less about getting someone into bed than about the difficulty of making it out the next morning. And there’s domestic bliss. Jepsen became a mother in March, which she “didn’t always think was on the cards”.View image in fullscreenA new-mother post on Jepsen’s Instagram.Photograph: @carlyraejepsen / InstagramShe remembers working in a Vancouver coffee shop 20-odd years ago, seeing young kids and thinking: “I would love to hold that cute baby.” But, she says, “I always had this very clear vision for my life; that I was on a mission to make music, and that was, for a very long time, my priority. Similar with getting married.” There was never a bridal Pinterest board for Jepsen, hardly even the thought of a husband. “All of these things were nice, hypothetical ideas that belonged to other people. Maybe I almost romanticise this idea that, as an artist, it was more my job to be an observer of life than to wildly participate.”Now she’s left being a bystander behind. “At this stage in my life, I feel much more comfortable with the parts that I don’t have full control over,” she says. “There is nothing more vulnerable than having a child. It’s this whole heartbeat that breathes outside you. I’ve never been happier and more terrified – but I feel very, very alive.”After Day and Night, Jepsen’s focus will be on the result of a phone call with the theatrical producer Mike Bosner, five years ago. Having heard that she was interested in writing for Broadway, Bosner rang Jepsen and said: “Lena Dunham, 10 Things I Hate About You.” She slaps her palms on the table and mimes an awestruck face.View image in fullscreenJepsen performs at the 2024 Bonnaroo Music and Arts festival.Photograph: Douglas Mason/WireImageJepsen had wanted to work with Dunham for years, having met her through their shared friend and collaborator Jack Antonoff. “She’s been a support from the beginning, always so sweet about certain songs,” Jepsen says, recalling the Girls creator’s love of Guitar String/Wedding Ring, from Kiss. (Dunham used a key line from the song – “If you cut a piece of guitar string / I would wear it like it’s a wedding ring” – as an epigraph for the “Falling in Love” chapter of her 2014 autobiography, Not That Kind of Girl.) “I’ve always thought – and I think everyone feels this way – that the way she puts words together is hilarious and brilliant,” says Jepsen.View image in fullscreenHeath Ledger and Julia Stiles in 1999’s 10 Things I Hate About You.Photograph: Touchstone Pictures/AllstarTheir adaptation of Gil Junger’s 1999 teen comedy 10 Things I Hate About You – a collaboration with co-composer Ethan Gruska and playwright Jessica Huang – is due to open next August. The task of scoring an existing story, let alone one that’s a spin on Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, with a lead character to whose “anger and passion” Jepsen thinks every woman relates, “is a completely different energy of approaching music. You want to honour the 90s and really do it justice.”Having caught a workshop presentation of the production earlier this year, I tell Jepsen how I heard her voice throughout the cast’s. “That is the best part,” she beams, adding that she has enjoyed the challenge of writing for different characters, particularly men. But, she adds: “I do believe if you haven’t felt it you can’t write it – you have to really feel them in order to have anything for them to say.“When you’re singing on Broadway, when you think about the reason one would need to sing in real life, the emotion has to be so potent that words are no longer doing it,” Jepsen says. “There’s only a song when the feeling erupts.”Day and Night is released via Schoolboy and Interscope on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsCarly Rae JepsenThe big interviewBroadwayfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sunday in the Park With George musical cancelled, after Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey both drop out | Musicals | The Guardian
description: The star-studded Sondheim musical has hit the buffers after a second star, Jonathan Bailey, joined his Wicked colleague Ariana Grande and left the production
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: The star-studded Sondheim musical has hit the buffers after a second star, Jonathan Bailey, joined his Wicked colleague Ariana Grande and left the production
Content: Never on a Sunday … Ariana Grande, left, and Jonathan Bailey have both now left the production of Sunday in the Park With George.Composite: Shuttershock, GettyView image in fullscreenNever on a Sunday … Ariana Grande, left, and Jonathan Bailey have both now left the production of Sunday in the Park With George.Composite: Shuttershock, GettyMusicalsSunday in the Park With George musical cancelled, after Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey both drop outThe star-studded Sondheim musical has hit the buffers after a second star, Jonathan Bailey, joined his Wicked colleague Ariana Grande and left the productionTim JonzeMon 14 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst, it wasAriana Grande who dropped out. Then her co-starJonathan Baileyfollowed her out the door. Now, the London revival of Sunday in the Park With Georgehas been cancelled altogether, with organisers perhaps anticipating that it would be hard to sell tickets for a star-studded musical without the stars.Grande and Bailey, who appeared together as Glinda and Fiyero in Wicked andWicked: For Good, had originally been cast as Dot and George in Stephen Sondheim’s hit musical. It was set to debut at the Barbican in the summer of 2027.But in August, Grande pulled out, citing the need to take a break from “endless public scrutiny”. The pop star, who was coming to the end of her Eternal Sunshine tour, had been the subject of press speculation surrounding her weight loss and general health, which intensified after the release of the music video for her song Petal.The production vowed to soldier on, with new casting promised, but was then hit with the news earlier this month that Bailey had also had second thoughts. In a statement, the Bridgerton star announced his departure, saying: “Ari is one of my dearest friends. After much consideration, I have decided to also step back from Sunday in the Park With George. This brilliant, introspective musical has been a real passion project for me, and I feel incredibly lucky to have shared in its journey with this team. I look forward to seeing what the team, and the two actors who will now take on these roles, will create with it.”Sadly, it seems that what production company Empire Street Productions have decided to do with it is cancel it, at least in the short term. A statement from the company said: “The planned 2027 production of Sunday in the Park With George at the Barbican will no longer proceed as scheduled. Empire Street Productions will retain the rights with a view to presenting the production in 2028. Further details will be announced in due course.”The musical, created by Sondheim and James Lapine, made its Broadway debut in 1984, starring Mandy Patinkin and Bernadette Peters as George and Dot. A year later it won the Pulitzer prize for drama. The musical’s story is inspired by the Georges Seurat painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, and follows the artist as he attempts to finish the pointillist masterpiece, while exploring his relationship with Dot, his lover and muse.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsStephen SondheimAriana GrandeWickedWicked: For GoodJonathan BaileynewsShareReuse this content

title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after ‘free Palestine’ speech | Macklemore | The Guardian
description: The American rapper will no longer support Sheeran’s US leg of Loop tour after comments at MetLife Stadium show
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The American rapper will no longer support Sheeran’s US leg of Loop tour after comments at MetLife Stadium show
Content: Macklemore performing on stage at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts on 3o August.Photograph: Arnaud Finistre/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMacklemore performing on stage at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts on 3o August.Photograph: Arnaud Finistre/AFP/Getty ImagesMacklemoreMacklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after ‘free Palestine’ speechThe American rapper will no longer support Sheeran’s US leg of Loop tour after comments at MetLife Stadium showAdrian HortonMon 14 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMacklemorehas been dropped from the remainder of the US leg ofEd Sheeran’s Loop tour, after the American rapper drew headlines for saying “free Palestine” on stage at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.In a brief speech between songs on 4 September, the Grammy-winning artist told the audience he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”, prompting apetitionfrom the Israeli American Council demanding his removal from the tour.Messina Touring Group, the promoter of the US leg of Sheeran’s tour,toldRolling Stone: “As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s US Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming US tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans. After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” Sheeran did not immediately reply to requests for comment.The Seattle-bred rapper was slated to open for Sheeran at eight of the remaining 10 shows of his US Loop tour, which will resume on 19 September in Philadelphia. The venues that allegedly objected to Macklemore’s return include stadiums in that city as well as outside Boston, Atlanta, Charlotte, Indianapolis, Dallas and Tampa.Macklemore, long anoutspokensupporterof the rights of Palestinians and those in Gaza, delivered the remarks at his first appearance on the Loop tour on 4 September. “A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: ‘Free Palestine,’” he said in atwo-minute speech. “I said: ‘Free Palestine!’ I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.”Alluding to possible controversy, he added that not “speaking my heart in order to keep my own comfort, and the audience’s comfort … is the day that I no longer deserve to be on stage”, and called US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) a “terrorist organization”. He also showed images of the devastation from Israeli military attacks in Gaza during his protest anthem Hind’s Hall, which celebrated protesters’ occupation of a building they named in honor ofHind Rajab, a six-year-oldkilled by the Israeli militaryin 2024.The comments spurred the group StopAntisemitism to accuse the musician of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda” in an Instagram post that was amplified by the singer Pink. In another post, Pinkexplainedthat she did not object to Macklemore saying “free Palestine” but added: “I have never asked for another artist to be silenced and I’m not asking now. I don’t need anyone fired, and I don’t need a refund. What I need is to be able to say, as a Jewish mom, ‘that scared me, and it scared people I love,’ without being told our fear is just propaganda, and without being told I’m somehow cool with genocide because I noticed?”The Israeli American Council also called for Macklemore to be removed from the tour, claiming his statements raised the question of “where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda”.At the second of his appearances at MetLife on 5 September, Macklemore reiterated his support forPalestineand addressed Jewish members of the audience: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”In a lengthyInstagram poston Monday morning, Macklemore confirmed that Sheeran and his team had decided to remove him from the tour, but noted that he, Sheeran and Pink were not victims. “We have careers, money, opportunities, safety and audiences around the world,” he wrote. “Whatever consequences any of us face for what we say, we get to go home to our families.“The victims are the Palestinian people. The men, women and children who have been killed, starved, displaced and forced to live through unimaginable violence,” he added,citingthe more than 20,000 children killed in Gaza by the Israeli military since the 7 October 2023 terrorist attacks by Hamas.Macklemore explained that the decision came after a week of “difficult conversations” with Sheeran, a friend of 13 years whom he considers a “brother”, though “as I told Ed multiple times on the phone, our friendship can’t change my responsibility to tell the truth about what happened.” According to Macklemore, Sheeran was under pressure from stadium owners rallied by Robert Kraft – the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and their Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, where Sheeran was next slated to play – to drop Macklemore from the tour, lest the English singer be barred from their venues. “Ed was in a fucked up position,” the rapper wrote. “He knew it. His typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it had never been before.“What I said at MetLife I have been saying on stages around the world for almost three years,” he added. “So why is it an issue now? Because now I’m sharing the stage with one of the biggest artists in the world, in some of the biggest stages in America.”Macklemore ended his multi-page post by reiterating his call to “free Palestine”: “If those words cost me the stage, while turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I’ve ever been on.”In a statement provided toNBC News, Kraft said the decision to bar Macklemore from Gillette Stadium, which is intended to be “a welcoming environment for all guests”, was made after the comments at the MetLife shows and “a broader history of rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.“I would welcome the opportunity to sit down with Macklemore and discuss the facts, because ultimately our goal is the same – peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate,” he added. He also blamed Hamas for actions that “have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike”.“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” he said. Kraft, who is Jewish, created the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, now known as the Blue Square Alliance Against Hate, in 2019. He is a longtimesupporterof the state of Israelas well as its allyin the White House, Donald Trump.The North American leg of Sheeran’s tour will conclude in November at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, Florida, which earlier this year hosted two shows by Ye, the rapper formerly known as Kanye West, who has ahistoryofantisemiticstatements. Tour openers Lukas Graham and Aaron Rowe are set to take the stage as planned.Explore more on these topicsMacklemoreEd SheeranIsrael-Gaza warPalestinePop and rockGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: Jack Thorne warns some fellow scriptwriters are using AI ‘to cheat’ | Jack Thorne | The Guardian
description: Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate scripts
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate scripts
Content: ‘If publishers, studios, streamers, can point to the writer as the problem, that gives them the excuse to behave however they’d like with content,’ Thorne said.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/WireImageView image in fullscreen‘If publishers, studios, streamers, can point to the writer as the problem, that gives them the excuse to behave however they’d like with content,’ Thorne said.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/WireImageJack ThorneJack Thorne warns some fellow scriptwriters are using AI ‘to cheat’Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate scriptsMichael SavageMedia editorMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 04.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJack Thorne, one of Britain’s most successful screen and stage writers, has warned that some people in his profession are using AI “to cheat”, as he called for laws banning the secret use of the technology to generate scripts.Thorne, who co-wrote the hit Netflix dramaAdolescenceand wrote the stage play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, said that “writers need to be squeaky clean” in the face of AI models that “steal” the creative industry’s work.In a wide-ranging speech in London, Thorne attacked government inaction over the AI industry’s mass-scraping of material to train their models. He said Keir Starmer’s government had been “a bit dazzled by tech” and lamented a failure to protect the copyright of writers.However, he also said he had heard worrying stories about the misuse of AI among writers that risked undermining the profession.“I have spoken to a number of execs and studio heads about their use of AI, and got hugely different responses, but what I did hear from them – and what anecdotally I’ve heard from a few writers close to me – is that some in my profession are using AI to cheat,” he said.“What I’m not talking about here is using AI to help – to discuss things with, to check for spelling errors or help with layout. I’m talking about using AI as a replacement for endeavour, as a replacement for writing at all. Using prompts instead of writing words.“That is, simply put, failing to write, they’re cheating their employers in doing so, and they’re cheating their fellow writers.”Thorne, who is the president of the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain, warned that “if publishers, studios, streamers, can point to the writer as the problem, that gives them the excuse to behave however they’d like with content”.He added: “Passing AI work off as your own needs to be unlawful. If you use AI to generate content and you do not declare it as such, then that is fraud and the companies you do it to should be entitled to prosecute you.“To discourage it, the impact should be sizeable, and that requires laws but also us as an industry responding. Just as it should get you threatened with expulsion at university if you use it for essays, so it should have some professional impact on your career if you use it for text.”Thorne said broadcasters such as the BBC and Channel 4 should threaten sanctions against those found to have used AI to generate their work.“To protect the most vulnerable, it is essential,” he said. “As writers, what we are is what we make, and both the law and our industry should be absolutely crystal clear on that.”Thorne also said AI must not be allowed to impersonate actors, directors and writers.He criticised inaction by the government to protect the intellectual property of writers from AI models and said the way ministers acted in the next five years “will define what the next hundred years looks like for every writer in this country”.Last year, Starmer’s governmentabandoned a proposalthat would have required artists and copyright holders to actively opt out of having their material fed into AI systems,after a backlash. Ministers instead held a consultation on the issue.“There are so many things the government could be doing,” Thorne said. “Crucially, observation without intervention for fear of upsetting their apple cart could be replaced by observationwithintervention for fear of upsettingourapple cart.“The pieces of AI we use cannot be built using thievery. Cannot be built on a copyright crime. That’s what government is there for, to set lines in an argument. While adaptation is probably necessary, legislating so that you are protecting us from the worst excesses is essential.”He added: “This requires government leadership. In fact, it requires our government to take global leadership.”A government spokesperson said: “Copyright laws must protect the UK’s position as a creative powerhouse while unlocking the extraordinary potential of AI-driven innovation. We are doing the work that’s required to get the right outcomes so both the creative and technical sectors can flourish in this country.”Explore more on these topicsJack ThorneAI (artificial intelligence)Television industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZA  | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Miki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’
Content: NAZA directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor at the Venice film festival. There are now calls to strip them of their Israeli citizenship.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNAZA directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor at the Venice film festival.
