There are now calls to strip them of their Israeli citizenship.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesNAZAIsraeli minister threatens to strip Israeli film-makers of citizenship over Gaza documentary NAZAMiki Zohar accuses Oscar-winning directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of ‘treason against the state’‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceSian Cain,Lorenzo Tondoin Jerusalem and agenciesMon 14 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTFirst published on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s culture minister has called for the Oscar-winning Israeli directors ofNAZA, a documentary about the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, to be stripped of their citizenship, accusing them of “treason against the state”.NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, is named for an acronym used by Israel’s intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza.In the film, the Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor spoke to 24 Israeli military or intelligence whistleblowers who outlined the AI-powered targeting systems used to bombardGazathat have killed tens of thousands of civilians. In one interview, a source claims that approval had been given to kill 500 NAZA in order to kill one Hamas member.The 80-minute documentarywon a special jury prizeat this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receivinga 25-minute standing ovation– a festival record.0:50NAZA director says ‘it’s important Israelis watch this film’ after win at Venice festival – videoOn Sunday, Israel’s culture minister, Miki Zohar, accused the directors of being willing to “harm their homeland in order to receive applause from antisemites around the world”.“I will act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators for treason against the state,” Zohar wrote on X.On Monday, Zohar expanded on these comments, issuing a statement saying: “This morning, I wrote to the director general of the Population and Immigration Authority and the director general of the interior ministry, asking them to examine the possibility of revoking the Israeli citizenship of the creators of the anti-Israel film NZA [sic] for breach of loyalty to the state and collaboration with the enemy.“I also asked them to investigate how the materials used in the film were obtained, who was responsible for obtaining them, and whether any actions carried out in acquiring or disseminating them could amount to assisting the enemy during wartime.“Freedom of expression is not a licence to betray the state. Anyone who acts against Israel during a war must know that there will be a price to pay.”The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, condemned the film. “It’s shocking. We ⁠are fighting global antisemitic incitement and when it comes from within us it is intolerable,” he said in a video posted on social media. “And ‌now two Israeli directors portraying ‌the IDF as war criminals receive applause at the Venice festival.”Other Israeli ministers also took aim at the directors, who won an Oscar in 2025 for their film No Other Land about Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank.‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceRead more“You are a disgrace and an embarrassment to the entire people of Israel. Go away!” the far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said on X.“I am certain that your friends, that is to say our enemies Hamas in Gaza, will welcome you with open arms.”On Monday, the chief of general staff of the Israeli military claimed the film was “based on blood libels, deliberate distortions of reality and grave, false accusations against IDF soldiers and commanders”.Eyal Zamir said military lawyers were examining “possible legal measures concerning the film and those involved in it”.The former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman called Abraham and Szor “haters of Israel”, while the former prime minister Naftali Bennett described it as “a horrific blood libel against our sons and daughters”.The revocation of nationality is legally possible in Israel, although it is rarely applied. In 2022 the supreme court confirmed that the state may strip people of their nationality if they have failed to show “loyalty”, for example by committing acts of espionage or treason. The law was also expanded in 2023 to apply to people convicted of “terrorism”. The law requires the interior minister to submit the revocation request, the justice minister to approve it and judges to validate it.Abraham’s family home wastargeted by a rightwing mobafter the world premiere of 2024’s No Other Land, which focused on the destruction of Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank.“We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic,” hetold the Guardian, adding: “For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons.“Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”The Israeli military initially responded toNAZAby saying it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary and criticised the use of anonymous testimonies, saying the identities of the whistleblowers “cannot be verified”. In a later response, the military said “the allegations required a detailed, evidence-based response rather than a blanket dismissal”.Some figures on the Israeli left praised the film and its directors. The former lawmaker Yousef Jabareen, chair of the leftwing Hadash party, congratulated the directors on the award, thanking them for bringing “these horrific crimes and the brutal reality in Gaza” before millions of people.Anat Saragusti, the head of press freedom at the Union of Journalists in Israel, said: “The Israeli public has not received anything close to adequate coverage in Hebrew of what has happened in Gaza. For much of the war, Israeli media barely showed the Palestinian side of the story – the civilian casualties, the children killed, the destruction. People could find that information elsewhere if they actively looked for it, but they were not seeing it in the mainstream Hebrew-language media.”In an editorial, the Haaretz newspaper urged Israelis to confront what it described as the reality of Israel’s actions in Gaza. “By screening their film at the Venice film festival,Abrahamand Szor are trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that there’s a black stain on the way Israel is conducting war in Gaza, to put it mildly,” Haaretz wrote.The Palestinian militant group Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an Agence France-Presse tally based on official Israeli figures. Hamas militants also took 251 hostages to Gaza.The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the subsequent three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties.A Guardian News & Media spokesperson said: “The Guardian is disturbed to see the authoritarian response toNAZAin Israel.“Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are brave journalists and film-makers. The attacks against them come from people who have not yet seen the film.“NAZA is based on more than three years of investigative journalism. The testimonies it contains are true and we believe they deserve to be heard. The interviews were given by confidential journalistic sources.“We will robustly defend NAZA – and the team behind it – from any attacks or attempts at censorship.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaGazaPalestineIsrael-Gaza warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Somerset ‘festival of ideas’ to measure whether its talks change people’s outlook | Festivals | The Guardian
description: Attenders will be asked to take part in tests to see if they have become more open to views they do not agree with
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Attenders will be asked to take part in tests to see if they have become more open to views they do not agree with
Content: The Big Brue founders (left to right) Mariella Frostrup, Catherine Fairweather, Eleanor O'Keeffe and Jason McCue in front of the Radić Pavilion at Hauser & Wirth Somerset.Photograph: © donmccullinphotographyView image in fullscreenThe Big Brue founders (left to right) Mariella Frostrup, Catherine Fairweather, Eleanor O'Keeffe and Jason McCue in front of the Radić Pavilion at Hauser & Wirth Somerset.Photograph: © donmccullinphotographyFestivalsSomerset ‘festival of ideas’ to measure whether its talks change people’s outlookAttenders will be asked to take part in tests to see if they have become more open to views they do not agree withSteven MorrisMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 04.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFestivalgoers sometimes report feelingthey have a fresh perspective of the worldwhen they make their weary way home after a stimulating cultural gathering.A new “festival of ideas” in Somerset is aiming to measure whether the beliefs and ideas of attenders and speakers really are changed by their event.People attending theBig Bruein the town of Bruton next weekend will be asked to take part in tests before and after to try to discover if what they have listened to has made them more open, optimistic, empathetic and tolerant of people with views they do not agree with.Beau Lotto, a neuroscientist and educator, said the idea was to turn the festival into an experiment“We have set up a number of panels with strongly opposing views. We want to examine if the festival can change perception of conflict. Can conflict be generative rather than degenerative?”Lotto said that finding out ways of understanding other people who see things in a different way was important given the febrile nature of much national and global debate.“Because of the polarisation in the world, there’s so much pessimism and negativity, partly because views are incredibly non-nuanced. Which means it feels very fragile. It’s very extreme.”Lotto did something similar at a Cirque du Soleil performance to test whether thewonder and awe people felt changed the way they interactedwith other people.One of the experiments there was for an interviewer to drop their pens and see how people responded both before and after watching Cirque du Soleil performers.They found people were more likely to bend and pick up the pens afterwards. “People were much more pro-social than they were before. Much more willing to help than they were before.”Big Brue festivalgoers will be asked to fill in questionnaires and carry out simple tasks such as finding the midpoint of a line.Lotto said the line task could indicate which side of the brain the respondent was using – and might be different at the start and end of the festival, indicating a change. Panellists will also be invited to take part in the experiment.An ethos of the Big Brue, taking place in the grounds of theHauser & Wirth Somersetgallery, is that conflicting views can be a good thing if they are aired under conditions that encourage curiosity, compassion, creativity and learning.So rather than bringing together speakers likely to have similar views, the festival has deliberately put together panels of people likely to have contrasting opinions.Lotto said he expected a session on artificial intelligence involving the former UK chancellor George Osborne,who now works for OpenAI,and Misha Glenny,who has written about the global race for dominance of the technology,to be lively.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTwo sessions with the Reform UK MP Danny Kruger may also be sparky. In one, he will discuss migration, in another, called Family Matters, he will be in conversation with his mother, the cookery writer and broadcaster Prue Leith.Parent and child disagree over subjects such as assisted dying and abortion.Even a literature session is being billed as a “poetry battle” in which the actor Dominic West and singer and activist Bob Geldof “go head-to-head to champion the poems they believe everyone else should love”.The journalist and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup, one of the festival founders and the host for the Kruger/Leith face-off, said: “The idea is not just to hold another talks festival. We’re creating a space where ideas are presented and tested, where disagreement is welcome so long as its agreeable, and audiences are participants as well as spectators.”Festival organisers also hope the rural setting – away from the “fray of the city” may be a good location for working out how to “disagree agreeably” – the theme for the talks programme.Another of the founders, the human rights lawyer Jason McCue said: “We firmly believe that progress comes from difference and disagreement, so we are here to stir things up and help make sense of the world.”The Big Brue takes place on 19 and 20 September at Hauser & Wirth Somerset. For details:https://bigbrue.com/Explore more on these topicsFestivalsMariella FrostrupPsychologynewsShareReuse this content

title: Sydney Sweeney under fire for ‘sexualising women’s sport’ in sports prediction ad  | Sport | The Guardian
description: Olympic athletes have come out in force to condemn a sports betting advert featuring actor Sydney Sweeney in various states of undress
Author: Jo Khan
Headline: Olympic athletes have come out in force to condemn a sports betting advert featuring actor Sydney Sweeney in various states of undress
Content: Sydney Sweeney in an advertisement that has prompted backlash from several Olympic athletes.Photograph: NovigView image in fullscreenSydney Sweeney in an advertisement that has prompted backlash from several Olympic athletes.Photograph: NovigSportSydney Sweeney under fire for ‘sexualising women’s sport’ in sports prediction adActor appears naked while mock playing various sports‘A kick in the face,’ says Olympic champion TitmusJo KhanMon 14 Sep 2026 00.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlympic athletes have come out in force to condemn a sports betting advert featuring actorSydney Sweeneyin various states of undress, while showcasing the real skill, strength and beauty of women’s sport.The campaign, for US sports prediction market company Novig, depicts Sweeney in minimal to no clothing while she pretends to play several different sports.It has been widely criticised for sexualising women’s sport, with retired Olympic swimmer Ariarne Titmus saying she thought this type of “bullshit” marketing was a thing of the past.View image in fullscreenAriarne Titmus with one of her many gold medals.Photograph: Ashley Landis/AP“I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” the four-time Olympic gold medallistwrote on Instagram. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who had dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every women who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellent, unity …“How do we live in a world where monetising a women’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?”Sydney Sweeney’s prediction ad is cynical, unhealthy and reveals plenty about modern sportsRead moreThe response from athletes has been swift, not only to denounce the ad but to use it as an opportunity to highlight the excellence of women’s sport. The British sprinter and four-time European champion, Amy Hunt spoke directly to the actor after finishing fourth in the 200m at athletics’ new showpiece event, the Ultimate Championships on Sunday evening. “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like,” Hunt told the BBC.11:05Sydney Sweeney naked sports ad controversy: what’s she playing at? - The LatestReferring to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden’s winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth fastest ever over the distance, Hunt said: “21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears” before telling journalists “when you’re a woman in sport, it’s not pretty. It’s not glamorous. It’s not sexy all the time, definitely.”Taking inspiration fromAmerican gymnast Gracie Kramer, who kickstarted a trend of responses centred around her line “this is what a woman in sport looks like”,Australian Olympic swimmer Lani Pallistershared an Instagram video of her training regime, races and medals.Track sprinter Bree Rizzo alsoposted a highlights reelof her career on the track while theAustralian Institute of Sport’s versionfeatured archery, gymnastics, boxing, softball, and a peek behind the scenes at women’s sport science in action.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAllow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueWater polo silver medallistTilly Kearns wrote, “I absolutely fking hate Sydney Sweeney’s new sports ad”, while world champion boxerSkye Nicolson saidthe backlash was about making a “mockery” of women in sport rather than judging how women look.“There’s a big difference between looking ‘sexy’ because you do sport compared to use sex to sell ‘sport’,” she wrote in an Instagram story. “There is nothing wrong with looking good and doing sport and there’s nothing wrong with embracing your femininity while also being a badass athlete.”While some social media users suggested anger should be directed at Novig rather than Sweeney, the actor is not just the face of the campaign, having joined as “strategic partner and equity holder”, according to a Novig statement.View image in fullscreenSkye Nicolson takes part in a training session.Photograph: Mark Robinson/Mark Robinson Matchroom BoxingNovig and Sweeney are the beneficiaries of the attention, which is similar to the outrage caused by American Eagle’s “Sydney Sweeney has great jeans” campaign in 2025. That campaign washeavily criticisedfor appearing to use the language of eugenics, with Sweeney saying in a now-deleted video: “Genes are passed down from parents to offspring, often determining traits like hair colour, personality, and even eye colour. My jeans are blue.”Several months after the ad’s release, theactor acknowledgedher silence on the controversy had only “widened the divide”. “I was honestly surprised by the reaction,” she said. “I’m against hate and divisiveness.”Explore more on these topicsSportSydney SweeneyAustralia sportSport filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: We Are Family: photography from Images Vevey 2026 – picture essay | Photography | The Guardian
description: We visited the idyllic Swiss lakeside town of Vevey for its 10th Biennale of photography. Global head of photography Fiona Shields picks out some of her favourite projects on display
Author: Fiona Shields
Headline: We visited the idyllic Swiss lakeside town of Vevey for its 10th Biennale of photography. Global head of photography Fiona Shields picks out some of her favourite projects on display
Content: One of Sian Davey’s The Garden images of Martin Parr on display. Photograph: Laetitia GesslerWe visited the idyllic Swiss lakeside town of Vevey for its 10th Biennale of photography. Global head of photography Fiona Shields picks out some of her favourite projects on displayDiscover the 50 artworks on display at the 10th edition of theBiennale Images Vevey, 5-27 September 2026ByFiona ShieldsMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 08.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery two years, on the shores of Lake Geneva at the foot of the Swiss Alps, the town of Vevey transforms its public spaces and buildings with 50 installations of artistic projects from 21 countries, which are free and open to the public. With such a breathtaking natural setting as its backdrop, the photography displayed at Images Vevey has to strike its own particular note of magnificence to hold the gaze.Rising six storeys high, Sian Davey’s portrait of the renowned photographer Martin Parr, who died at the end of last year, sets the tone for this year’s festival. Taken in a splendid garden that seems to have flourished straight from Eden, the monumental portrait overlooks the town.Martin was a significant and much-loved member of the Images Vevey family, having exhibited his own work here on a number of occasions. It is fitting then, that he should embody this year’s theme, “We Are Family”.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenWhen Martin arrived to visit Sian he had recently received a terminal cancer diagnosis but Sian recalls the serenity he experienced in the garden. That sense of peace radiates from the portrait as he watches over the town in a fitting tribute.The creation of the garden itself was a labour of love for Sian and her son Luke. As you can see in the portrait of Martin and in the other photographs in the display, it’s also the playground of Sian’s daughter, Alice, making this in every sense a family affair.View image in fullscreenAlice from The GardenMany of this year’s family-themed projects are a study of love and loss, connection and separation. In Barbara Davatz’s series As Time Goes By the starting point is the relationship between couples who visited her studio from 1982 onwards. Over the course of three decades, she charts their changing relationships creating a fascinating kind of family tree.View image in fullscreenPrints by Barbara Davatz in the central squareUncomplicated by props or elaborate staging, her subjects are presented in their purest form, inviting us to contemplate the course of their lives and the shifting nature of family bonds over time.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenBarbara, Aniko, Sascha – 1997. Barbara + Béla – 2014View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenCarlos + Aniko – 2014, Barbara + Sascha – 1982One of the most joyful series on display is Martina Bacigalupo’s Showing How Big the Sky Is, a project that charts 10 years of personal correspondence and amusing snapshots exchanged via WhatsApp and Skype with her former nanny, Chiou Taur Wu, who she affectionately describes as “auntie”.View image in fullscreenOne of Martina Bacigalupo’s prints on display at the festival“I love being barefoot. Because when your feet are not tied you are free.” Chiou told Martina, offering a glimpse into the context of her life.Born into poverty inTaiwanin 1948 and deprived of an education, Chiou left the country to marry an Italian sailor and began new life with him in Rapallo. But her hopes for a brighter future were dashed when she discovered he had mounting gambling debts which she then spent decades paying off.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenChiou Taur Wu (45, and 46)One of the jobs she took on was caring for Martina and her brother, Tomaso. In all she spent 32 years with the family until retiring back to Taiwan. There, at the age of 70 she resolved to live on her own terms. She returned to education, took dance classes and began an adventure travelling around Asia.Now she is playing and sharing her enchantment with the world with Martina. These vibrant and witty photographs tell of the love and the lasting bond between the two.When Karolina Wojtas was a little girl, she was perfectly content as an only child. The very idea of a sibling filled her with dark thoughts. “I’ll kill them and eat them,” she told her parents when the subject was raised. So when her little brother arrived when she was 13, turbulence was perhaps inevitable.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenWe can’t live – without each other © Karolina WojtasHer project bravely delves into the complex territory of sibling rivalry. The scenes she creates with her brother are infused with humour, tenderness, and at times, a touch of cruelty – decorating him with frankfurters or vegetables for example. Presented at the festival in an anarchic, staged playroom, the images confront us with the messy, funny and sometimes uncomfortable truth of growing up together.View image in fullscreenWe can’t live – without each other © Karolina WojtasThe chains of generations of oppression and poverty link together the story of the Appalachian people explored by the photojournalist Stacy Kranitz, winner of the Images Vevey book award 2025/2026 for her photobook project Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down.View image in fullscreenFamily standing in front of cabin, near Mt. Sterling, North Carolina © Great Smoky Mountains National Park ArchiveDrawing on archive photographs dating back more than a century, alongside newspaper reports charting the heroic early pioneers’ descent into poverty and isolation, the work examines the purpose of photography: is it to bear witness or a tool of propaganda?Stacy tells the story of how these once proud and courageous people made their way to the mountain ranges of the easternUnited States, only to be exploited by mining companies who left them economically impoverished and socially isolated.View image in fullscreenMiner standing at a drift mouth with a coal cart he loaded by hand © William O. Trevey Glass Slide Collection, Radford University 1895-1925During the 1960s, the American author and historian Harry M. Caudill further stigmatised the Appalachian people by arguing that their circumstances couldn’t be fixed. In film footage unearthed by Stacy, Caudill claims that genetic deficiencies had amplified their plight, a theory later echoed in JD Vance’s memoir Hillbilly Elegy,which traces his own family’s Appalachian roots.View image in fullscreenThe exhibition Ain’t no grave gonna hold me down by Stacy Kranitz at Images Vevey 2026Fast forward to the present and, in the photographs Stacy has made of Pat Greene and his friends and family, we see a cycle of deprivation that remains unbroken. Through this project, Stacy challenges stereotypes and assumptions that allow a single image to define people and their circumstances. She draws attention to a system stacked against those who need help most.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenPat with his daughter Vicky on her birthday. Untitled, possibly related to ‘The Blizzard family’, Kempton, West Virginia, 1939 © John Vachon, Farm Security Administration, Stacy Kranitz.View image in fullscreenWest Columbia, West Virginia, 2013Fiona Shields attended Images Vevey atits invitationExplore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayPhotographySwitzerlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: inside the Bayeux Tapestry’s ‘treacherous’ journey to London | Television | The Guardian
description: Michael Palin tells the story of the artwork that has caused such a stir – and nightmares! Plus, a juicy drama based on Graham Norton’s novel. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Michael Palin tells the story of the artwork that has caused such a stir – and nightmares! Plus, a juicy drama based on Graham Norton’s novel. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Dodgy dossier? … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Blast Films/Bernadette RossView image in fullscreenDodgy dossier? … the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Blast Films/Bernadette RossTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: inside the Bayeux Tapestry’s ‘treacherous’ journey to LondonMichael Palin tells the story of the artwork that has caused such a stir – and nightmares! Plus, a juicy drama based on Graham Norton’s novel. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Hannah J DaviesandEllen E JonesMon 14 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecrets of the Bayeux Tapestry: Inside the Museum9pm, BBC TwoState guests can only dream of the sort of welcome the Bayeux Tapestry has received in London. No wonder one of the French conservators in this documentary was having nightmares about its “treacherous journey beneath the channel”. Michael Palin narrates the events of its move to the British Museum, while historians such as David Olusoga and Janina Ramirez help tell the story behind the stitches, with Rory Stewart also explaining why some call it a “dodgy dossier”.Hollie RichardsonEpstein: Money, Power and Abuse8pm, BBC OneHow did Jeffrey Epstein get away with it for so long? This report explores the paedophile and sex trafficker’s network of contacts among the super-rich and looks at his related cashflows. Clearly, this is a story with implications that remain important – so how much information still remains hidden?Phil HarrisonForever Home9pm, Channel 5Adapted from Graham Norton’s 2022 novel, this moreish six-parter sees a dementia diagnosis amplify the fault lines in a family. As her older partner Robert (Douglas Henshall) becomes unmoored, Carol (Amy Nuttall) begins to wonder what really happened to his runaway wife decades ago. Continues Tuesday and Wednesday.Graeme VirtueColin from Accounts10pm, BBC TwoAfter a three-year time jump, the superb Aussie romcom has seen its central couple Ash (Harriet Dyer) and Gordon (Patrick Brammall) settle down with other partners. But does a frisson remain? They attempt to clear the air with a brutally funny face-off at a swanky restaurant. Continues Tuesday.GVGeordie Coppers10pm, Channel 4This new series sets itself apart from most fly-on-the-wall UK cop documentaries by shadowing Newcastle’s neighbourhood policing unit. These public-facing bobbies and auxiliary street rangers remain remarkably upbeat as they deal with unpredictable incidents ranging from Lurpak heists to drunken brawls.GVLubaina Himid: This Cultural Life10.30pm, BBC FourJohn Wilson interviews Turner prize-winner Lubaina Himid, in a televised version of a programme previously broadcast on Radio 4 earlier this year. Their conversation is wide-ranging but – naturally – hinges on this feted British artist’s pioneering place in the Black arts movement, and her bold mixed-media works with a satirical bent.Hannah J DaviesFilm choiceView image in fullscreenA classic … Kevin Costner in Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarRobin Hood: Prince of Thieves (Kevin Reynolds, 1991)5.35pm, Sky Cinema GreatsThis month two entirely different films are out in cinemas, offering alternative takes on the legendary, wealth-redistributing outlaw. But neither the mortality-contemplating Hugh Jackman one, nor the mud-splattered Andrew Garfield one, can compete with this Kevin Costner-starring 90s classic. Alan Rickman was a deserved Bafta-winner for his definitive take on the Sheriff of Nottingham, but the real villain was that Bryan Adams theme song.Ellen E JonesGet Carter (Mike Hodges, 1971)11.05pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenCharismatic and menacing … Michael Caine in Get Carter.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyIt’s one of the all-time great gangster films, offering a peer down the sidestreets and back alleys of late-60s Newcastle, plus Michael Caine in his charismatic, menacing prime. He plays Jack Carter, the titular hardman who returns to his home town after years spent in London’s underworld in order to investigate, then avenge, his brother’s death. Writer-director Mike Hodges cleverly incorporated aspects of real-life local crimes into his script, especially the notorious “one-armed bandit murder” of 1967, helping to usher in a gritty new era of realism for British crime drama.EEJExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightBayeux tapestryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Farewell to Eden by Sebastian Faulks review – conflict and compromise, from a veteran of the genre | Fiction | The Guardian
description: A returning British soldier is haunted by his time in Palestine in this panoramic epic set after the second world war
Author: Michael Donkor
Headline: A returning British soldier is haunted by his time in Palestine in this panoramic epic set after the second world war
Content: Sebastian Faulks ‘is deft in the management of his ample material’.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyView image in fullscreenSebastian Faulks ‘is deft in the management of his ample material’.Photograph: Cheese Scientist/AlamyFictionReviewFarewell to Eden by Sebastian Faulks review – conflict and compromise, from a veteran of the genreA returning British soldier is haunted by his time in Palestine in this panoramic epic set after the second world warMichael DonkorMon 14 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSebastian Faulks’s latest book focuses on the most irreconcilable geopolitical struggle of our age, the Israel-Palestine conflict. While “the sound of mortar and machine gun, the collision of flesh and metal” are integral to Faulks’s best known works, such as Birdsong, in his 17th novel the military presence is a peacekeeping one. It’s 1946 and infantry officer Philip Deval, who saw action in Normandy, is deployed to the Holy Land to take part in maintaining Britain’s mandate in Palestine. Initially Philip is second in command of a battalion overseeing febrile relationships between Jewish and Arab communities. Britain’s profound failures and manipulation in the region, and the imminence of its disastrous departure from the territory, come under scrutiny.While able to drum up motivation and cheer for the men in his battalions, privately Philip wrestles with inner melancholy. He is “shrouded” in a “loneliness … that insulates him from the world”. Experiences on the battlefield and other, slowly elucidated tragedies have led to his pessimistic bent. Much of what Philip observes in the Middle East, and his “foreboding” sense of its intractable problems, only confirms his despairing sense of human nature. It also underlines his ambivalence towards notions of divine benevolence.double quotation markThe lamenting tone of the title reflects a work mourning seeming certaintiesIn Jerusalem, Philip and some of his men find themselves in a raucous bar. They jostle along among multicultural crowds, those “with yarmulkes, tarbushes … barehead Armenians and Greeks … [all] playing dice and cards in a mix of tongues”. Philip knows that “soon they would [all] be killing each other … Humans had worked out the movements of the planets and prised apart the indivisible atom; they cured mysterious diseases and found a new way, by trade, of making themselves richer than the sum of their possessions … But a group of closely related people in a fertile landscape couldn’t find a way to coexist.”This inability to coexist does, indeed, frequently erupt into shocking violence and inevitable reprisals. Faulks captures these with his typically steady and unblinking attention, in scenes where both the seriousness of his research and his instinct for affecting fictive detail is clear. Not long after Philip’s arrival in the region, Zionist paramilitaries bomb the King David Hotel, location of the headquarters of the Palestine police and the British administration. While helping to rescue survivors from the debris, “in a Remington [typewriter] that Philip lifted clear, there were three severed female fingers jammed between the keys”.Faulks’s plots often cultivate friendships formed in duress. Here, Matthew Kilvert, a priest attached to the peacekeeping mission, has a “genial energy”. He’s fantastically enthusiastic about staging a Christmas production, cast with officers and locals of all backgrounds, of The Importance of Being Earnest. His uproarious Lady Bracknell becomes the talk of the town. Matthew forms an enduring closeness with Philip; their dialogue often glitters with an easy, youthful humour and they are able to share opposing views of what it means to have faith with an instructive conviviality and curiosity. There is a beautiful, strangely rendered moment when Matthew thinks he has had a vision of Christ. Philip listens to Matthew’s retelling of the encounter with quiet interest.A different friendship also shapes Philip’s progress in the novel. With postwar employment opportunities limited, after demobbing Philip retrains as a French teacher and takes up a post at a girls’ boarding school where he and music mistress Frances Darwood – as stiff as Philip is wont to be – strike up a delicate and important confidence. Over evenings listening to recordings of Ravel and Bach, the two gradually share stories of their pasts and the historical forces that have shaped them. This process proves especially harrowing for Frances. Alongside Philip’s detailed recounting of his time in the Holy Land and the desolate realities of weary postwar Britain, Frances’s horrific wartime recollections contribute to the panoramic ambitions of the novel. Faulks is deft in the management of his ample material, throwing in the odd, energising shift in narrative perspective too – an echo of the more sustained polyphony ofA Week in December. There is a lightness and unpredictability in the movement between stories and periods, a kind of deliberate structural restiveness that is of a piece with Philip’s psychic disquiet. This mobility in the organisation of the story culminates in some thrillingly clever late-stage plot developments that are every bit as dramatic as the concluding sections of Faulks’s 2007 novel,Engleby.While characteristically expansive in its scope, at its core Farewell to Eden is about disillusionment and morally compromised nations, peoples and individuals. The lamenting tone of the title – and indeed of the text at large – reflects a work mourning seeming certainties or easy categorical distinctions. It is a novel that asks us what we might do when unavoidably faced with our own imperfection and fallibility, and is wise and sober in its refusal to trumpet answers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
