title: Ancestors review – messy but moving ghostly drama about the Aids crisis | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Saipan standout Éanna Hardwicke is a soulful gay man looking for a missing friend in a striking yet muddled debut
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Saipan standout Éanna Hardwicke is a soulful gay man looking for a missing friend in a striking yet muddled debut
Content: Éanna Hardwicke in Ancestors.Photograph: Leanne SullivanView image in fullscreenÉanna Hardwicke in Ancestors.Photograph: Leanne SullivanFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewAncestors review – messy but moving ghostly drama about the Aids crisisToronto film festival:Saipan standout Éanna Hardwicke is a soulful gay man looking for a missing friend in a striking yet muddled debutBenjamin Leein TorontoMon 14 Sep 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 10.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not normal to regularly contemplate mortality in your twenties, to ask questions about where we might go after we die and whether any part of our legacy will even matter in the years following. But for gay men in the 1980s, death was everywhere.Prima Facie review – fiery one-woman play is flattened into a bland movieRead moreIn David Turpin’s intermittently impactful debut Ancestors, the director tries to make a connection with those men who lived through the very worst years of the Aids crisis. Turpin, born in 1982, might not have the first-hand experience but he bears the scars passed on from generation to generation and like many young gay men coming of age in the years after, likely experienced a watered down version of the shame and fear those before him once felt.His film is about how bridges are built between past and future, living and dead, old and young, and how those who have been pushed out of society work about trying to create and sustain their own. Set in a foggy, ghostly London in 1988, Turpin’s dreamy and mysterious film is trying to cast a spell (he hasreferredto it as a “séance” in interviews) and it’s one that works incredibly well at times and wears off far too easily at others. As with many a first movie, there’s a lot thrown at the wall here with scrappy ambition prioritised over laser focus and while that’s admirable, it can also be a little frustrating.What’s most consistent is a mesmerising performance from Éanna Hardwicke, the Irish actor who was also one of the best things about last year’s Toronto film festival, playing Roy Keane in underseen World Cup workplace dramaSaipan. Again he brings real, combustible angst to the role but here it’s of a far different kind, aimed at the rapidly disintegrating world around him and the one person he wants to save from disintegrating with it. He plays Beau, a gay man working in a caff owned by “Auntie” Maurice (Rupert Everett), an old queen who collects both framed pictures of the female actors he idolises as well as young strays. The latest of whom is Tiny (Jack Wolfe), a 20-year-old in need of work. When Beau later sees him cruising in the park and finds out he has nowhere to stay, he brings him back to stay in an apartment shared with his best friend, Shell (a luminous Jessica Reynolds).Refreshingly there’s no sexual tension between the pair (Beau says early on that Tiny isn’t his type) and instead they become friends, a far more compelling and under-explored gay male dynamic. Like Maurice did with him, Beau also feels a sense of responsibility for Tiny, an overwhelming weight at such a grim time and after Tiny reveals that he is positive, the objective changes from keeping him safe to keeping him alive. The film jumps back and forth in time, and to other places, as Tiny goes missing and Beau must try to find him. Early on Beau tries to get Tiny to read his collection of Jean Genet novels but he tells him that he isn’t interested in tales of detectives and instead prefers “love stories and ghost stories”. Turpin also has little interest in the fact-finding grind of actually tracking someone down and more about the love between the pair and the ghosts that surround them.From Chris Rock to Helen Mirren: 10 films to look out for at the Toronto film festival 2026Read moreFor a film that plays with reality, dreams, nightmares, the past, the future and the afterlife and slips between timelines and from colour to black and white, it often works best in its more grounded conversational scenes. His direction might get overly precious but Turpin’s dialogue is natural and direct and we never doubt Hardwicke’s authenticity. The film around him can meander a little, in its worst moments feeling like a short that’s been expanded beyond its means, and while some of the atmosphere is entirely enveloping, sometimes the visuals can be a little ropey. There are misfiring gambits like a transfixing but inconsequential Christina Hendricks as a golden age actor who comes to life and a few too many underwhelming musical interludes at a local gay bar (save for one wrenching cover of Tim Buckley’s Song to the Siren which is wisely played again at the end). I was moved by so much – a picture of Tiny added to an expanding wall filled with other gay men who got sick, Beau’s anxiousness over whether he might also have it and how intimate he should then be with Shell or Maurice, how Beau grapples with the idea of hopelessness without despair – but then alienated by so many others.The last act hinges on a more conventional reveal that feels a little at odds with the stranger, fuzzier movie that Turpin seems more focused on making. It doesn’t quite have the gut-punch impact it should, a more conceptually interesting idea than an emotionally effective one, but the very last scene does bring us back under that spell. In its swirl of emotions, ideas and styles, Ancestors can get a little lost in the mist but when, in its finest moments, it all clears, there’s something haunting in front of us.Ancestors is premiering at theToronto film festivaland is seeking distributionExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalFestivalsDrama filmsAids and HIVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Barrio Triste review – raw and dynamic portrait of anarchic slum life in 1980s Medellín | Movies | The Guardian
description: Bad Bunny collaborator Stillz’s debut feature shot using Betacam focuses on vibes over plot
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Bad Bunny collaborator Stillz’s debut feature shot using Betacam focuses on vibes over plot
Content: Barrio Triste.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreenBarrio Triste.Photograph: PRMoviesReviewBarrio Triste review – raw and dynamic portrait of anarchic slum life in 1980s MedellínBad Bunny collaborator Stillz’s debut feature shot using Betacam focuses on vibes over plotPhuong LeMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBest known as the creative mind behind the music videos of Puerto Rican rapper and singer Bad Bunny, Stillz has risen to the top of the industry as an in-demand director and photographer. Interestingly, for his feature-film debut, Stillz has turned away from the glitz and glamour of celebrity to fix his lens on the underdog. Shot on Betacam video and set in the crime-ridden neighbourhoods of 1980s Medellín, Barrio Triste opens with an unexpected act of rebellion: having snatched a camera from a television crew, a group of young men head out on an anarchic joyride and film their exploits in the process. Previously rendered invisible by the system, they have inserted themselves into a tool of mainstream media.There are moments of crisis here and there – the restless band of youths attempt a robbery and even kill a hostage – yet the primary focus seems to be on vibes rather than plot. The ever-roving camera not only channels the agitated psyche of the main characters but also drums up the chaotic pace of Medellín’s underbelly. One particularly memorable sequence moves from the peculiar sight of a punk duo practising on a rooftop to the garbage-strewn streets, during which seemingly benign interactions can quickly escalate into heated altercations. Echoing the handheld cinematography, life in the slums is unmoored and precarious, as if the ground might give way at any second.These moments of visual and emotional rawness are undermined by creative choices that err on the side of superfluousness. Arca’s electronic score is stunning, with scattering beats that resemble gunshots, yet its omnipresence in the film overwhelms the dynamism of the camerawork. Also intrusive are asinine sequences where one of the kids answers vague questions about his hopes and dreams, asked by an unseen presence. Though produced by Harmony Korine’s company EDGLRD, the film doesn’t quite measure up to classic portraits of wasted youth, offering little substance behind its propulsive style.Barrio Triste is in UK cinemas from 18 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsColombiaAmericasreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Prima Facie review – fiery one-woman play is flattened into a bland movie | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Cynthia Erivo takes on the role Jodie Comer made famous for a pointless adaptation of a story about rape and retribution that loses the power it once had
Author: Richard Lawson
Headline: Cynthia Erivo takes on the role Jodie Comer made famous for a pointless adaptation of a story about rape and retribution that loses the power it once had
Content: Cynthia Erivo as Tessa in Prima Facie, ‘an Olivier-winning play somehow reduced to Law & Order blandness’.Photograph: Nicola Dove/Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenCynthia Erivo as Tessa in Prima Facie, ‘an Olivier-winning play somehow reduced to Law & Order blandness’.Photograph: Nicola Dove/Toronto film festivalFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewPrima Facie review – fiery one-woman play is flattened into a bland movieToronto film festival:Cynthia Erivo takes on the role Jodie Comer made famous for a pointless adaptation of a story about rape and retribution that loses the power it once hadRichard Lawsonin TorontoMon 14 Sep 2026 00.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuzie Miller’s award-winning2019 play Prima Facieemploys a familiar narrative device: a hotshot London barrister finds herself on the other side of the bar, subject to the very legal tactics she once so ruthlessly employed. Not as a defendant, but as the accuser in a rape case.We’ve seen versions of this before – a powerful figure suddenly caught in a struggle against a system they helped perpetuate – but Miller’s play distinguishes itself by putting the onus on to one actor.The wonder of Prima Facie is not really its narrative acuity nor its urgent point-making but the breathless and prodigious effort of its performer – most famouslya magnificent, tireless Jodie Comerin London and New York.How could a traditional film hold its focus on one monologuing person for nearly two hours? A rare few have tried that but most financiers and producers seem to think that it might be a good idea to have a few more cast members.And thus the fate of Prima Facie, which Miller and the director, Susanna White, have turned into a cinematic vehicle forCynthia Erivo. Unlike Comer, Erivo has to share the space with other people and must perform in real time what was, on stage, only recollection. In doing so, much of the exciting punch of Prima Facie has been washed away; what remains is a fairly conventional treatise on a pervasive societal ill.The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd review – Amanda Seyfried compels in wrenching prison dramaRead moreErivo plays Tessa, a criminal defense lawyer who is quickly gaining a reputation around the Old Bailey for her wily cunning in pleading her clients’ innocence. She is assigned a lot of sex crimes cases because, as a colleague glumly sums up, it looks good for a man accused of rape to have a female attorney arguing on his behalf.Tessa doesn’t seem to mind; she is simply providing the defense to which everyone is entitled. Morality has no place in the equation, she coolly figures.Tessa is perhaps especially driven because she is trying to transcend humble beginnings. Her mother, June (Noma Dumezweni), works as a cleaner, while her younger brother, Johnny (Toheeb Jimoh), is in construction. Tessa was clever enough to get a scholarship to Cambridge and now lives a flashy, important life in London, stylish Thames-adjacent apartment and all.All of that momentum is horribly disrupted when Tessa is raped by a colleague and lover, Julian (Daniel Ings), a terrible, frightening violation that punctuates what had been a lovely “are we getting serious?” date. Tessa reports to the police and thus sets herself on course for a trial, during which her motives and character will be intensely scrutinized on the way to a likely acquittal. That is just the way things tend to work, a fact Tessa understands all too well. But she goes ahead anyway, trying to rescue some sense of justice from this awful mess.In the play, the actor playing Tessa gets to wax long and rhapsodic on what she loves about the law, describing with relish the minute strategies of cross-examination and reveling in the sport of it all. That actor also has ample time to explicate what is happening inside Tessa’s head: the agonizing doubt, the anger, the fear, the bewilderment that she has become the figure she once easily dismantled in court.Miller and White throw in a little of that internal monologue but sparingly enough that it comes across as merely a half-hearted gimmick. We never get too deep with Tessa, which turns her story into something far more generic than I think the film-makers intended.It does not help matters that White films everything so flatly, with only the occasional attempt to add some visual texture to the proceedings.Erivo approaches the role with a focused rigor and yet she oddly doesn’t have all that much to play. Perhaps part of the problem is that the film makes a three-year time jump from the police report to the trial, which means we’ve no time to sit in the long fallout of the incident, to watch Erivo evolve her characterization as Tessa passes through the crucible of processing what has happened to her. The film becomes quite procedural, slowing down for a long recounting of what we just saw; an Olivier-winning play somehow reduced to Law & Order blandness.Of course, the film’s messaging – about the boggling frequency of sexual assault, about the vexing and myriad struggles of bringing perpetrators to justice – is well worth issuing out. And yet, White delivers all that in far too blunt a fashion. One sorely misses the darkly engrossing journey of the play’s performance, its energetic peaks, its shattering valleys, its spiky humor. All that has been bowdlerized in favor of something far more straightforward and thin.In expanding its view beyond one woman and the fire of her personal testimony, Prima Facie makes itself not universal but frustratingly anodyne.Prima Facie is premiering at theToronto film festivaland is seeking distributionExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalCynthia ErivoDrama filmsFestivalsJodie ComerRape and sexual assaultreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Route to Cappyness review – capybara boosterism is an ode to the internet’s favourite rodent | Movies | The Guardian
description: From a cappy-cafe owner in Japan to an escaped capybara in the UK, this homespun film takes the temperature of an international obsession
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: From a cappy-cafe owner in Japan to an escaped capybara in the UK, this homespun film takes the temperature of an international obsession
Content: Charming effort … The Route to Cappyness.Photograph: Darkwings WildlifeView image in fullscreenCharming effort … The Route to Cappyness.Photograph: Darkwings WildlifeMoviesReviewThe Route to Cappyness review – capybara boosterism is an ode to the internet’s favourite rodentFrom a cappy-cafe owner in Japan to an escaped capybara in the UK, this homespun film takes the temperature of an international obsessionLeslie FelperinMon 14 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Midlands-based film-maker Sharon Walia’s previous works wasThe Keepers of the Pigs, proudly described on her production company’s website as “the first ever documentary about guinea pigs”. So it makes zoological sense that her latest film takes on capybaras, guinea pigs’ ridiculously cute semi-aquatic cousins that are indigenous to Latin America, andrelatively recently became ubiquitouson social media in memes and short films alike. As glimpsed here, there was even a capybara in the recentAcademy Award-winning animated feature Flow, some pro-cappy boosterism that captured the creatures’ chill vibe and snuffly sweetness.Walia’s celebration of the species stays on script, rejoicing in the animals’ natural geniality, friendliness to other species in their natural habitat, and their compelling, remunerative charm that seems to have bolstered the fortunes of several animal attractions around the world.Equipped with a fairly basic camera, a drone and her five-year-old son for company, Walia visits a variety of venues offering capybara-centric attractions, starting in the species’ home turf in Brazil; there she meets Luciano Mochinski, whose smartphone-shot footage of himselfsitting under an umbrella with an large inquisitive male cappywent viral. (In fact, having achieved virality is often cited as a measure of success for several people here, which is little sad but that’s the times we live in.)Other interlocutors include a cappy-cafe owner in Japan who’s found a great way to get out of the rat race doing what he loves and makes no claims to expertise on the creatures. By contrast, American cappy shillers love to reel off factoids and anecdotes and all sound like they’ve had media training should a camera crew or schoolbus full of kids pull up to the gates. The British cappy-keepers are endearingly more amateur, yet noticeably a little defensive, especially the owners of the park from where Cinnamon, a young female capybara, escaped andmade the newsand, once again, social media.Indeed, the film-making here sometimes resembles the amateur efforts you’d see on social media, especially YouTube; the abrupt music transitions and off-the-shelf graphics look a little more naff than if you were watching this for free. But the homemade quality is part of The Route to Cappyness’s charm, along with the cuddly giant rodent stars themselves.The Route to Cappyness is in UK cinemas from 17 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsAnimalsSocial mediaDigital mediaYouTubereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I never pass up a rewatch’: why Valley Girl is my feelgood movie | Nicolas Cage | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films brings us back to 1980s LA
Author: Annie Zaleski
Headline: The latest in our series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films brings us back to 1980s LA
Content: Nicolas Cage and Deborah Foreman in Valley Girl.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenNicolas Cage and Deborah Foreman in Valley Girl.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyMy feelgood movieNicolas Cage‘I never pass up a rewatch’: why Valley Girl is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films brings us back to 1980s LAAnnie ZaleskiMon 14 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a teenager growing up in the 1990s, I was deeply obsessed with all things 1980s pop culture. Chalk it up to nostalgia for my Care Bears-filled childhood – or a stubborn adolescent desire to separate myself from the Dave Matthews Band-loving, khaki-wearing kids at my high school. (Mission accomplished: it’s safe to say I was the only person I knew rocking a bandana tied around my pants leg or a Wild Boys-eraDuran Duranshirt.)‘Swiftly enchanted’: why Bedknobs and Broomsticks is my feelgood movieRead moreBack then, I was especially drawn to 1980s teen movies. In my own life, I was having zero luck finding a New Romantic Romeo; instead, I pined after artsy, sensitive boys who didn’t know I existed. But throughout these films, even the most awkward characters managed to find a happy ending, with the ultimate examples being Samantha (Molly Ringwald) in Sixteen Candles landing hunky Jake Ryan or Stacy (Jennifer Jason Leigh) linking up with Rat (Brian Backer) in Fast Times at Ridgemont High.Out of these teen movies, 1983’s Valley Girl emerged as my hands-down favorite, a permanent feelgood film I never pass up for a rewatch. It’s best described as a new wave Romeo and Juliet. The film focuses on wholesome Julie (Deborah Foreman), the child of two ageing, laid-back hippies who run a health food store and restaurant. Although her parents embarrass her, they give Julie the freedom to find her authentic self. That extends to her romantic life, especially after she connects with Randy (a chiseledNicolas Cage, in one of his first film roles) at a party.They’re polar opposites – he’s a scruffy punk who hangs out in dingy clubs, she’s often found gossiping in a mall food court – but fall head over heels. This causes issues with Julie’s friends, who are uncomfortable that Randyseemsso different from them; in fact, they encourage her to take back her boorish boyfriend, Tommy, with whom she broke up with at the film’s start. Julie is hesitant, for good reason. Randy is actually quite tender despite his edgy exterior. And Tommy’s loutish post-split behavior involved secretly seducing one of Julie’s good friends to use as extortion fodder and, separately, publicly assaulting Randy at a party.After caving in to peer pressure and agreeing to go to prom with Tommy, Julie eventually realizes she’s made a huge mistake. Luckily, Randy hasn’t given up on their relationship – and, like all the best teen movies, Valley Girl culminates in a dramatic prom scene in which he goes to great lengths (and sparks a major food fight) to win her back.The movie arrived not long after Frank Zappa’s 1982 hit song Valley Girl, which satirized a very specific teenage California subculture. (Zappa wasn’t thrilled about the film; he evensued the producers, who subsequently denied the movie had anything to do with the song.) But the movie doesn’t mock the valley girl trend.Instead, Valley Girl meets these teenagers where they are: going shopping, hanging out and eating junk food, and attending house parties with then-novel foods like sushi. They’re shockingly normal, not exaggerated caricatures or curiosities. That’s probably why, years later, I still related to Julie and her friends. The scene of them flipping through racks of colorful clothes reminded me of my own 1990s teenage mall excursions.Chalk up this endurance to Valley Girl director Martha Coolidge, who had a background in documentary film-making and brought an observant eye to the movie. More than once, we see Julie absolutely awed by scenes of gritty 1980s Los Angeles: movie theater marquees, flashy neon signs, and famous locations such as Grauman’s Chinese Theater, the Roxy and the Rainbow Bar & Grill. I recognized her reaction: I had the exact same mind-expanding experience when I finally visited bigger cities and saw things I had only glimpsed in movies.I was also envious of the music in Valley Girl. Julie and Randy go to a cool underground club to watch powerpop legends the Plimsouls rip through an urgent set. Elsewhere, the teens dance to Sparks and the Flirts at a house party, or have a prom where the musical entertainment comes from new wave cult figure Josie Cotton. You felt cool by association because of the soundtrack.When a Valley Girl remake was released in 2020, I couldn’t bring myself to watch it. The magic of the original film was how unselfconscious it was. The movie used a very specific era and location to illustrate something timeless about growing up and navigating complicated relationships. I was a goody two-shoes who grew up in a super-preppy town, so I related to having a sheltered life exploded by new experiences. As an adult, the idea of being bold, meeting new people and going to exciting places continues to inspire me. As much as the Valley Girl plot centered on romance, the movie was also a story about self-discovery and being brave enough to carve out your own offbeat path.Valley Girl is available to watch on Amazon Prime in the US, the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsNicolas CageMy feelgood movieComedy filmsRomance filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Goody Goody review – intriguing natural childbirth horror lurches into demonic occult blowout | Movies | The Guardian
description: After Samantha Robinson decides a forest cabin in deep winter is the perfect spot to bear her child, it’s going to be a very bad shift for the doula and midwife
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: After Samantha Robinson decides a forest cabin in deep winter is the perfect spot to bear her child, it’s going to be a very bad shift for the doula and midwife
Content: Pangs for nothing … Goody GoodyPhotograph: PRView image in fullscreenPangs for nothing … Goody GoodyPhotograph: PRMoviesReviewGoody Goody review – intriguing natural childbirth horror lurches into demonic occult blowoutAfter Samantha Robinson decides a forest cabin in deep winter is the perfect spot to bear her child, it’s going to be a very bad shift for the doula and midwifePhil HoadMon 14 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConception, pregnancy and childbirth are defining human experiences, and so remain perennial themes for horror, from Rosemary’s Baby to the Alien franchise toPrevenge. Occupying a no-woman’s-land between life and death, they’re innately anxiety-inducing, perhaps making it harder for film-makers to supply a truly individual take. Debut director Raymond Creamer comes close by initially digging into the interpersonal dynamics around the home-birthing pool of a headstrong mother-to-be, before he defaults into a schlocky creature feature.Goody (Samantha Robinson) is in the pool, ready for battle, soaking in good vibes beamed at her by husband Jayson (Colby Hollman), his doula sister Candace (Zoe Renee) and their rock, midwife Sarah (Colleen Foy). But shaken by weirdly spaced contractions, Sarah takes Jason aside and admits that she has a bad feeling. It’s not purely premonition: a flashback reveals, in contrast to the new-age love-in around the tub, Goody’s insistence against Sarah’s advice that she give birth in winter at their forest cabin. The midwife fears it will make going to hospital too difficult should anything go wrong – and only agrees to supervise because Goody will probably go ahead solo if she pulls out.Creamer starts out by layering telling details that insinuate the stifling boho perfectionism ruling this household: a faux Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan cover featuring the couple, their disdain for teabags, the cloying veneer of positivity. He films the damning flashback with psychological finesse to show Jayson’s status as junior partner; back on the natal frontline, Candace sometimes slips into a grandstanding bolshiness that threatens to tip Sarah’s carefully nurtured equilibrium out of balance.Given this careful familial setup, it’s a bit bewildering when the film takes a sudden demonic swerve. What was initially an exercise in cannily undermining Goody’s (and the audience’s) need for an authority figure turns into a hurdy-gurdy occult blowout. As Goody starts raving about Asmodeus, Sarah lurches between panic and calm in a manner that feels increasingly nonsensical. (It’s probably fair enough, though, when she’s being dragged underwater by greasy tentacles.) Jayson’s disappearance is left unexplained and not in a productively disturbing way.Amid the mayhem, Creamer still manages the odd visual flourish, including Candace’s final esoteric vision. But if Goody Goody really had to take The Omen route, he needed to deliver the transition with far more delicacy.Goody Goody is on Shudder and AMC+ from 18 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsChildbirthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Onwards and Sideways review – Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney lift solid Parkinson’s drama | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Toronto film festival: Shakespeare in Love director John Madden’s feelgood – and bad – comedy-drama is powered by excellent performances and authenticity
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Toronto film festival: Shakespeare in Love director John Madden’s feelgood – and bad – comedy-drama is powered by excellent performances and authenticity
Content: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney in Onwards and Sideways.Photograph: Jonathan Birch/BBCView image in fullscreenRhys Ifans and Laura Linney in Onwards and Sideways.Photograph: Jonathan Birch/BBCFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewOnwards and Sideways review – Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney lift solid Parkinson’s dramaToronto film festival:Shakespeare in Love director John Madden’s feelgood – and bad – comedy-drama is powered by excellent performances and authenticityBenjamin Leein TorontoSun 13 Sep 2026 21.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSo far at this year’sToronto film festival, I have seen three films involving someone with dementia and two featuring someone who has Aids. It’s not just a sign that the lineup could perhaps benefit from some more light relief but also that certain conditions and illnesses still tend to be covered more often than others on screen.Babies review – Anna Kendrick and Seth Rogen embrace childlessness in breezy comedyRead moreLast year’s festival saw Scottish hitI Swearbring an unprecedented level of awareness to people who live with Tourette’s and while there’s perhaps less of an obvious edge to John Madden’s more politely framed comedy-drama Onwards and Sideways, it too acts as both narrative movie and potential educational tool. Our knowledge of Parkinson’s is usually restricted to the celebrities who have it, from Muhammad Ali to Michael J Fox to, most recently, Carly Simon, but for many of us, it’s still seen in an abstract way, a handful of symptoms we know about, but so many more that we don’t.Onwards and Sideways is written by Paul Mayhew-Archer, a TV writer best known for The Vicar of Dibley, and who was diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 2011. He knows the disease’s hardships – but he also knows comedy, and this film is an attempt to remain honest about the hell of it while not getting too lost in the dark.Director Madden, whose post-Shakespeare in Love career has included two fun trips to the Marigold Hotel and two serviceable Jessica Chastain thrillers, knows how to pull the right strings and Onwards and Sideways is a sturdy film of substance over style. It’s made with the BBC and often feels like it would be more at home on the small screen, but it is hard to deny that its grander purpose could do with a larger audience.As could the deserving lead performances, from Laura Linney and a never-better Rhys Ifans, who play two people who receive their Parkinson’s diagnosis right after the other. Ifans is Tony, a widowed deputy headteacher, and Linney is Emma, an American composer and single mother, and they are both told by a believably brisk and disinterested doctor (Rory Kinnear) that they have “five good years” left before things really go downhill.Tony’s son lives abroad and his only real support comes from the prim, nagging Liz (Monica Dolan, doing the most she can with a duff, one-note character). He decides to keep his diagnosis a secret at work, out of shame but also fear of losing his job. Tony is lonely and in need of someone who knows what he’s going through and, after a few interactions with Emma (the film introduces the passing of each “good” year), the pair grow closer, first as friends and then romantically.Tony and Emma attend a regular group for those who have Parkinson’s, a so-called “ballet” class that provides both exercise and support. Tony has a believable feeling of revulsion and annoyance when he first meets them, a nice and unexpected detail. Screenwriter Mayhew-Archer plays a sharp-tongued realist in the group, calling the disease “one humiliation after another”, which “takes everything from you”. His character, along with his script, nails an effective sense of realistic optimism. There’s no curing Parkinson’s – one of the most heart-wrenching moments sees Emma’s hand tremor return after she thought a new drug regimen had fixed it – so these characters have to figure out how to live with it, both physically and mentally.There’s so much here that I, embarrassingly, wasn’t aware of, such as how certain Parkinson’s medications can sometimes lead to hypersexuality or a gambling compulsion; that a form ofbrain-drilling surgery called DBScan help; that it can lead to extreme nightmares which are harder to wake up from. Mayhew-Archer’s direct, lived experience gives the film a rare authenticity while Ifans and Linney also help to stop it from feeling too much like a pamphlet come to life, with the former particularly impressive and in moments rather heartbreaking.I Play Rocky review – crowd-pleasing Stallone biopic is heavy on fan service, light on real emotionRead moreI wanted a little more spark and wit to some of their dialogue, which often feels a little too plain and safe. While we might not know enough about the disease itself, we certainly know enough about the kind of crowd-manipulating, laugh-until-you-cry British dramedy this is aiming to be; both Mayhew-Archer and Madden could have afforded to break the mould a little more. (An overly sentimental Thomas Newman score doesn’t help there either.)The film’s messaging and more distinctive personality do come through strongest in a cleverly crafted finale that feels less obviously borrowed from elsewhere. Mayhew-Archer injects the right amount of realistic optimism, in a way that will strike a chord not only for audiences with Parkinson’s but those living with other life-interrupting diseases and disorders. Providing hope without an empty promise is no easy feat, but Mayhew-Archer finds his way there and offers his hand for us to follow.Onwards and Sideways is premiering at the Toronto film festival and will be released in UK cinemas on 6 November and will be on BBC One later, with US and Australia dates to be announcedExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalFestivalsRhys IfansLaura LinneyComedy filmsParkinson's diseasereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Royal Ballet: The McRae/Vassilev Project review – an encounter between two masterful ROH performers | Dance | The Guardian
description: Directed by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, this is an evening of many parts that sometimes feels bolted together
Author: Sanjoy Roy
Headline: Directed by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, this is an evening of many parts that sometimes feels bolted together
Content: Spellbinding … Vasko Vassilev and Steven McRae in The McRae/Vassilev Project.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSpellbinding … Vasko Vassilev and Steven McRae in The McRae/Vassilev Project.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewRoyal Ballet: The McRae/Vassilev Project review – an encounter between two masterful ROH performersLinbury theatre, LondonDirected by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, this is an evening of many parts that sometimes feels bolted togetherSanjoy RoyMon 14 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s an evening of two halves and many, many parts, some that dovetail snugly, others more clunkily bolted together. And perhaps that’s because The McRae/Vassilev Project is just that: a project more than a piece.Directed by Natalie Abrahami and choreographed by Loughlan Prior, it is essentially an encounter between two masterful performers with long careers at the Royal Opera House, dancerSteven McRaeand violinist Vasko Vassilev, entwined with the near mythical figure of another virtuoso artist, Niccolò Paganini.The first half opens with Vassilev centre stage playing Bach (for some reason); he backs off to cede space for a luxurious pas de deux by McRae and partner Sarah Lamb, all exquisite lines, spins and lifts. From this “front stage” scene, the set switches to a backstage studio, artists McRae, Vassilev, Lamb and pianist Pamela Tan Nicholson entering as if for rehearsal. The rest of this section is a light-touch show-and-tell of McRae and Vassilev’s backstories – one a homespun Australian who happened upon dance as a child, the other a Bulgarian prodigy hothoused within a musical family – illustrated with old photos and videos, supplemented by comments from Lamb and Nicholson, and interspersed with consummate yet seemingly off-the-cuff demonstrations of their skills in music and dance.View image in fullscreenL-r: Vasko Vassilev , Pamela Tan Nicholson, Steven McRae and Sarah Lamb in The McRae/Vassilev Project.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThe scene is at once charming – personalising the figure of the professional performer – and contrived: even as you warm to the characters you feel the joins in the script (voice acting is not their forte) and the jolts between the attempted naturalism of their conversation and the executed artifices of classical performance.The second half is a complete change of tack. Everyone returns as devilish Paganinis in tailcoats and cummerbunds, hair dyed dark and tastefully tousled. As well as flourishing a violin bow like a baton, sword or spear, McRae uses his tap dance training in fiendish zapateado and brilliant Cossack spins, sometimes melding his commanding footwork in partnership with Lamb’s airy pointe-work and lean lines. Still, it’s perhaps Vassilev who holds the stage most, simply by putting his body into playing Paganini; the laser focus is spellbinding.Shame, then, that there are so many distracting effects, from back-projected dancers to billowing smoke and glaring lights, and a busy abstract animation that visualises the musical dynamics. With performers like these, it’s enough for them to just do their thing.At theLinbury theatre, London, until 19 September.Explore more on these topicsDancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: A great time with Uncle Junior from the Sopranos: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Fans of the show will not want to miss this revealing new series with Dominic Chianese and his son. Plus, a political drama that’s as thrilling as a Bourne novel
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Fans of the show will not want to miss this revealing new series with Dominic Chianese and his son. Plus, a political drama that’s as thrilling as a Bourne novel
Content: Dominic Chianese presents Dominic & Junior podcast.Photograph: Pacific Press Media Production Corp./AlamyView image in fullscreenDominic Chianese presents Dominic & Junior podcast.Photograph: Pacific Press Media Production Corp./AlamyBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioA great time with Uncle Junior from the Sopranos: best podcasts of the weekFans of the show will not want to miss this revealing new series with Dominic Chianese and his son. Plus, a political drama that’s as thrilling as a Bourne novelHannah J DaviesandHollie RichardsonMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDominic & JuniorThe Sopranos star Dominic Chianese (95) and his son Dominic Chianese Jr (62) helm this new series – a cosy father-soncatchup, and all the better for it. Choice cuts include Chianese Sr’s admission that he thought the show was a spoof at first, playing his first scene as crime boss Junior for laughs. As for “Jimmy” Gandolfini, he was “in the same stratosphere as Al Pacino ... acting with him was so easy because he was so real and so believable”. Hannah J DaviesWidely available, episodes weeklyBear HuntThe Rest Is … stable has form inaudio drama. This new one – an action-heavy political thriller about beef between Britain and Russia – is described by its creators as “a British Bourne”. The dramatic writing and input of real-life defence experts makes for an atmospheric listen that blurs the lines between fiction and present reality. HJDWidely available, episodes weeklyUnderGround Zero: 9/11 & The MobView image in fullscreenMichael Imperioli.Photograph: Deadline/Getty ImagesMore Sopranos-adjacent podcasting, with Michael Imperioli and Steve Schirripa in thisnew dramaabout how the mafia exploited the chaos caused by 9/11. Drawing on true events, it is a solid gangland drama elevated by a strong cast – not least Imperioli as brave cop Frank Sturiano. HJDWidely available, all episodes out nowA Matter of FatRose Stokes is a journalist who has always had issues with her weight. Prof Giles Yeo is an obesity scientist. In this nuancedseries, they exchange views and facts on how the age of GLP-1s has disrupted our relationship with weight and bodies. They unpick the issues from all angles, from how these drugs work to the marketing of them and their own experiences of using them. Hollie RichardsonWidely available, weekly from Tuesday 15 SeptemberLight BoxMark Henry Phillips has spent 20 years composing music for podcasts such as Serial and This American Life. But how might AI music change his job? From copyright issues to the uncanny valley quality of much AI output, Phillips’sseriesis straight-talking – but not overly doomy – as it centres on the insights of those affected by this huge tech shift. HJDWidely available, from Tuesday 15 SeptemberWhat are you listening to this week? title: Burrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, Italy | Italy holidays | The Guardian
description: It’s the birthplace of the popular cheese, but the Barletta-Andria-Trani province in southern Italy has an array of local delicacies – from olive oil and yellow tomatoes to goat prosciutto
Author: Liz Boulter
Headline: It’s the birthplace of the popular cheese, but the Barletta-Andria-Trani province in southern Italy has an array of local delicacies – from olive oil and yellow tomatoes to goat prosciutto
Content: The Norman cathedral in Barletta.Photograph: Giovanni Ruggiero/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Norman cathedral in Barletta.Photograph: Giovanni Ruggiero/AlamyItaly holidaysBurrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, ItalyIt’s the birthplace of the popular cheese, but the Barletta-Andria-Trani province in southern Italy has an array of local delicacies – from olive oil and yellow tomatoes to goat prosciuttoLiz BoulterMon 14 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 05.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Idon’t eat mozzarella outside Puglia,” says our friend Savio. “It’s not the same.” Savio is a very opinionated foodie, so I take his words with a pinch of good Puglian sea salt (see below). He was adamant about the superiority of the stretched-curd cheese from his home turf.Puglia is also the birthplace of ingredientdu jourburrata, which originated in Andria, a few miles from Savio’s home town of Barletta. Andria forms one part of the triangular Barletta-Andria-Trani (BAT) province, but despite the cheese connection and Barletta having miles of palm-backed, sandy beaches, it is often passed over for better-known parts of Puglia. So I asked Savio’s company,Unexpected Italy, an app that calls itself the antidote to overtourism, to organise a trip to the area.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsAbout a century ago, in the hills outside Andria, farmer Lorenzo Bianchino was snowed in and couldn’t get his milk to market. To save what he could, he revived an old technique for preserving butter (burro, hence burrata), stuffing cream mixed with mozzarella scraps (stracciatella) in a casing of the stretched-curd cheese.There are now several burrata makers in Andria, the most famous beingCaseificio Olanda, which offers demos, tastings and a museum. Late one morning, we watch Riccardo “Dino” Olanda, son of the founders, work his magic. He adds almost-boiling water to the curds, then mixes with hands red from doing this every day. As he stretches and massages the curds, a smooth velvety mass forms. “See how it’s shiny?” he says. “Means it’s ready.” Working quickly, he squeezes out round lumps between thumb and forefinger into the familiar mozzarella balls. This action ismozzare, hence the name.He also makes little knots and plaits before moving on to burrata. Taking a warm mozzarella ball, he works it into a hollow bag with his fingers then fills it with cream andstracciatellabefore tying the top with string.View image in fullscreenRiccardo Olanda making burrataAfterwards, a dairy-heavy meal totally worth the cholesterol and calories: mozzarella and burrata to start, then bread with chunks ofcaciocavallo(a stretched-curd cheese), and a dessert of heart-shaped fresh ricotta with strawberry jam or cocoa.And, I have to say, Savio is right. The mozzarella and burrata have a juicy, elastic texture and a gorgeous cheesy, umami flavour; the salt and flavour leached out by the whey the cheeses later sit in. How will I ever settle for Tesco Finest after this?double quotation markThe mozzarella and burrata have a juicy, elastic texture and a cheesy, umami flavourOver the next few days, eating our way around the province’s restaurants and food producers, I wonder whether it’s because the ingredients are so good that this area has so many food obsessives, or the other way round.Barletta sees few foreign tourists, but it is full of Italian life. There are lots of independent shops, a Norman castle and cathedral to visit, and every evening people pour into the bars, clubs andgelaterieof thesette strade, seven parallel streets in the old town.Down the coast, Trani, with its sea-facing romanesque cathedral and pretty harbour, attracts some tourists, but they are not in evidence at 7am when the fishing boats return. The men complain of rough seas and a poor catch, but from the back of the boats they’re soon selling mullet, octopus, skate, fat sea snails, monkfish andpalombo(small shark) to restaurateurs and fishmongers. Thirtysomething Nicola says he went out at midday and got back at 3am. When does he sleep? “Never.” A fifth-generation fisher, he began helping on the boats aged six.View image in fullscreenFish straight off the boat at Trani docks.Photograph: Vittorio Sciosia/AlamyWe’ll eat fish later, but today is for pizza.Portentoin Barletta is run by food nut Luigi Lacerenza. He has us try so many local products asantipasti–caprinogoat’s cheese tasting of green mountains, grilledcaciocavallo from an old couple who make just six a week and small-batch salami – that we’re almost too full for pizzas. But they are wonderful: one with sausage, olives, oyster mushrooms and yellow tomatoes; another with aubergines and gratedcacioricotta.‘It’s like bringing the kitchen into the piazza’: seven of the best Italian village food festivalsRead moreIn Cerignola, west of Barletta, Rosario Didonna used the money he won on a TV standup competition to turn his family’s deli into a cosy, wood- panelled restaurant,U’ Vulèsce(dialect for “peckish”). Rosario knows fishers by name, works with small farmers and wine producers, and invitesnonnefrom all over southern Italy to demonstrate recipes in his kitchens.double quotation markI wonder whether it’s because the ingredients are so good that this area has so many food obsessives, or the other way roundWe start with tasty goat prosciutto and plum-sized local olives calledbella di Cerignola. Then an unforgettable prawn tartare served in sea urchin shells, hairy crab spaghetti (“the juice is better than lobster”), octopus with bean puree, and sea bass with orange mayo. He waves away our thanks: “I’m doing the best job in the world!”Nicola Barbera atMasseria Barbera, a farm restaurant in the Alta Murgia national park, is equally inspired, but rather by what grows on the estate founded by his great-great-great-great-grandfather Riccardo, who fought with Garibaldi.Exuberantly bouncing us around the farm – it produces 90% of what the 100-cover restaurant needs – he shows us olives and vines, but also the “weeds” growing around them. “They’re eatable,” he says, grabbing handfuls of peppery rocket, and bitter but delicate wild chicory. From the abundant kitchen garden, he makes eight varieties of tomato sauce.View image in fullscreenMasseria Barbera farm restaurantWe tuck into a lot of this for lunch: a pie with white onions, anchovy and sultanas; courgettes with mint and garlic; spaghetti with yellow tomatoes. (“I call it bastard sauce,” says Nicola. “Those tomatoes take three times as long to pick.”) Then, something I never thought I’d eat: grilled donkey fillet. I feel bad about the patient, mild-tempered beasts, but this is healthy, low-fat food, never intensively farmed. It’s also the best meat I’ve ever tasted.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGood food is made better by good olive oil, and producers here includeMuraglia, known for organic oil in hand-painted, rainbow-stripe ceramic bottles, andSabino Leone, offering tours of its ancient groves and oil mill for €15, plus tastings.View image in fullscreenSabino Leone olive oilThis area also offers plenty to do between meals. Barletta was the home of Italian painter Giuseppe De Nittis, who hung out with Degas and Manet, and took part in the first impressionist exhibition in Paris, in 1874. Over 200 of his works are now displayed in the 16th-centuryPalazzodella Marra(€6).At Europe’s biggest salt pan,Salina Margherita di Savoia, there’s an expanse of peaceful ponds with a snow-white salt mountain to climb. Another day, an exhilarating ebike ride in the Alta Murgia with Filippo Tito ofCycling ’n’ Trek, through dense forest to peer with awe into an old bauxite mine that resembles a mini grand canyon. We get back ravenous, but in this corner of northern Puglia, that’s a blessing.Where to stayUntil this century, Barletta had little tourist accommodation. Pick of the few B&Bs isAntica Dimora(doubles from €97), a restored 17th-century palazzo run by Lilly and Riccardo Manna. There are three smart bedrooms with lots of plants and breakfast features different local specialities each day.Lama di Luna(doubles from €230) is an organic farm in deep countryside, with six rooms set around an 18th-century stone courtyard. A well and solar panels make it energy and water self-sufficient; half of its 200 hectares are left wild, the rest are planted with olives, vines, almonds and cherries. There’s a cinema, a library and a large pool shaded by 600-year-old olive trees.Where (else) to eatView image in fullscreenThe view from A Sud dell’Anima restaurant, MinervinoBarletta’s 60-year-oldMosébakery is revered for itskrapfenfilled doughnuts and sourdough croissants. There are also chocolates, ice-cream and cakes, all housemade, and great coffee.Puglia has hundreds ofgelateriebut experts rateScoopin Canosa (which is called Puglia’s “Little Rome” for its catacombs, temple ruins and Roman bridge). Francesco Di Nunno makes ice-cream with local seasonal ingredients: raspberry and strawberry sorbets are available only in early summer; percoca yellow peach until mid-August.There’s affordable fine dining at chef Luciano Matera’sIl Turraccioloin central Andria. Highlights for me are broad bean and chicory “meatballs”, bright green inside; a “hidden mushroom” under baked eggy topping; and pasta discs with whole and pureed green beans and peas.AtA Sud dell’Anima, chef Nadia Tamburrano uses modern techniques and hyper-local ingredients to make food of astonishing quality for a small hilltop town (Minervino, population under 8,000). Her antipasti explode with flavour thanks to house-cured capers and homemade mustard, syrups and purees. A main of sweetbreads wrapped in intestines feels a bit out-there, but is delicious, the intestines crispy as crackling.The trip was organised byUnexpected Italy, which offers personaliseditineraries for Barlettaand the surrounding areaExplore more on these topicsItaly holidaysFood and drinkEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt | Lamb | The Guardian
description: Intimidated by the thought of midweek entertaining? Three simple rules make it simple…
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Intimidated by the thought of midweek entertaining? Three simple rules make it simple…
Content: Rosie Mackean’s lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenRosie Mackean’s lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurt.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Wilkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.Quick and easyLambRosie Mackean’s quick and easy recipe for lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurtIntimidated by the thought of midweek entertaining? Three simple rules make it simple…Rosie MackeanMon 14 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEntertaining midweek can feel daunting, but if you employ a couple of tricks, things can very quickly go from mayhem to magic. First, choose a dish that goes perfectly with good bread, so your carb is covered. Second, choose a protein that is quick to cook and great for sharing – little lamb chops are perfect for this, while also being a treat. And, finally, use other ingredients that don’t need much help. Here, the walnuts just get cooked in butter and the lamb juices, the courgettes are simply boiled and dressed, and the yoghurt is, well, yoghurt. Suddenly you’ve conjured up a masterpiece ready for many hands to dig in.Lamb chops with courgettes, walnuts and yoghurtPrep10 minCook30 minServes4For the chops800g french-trimmed lamb chops(ie, 12-14 chops from 2 lamb racks – I like small, leaner ones)1½ tbsp flaky salt1 tsp black pepper1 tspground cumin1 tspground coriander½ tsp ground cinnamon2 tbspvegetable oil90g saltedbutter2 garlic cloves, unpeeled and bashed1 banana shallot, peeled and sliced100g walnuts½ tsp smoked paprikaJuice of ½lemonFor the courgettes1 generous pinchflaky sea salt, plus fine salt for the boiling water1kg courgettes, cut into roughly 1½cm-thick slices75g extra-virgin olive oilZest of 1 unwaxed lemon1garlic clove, peeled and grated1 big handfulfresh mint, leaves pickedTo serve500ggreek yoghurtFlatbreadsIf the chops are in the shape of a rack, use a sharp knife to separate them. Sprinkle the salt and spices all over the chops, then rub in and leave to sit at room temperature for a few minutes.Meanwhile, bring a large pan of water to a boil and season it generously with salt. Tip in the courgettes and simmer for seven minutes, until just tender. Combine the olive oil, lemon zest and garlic in a large bowl and use a slotted spoon to transfer the cooked courgettes straight into it. Stir, season with salt and leave to sit while you cook the chops.Put a cast-iron (or nonstick) pan on a high heat. Add the oil and the chops, taking care to render any thicker bits of fat before searing them on their flat sides for two minutes each. You may need to do this in batches; pop any seared chops on a rack while you finish the rest.Return all the chops to the pan with about half the butter and the bashed garlic cloves, then let the butter foam and bubble while you gently spoon it over the lamb for another minute. Lift out the chops and set aside to rest.Add the remaining butter to the pan with the shallot, walnuts and smoked paprika, turn down the heat to medium and let the butter foam and brown as the walnuts toast for about six minutes. Add a squeeze of lemon juice to stop the butter cooking further, then take the pan off the heat.Stir the mint into the courgettes, then scoop the yoghurt on to plates. Pile the courgettes around it, then lay the chops on top. Pour over the walnuts and their smoky butter and serve with plenty of flatbread for smooshing and sandwiching.Good Time Cooking: Show-Stopping Menus for Easy Entertaining, by Rosie Mackean, is published by Pavilion Books at £26. title: Hot and sour, vegetarian mapo and in spicy sauce: Fuchsia Dunlop’s tofu recipes | Food | The Guardian
description: Wobblesome, firm or silken, tofu is a star ingredient in Chinese cooking. These dishes show why
Author: Fuchsia Dunlop
Headline: Wobblesome, firm or silken, tofu is a star ingredient in Chinese cooking. These dishes show why
Content: Fuschia Dunlop’s juicy tofu in a spicy sauce.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.View image in fullscreenFuschia Dunlop’s juicy tofu in a spicy sauce.Photograph: Patricia Niven/The Guardian. Food styling: Tamara Vos. Prop styling: Anna Willkins. Food styling assistant: Katie Smith.FoodHot and sour, vegetarian mapo and in spicy sauce: Fuchsia Dunlop’s tofu recipesWobblesome, firm or silken, tofu is a star ingredient in Chinese cooking. These dishes show whyFuchsia DunlopMon 14 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the west, tofu is often viewed as a substitute for meat, which may explain why firmer types that can be cut into chunks and fried or grilled like meat have become so ubiquitous. In China, however, where tofu has been eaten for at least 1,000 years, it isn’t a substitute for anything; it’s simply a protein-rich ingredient that forms part of most people’s diets, can be cooked with meat and fish, and comes in myriad forms, from the tender, wobbly tofu used to make Sichuanese mapo tofu to firm smoked tofu, sheets of tofu “skin” and the silken tofu that can be as soft as creme caramel. Many Chinese tofu recipes are so delicious that habitual meat-eaters will devour them as keenly as vegetarians.Juicy tofu in a spicy sauceIn Yunnan, eating tofu is a social activity. All over the south of the province, people gather around grills tended by cooks who slowly toast chunks of cured tofu until they are crisp and golden on the outside, soft and slightly juicy within, and customers help themselves, dipping the tofu pieces into soy sauce, chilli, garlic and herbs. Aside from the ubiquitous tofu grills, there are many delicious local tofu recipes, including this one. In Yunnan, they make it with slices of fresh tofu soaked in an alkaline solution, which makes the texture particularly custardy after frying: a sort of artisanal molecular gastronomy (such tofu is described as “enclosing milkiness”). At home, however, I use tofu that is very tender but just holds its shape and is similarly sumptuous when bathed in a spicy sauce with minced pork (to make this vegetarian, simply omit the pork). The tofu can be deep-fried a few hours ahead and chilled until you wish to finish cooking. I use a combination of Sichuan chilli bean paste and sambal oelek instead of Yunnan fermented sauces, which are hard to find outside China.Prep10 minCook20 minServes4 with rice and 2-3 other dishes600g tender plain white tofuCooking oil, for deep-frying, plus 3 tbsp extra for the wok100g minced pork1 tbspShaoxing wine2 tbsp Sichuan chilli bean paste1 small red onion(about 50g), peeled and finely chopped1½ tbsp finely chopped garlic1 tbsp finely chopped ginger2 tbsp finely chopped red chilli1 tbspsambal oelekA few pinches of ground white pepper, to taste1 tsp potato starch mixed with 1 tbsp cold water3 tbsp finely sliced spring onions, green parts onlyCut the tofu into even, 1-1½cm-thick bite-size pieces, then gently pat dry with kitchen paper.Heat oil for deep-frying to 180C. Working in batches, fry the tofu for about five minutes, until golden brown, then drain on kitchen paper. You can do this step a few hours in advance.Put three tablespoons of oil in a seasoned wok on a high heat. Add the pork and stir-fry, breaking up the meat, then, when it turns pale, add the Shaoxing wine. When the meat is a little golden, turn down the heat to medium, add the chilli bean paste and stir until the oil reddens. Add the onion, fry until it smells delicious, then do the same with the garlic, ginger and chilli. Finally, stir in the sambal oelek. You should have a rubbly mass of utter deliciousness.Pour in 250ml water and add a little white pepper to taste. Drop in the fried tofu, nudge the pieces into the sauce, then return to a boil and simmer for a minute or so, to “send the flavours in”. Give the starch mixture a stir and, in a couple of stages, add just enough to thicken the sauce to a lazy gravy. Stir in the spring onion greens and serve.Mushroom mapo tofuView image in fullscreenFuchsia Dunlop’s mushroom mapo tofu.People often ask me how to make mapo tofu vegetarian and, to be honest, I normally just omit the beef from the classic recipe. If you miss the mouthfeel of the meat, this version, made with mushroom mince, is highly satisfying (you can also make the mince a day in advance, if you like). Do finish the dish with a scattering of freshly roasted and ground Sichuan pepper, which is one of the signatures of real mapo tofu. To make the perfect mapo tofu, use the tenderest, silkiest tofu that will hold its shape – as the Sichuanese chef Yu Bo puts it, you want the edges of the cubes to look as if they are straining to contain its voluptuousness. The more wobblesome the tofu, the greater the joy! It’s best to buy fresh tofu in water from Chinese shops; supermarket versions tend to be drier and nubblier. The same mince makes a fabulous pork substitute in dan dan noodles or anywhere, really, where you want to replace mince with something meatless. (Perhaps in lasagne or moussaka, for example.)Prep10 minCook25 minServes4 with rice and 2-3 other dishesFor the mushroom mince200g chestnut mushrooms, or other mushrooms3 tbsp cooking oil2 tsp finely chopped garlic2 tsp finely chopped ginger1 tsp dark soy sauceSaltFor the dish500g tender plain white tofu2 baby leeks, or spring onions, green parts only3 tbsp cooking oil2½ tbsp Sichuan chilli bean paste1 tbsp fermented black beans, rinsed2 tsp ground chillies1 tbsp finely chopped garlic1 tbsp finely chopped ginger¼ tsp ground white pepper1 tbsp potato starch mixed with 2½ tbsp cold water¼-1 tsp ground roasted Sichuan pepper, to toastCut off and discard the dry ends of the mushroom stalks, cut the stems and caps into roughly 5mm-thick slices, then cut into 5mm cubes. Put the oil in a seasoned wok on a high heat, then cook the mushroom cubes for two to three minutes, until greatly reduced in volume and tinged with gold. Add the garlic and ginger, stir briefly until you can smell them, then add the soy sauce and salt to taste. When it’s all sizzly and delicious, take off the heat.Cut the tofu into 2cm cubes and leave it to steep in very hot, lightly salted water while you prepare the other ingredients. Cut the leeks into 2cm lengths.Put the oil in a seasoned wok on a medium heat. Add the chilli bean paste, stir-fry until the oil turns red, then add the black beans and chillies, and stir-fry until they smell delicious. Do the same for the garlic and ginger, taking care not to burn them, then pour in 175ml water. Use a slotted spoon to transfer the tofu from its soaking water to the hot wok, then add the mushroom mince and white pepper, and bring to a boil. Simmer for a couple of minutes, so the tofu absorbs the flavours. If you’re using baby leeks, stir them in and cook for a few moments (if you’re using spring onions instead, add them later). In a few stages, stir in just enough of the starch mixture to thicken the sauce so it clings to the tofu (if using spring onion greens, stir them in now).Pour everything into a deep serving bowl, sprinkle with the ground roasted Sichuan pepper to taste and serve.Sour-and-hot silken tofuView image in fullscreenFuchsia Dunlop’s sour-and-hot silken tofu.The soft wobbliness of “flower tofu”, otherwise known as “tofu brain” or silken tofu, is soothing at any time of day, but I particularly love it for breakfast. It is as satisfying and comforting as porridge, but lighter. You can eat it sweet, with a drizzle of brown sugar syrup or even fruit salad, but I prefer mine with savoury seasonings. There are countless ways to serve silken tofu. In the north, including Beijing, they bathe it in a kind of gravy, thick with morsels of dried lily, mushrooms and wisps of egg. In the Jiangnan region around Shanghai, on the other hand, the adornments are more delicate: tiny dried shrimps and seaweed, preserved vegetables and sliced spring onions. In Sichuan, of course, they like a bit of spice. This recipe, which serves one or two people, depending on appetite, is inspired by the exquisite version dreamed up by Chengdu chef Lu Ziqiang atBirds of a Feather in Brooklyn, New York. I’ve substituted the traditional deep-fried soya beans and noodles for Bombay mix, which is similar in appearance and crunchiness.Prep10 minCook5 minServes1-2300g silken tofu2 tsp Chinese sesame paste1 tspChinkiang vinegar2 tsp light soy sauce1 tsp white sugar1½ tbsp chilli oil, plus ½–1 tbsp chilli sediment½ tsp red or green Sichuan pepper oil2 tbsp finely chopped Sichuan preserved vegetables2 tbsp finely sliced spring onions, green parts only1 small handful Bombay mixTip the silken tofu into a saucepan of boiling water and simmer gently for a few minutes, until heated through. Gently break it up into large, cloud-like clumps, but don’t stir or it will disintegrate.Meanwhile, put the sesame paste in a small bowl and smooth it with the back of a spoon. Gradually stir in the vinegar and soy sauce to create a satiny emulsion, then add the sugar. Stir in the chilli oil and sediment, and the Sichuan pepper oil.When the tofu is ready, gently lift it from the water and transfer to a bowl. Pour the sauce over the top, then sprinkle over the other ingredients. Mix well before eating.These recipes are edited extracts from Five Tastes: The Magic of Flavour in a Chinese Kitchen, by Fuchsia Dunlop, published by Particular Books at £30.
